Lesson 1.1/Accounting Foundations

Why Accounting Matters for Deals

20 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson explains why accounting is the language of every deal conversation. It shows how accrual accounting differs from cash accounting, using a worked example, and it sets out the question that each of the three financial statements answers.

  1. 1.1.1The language of business — and of every deal
  2. 1.1.2Cash accounting: the intuitive (and wrong) starting point
  3. 1.1.3Worked example: same business, two very different pictures
  4. 1.1.4The three statements at a glance
  5. 1.1.5Why deal teams care so much
  6. 1.1.6What's coming in this module

§1.1.1The language of business — and of every deal

Every private equity deal is, at its core, a bet expressed in numbers. When a deal team says "we're paying 8x EBITDA for a business doing £10m", every word apart from "we're paying" is an accounting concept. When an investment committee asks "what's the cash conversion?" or "how much of that margin is real?", it is asking accounting questions. So you can't follow a deal discussion, let alone contribute to one, unless you're fluent in how businesses keep score.

That score is kept in three documents. Every company of any size produces them, and it does so on a regular rhythm: monthly for management, and annually for its statutory filings. The three are:

  • the income statement, which is also called the P&L, short for "profit and loss";
  • the balance sheet; and
  • the cash flow statement.

Together, they're known as "the financial statements", or simply "the financials". Almost everything in this course is built on top of them, from valuation multiples and leverage ratios to quality of earnings and returns maths. And if you work in a PE data team, these statements are the schema behind most of the data you'll ever be asked to analyse.

Here's the thing that surprises people who come from a data background. The financials are not raw data. They are the output of a model, which is to say a set of rules and judgements applied to raw transactions. Two accountants can look at the same business and produce legitimately different numbers. Understanding that model, and knowing where its outputs can bend, is the entire game.

§1.1.2Cash accounting: the intuitive (and wrong) starting point

The naive way to measure a business is to track the money coming in and the money going out, just like your own bank statement. When money arrives, you count it as income, and when money leaves, you count it as a cost. This is called cash accounting, and it genuinely is how many very small businesses and sole traders think.

The trouble is that the timing of cash and the timing of economic activity are two different things. A business can do the work in March, send the invoice in April, and get paid in June. It can buy a year's insurance in January to cover it right through to December. Or it can buy a machine today that will go on producing goods for a decade. Cash accounting smears or spikes all of this, in ways that make performance impossible to read.

Accrual accounting is the system every real company uses, and it fixes the problem with two core ideas.

  1. The first is to recognise revenue when it is earned, rather than when the cash is received. Once you've delivered the goods or performed the service, you have revenue, even if the customer doesn't pay for another 60 days.
  2. The second is to match costs to the revenue they generate, which is known as the matching principle. The cost of the goods you sold this period is this period's cost, even if you bought the stock last period. Likewise, a machine that lasts ten years is spread across ten years of P&Ls, rather than being dumped into one.

Accrual accounting answers the question "how did the business perform this period?" Cash accounting answers a different one: "what happened to the bank balance this period?" Both questions matter, and that is exactly why there are separate statements for each.

§1.1.3Worked example: same business, two very different pictures

Let's meet a tiny fictional business: a consultancy that signs a single project in January. Here's how its year unfolds.

  • In January, it signs a £120k project, and the client pays a £30k deposit upfront.
  • From January to March, it does the work, paying £20k a month to contractors. That's £60k in total, paid in cash as the costs are incurred.
  • In March, it delivers the project and invoices the remaining £90k, on 90-day payment terms.
  • And in June, the client pays the £90k.

So what did the first quarter, from January to March, look like?

£k, Q1 (Jan–Mar) Cash view Accrual view
Revenue / cash in 30 (deposit) 120 (work delivered)
Costs / cash out (60) (60)
Result (30) — a loss? 60 profit

On a cash basis, the first quarter looks like a disaster, because £30k more went out of the door than came in. On an accrual basis, though, it was an excellent quarter. The firm earned £120k of revenue, incurred £60k of matched costs, and made £60k of profit. The £90k it is still owed sits on the balance sheet as a receivable, which is an asset, until June.

Now look at the second quarter, from April to June. No work happens at all, but £90k of cash arrives.

£k, Q2 (Apr–Jun) Cash view Accrual view
Revenue / cash in 90 0
Costs / cash out 0 0
Result 90 "profit"? 0

Cash accounting says the second quarter was the best one ever, when in reality nobody did anything. Accrual accounting correctly says that the performance happened in the first quarter, and the cash simply caught up in the second. Over the full half-year, the two views agree: £120k in, £60k out, and a £60k surplus. That's because over long enough periods, profit and cash converge. Within any single period, though, they can diverge wildly, and that divergence is one of the most important things deal teams scrutinise.

Hold on to this example, because it contains, in miniature, the single most important idea in this module. Profit is an opinion about performance, while cash is a fact about the bank account. You need both, and the gap between them is where the interesting questions live.

§1.1.4The three statements at a glance

Each statement answers one question. It's worth learning the questions first; the mechanics follow in the next three lessons.

Statement The question it answers Type of measure
Income statement (P&L) "How did the business perform over the period?" Flow — covers a period (a year, a quarter)
Balance sheet "What does the business own and owe right now?" Stock — a snapshot at a single date
Cash flow statement "Where did cash actually come from and go to over the period?" Flow — covers a period

Here's a useful analogy if you think in data terms. The balance sheet is a table of current state, while the P&L and the cash flow statement are aggregations over an event log between two snapshots. And just as you'd expect from that framing, the statements have to reconcile. The profit for the year, from the P&L, explains part of the change in the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement explains how the cash line moved from one balance sheet to the next. Lesson 5 traces those links in detail. They are what make the three statements a closed, self-checking system, rather than three unrelated reports.

The income statement starts with revenue at the top, which is why revenue is called the "top line". It then subtracts costs in layers, and it ends with net profit at the bottom, hence the "bottom line". Those layers matter. Deal teams rarely talk about net profit, but they constantly talk about the lines in between, such as gross profit and EBITDA.

The balance sheet lists everything the business owns. These are its assets, such as cash, money owed by customers, stock, machinery and brands. It then sets them against how those assets were funded, either by borrowing, which gives liabilities, or by the owners' money and accumulated profits, which gives equity. By construction, assets always equal liabilities plus equity.

The cash flow statement reconciles profit back to actual cash movements, and it splits them into three buckets. The first is cash from running the business, called operating cash flow. The second is cash spent on, or received from, long-term assets, called investing. And the third is cash raised from, or returned to, lenders and shareholders, called financing.

§1.1.5Why deal teams care so much

Everything a PE fund does maps onto these statements.

  • Pricing the deal. Valuations are usually quoted as a multiple of EBITDA, which is a number derived from the P&L. So "8x £10m" means an enterprise value of £80m. Get the EBITDA wrong by £1m, and the price moves by £8m. That's why so much diligence effort goes into testing whether the reported EBITDA is real, as you'll see in lesson 6 and throughout the due diligence module.
  • Funding the deal. LBOs are funded largely with debt, and lenders size that debt off EBITDA and cash flow. Meanwhile, the balance sheet shows what debt already exists, and what assets support it.
  • Servicing the debt. Once the deal has closed, it's the company's cash, not its profit, that pays the interest. A profitable company that generates no cash is a company that defaults. The cash flow statement is where that risk shows up first.
  • Judging the business. Margins, working capital behaviour, capital intensity and cash conversion are all computed from the statements, and so is every other quality signal a deal team looks for.

So what looks good? Profit that reliably turns into cash; clean, simple statements; and numbers that reconcile across all three statements without any gymnastics. And what looks bad? Profit growing while cash stands still; a widening gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow; and frequent "one-off" items. The question deal teams actually ask, over and over again, is this: "is the profit real, and does it convert to cash?" By the end of this module, you'll understand precisely what that question means and how the statements answer it.

§1.1.6What's coming in this module

The next three lessons build each statement from scratch, using one consistent fictional company. It's called Bramley Foods Ltd, a UK speciality food manufacturer with £50m of revenue. Because every number carries across, you'll be able to see the statements as one connected system. Lesson 5 then follows a single transaction, a £5m machine bought with debt, through all three statements over two years. Lesson 6 closes with an uncomfortable truth: many of these numbers involve judgement, judgement can be stretched, and that's why diligence teams never take reported numbers at face value.

There's one mindset worth carrying all the way through. Whenever you meet a number in this course, ask yourself which statement it lives on, and whether it's a flow or a snapshot. That one habit prevents most of the confusion beginners run into. And it's exactly the same discipline you already apply when you ask whether a column is an event or a dimension.

Lesson 1.2/Accounting Foundations

The Income Statement: From Revenue to EBITDA

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson builds a full P&L, line by line, for a fictional company with £50m of revenue. Along the way it covers revenue recognition, the difference between COGS and opex, gross, operating and net profit, D&A, and EBIT and EBITDA. It finishes by explaining why EBITDA dominates PE conversations, and where it misleads.

  1. 1.2.1The shape of a P&L
  2. 1.2.2Revenue: recognised, not received
  3. 1.2.3COGS vs opex: direct costs vs overheads
  4. 1.2.4Building the P&L: Bramley Foods Ltd
  5. 1.2.5EBITDA and EBIT: the deal world's favourite acronyms
  6. 1.2.6The limitations — where EBITDA misleads
  7. 1.2.7Margins: the P&L as percentages

§1.2.1The shape of a P&L

The income statement is a subtraction ladder. You start with everything the business earned in the period, then subtract costs in a deliberate order, and each rung of the ladder is a named profit measure. That order isn't arbitrary. Each rung strips out a different kind of cost, so each profit line answers a different question.

Line What has been deducted so far Question it answers
Revenue Nothing How much did we sell?
Gross profit Direct costs of what was sold (COGS) Is the core product profitable?
EBITDA + all operating overheads (opex) How profitable are operations, before asset and funding costs?
EBIT / operating profit + depreciation & amortisation How profitable are operations, after wearing out the assets?
Profit before tax + interest What's left after paying the lenders?
Net profit + tax What's left for the shareholders?

Reading from top to bottom, you deal first with the product, then the operation, then the assets, then the funding, and finally the taxman. Everything below EBIT depends on how the company is financed and taxed, whereas everything above it depends on how the business actually runs. That split is why deal teams spend their lives in the top half.

§1.2.2Revenue: recognised, not received

The top line is revenue, which British accounts often call "turnover". Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised when the performance obligation is satisfied. In other words, it's recognised when the goods are delivered or the service is performed, not when the cash arrives.

Three patterns cover most businesses.

  • Point-in-time delivery, such as a manufacturer shipping pallets of goods. Here you recognise the revenue on delivery. If the invoice isn't paid for another 60 days, it's still this period's revenue, and the unpaid amount sits on the balance sheet as a receivable.
  • Over-time services, such as a 12-month, £1.2m support contract that's billed upfront. Here you recognise £0.1m a month as the service is delivered. The cash that's been received but not yet earned sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue. That's a liability, because the company still owes the customer eleven months of service.
  • Long projects, such as construction or big consulting engagements. Here you recognise revenue in proportion to progress, which means estimating how far through the project you are. That estimate is a judgement, and so it's a place where numbers can bend, as lesson 6 explains.

Let's quickly check the over-time logic. Suppose a company with a 31 December year end signs that £1.2m annual contract on 1 October, and bills all of it immediately. Its revenue this year is 1.2×312=£0.3m1.2 \times \tfrac{3}{12} = £0.3\text{m}1.2×123​=£0.3m, and the remaining £0.9m is deferred revenue. Recognising the full £1.2m would overstate this year's performance by £0.9m, and that's one of the classic revenue games.

§1.2.3COGS vs opex: direct costs vs overheads

Costs fall into two families, and the split between them drives the two most-quoted margins.

Cost of goods sold, or COGS, is also known as "cost of sales". It's what it directly cost to produce the things you sold this period: raw materials, direct production labour, and the costs of running the factory. Its key property is that COGS scales roughly with volume. Sell 10% more units, and you'll incur roughly 10% more COGS.

Operating expenses, or opex, are the overheads of running the business, regardless of exactly how much was shipped this month. They include sales and marketing, distribution, head-office salaries, rent, IT and insurance. Opex is stickier. It steps up as the business grows, but not sale by sale.

So why does the split matter? Gross profit, which is revenue minus COGS, tells you about the underlying economics of the product. In a high-gross-margin business, most of each extra pound of sales drops straight through to profit, which is known as "operating leverage". A business with 60% gross margins and heavy opex can scale beautifully. A business with 15% gross margins, on the other hand, has almost no room for anything else, however lean its overheads. That's why deal teams check the gross margin trend first. A falling gross margin means pricing pressure, or input-cost inflation that the company can't pass on, and that's a structural problem no amount of opex cutting can fix.

§1.2.4Building the P&L: Bramley Foods Ltd

Bramley Foods Ltd is the fictional company we'll use throughout. It's a UK speciality food manufacturer, selling premium sauces and condiments to supermarkets and food-service distributors. Here is its FY24 P&L, built up line by line. To keep the arithmetic round, we use a 20% tax rate throughout the module, although the actual main rate of UK corporation tax is 25%.

Bramley Foods — FY24 P&L (£m) % of revenue
Revenue 50.0 100%
Cost of goods sold (30.0) 60%
Gross profit 20.0 40%
Distribution costs (4.0)
Sales & marketing (3.5)
Administrative expenses (4.5)
EBITDA 8.0 16%
Depreciation (1.8)
Amortisation (0.2)
EBIT (operating profit) 6.0 12%
Interest expense (1.0)
Profit before tax 5.0 10%
Tax (20%) (1.0)
Net profit 4.0 8%

Let's walk down the ladder.

  • Revenue is £50.0m. That's the goods delivered to customers during FY24, whether or not they've been paid for yet.
  • COGS is £30.0m. That's made up of ingredients at £18m, direct factory labour at £8m, and factory energy and running costs at £4m. The gross margin is 20.0 divided by 50.0, which is 40%. That's healthy for premium food manufacturing, where 25 to 40% is a typical range.
  • Opex is £12.0m, in three buckets: £4.0m on getting the product to customers, £3.5m on winning and keeping customers, and £4.5m on running the company.
  • EBITDA is £8.0m, which is 20.0 minus 12.0. That's a margin of 16%.
  • D&A is £2.0m. The factory's machines wear out, giving £1.8m of depreciation, and some purchased software and brand assets are written down over their lives, giving £0.2m of amortisation. These are real economic costs, but no cash leaves the business this period because of them. The cash left when the assets were bought. Lesson 3 covers the mechanics.
  • EBIT is £6.0m, which is 8.0 minus 2.0. That's a margin of 12%.
  • Interest is £1.0m. Bramley has £15m of bank debt, as we'll see in lesson 3, and this is what it costs.
  • Tax is £1.0m, which is 20% of the £5.0m profit before tax. That leaves net profit of £4.0m, an 8% net margin. This is the number that flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet, as lesson 5 shows.

Here's a sanity-check habit worth building. Every profit line should equal the line above it, minus the deductions in between. So, 50.0 − 30.0 = 20.0; 20.0 − 12.0 = 8.0; 8.0 − 2.0 = 6.0; 6.0 − 1.0 = 5.0; and 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0. If a P&L you're handed doesn't add up like this, something is being hidden between the lines, and that happens more often than you'd think.

§1.2.5EBITDA and EBIT: the deal world's favourite acronyms

EBIT stands for Earnings Before Interest and Tax. It's operating profit: what the business earned from its operations, before anyone asks how it's financed. EBITDA stands for Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation. It goes one step further, and adds back the non-cash charges for assets.

EBITDA=EBIT+Depreciation+Amortisation\text{EBITDA} = \text{EBIT} + \text{Depreciation} + \text{Amortisation}EBITDA=EBIT+Depreciation+Amortisation

For Bramley, EBITDA is 6.0 plus 2.0, which gives £8.0m. In practice, you'll compute it both ways, either down from gross profit or up from EBIT, and the two answers must agree.

So why does EBITDA dominate PE conversations?

  1. It approximates the cash that operations generate. Because it excludes non-cash D&A, EBITDA is a rough proxy for the cash the operations throw off. That's the pool available to pay interest, fund capex and reward shareholders. "Rough" is the key word here, as we'll see below.
  2. It's neutral to the capital structure. A PE buyer is going to replace the company's financing anyway. So a profit measure taken before interest lets you compare targets, regardless of how their current owners chose to fund them.
  3. It irons out differences in how assets are accounted for. Two identical businesses can show different EBIT purely because of their depreciation policies or their acquisition accounting. EBITDA strips out that noise, which makes comparisons across companies cleaner.
  4. It's the unit the market prices and lends in. Deals are priced as multiples of EV to EBITDA, leverage is quoted as debt to EBITDA, and loan covenants are written against EBITDA. When everyone transacts in one currency, you learn that currency.

§1.2.6The limitations — where EBITDA misleads

Every deal professional can recite the famous warning that EBITDA is not cash flow. More concretely, EBITDA ignores four real demands on cash.

  • Capex. Depreciation may be non-cash, but the machines still have to be replaced, and that takes cash. A haulage firm and a software firm can post identical EBITDA, even though one of them has to plough half of it back into trucks every year. EBITDA treats them as equals, but free cash flow, which we'll meet in lesson 4, does not.
  • Working capital. A growing business ties up cash in stock and unpaid invoices before a single penny of EBITDA becomes money in the bank. The worked example in lesson 4 shows a profitable company running out of cash in exactly this way.
  • Interest and tax. These are real, contractual cash outflows, and they aren't optional. A company leveraged at 6x EBITDA lives a very different life from one leveraged at 1x, and EBITDA simply can't see the difference.
  • Definitional games. Because EBITDA isn't a statutory measure, sellers present an "adjusted EBITDA", which adds back costs that are supposedly one-offs. Some of those add-backs are legitimate, and some are fiction. Lesson 6 opens this can of worms properly.

So what looks good? EBITDA margins that are stable or rising, and operating cash flow that tracks EBITDA closely, year after year. What looks bad? EBITDA growing while cash conversion deteriorates, or an adjusted-EBITDA bridge full of small add-backs that all conveniently push the number up. The question deal teams actually ask is this: "what's the bridge from reported EBITDA to adjusted EBITDA, and how much of it would survive diligence?" That matters because, at an 8x multiple, every £1m of contested EBITDA is £8m of contested price.

§1.2.7Margins: the P&L as percentages

If you divide each profit line by revenue, you get margins. They show the P&L in a comparable form that doesn't depend on the size of the business.

Margin Bramley FY24 Formula
Gross margin 40% Gross profit / revenue = 20.0 / 50.0
EBITDA margin 16% EBITDA / revenue = 8.0 / 50.0
EBIT margin 12% EBIT / revenue = 6.0 / 50.0
Net margin 8% Net profit / revenue = 4.0 / 50.0

Margins are how you compare a £50m business with a £500m one, and how you spot drift over time. Picture a gross margin sliding from 40% to 37% and then to 34% over three years. That's a story about pricing power, and no amount of top-line growth should distract you from it. The financial statement analysis module turns margin analysis into a full toolkit. For now, the discipline is simply to always look at the percentage next to the pound figure.

Here's one closing reframe for the data-minded. The P&L is a period aggregation with a fixed roll-up hierarchy. Revenue sits at the root, cost categories are the deductions, and the profit measures are subtotals at each level. Once you see it that way, "EBITDA" stops being jargon. It becomes just a named subtotal: the one taken after operating costs, but before the costs of assets and funding. The next lesson moves from the flow to the snapshot, with the balance sheet.

Lesson 1.3/Accounting Foundations

The Balance Sheet: What a Business Owns and Owes

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson derives the equation "assets equal liabilities plus equity" from first principles. It explains the working capital items, PP&E and depreciation, intangibles and goodwill, and the difference between debt and equity funding. It then builds Bramley Foods' full balance sheet across two years.

  1. 1.3.1The equation from first principles
  2. 1.3.2A snapshot, sorted by time
  3. 1.3.3Working capital: the operating engine's float
  4. 1.3.4PP&E and depreciation: spreading the cost of long-lived assets
  5. 1.3.5Intangibles and goodwill
  6. 1.3.6Debt vs equity: the two flavours of funding
  7. 1.3.7Bramley Foods: the full balance sheet

§1.3.1The equation from first principles

Let's strip a business down to its simplest possible form. On day one, two founders put £100k into a company bank account, and a bank lends the company another £50k. The company now has £150k of cash. But that cash isn't free-floating, because every pound of it is claimed by someone. In an economic sense, £50k belongs to the bank, since it has to be repaid, and £100k belongs to the founders, since it's their stake.

That's the entire idea behind the balance sheet. Everything a company has, its assets, was funded by someone. And that funding came from exactly two kinds of source: money that must be paid back, which we call liabilities, or the owners' money and accumulated profits, which we call equity. So, always, and by construction:

Assets=Liabilities+Equity\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}Assets=Liabilities+Equity

This isn't an observation that might occasionally fail. It's an identity, like a ledger that records every transaction twice. If you buy a £20k van with cash, your assets simply rearrange: cash goes down by £20k and vans go up by £20k, so the totals don't change. If you buy it on credit instead, assets rise by £20k and liabilities rise by £20k. And if you make £10k of profit, assets rise, say in cash, and equity rises through retained earnings. Every transaction moves at least two lines, and every one preserves the equation. So if a balance sheet doesn't balance, someone has made a mistake. The format checks itself, which is precisely why accountants love it.

That means equity is best understood as a residual: equity equals assets minus liabilities. It's what would notionally be left for the owners if the assets were sold at book value and all the liabilities were repaid. Because it's a residual, equity holders sit at the back of the queue. It's also why, in leveraged deals, small changes in the value of the assets produce large swings in the value of the equity. That lever is the beating heart of the LBO module later on.

§1.3.2A snapshot, sorted by time

Unlike the P&L, the balance sheet is a snapshot at a single date, usually the last day of the financial year. By convention, both sides are sorted by time horizon.

  • Current assets are cash, or things expected to turn into cash within 12 months, such as customer receivables, inventory and prepayments.
  • Non-current assets are things the business holds in order to operate, rather than to sell. They include property, plant and equipment, known as PP&E, along with intangible assets and goodwill.
  • Current liabilities are amounts due within 12 months, such as supplier payables, accrued expenses and tax owed.
  • Non-current liabilities are amounts due later than that, which mainly means long-term debt.

Splitting current from non-current lets you ask questions about liquidity, such as "can it pay its bills this year?", separately from questions about solvency, such as "is it worth more than it owes overall?"

§1.3.3Working capital: the operating engine's float

Three current items deserve special attention, because they arise directly from running the business. Together, they make up trade working capital, often just called working capital.

  • Trade receivables, also called debtors, are sales that have been delivered and invoiced but not yet paid for. In effect, you've lent your customers this money.
  • Inventory, also called stock, is raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods waiting to be sold. It's cash that has been turned into things sitting in a warehouse.
  • Trade payables, also called creditors, are what you owe your suppliers. In effect, they've lent you this money.

Working capital=Receivables+Inventory−Payables\text{Working capital} = \text{Receivables} + \text{Inventory} - \text{Payables}Working capital=Receivables+Inventory−Payables

Positive working capital means the business has cash tied up in its operating cycle. It pays for ingredients, holds stock, delivers to customers, and then waits for them to pay, funding that whole pipeline itself. The crucial consequence is this: when the business grows, its working capital grows too, and that growth consumes cash. A company that doubles its revenue roughly doubles its receivables and inventory, and the cash to fund them has to come from somewhere before the profit arrives. That single mechanic explains most stories of profitable companies running into a cash crisis, and lesson 4 works through one.

So the question deal teams actually ask is: "how much working capital does each pound of growth consume?" That's because it directly determines how much of the growth in EBITDA turns into cash that can be distributed.

§1.3.4PP&E and depreciation: spreading the cost of long-lived assets

Suppose Bramley buys a £3m filling line that will run for ten years. Charging the whole £3m against a single year's profit would be absurd, because the machine serves a decade of revenue. So instead, three things happen.

  1. First, the purchase is capitalised. It lands on the balance sheet as PP&E, rather than going through the P&L.
  2. Second, each year a slice of the cost is charged to the P&L as depreciation. Spread on a straight line over ten years, with no residual value, that's £0.3m a year.
  3. Third, the balance sheet carries the asset at its net book value, which is the original cost minus the accumulated depreciation. After year 4, that's 3.0 minus 1.2, or £1.8m.

If an asset is expected to have some salvage value at the end, you depreciate the cost minus that salvage value. For example, a £12m asset with a £2m residual value, depreciated over five years, gives (12−2)/5=£2.0m(12-2)/5 = £2.0\text{m}(12−2)/5=£2.0m a year.

Notice what depreciation is not. It is not cash. The cash left the business when the machine was bought, and that shows up as capex on the cash flow statement. Depreciation is simply the P&L's way of matching that past cash cost to the periods that benefit from it. That's why it gets added back to reach EBITDA, and why it appears on all three statements, a link that lesson 5 makes explicit.

Useful lives and depreciation methods are choices. Is a van's life five years, or eight? That makes depreciation one of the softer numbers in the accounts, and it's another entry on lesson 6's list.

§1.3.5Intangibles and goodwill

Not every long-term asset is physical. Intangible assets include purchased software, licences, patents, acquired brands and customer relationships. They sit on the balance sheet and are amortised over their useful lives; amortisation is simply the word used for depreciating an intangible asset.

Goodwill is the strangest line on any balance sheet, and in PE you'll meet it constantly. When one company buys another for more than the fair value of its identifiable net assets, the excess is recorded as goodwill. So if you buy a company for £30m when its identifiable net assets are worth £22m, £8m of goodwill appears. It represents everything you paid for that can't be listed separately: the workforce, the reputation and the expected synergies, and sometimes plain overpayment.

There are two things to know for now. First, under modern accounting rules, IFRS, goodwill is not amortised. Instead, it's tested every year for impairment, and written down if the acquired business underperforms. A big goodwill impairment is effectively a public confession of having overpaid. Second, because PE deals are acquisitions, post-deal balance sheets are full of goodwill, so learn to read past it to the operating assets underneath.

§1.3.6Debt vs equity: the two flavours of funding

The right-hand side of the balance sheet answers the question "whose money funded all this?" There are two possible answers, and they have profoundly different characters.

Debt Equity
Obligation Contractual — interest and repayment on schedule None — dividends discretionary
Cost to company Interest (tax-deductible) Share of all future value
Risk to provider Lower — paid first, often secured Higher — paid last, can be wiped out
Upside to provider Capped at interest Unlimited
If things go wrong Can enforce, appoint administrators Absorbs the loss

Debt is cheaper, because it's less risky for the lender and the interest is tax-deductible, but it's rigid. Equity is expensive, but it's forgiving. Private equity's core trick is to deliberately load a company with far more debt than it would naturally carry. It does this precisely because debt's fixed claim concentrates all of the upside into a small slice of equity. And here's a number to start tracking now: net debt, which is total debt minus cash, and which is usually quoted as a multiple of EBITDA.

§1.3.7Bramley Foods: the full balance sheet

Here is Bramley's balance sheet at the last two year ends. It's the same company whose FY24 P&L we built in lesson 2, with revenue of £50.0m, EBITDA of £8.0m and net profit of £4.0m.

Bramley Foods — Balance sheet (£m) FY23 FY24
Cash 2.5 3.0
Trade receivables 7.0 8.0
Inventory 5.5 6.0
Prepayments 1.0 1.0
Current assets 16.0 18.0
PP&E (net) 18.8 20.0
Intangible assets 2.2 2.0
Goodwill 5.0 5.0
Non-current assets 26.0 27.0
Total assets 42.0 45.0
Trade payables 6.5 7.0
Accruals 2.0 2.0
Tax payable 1.0 1.0
Current liabilities 9.5 10.0
Bank debt 16.0 15.0
Total liabilities 25.5 25.0
Share capital 5.0 5.0
Retained earnings 11.5 15.0
Total equity 16.5 20.0
Total liabilities + equity 42.0 45.0

Let's check the identity in both years: 25.5 + 16.5 = 42.0 ✓, and 25.0 + 20.0 = 45.0 ✓.

Now let's read it the way a deal person would.

  • Working capital in FY24 is 8.0 + 6.0 − 7.0, which gives £7.0m. In FY23 it was 7.0 + 5.5 − 6.5, which gives £6.0m. So growth consumed £1.0m of cash this year, and that's a number worth remembering for the cash flow statement.
  • PP&E rose from 18.8 to 20.0. That's because Bramley spent £3.0m on capex and charged £1.8m of depreciation, so 18.8 + 3.0 − 1.8 = 20.0. Meanwhile, intangibles fell from 2.2 to 2.0, through £0.2m of amortisation.
  • Goodwill of £5.0m dates back to Bramley's acquisition of a smaller sauce brand some years ago. It just sits there, unless it's impaired.
  • Net debt is 15.0 minus 3.0, which gives £12.0m. Divide that by EBITDA, 12.0 / 8.0, and you get 1.5x EBITDA. That's modest, and a PE buyer would see a lot of unused debt capacity here.
  • Equity rose from 16.5 to 20.0, an increase of £3.5m. Net profit of £4.0m came in through retained earnings, and £0.5m went out as a dividend, so retained earnings moved from 11.5, plus 4.0, minus 0.5, to 15.0. That roll-forward of equity is one of the key links between the statements that we'll explore in lesson 5.

So what looks good? Working capital growing more slowly than revenue; net debt comfortably low relative to EBITDA; and equity building steadily through retained profits. What looks bad? Receivables or inventory ballooning faster than sales, which means cash is quietly leaking into the operating cycle, or worse, that revenue is being booked which customers aren't actually paying. Goodwill dwarfing the tangible assets is another warning sign, as is debt creeping up to fund ordinary operations. The question deal teams actually ask is: "what's the normalised working capital, and what's the real net debt?" Both of those numbers move the purchase price pound for pound, as the structuring module will show.

Here's one final way to frame it. The P&L told you how Bramley performed, and the balance sheet shows the position that performance left behind. The third statement, in the next lesson, explains the one line here that nothing so far fully accounts for: why cash only moved from 2.5 to 3.0 in a year when the company "made" £4.0m.

Lesson 1.4/Accounting Foundations

The Cash Flow Statement: Where the Money Actually Went

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson covers the three sections of the cash flow statement, and walks through the indirect method line by line using Bramley Foods' numbers. It then introduces free cash flow, and finishes with a worked example of a profitable company that runs out of cash.

  1. 1.4.1Why a third statement exists at all
  2. 1.4.2The three sections
  3. 1.4.3The indirect method, line by line
  4. 1.4.4Free cash flow
  5. 1.4.5Why profit ≠ cash: a company that profits itself to death
  6. 1.4.6What deal teams look for

§1.4.1Why a third statement exists at all

Lesson 3 ended on a puzzle. Bramley Foods made £4.0m of profit in FY24, and yet its cash rose by only £0.5m, from 2.5 to 3.0. Neither the P&L nor the balance sheet explains that gap. The P&L deliberately ignores the timing of cash, and the balance sheet only shows the end points. The cash flow statement is the bridge between them. It reconciles the profit for the period to the actual movement in cash, item by item.

For deal teams, this is arguably the most important of the three statements, and the reason is blunt: debt is serviced with cash, not profit. An LBO's leverage is sized against the cash the business generates. Covenant headroom is measured in cash. And a portfolio company dies when it runs out of cash, never when it runs out of profit. Profit is also the easier number to flatter, as lesson 6 shows, whereas cash is much harder to fake. That's why "does the profit convert to cash?" is the standard first check on the quality of any target.

§1.4.2The three sections

Every cash flow statement sorts the period's cash movements into three buckets, according to why the cash moved.

Section Question Typical contents
Operating (CFO) Did the day-to-day business generate cash? Profit, add back non-cash charges, working capital movements
Investing (CFI) What was spent on the long-term asset base? Capex, acquisitions, disposal proceeds
Financing (CFF) What moved between the company and its funders? Debt drawn/repaid, dividends, share issues

A healthy, mature business has a recognisable signature. Operating cash flow is strongly positive; investing cash flow is moderately negative, because the business is reinvesting; and financing cash flow is modestly negative, because it's repaying debt and paying dividends. Variations on that pattern tell stories. A start-up shows negative operating cash flow, funded by positive financing cash flow. A business in decline sometimes shows positive investing cash flow, because it's selling off the family silver. Reading the three signs together is a 30-second diagnostic that's well worth internalising.

§1.4.3The indirect method, line by line

There are two ways to build the operating section. The direct method lists the actual cash receipts and payments. It's intuitive, but it's rarely used. The indirect method, which virtually every company publishes, starts from profit and then adjusts away everything that isn't cash. It looks odd at first, but it soon becomes second nature. Here is Bramley's FY24 statement, followed by the logic behind each line.

Bramley Foods — FY24 cash flow statement (£m)
Net profit 4.0
Add back: depreciation & amortisation 2.0
(Increase) in trade receivables (1.0)
(Increase) in inventory (0.5)
Increase in trade payables 0.5
Cash from operating activities 5.0
Capital expenditure (3.0)
Cash used in investing activities (3.0)
Repayment of bank debt (1.0)
Dividends paid (0.5)
Cash used in financing activities (1.5)
Net movement in cash 0.5
Opening cash 2.5
Closing cash 3.0

Let's walk through it.

  • We start with net profit of £4.0m. That's the accrual measure of the period, which we now convert to cash by undoing everything in it that isn't cash.
  • Then we add back D&A of £2.0m. Depreciation reduced profit, but no cash left the building this year because of it, so we add it back. The cash cost of the assets shows up further down, as capex, in the year they were bought.
  • Next, we subtract the increase in receivables, which is £1.0m. Receivables rose from 7.0 to 8.0, as we saw on lesson 3's balance sheet. That means £1.0m of the revenue counted in profit is still sitting with customers, rather than in Bramley's bank account, so profit overstates cash by that amount.
  • We also subtract the increase in inventory, which is £0.5m. Stock rose from 5.5 to 6.0. Cash was spent filling the warehouse, but none of it hit the P&L, because the goods haven't been sold yet.
  • Then we add the increase in payables, which is £0.5m. Payables rose from 6.5 to 7.0. In other words, Bramley put £0.5m of costs through the P&L that it hasn't yet paid its suppliers for. That's free short-term funding.

The three working capital lines net off to minus £1.0m, which is exactly the increase in working capital, from 6.0 to 7.0, that we worked out from the balance sheet. That gives us a general rule worth memorising: an increase in working capital is a cash outflow, and a decrease is an inflow. That sign convention trips everyone up at least once. The fix is to ask yourself, "did this tie cash up, or release it?"

  • So operating cash flow is £5.0m, which is 4.0 + 2.0 − 1.0 − 0.5 + 0.5. Set that against £8.0m of EBITDA, and you have the "cash conversion" figure that a deal team would work out immediately.
  • In investing, there's capex of £3.0m. That's the investment in the filling line, and it also explains the movement in PP&E: 18.8 + 3.0 − 1.8 = 20.0.
  • Financing comes to minus £1.5m. That's £1.0m of scheduled debt repayment, taking debt from 16.0 down to 15.0, plus the £0.5m dividend from the equity roll-forward.
  • The net movement is plus £0.5m, which leaves closing cash of £3.0m, matching the balance sheet to the penny. So the puzzle is solved. Of the £4.0m profit, £2.0m was offset by capex net of the D&A add-back, that's 3.0 minus 2.0. Another £1.0m was absorbed into working capital, and £1.5m went to the people who fund the business. That leaves £0.5m.

There's a deep structural point to notice here. Apart from the opening and closing cash, every line came from the other two statements. Profit and D&A came from the P&L, and the working capital and debt movements came from changes in the balance sheet. The indirect-method cash flow statement is derived. That's why a three-statement model always builds it last, and why lesson 5 can treat the three statements as a single machine.

§1.4.4Free cash flow

Deal teams compress the whole statement into one number, called free cash flow, or FCF. It's the cash the business generates after the reinvestment needed to keep it running. In other words, it's the cash that is genuinely free to pay lenders and owners. The simplest common definition is:

FCF=Operating cash flow−Capex\text{FCF} = \text{Operating cash flow} - \text{Capex}FCF=Operating cash flow−Capex

For Bramley, that's 5.0 minus 3.0, which gives £2.0m. Definitions do vary, for instance whether you measure before or after interest and tax, so be precise about which one you're using; the valuation module formalises the variants. But the idea stays the same. EBITDA of £8.0m is the headline, and £2.0m is what actually landed. The ratio between the two, 25% here, is the single most revealing quality-of-earnings statistic there is. A business converting 80% of its EBITDA into free cash is a compounding machine, while one converting 20% is running hard just to stand still. Same EBITDA, completely different deals.

§1.4.5Why profit ≠ cash: a company that profits itself to death

Now for the promised cautionary tale. Growfast Trading Ltd, which is fictional, distributes electronic components. It buys stock, holds it, and sells it on 60-day credit terms, and it's growing ferociously. Revenue is up 60% this year, from £20.0m to £32.0m. The P&L looks great, with net profit of £1.6m, a 5% margin, and £0.4m of depreciation. Time to open the champagne?

Look at what all that growth did to the balance sheet.

Growfast (£m) Opening Closing Cash effect
Trade receivables 3.0 5.0 (2.0)
Inventory 2.5 4.5 (2.0)
Trade payables 2.0 3.0 1.0
Working capital 3.5 6.5 (3.0)

Sixty percent more sales means roughly sixty percent more invoices outstanding, and a much bigger warehouse full of stock, only partly offset by stretching out the suppliers. Now let's put the cash flow statement together.

Growfast — cash flow (£m)
Net profit 1.6
Add back: depreciation 0.4
Working capital increase (3.0)
Operating cash flow (1.0)
Capex (0.6)
Free cash flow (1.6)
Debt repayment due (0.5)
Net cash movement (2.1)
Opening cash 1.5
Closing cash (0.6)

A company that has just reported £1.6m of profit finishes the year £0.6m overdrawn. Nothing fraudulent happened, and nothing even went wrong operationally. The profit is real; it's just trapped in stock and unpaid invoices, while the wage bill, the suppliers and the bank all want actual cash on actual dates. Unless Growfast raises new funding, slows its own growth, or tightens its working capital cycle, it will start bouncing payments while its P&L glows. Insolvency practitioners have a name for this: overtrading. It kills growing companies with real products and real customers.

The general law is this. Profit and cash differ because of three things: first, non-cash charges such as D&A; second, movements in working capital; and third, items that hit cash but not profit, such as capex, repayments of debt principal, and dividends. Fast growth maximises the second, and often the third as well. That's why growth is a use of cash long before it becomes a source of it.

§1.4.6What deal teams look for

So what looks good? Operating cash flow consistently at or above 80 to 90% of EBITDA; capex comfortably covered; and a cash flow statement that's "boring", with the same shape every year. What looks bad? A widening gap between EBITDA and cash, which is a classic early warning of aggressive revenue recognition or stock problems. Chronic negative operating cash flow, dressed up as "investment in growth". Or one-off releases of working capital that flatter a single year, such as squeezing payables in December so you look great at the year end, and then paying for it in January. What deal teams actually ask for is this: "show me EBITDA to free cash flow, line by line, for the last three years". That's the so-called cash conversion bridge. If you remember one exhibit from this lesson, make it that one, because it's the P&L's claims, audited by the bank account.

Next, lesson 5 ties everything together. It traces a single transaction through all three statements over two years, so that the links stop being rules to memorise and become mechanics you can actually see.

Lesson 1.5/Accounting Foundations

How the Three Statements Link

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson follows a £5m machine, bought with debt, through all three statements over two years. Along the way, it makes the standing links between the statements explicit: net income flowing into retained earnings, depreciation's triple appearance, and the movements in working capital.

  1. 1.5.1One machine, three statements, two years
  2. 1.5.2Day one: nothing hits the P&L
  3. 1.5.3Year 1: the costs begin to flow
  4. 1.5.4Year 2: the pattern repeats
  5. 1.5.5The standing linkages
  6. 1.5.6Why this matters beyond exams

§1.5.1One machine, three statements, two years

The quickest way to stop thinking of the statements as three separate reports is to push a single transaction through all of them, and watch each one react. Here's our test transaction. On the first day of Year 1, a company buys a £5.0m production machine, funded entirely by a new £5.0m bank loan. We'll keep the assumptions deliberately clean.

  • The machine is depreciated on a straight line over 10 years, with no residual value. That gives £0.5m of depreciation a year.
  • The loan carries 6% interest, which is £0.3m a year. It's interest-only for now, so there are no principal repayments in our window.
  • The tax rate is 20%, and tax is paid in the year it's incurred.
  • And we isolate only the effects of this transaction, as if everything else in the company stood still. In reality, the machine would earn revenue too, and we'll come back to that at the end.

This is the classic interview drill: "walk me through £5m of capex funded by debt". It's asked precisely because you can't answer it correctly without understanding every link in this lesson.

§1.5.2Day one: nothing hits the P&L

On the day the machine is bought, the company has spent £5.0m, and yet it reports no impact on profit at all. That feels wrong to newcomers, but it's exactly right. The machine isn't a cost of this period; it's an asset that will serve ten periods. So the purchase is capitalised.

  • On the P&L, there's no effect, because nothing has been used up yet.
  • On the cash flow statement, there are two entries that cancel each other out: capex of minus 5.0 in investing, and the loan drawdown of plus 5.0 in financing. So the net movement in cash is nil.
  • On the balance sheet, PP&E goes up by 5.0 on the asset side, and bank debt goes up by 5.0 on the liability side. The equation grows by £5m on each side and stays balanced, while equity is untouched.

You can already see the division of labour. The cash flow statement recorded the event, the balance sheet recorded the position, and the P&L quite rightly stayed silent.

§1.5.3Year 1: the costs begin to flow

Over Year 1, the machine wears out a little, which is depreciation, and the loan costs money, which is interest.

Here's the impact on the P&L in Year 1, in £m.
Depreciation (0.50)
Interest expense (0.30)
Profit before tax (0.80)
Tax saving at 20% 0.16
Net income impact (0.64)

Notice the tax line. Because depreciation and interest are both deductible, a pre-tax cost of £0.8m reduces the tax bill by £0.16m. That's known as the "tax shield". This shield, especially on interest, is one of the quiet subsidies that makes leveraged structures attractive, and the LBO module comes back to it.

Here's the cash flow statement for Year 1, in £m. We start from net income, and undo the items that aren't cash.
Net income impact (0.64)
Add back: depreciation (non-cash) 0.50
Operating cash flow impact (0.14)
Investing 0.00
Financing 0.00
Cash impact (0.14)

Only £0.14m of actual cash left the business in Year 1. That's the £0.30m of interest paid out, minus the £0.16m of tax genuinely saved. The £0.5m depreciation charge cost nothing in cash this year, because its cash left on day one.

And here's the balance sheet at the end of Year 1, showing the changes compared with the day before the purchase.

Δ £m
PP&E (5.0 cost − 0.5 accumulated depreciation) +4.50
Cash (0.14)
Assets +4.36
Bank debt +5.00
Retained earnings (0.64)
Liabilities + equity +4.36

It balances: plus 4.36 on both sides. And every one of those four changes came from one of the flows above. Nothing was plugged.

§1.5.4Year 2: the pattern repeats

Year 2 is a carbon copy of Year 1's flows. There's depreciation of 0.50, interest of 0.30, a tax saving of 0.16, a hit to net income of 0.64, and a cash impact of 0.14. The balance sheet simply accumulates another year of the same.

End of Year 2 (cumulative Δ, £m)
PP&E (5.0 − 1.0 accumulated depreciation) +4.00
Cash (2 × 0.14) (0.28)
Assets +3.72
Bank debt +5.00
Retained earnings (2 × 0.64) (1.28)
Liabilities + equity +3.72

It's balanced again. Now run the film forward in your head. After ten years, PP&E reaches zero, a cumulative £5.0m of depreciation has flowed through the P&L, and the total cost on the P&L equals the cash spent on day one. It's just been spread over the machine's life. Accrual accounting never changes what things cost, only when the cost is recognised. And in real life, of course, the machine would be generating revenue all along. A machine that only shows up in a model as costs is a machine that shouldn't have been bought. The point of isolating the costs is simply to see the plumbing.

It's worth pausing on how each statement did its own distinctive job across the two years. The cash flow statement told the truth about timing: a £5.0m outflow on day one, and then only £0.14m a year. The P&L told the truth about economics: no cost on day one, and then £0.64m a year of after-tax burden, as the machine wears out and the loan accrues interest. And the balance sheet kept the running score: an asset shrinking by £0.5m a year, a debt sitting unchanged until it's repaid, and equity quietly absorbing the accumulated after-tax cost. Ask any one statement on its own, and you get a misleading answer. The cash view on day one says "we spent £5m and there was no impact on profit". The P&L view says "this machine only costs £0.64m a year", ignoring all the capital tied up in it. Ask all three, and the picture is complete. That's the design. The statements aren't three opinions; they're three projections of one underlying event log.

§1.5.5The standing linkages

The machine story used every major connection between the statements. Here they are as a checklist you can reuse, because they hold for every company in every period.

1. Net income flows into retained earnings. The P&L's bottom line doesn't vanish at the year end; it rolls into equity.

Closing RE=Opening RE+Net income−Dividends\text{Closing RE} = \text{Opening RE} + \text{Net income} - \text{Dividends}Closing RE=Opening RE+Net income−Dividends

For Bramley Foods, from lessons 2 and 3, that's 11.5 + 4.0 − 0.5 = 15.0 ✓. This is the bridge from the P&L to the balance sheet. It's also the reason a profitable company that pays out little in dividends shows equity compounding steadily.

2. Depreciation appears three times. This is the most-tested link in every modelling interview.

  • On the P&L, it's an expense, which reduces EBIT and net income.
  • On the cash flow statement, it's added back to net income in the operating section, because it isn't cash.
  • On the balance sheet, it accumulates against PP&E, which reduces the net book value.

So that's one economic event, with three coordinated appearances. If you change depreciation in a model and only one statement moves, the model is broken.

3. Working capital links changes in the balance sheet to operating cash flow. Every change in receivables, inventory and payables between two balance sheets shows up in the operating section, with the sign flipped for the assets. So Bramley's receivables going up by 1.0, inventory up by 0.5 and payables up by 0.5 became minus 1.0, minus 0.5 and plus 0.5 in operating cash flow.

4. Capex links investing cash flow to PP&E, and D&A closes the loop. Closing PP&E=Opening PP&E+Capex−Depreciation\text{Closing PP\&E} = \text{Opening PP\&E} + \text{Capex} - \text{Depreciation}Closing PP&E=Opening PP&E+Capex−Depreciation. For Bramley, that's 18.8 + 3.0 − 1.8 = 20.0 ✓. Given any three of those numbers, you can solve for the fourth, and that's a standard diligence cross-check on the numbers in a data room.

5. Financing flows link financing cash flow to debt and equity. Debt drawn or repaid moves the debt balance; for Bramley, 16.0 minus 1.0 gives 15.0. Dividends and share issues move equity, alongside retained earnings.

6. The bottom line of the cash flow statement is the cash line on the balance sheet. Opening cash plus the net movement in cash equals closing cash; for Bramley, 2.5 plus 0.5 gives 3.0. This is the master check. If a three-statement model balances and the cash reconciles, every flow has been accounted for somewhere.

§1.5.6Why this matters beyond exams

Because the linked system audits itself, deal teams exploit it all the time.

  • Models are built on it. Every LBO model is a three-statement machine. The P&L drives cash flow, cash flow pays down debt, and the debt sets next year's interest, which feeds back into the P&L. So the links aren't a nicety; they're the simulation loop.
  • Inconsistencies expose problems. Suppose a management pack shows EBITDA up 20%, but debt is creeping upwards and cash is flat. The links tell you the profit isn't converting into cash, which means something is absorbing it. It might be working capital, capitalised costs, or optimistic revenue. You don't need anyone to tell you where to look, because the system tells you.
  • Data work depends on it. When you reconcile a portfolio company's reporting into a warehouse, these links are your integrity constraints: the roll-forward of retained earnings, the roll-forward of PP&E, and the cash reconciliation. A monthly pack that fails them is a data quality incident with a financial name.

So what looks good? Statements that tie out exactly, with roll-forwards you can reproduce from the disclosed flows. What looks bad? "Adjusted" figures that can't be reconciled back to any statement, or movements on the balance sheet with no matching flow, which go by the polite name of "other". What deal teams actually ask is: "does the model balance?" And of an analyst, they'll ask: "walk me through £5m of capex funded by debt." You can now do that, to the decimal point.

There's one lesson left in this module, and it changes register. So far, we've treated the rules as mechanical. In practice, though, several of the numbers you've just learned to trace, such as depreciation lives, the timing of revenue, and what counts as an asset, are chosen rather than observed. Lesson 6 is about who chooses them, how they bend, and why diligence exists.

↑ Module 1

Lesson 1.6/Accounting Foundations

Accounting Judgement & Where Numbers Bend

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson looks at where reported numbers involve judgement: accruals and provisions, capitalising versus expensing, revenue recognition games, and one-offs and exceptional items. It also explains why diligence teams adjust the reported figures before they price a deal.

  1. 1.6.1The uncomfortable truth about "the numbers"
  2. 1.6.2Accruals and provisions: profit by estimate
  3. 1.6.3Capitalisation vs expensing: the EBITDA machine
  4. 1.6.4Revenue recognition games
  5. 1.6.5One-offs, exceptionals, and the adjusted-EBITDA bridge
  6. 1.6.6The instinct to carry forward

§1.6.1The uncomfortable truth about "the numbers"

So far in this module, we've treated accounting like arithmetic: rules go in, and statements come out. Now it's time to complicate that picture. Accounting standards are a framework, not a formula. They require estimates, such as how long a machine will last. They require judgements, such as whether a project is 60% or 80% complete. And they require classifications, such as whether a cost is an asset or an expense. Reasonable people can answer these questions differently, and the answers move profit.

Most of the time, management makes these calls in good faith. But look at the incentives. Bonus schemes pay out on profit targets, covenants are tested on EBITDA, and, most relevant for us, companies being sold are valued at a multiple of EBITDA. At an 8x multiple, every extra £1m of EBITDA a seller can present is worth £8m of extra price. Nobody needs to commit fraud for the numbers to drift towards optimism, because the drift is built into the situation. This is the reason financial due diligence exists. It isn't there to re-add the columns; it's there to remake the judgements from the buyer's side. This lesson is your first tour of the four places where numbers bend the most. The due diligence module goes much deeper, but here we're building the instinct.

§1.6.2Accruals and provisions: profit by estimate

Accrual accounting requires you to estimate costs that haven't been billed yet. An accrual is a cost recognised before the invoice arrives, such as December's electricity, or bonuses that haven't been paid yet. A provision is its bigger, less certain cousin. It's a liability whose timing or amount is uncertain, such as warranty claims, a lawsuit, restructuring costs, or receivables that may never be collected.

Every accrual and every provision is an estimate, and estimates come with a dial. Here's a worked example. A machinery manufacturer sells £40.0m of equipment with two-year warranties. History says warranty costs run at about 3% of sales, so prudent accounting books a £1.2m provision, charging it against this year's profit. But suppose that management, in a year when they're being measured, decide that "quality has improved", and book 1.5% instead. The charge falls to £0.6m, and so profit is £0.6m higher, without any change whatsoever in the business. The claims will arrive regardless, and next year's P&L will have to absorb the shortfall.

Provisions also make the opposite game possible. You over-provide in a bad year, when the market has written the year off anyway. Then, in a later year when you need to hit a target, you quietly release the excess provision back into profit. Those releases boost profit without any cash or performance behind them. This kind of smoothing is sometimes called "cookie-jar accounting".

So the questions deal teams actually ask are these: how have the provision balances moved over three years, and were any releases booked into EBITDA? A provision that only ever moves in the direction that helps profit is a red flag that comes with a paper trail.

§1.6.3Capitalisation vs expensing: the EBITDA machine

Remember the boundary from lessons 3 and 5. Spending that creates a long-term asset is capitalised: it goes on the balance sheet, and is then depreciated or amortised over a number of years. Spending that's used up now is expensed: it goes straight through the P&L. That boundary is genuinely fuzzy, and it sits right on top of EBITDA.

Here's a worked example. A software company spends £3.0m a year on developers, and there are two defensible ways to treat that cost.

£m Expense it all Capitalise £2.0m as development
Revenue 20.0 20.0
Staff costs in P&L (3.0) (1.0)
Other opex (12.0) (12.0)
EBITDA 5.0 7.0
Amortisation of capitalised dev (over 4 years) — (0.5)

It's the same company, with the same cash going out of the door, and yet EBITDA is 40% higher under the second treatment. That's because the capitalised £2.0m only comes back into the P&L as amortisation, which sits below the EBITDA line and gets added straight back. At an 8x multiple, that choice of treatment is worth £16m of headline price. In a steady state, amortisation does catch up; by year 4, there's £2.0m of annual amortisation from four overlapping years of spending. But EBITDA never sees it, and EBITDA is what the deal is priced on.

Capitalising development costs can be entirely legitimate, and the standards allow it when specific criteria are met. The diligence questions are these. Is the policy stable, or did the capitalisation rate creep up before the sale? And what happens to "EBITDA minus capitalised development", which is the cash-honest version? A capitalisation rate that rises in the two years before a sale process is one of the most reliable tells in the book.

§1.6.4Revenue recognition games

Revenue is the biggest number on the P&L, and it's the first thing every buyer looks at. And because recognising it depends on judgements about delivery, completion and contract terms, it's the place where being aggressive has the biggest consequences. Here are the classic moves.

  • Pulling revenue forward. This means shipping heavily in the last week of the period, often helped along by discounts, which is known as "channel stuffing". It also covers invoicing ahead of delivery, or recognising an annual contract upfront instead of over its life. Remember lesson 2's example: booking a £1.2m contract running from October to September entirely in this financial year overstates revenue by £0.9m. The tell is a receivables or deferred-revenue balance that has drifted out of line with revenue.
  • Optimistic percentage-of-completion. Businesses with long contracts recognise revenue according to their estimated progress. Nudge a project from 60% complete to 75%, and revenue appears out of thin air. Reality arrives later, in the form of a loss-making final phase. The tell here is contract assets, also called "accrued income", meaning revenue earned but not yet billed, growing faster than revenue itself.
  • Gross versus net presentation. Picture an intermediary that handles £100m of bookings and earns a 10% commission on them. It can present its revenue as £100m, which is the gross figure, or as £10m, which is the net figure. The profit is identical either way, but the scale, the optics of growth, and the revenue multiples look wildly different.
  • Bill-and-hold and side letters. This means recognising sales for goods that are still sitting in your own warehouse, or granting undisclosed rights of return that make the "sales" reversible.

There's one diagnostic that ties all of these together, and it's the reason lesson 4 matters so much: aggressive revenue makes profit grow faster than operating cash flow. That's because the fictional or early revenue piles up in receivables and contract assets, instead of arriving as cash. Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. When the two diverge for more than a year, diligence teams start pulling the contracts.

§1.6.5One-offs, exceptionals, and the adjusted-EBITDA bridge

Companies present certain items as exceptional, or "one-off", to argue that they don't reflect underlying performance. Typical examples are restructuring costs, a flood at the warehouse, deal fees, or a discontinued product line. The logic is fair enough: you shouldn't price a business off a year that was distorted by a fire. The abuse, though, is systematic, and it runs in one direction. Costs are forever one-offs, whereas gains somehow always turn out to be underlying. Some businesses report "exceptional" restructuring charges every single year for a decade, and at that point they aren't exceptional at all; they're the business model.

In a sale process, all of this comes together in the adjusted EBITDA bridge, which is the seller's walk from reported EBITDA to "underlying" EBITDA. Here's a typical one.

Project Orchard — adjusted EBITDA (£m) FY24
Reported EBITDA 6.0
Add: restructuring costs 0.8
Add: aborted-deal professional fees 0.4
Add: flood damage (uninsured portion) 0.3
Add: pro-forma synergies from new site 0.7
Add: normalised owner remuneration 0.3
Adjusted EBITDA 8.5

The reported £6.0m becomes a marketed £8.5m. That's a 42% uplift, and at 8x, the adjustments alone are asking for £20m. A diligence team would take each line on its merits. The aborted-deal fees are probably a fair add-back, because they're genuinely non-recurring and can be verified. The restructuring is suspect if there's one every year. The flood add-back needs the insurance file to back it up. The "pro-forma synergies" are a forecast dressed up as an add-back, and they usually get struck out or heavily discounted. And the adjustment for owner pay cuts both ways, because the real question is what a replacement on a market rate would actually cost. Notice, too, what these bridges rarely contain, which is deductions: the one-off gain on a property sale, the bonuses that weren't fully accrued, or the R&D that stopped being expensed. A bridge that only goes one way is evidence in itself.

So what looks good? A short bridge, where each item is large, documented and genuinely non-recurring, with deductions as well as add-backs. What looks bad? Lots of small add-backs, "one-offs" that recur year after year, and synergies presented as adjustments. What deal teams actually ask is: "rebuild the bridge: what EBITDA would we defend to our investment committee and to our lenders?"

§1.6.6The instinct to carry forward

Pull those four sections together, and you get the mental posture of a good diligence analyst, and of a good data person in PE.

  1. Reported numbers are a starting point, never an answer. They contain estimates made by people with incentives. So the question isn't "what is EBITDA?" It's "whose EBITDA, and under whose judgements?"
  2. Cash is the audit of profit. Nearly every game in this lesson, whether that's early revenue, skinny provisions or capitalised costs, shows up either as a gap between profit and operating cash flow, or as a balance sheet line drifting out of proportion. Those lines include receivables, contract assets, capitalised development and provision balances. The links between the three statements from lesson 5 are your lie detector.
  3. Trends beat snapshots. A single year's judgement calls are hard to assess. But three years of capitalisation rates, provision movements and the frequency of one-offs will tell you whether the dial has been turned. This is genuinely a data problem, and that's why data teams get pulled into diligence.
  4. Materiality is priced in multiples. At typical multiples, every contested £1m of EBITDA is worth £6 to £10m of price. That's why sellers polish their numbers, why buyers commission quality-of-earnings reports, and why this module ends here rather than with the mechanics.

None of this means that accounts are fiction. Audited statements are mostly reliable, and the self-checking structure you've learned makes gross manipulation hard to sustain. What it does mean is that the last 10 to 20% of any reported profit figure is soft, that the softness is usually on the optimistic side, and that deals are won and lost in exactly that band. The financial statement analysis module sharpens the tools, and the due diligence module turns them into weapons. You now speak the language they're written in.
