Lesson 2.1/Financial Statement Analysis

Reading Statements Like an Analyst

22 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson shows how analysts actually read a P&L. It covers common-size and trend analysis, and then works through five questions, on growth, margin, quality, trajectory and comparability, using a fictional company's three-year income statement.

  1. 2.1.1From bookkeeping to judgement
  2. 2.1.2Common-size analysis: divide everything by revenue
  3. 2.1.3Trend analysis: growth rates line by line
  4. 2.1.4The five questions to ask of any P&L
  5. 2.1.5Applying the five questions to Bramley
  6. 2.1.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.1.1From bookkeeping to judgement

Module 1 taught you what the three statements are. This module teaches you what deal teams do with them. The difference matters. An accountant asks, "has this been recorded correctly?" An analyst asks, "what is this business really like, and is it getting better or worse?"

When a deal team receives a target's financials, usually a three-year historical P&L plus a budget, nobody reads them from top to bottom like a novel. Instead, they convert them into two standard views, called common-size and trend, and then interrogate them with a handful of stock questions. The whole exercise takes about twenty minutes, and it tells you 80% of what you need for a first meeting. This lesson walks through exactly that process, using a fictional company called Bramley Foods Ltd, which makes branded chilled ready-meals.

Here is Bramley's summary P&L, as it might arrive in an information pack.

£m FY23 FY24 FY25
Revenue 80.0 92.0 100.0
Cost of goods sold (48.0) (56.4) (62.0)
Gross profit 32.0 35.6 38.0
Operating expenses (20.0) (22.0) (23.0)
EBITDA 12.0 13.6 15.0
Depreciation & amortisation (3.0) (3.2) (3.5)
EBIT 9.0 10.4 11.5
Interest (1.0) (1.2) (1.5)
Profit before tax 8.0 9.2 10.0
Tax (2.0) (2.3) (2.5)
Profit after tax 6.0 6.9 7.5

At first glance, everything is growing, and every subtotal is bigger each year. A seller would call this "a consistent record of profitable growth". Our job is to look harder.

§2.1.2Common-size analysis: divide everything by revenue

Common-size analysis restates every line of the P&L as a percentage of revenue. That strips out the effect of the company simply getting bigger, so you can see whether the shape of the business is changing. It also makes companies of different sizes directly comparable, so an £80m business and an £800m business can sit side by side.

Here's Bramley, common-sized.

% of revenue FY23 FY24 FY25
Revenue 100.0% 100.0% 100.0%
COGS 60.0% 61.3% 62.0%
Gross margin 40.0% 38.7% 38.0%
Opex 25.0% 23.9% 23.0%
EBITDA margin 15.0% 14.8% 15.0%
EBIT margin 11.3% 11.3% 11.5%
Net margin 7.5% 7.5% 7.5%

Suddenly, the story changes. The EBITDA margin looks flat at about 15%, but that flatness is hiding two opposing forces.

  • First, the gross margin is eroding, from 40.0% to 38.7%, and then to 38.0%. Bramley loses two full points of gross margin over two years. On FY25 revenue of £100.0m, two points is £2.0m of EBITDA, which is real money. Is it input-cost inflation that they can't pass on? Price pressure from their supermarket customers? Or a shift in mix towards lower-margin products? We don't know yet, but it's now question number one for management.
  • Second, opex is falling as a percentage of revenue, from 25.0% to 23.0%. That could be healthy operating leverage, where fixed costs are spread over more revenue, and there's more on that in Lesson 2. Or it could be under-investment: cutting marketing, delaying hires, or skimping on maintenance. Cost discipline that flatters the year before a sale is one of the oldest tricks in the book.

So what looks good? A gross margin that's stable or rising, with opex leverage on top. And what looks bad? Exactly Bramley's pattern, where a decline in gross margin is masked by cuts in opex. The headline margin is flat, but the quality of that margin has deteriorated. That's because gross margin reflects the fundamental economics of what you sell, whereas opex cuts are finite, and often reversible.

§2.1.3Trend analysis: growth rates line by line

The second standard view is the year-on-year growth of each line. The rule of thumb is that in a healthy business, the profit lines grow faster than revenue, which means margins are expanding, and no cost line keeps growing faster than revenue without a good reason.

YoY growth FY24 FY25
Revenue +15.0% +8.7%
COGS +17.5% +9.9%
Gross profit +11.3% +6.7%
Opex +10.0% +4.5%
EBITDA +13.3% +10.3%

There are two observations here. First, COGS grows faster than revenue in both years: 17.5% against 15.0%, and then 9.9% against 8.7%. That's the arithmetic mirror image of the gross margin erosion we saw above, and it's a pattern that compounds badly if it carries on. Second, revenue growth is slowing down, from 15.0% to 8.7%. Slowing growth isn't fatal, but a buyer paying a growth multiple needs to know where it settles. If FY26 comes in at 4%, this is a different business, and it deserves a different price.

A useful companion number is the CAGR, which stands for compound annual growth rate.

CAGR=(End valueStart value)1/n−1\text{CAGR} = \left(\frac{\text{End value}}{\text{Start value}}\right)^{1/n} - 1CAGR=(Start valueEnd value​)1/n−1

Bramley's two-year revenue CAGR is (100.0/80.0)1/2−1=11.8%(100.0/80.0)^{1/2} - 1 = 11.8\%(100.0/80.0)1/2−1=11.8%. Sellers love quoting CAGR, because it smooths the slowdown into a single flattering number. So always look at the year-by-year path behind any CAGR. "An 11.8% CAGR" and "15% fading to 9%" describe the same data, but they imply very different futures.

§2.1.4The five questions to ask of any P&L

The common-size and trend views are mechanical. The judgement comes from five questions that every analyst should be able to answer after reading any P&L. They're worth committing to memory.

1. Growth: how fast is it, and where is it coming from? It's not just the rate that matters, but the source. Is it volume or price? Existing customers or new ones? Organic, or bought through acquisitions? Ten million pounds of growth from a price rise on captive customers is worth more than the same amount from a one-off contract win. If the pack doesn't split volume from price, ask for it; it's one of the first data requests any deal team sends.

2. Margin: how profitable is the business, and is that normal? Work out the gross and EBITDA margins, and then benchmark them against the sector; Lesson 2 gives you the reference table. A 15% EBITDA margin is excellent for a food distributor, ordinary for a manufacturer, and alarming for a software business. And a margin far above the sector norm needs just as much explanation as one far below it. Outperformance has a cause, and if you can't find it, suspect the accounting.

3. Quality: is the profit real, and will it repeat? Are there one-off items in the numbers? Does EBITDA convert into cash, as covered in Lessons 3 and 4? Is the revenue recurring, or is it won deal by deal? A P&L on its own can't fully answer this; that's what Lesson 6, and later on quality of earnings work, are for. But you should form a first view of how far you trust the reported numbers.

4. Trajectory: which way is each line heading? Buyers buy the future. A business at a 14% margin and rising is more attractive than one at 16% and falling. For Bramley, growth is slowing, gross margin is falling, and the EBITDA margin is only being held flat by cuts in opex. So the read on trajectory is cautious, even though every absolute number went up.

5. Comparability: are all the years measured the same way? Trend analysis assumes that FY23, FY24 and FY25 are like for like, and often they aren't. There may have been changes in accounting policy, acquisitions part-way through a year, a 53-week year, costs reclassified between COGS and opex, or a change in how revenue is recognised. So before you trust any trend, check the basis on which the numbers were prepared. A margin "trend" that's really just a reclassification is noise. Worse, it's usually noise that flatters.

§2.1.5Applying the five questions to Bramley

Let's run Bramley through the framework, and write down what you'd actually say in a deal-team meeting.

  • On growth: it was 15.0% and then 8.7%, so it's slowing, with a two-year CAGR of 11.8%. We need the split between volume and price. With food inflation over the period, much of this could be pricing that's simply been passed through, on flat or falling volumes, and that's far less valuable than it looks.
  • On margin: in FY25, the gross margin is 38.0% and the EBITDA margin is 15.0%. For branded chilled food, a 15% EBITDA margin is towards the top of the normal range. That's good, but we need to check it's been earned honestly.
  • On quality: we can't tell from the P&L alone. We'll flag it for later. Does the £15.0m of EBITDA turn into cash, and is any of it a one-off?
  • On trajectory: this is the worrying one. Gross margin is down 2.0 points in two years, and the EBITDA margin is only flat because opex fell from 25.0% to 23.0% of revenue. If the opex cuts have run their course and gross margin keeps sliding, the FY26 EBITDA margin falls below 14%, even with decent growth.
  • On comparability: this still needs verifying. Has anything changed in how costs are split between COGS and opex? Has the depreciation policy changed? That wouldn't hit EBITDA, but it would hit EBIT. And are all the years 52 weeks long?

Notice how different this is from "revenue and profits grew every year". It's the same set of numbers, but a completely different conversation.

§2.1.6What deal teams actually ask

When this analysis lands in a meeting, the questions it raises are concrete. For a business shaped like Bramley, expect questions such as: "What's driving the decline in gross margin: input costs, pricing or mix?", "How much of the FY25 reduction in opex is sustainable, and how much is just deferred spending?", "Can you give us the volume and price bridge for revenue growth?", and "Were there any changes in accounting policy or cost classification over the period?"

There are three habits worth building from day one. First, always common-size and trend a P&L before forming any view, and never react to the absolute numbers. Second, be suspicious of flat lines. A suspiciously stable margin often means two movements offsetting each other, and you need to know what both of them are. Third, write your five answers down. The discipline of committing to something like "growth: slowing; margin: top of the range; trajectory: negative" forces clarity, and it's exactly the format an investment committee summary uses.

The rest of this module builds out the toolkit. There are margin benchmarks and returns ratios in Lesson 2, working capital in Lesson 3, cash conversion in Lesson 4, leverage in Lesson 5, and a first pass at the quality of earnings in Lesson 6. Every one of them ultimately serves the same five questions.

Lesson 2.2/Financial Statement Analysis

Margins and Profitability Ratios

24 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson climbs the margin ladder, from gross to EBITDA, operating and net, and gives typical ranges by sector. It then covers two returns ratios, ROCE and ROE, and operating leverage. That includes a worked example of what a 10% fall in revenue does to EBITDA in a fixed-cost business compared with a variable-cost one.

  1. 2.2.1The margin ladder
  2. 2.2.2What "normal" looks like by sector
  3. 2.2.3ROCE: the quality-of-business ratio
  4. 2.2.4ROE, and why PE treats it carefully
  5. 2.2.5Operating leverage: fixed costs cut both ways
  6. 2.2.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.2.1The margin ladder

Every P&L gives you a ladder of margins, and each one answers a different question.

  • Gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue. It's what's left after the direct cost of what you sell. This is the purest read on the economics of the product: pricing power, input costs and mix. It's also the hardest margin to improve. You can cut overheads within a quarter, but improving gross margin means changing what you sell, who you sell it to, and at what price.
  • EBITDA margin is EBITDA divided by revenue, where EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. It's the common language of PE. It approximates the cash profitability of the operations, before any choices about financing or capex policy. Almost every deal is priced as a multiple of EBITDA, and that's why so much of this course is about whether the reported EBITDA can be trusted.
  • Operating margin, or EBIT margin, is EBIT divided by revenue, where EBIT is EBITDA minus depreciation and amortisation. It's the honest margin for capital-intensive businesses. A haulier's EBITDA margin ignores the fact that its trucks are wearing out, but its EBIT margin doesn't. When the EBITDA and EBIT margins are far apart, the gap between them is the capital intensity.
  • Net margin is profit after tax divided by revenue, so it includes everything, financing and tax as well. It's useful for screening listed companies, but it's used less in deals, because a buyer is going to replace the capital structure anyway.

Let's work through the ladder for Bramley Foods' FY25, from Lesson 1. Revenue is £100.0m, gross profit is £38.0m, EBITDA is £15.0m, EBIT is £11.5m, and profit after tax is £7.5m. So the margins are 38.0% gross, 15.0% EBITDA, 11.5% operating and 7.5% net. The 3.5-point gap between EBITDA and EBIT tells you that Bramley carries meaningful fixed assets, such as factories and chilled logistics. That's worth remembering when we get to capex in Lesson 4.

§2.2.2What "normal" looks like by sector

Margins only mean something against a benchmark. A 6% EBITDA margin is a disaster for a software company, but a perfectly good result for a distributor. Here are typical ranges for established mid-market businesses.

Sector Gross margin EBITDA margin
Enterprise software / SaaS 75–90% 20–40%
Business & professional services 30–50% 10–20%
Healthcare services 25–45% 15–25%
Specialist manufacturing 25–40% 10–18%
Consumer brands 35–55% 10–20%
Distribution / wholesale 15–30% 4–8%
Food retail / grocery 20–30% 3–6%
Construction / contracting 10–20% 3–6%

Deal teams use this table in three ways. The first is placement: is the target at the top, middle or bottom of its range, and why? A distributor at an 8% EBITDA margin either has a genuinely differentiated niche, such as value-added services or exclusive product lines, or it has flattering accounting, and you need to find out which. The second is headroom. A services business at 11% when its peers make 18% is a value-creation thesis in a single line. The third is suspicion. A company above the top of its sector's range is a red flag until proven otherwise. Outperformance is possible, but it has a cause you can name, and "our margins are just better" is not an answer.

Notice, too, that low-margin sectors are unforgiving. A grocer at a 4% EBITDA margin loses half its profit if costs move 2 points against it. That fragility feeds directly into how much debt a business like that can carry, which we'll come to in Lesson 5.

§2.2.3ROCE: the quality-of-business ratio

Margins ignore how much capital it takes to earn them. Return on capital employed, or ROCE, fixes that.

ROCE=EBITCapital employed,Capital employed=Equity+Net debt\text{ROCE} = \frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Capital employed}}, \qquad \text{Capital employed} = \text{Equity} + \text{Net debt}ROCE=Capital employedEBIT​,Capital employed=Equity+Net debt

Capital employed can also be measured as total assets minus current liabilities. And you should use EBIT here, not EBITDA. Capital employed includes the fixed assets, so the return should be measured after the cost of wearing them out.

Here's a worked example. Bramley has EBIT of £11.5m, shareholders' equity of £40.0m, and net debt of £20.0m. So capital employed is £60.0m, and ROCE is 11.5 divided by 60.0, which gives 19.2%.

Is that good? Here are some rules of thumb. A ROCE below about 10% suggests a mediocre business that's barely covering its cost of capital. Between 15 and 20% is solid. And 25% or more is genuinely good, and usually signals some kind of moat. The real power of ROCE is in comparing businesses with identical margins. Imagine two companies that each earn £11.5m of EBIT, but one employs £60.0m of capital, giving a ROCE of 19.2%, while the other employs £130.0m, giving 8.8%. The first one compounds value; the second treads water. Businesses with a high ROCE also need less capital to grow, because every extra pound of revenue drags in less investment. That's exactly the cash-generative profile that PE is willing to pay up for.

§2.2.4ROE, and why PE treats it carefully

Return on equity, or ROE, is profit after tax divided by shareholders' equity. For Bramley, that's 7.5 divided by 40.0, which gives 18.8%.

But ROE has a trap: it rises with leverage. Suppose you refinance Bramley with £40.0m of net debt and only £20.0m of equity. After the higher interest, profit after tax might fall to, say, £6.3m, and yet ROE jumps to 6.3 divided by 20.0, which is 31.5%. Nothing about the business has improved. The equity cheque has simply become smaller and riskier. Since PE deliberately runs high leverage, ROE mostly measures the financial structure, not the company.

So here's the working rule. Judge the business on ROCE, judge the deal on equity returns, which means IRR and MOIC, covered in Module 7, and treat ROE as a number that needs taking apart before it tells you anything. If someone quotes you a high ROE, your first question should be how much of it is leverage.

§2.2.5Operating leverage: fixed costs cut both ways

Operating leverage describes how sensitive profit is to revenue, and it's driven by the cost structure. Costs fall into two types. Variable costs move with revenue, such as materials, freight and sales commissions. Fixed costs don't, at least in the short run, such as rent, salaried staff, IT and insurance. The more fixed the cost base, the more any change in revenue gets amplified in profit.

Let's compare two businesses, each with £100.0m of revenue and £15.0m of EBITDA.

£m FlexCo FixCo
Revenue 100.0 100.0
Variable costs (75.0) (45.0)
Fixed costs (10.0) (40.0)
EBITDA 15.0 15.0
EBITDA margin 15.0% 15.0%

The headline P&L is identical. Now let revenue fall by 10%, to £90.0m. The variable costs fall in proportion, but the fixed costs don't move.

£m FlexCo FixCo
Revenue 90.0 90.0
Variable costs (67.5) (40.5)
Fixed costs (10.0) (40.0)
EBITDA 12.5 9.5
EBITDA change −16.7% −36.7%

A 10% fall in revenue costs FlexCo 16.7% of its EBITDA, but it costs FixCo 36.7%, which is over a third of its profit gone. The shortcut for measuring this sensitivity is called the degree of operating leverage.

DOL=%ΔEBITDA%ΔRevenue=Contribution marginEBITDA margin\text{DOL} = \frac{\%\Delta \text{EBITDA}}{\%\Delta \text{Revenue}} = \frac{\text{Contribution margin}}{\text{EBITDA margin}}DOL=%ΔRevenue%ΔEBITDA​=EBITDA marginContribution margin​

Here, the contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs, divided by revenue. For FlexCo, that gives 25% divided by 15%, or 1.7×. For FixCo, it's 55% divided by 15%, or 3.7×. As a check, 3.7 × (−10%) ≈ −37%, which matches the table.

The same maths works in reverse. If revenue grows by 10%, FixCo's EBITDA jumps 36.7%, to £20.5m. Operating leverage is why growing fixed-cost businesses show expanding margins "for free". And it's why Lesson 1 told you to ask whether opex leverage is structural, or just the good half of a cycle.

A related number worth working out is break-even revenue. That's the level of revenue at which EBITDA hits zero, and you find it by dividing the fixed costs by the contribution margin.

Break-even revenue=Fixed costsContribution margin %\text{Break-even revenue} = \frac{\text{Fixed costs}}{\text{Contribution margin \%}}Break-even revenue=Contribution margin %Fixed costs​

FlexCo breaks even at 10.0 divided by 0.25, which is £40.0m of revenue. It could lose 60% of its sales and still not lose money. FixCo breaks even at 40.0 divided by 0.55, which is £72.7m, so a 27% fall in revenue puts it underwater. Here are two businesses with identical revenue and identical EBITDA, and one is roughly twice as far from the cliff edge as the other. When you later size debt against businesses like these, in Lesson 5, that distance to break-even is precisely the cushion the lender is relying on. That's why questions about cost structure appear in every lender's due diligence pack.

§2.2.6What deal teams actually ask

Margins and operating leverage come together in diligence questions like these.

  • "Give us the margin bridge." In other words, explain the year-on-year change in EBITDA margin, split into price, volume, mix, input costs and opex. If management can't produce this, they don't understand their own business, and that's a finding in itself.
  • "What's the split between fixed and variable costs?" This drives the downside case. A lender and an investment committee will both want to know what EBITDA looks like if revenue falls by 10% or by 20%. With FixCo's cost structure, a 20% fall in revenue means EBITDA of £4.0m, which is down 73%. That caps how much debt the deal can safely carry.
  • "Why is your margin above, or below, the sector?" The answer is the company's position in the benchmark table, with a cause you can name: a niche, scale, or the structure of its contracts. The wrong answer is accounting.
  • "Where does the margin go from here?" Operating leverage, combined with the growth outlook, gives you the trajectory. A 15% margin with an operating leverage of 3.7× and slowing revenue is fragile. The same margin with an operating leverage of 1.7× is robust.

There are two habits to take forward. First, always work out the full ladder, gross, EBITDA and EBIT. That's because the places where they diverge, such as gross margin falling while EBITDA holds, or EBITDA looking fine while EBIT sags, are where the real story hides. Second, never quote a margin without its benchmark and its trajectory. "A 15% EBITDA margin" is data. "Fifteen percent, top quartile for the sector, and only held flat by cuts in opex" is analysis.

Lesson 2.3/Financial Statement Analysis

Working Capital and the Cash Conversion Cycle

24 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson builds up net working capital and the cash conversion cycle from first principles. It works out DSO, DIO and DPO on a worked example, explains why growth consumes cash, looks at businesses with negative working capital, and shows how seasonality distorts the year-end balance sheet.

  1. 2.3.1Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact
  2. 2.3.2DSO, DIO, DPO: a worked example
  3. 2.3.3Why growth consumes cash
  4. 2.3.4Negative working capital: growth that pays you
  5. 2.3.5Seasonality: the year-end is not the year
  6. 2.3.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.3.1Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact

A business can report a profit every year and still run out of money. The usual culprit is working capital, which is the cash tied up in the day-to-day operating cycle. Money goes out to buy stock and pay staff before any money comes in from customers, and that timing gap has to be financed by someone: the company itself, its bank, or its suppliers.

For analysis purposes, net working capital, or NWC, is defined like this:

NWC=Trade receivables+Inventory−Trade payables\text{NWC} = \text{Trade receivables} + \text{Inventory} - \text{Trade payables}NWC=Trade receivables+Inventory−Trade payables

There are also some smaller items, such as accruals and prepayments, and they matter more than you'd think, as Lesson 6 and the case study will show. Receivables are sales you've made but haven't been paid for. Inventory is stock you've paid for but haven't sold. And payables are purchases you've made but haven't paid for yet. Receivables and inventory absorb cash, whereas payables are free credit from suppliers, so they provide cash.

Here's the single most important sentence in this lesson: an increase in NWC is cash flowing out of the business, even though none of it shows up in the P&L. If a company books £5m more revenue but hasn't collected any of it yet, it has £5m more profit, but £5m less cash than it appears to have.

A word on those "smaller items". Accruals are costs that have been incurred but not yet invoiced, such as staff bonuses that have been earned but not paid, or utilities that have been used but not billed. They behave like payables, and they should grow roughly in line with the cost base. Prepayments are the mirror image, such as insurance or rent paid in advance, and they behave like receivables. Deferred income is cash collected before the work has been done. It's a liability, and in subscription businesses it's a big one. Analysts watch accruals especially closely. If the accrual balance falls while revenue and headcount are growing, that usually means costs are being under-recognised, which inflates profit directly. Hold that thought for this module's case study.

§2.3.2DSO, DIO, DPO: a worked example

Raw working capital balances are hard to interpret. £23m of working capital means nothing until you know the scale of the business. So we convert each component into days, which can be compared over time and across companies. Let's take Fenwick Trading, a distributor of plumbing supplies.

£m FY25
Revenue 120.0
COGS 90.0
Trade receivables 20.0
Inventory 18.0
Trade payables 15.0

DSO, or days sales outstanding, measures how long customers take to pay.

DSO=ReceivablesRevenue×365=20.0120.0×365=60.8 days\text{DSO} = \frac{\text{Receivables}}{\text{Revenue}} \times 365 = \frac{20.0}{120.0} \times 365 = 60.8 \text{ days}DSO=RevenueReceivables​×365=120.020.0​×365=60.8 days

DIO, or days inventory outstanding, measures how long stock sits before it's sold. Notice that the denominator here is COGS, not revenue, because inventory is held at cost.

DIO=InventoryCOGS×365=18.090.0×365=73.0 days\text{DIO} = \frac{\text{Inventory}}{\text{COGS}} \times 365 = \frac{18.0}{90.0} \times 365 = 73.0 \text{ days}DIO=COGSInventory​×365=90.018.0​×365=73.0 days

DPO, or days payables outstanding, measures how long the company takes to pay its suppliers. It's also calculated on COGS.

DPO=PayablesCOGS×365=15.090.0×365=60.8 days\text{DPO} = \frac{\text{Payables}}{\text{COGS}} \times 365 = \frac{15.0}{90.0} \times 365 = 60.8 \text{ days}DPO=COGSPayables​×365=90.015.0​×365=60.8 days

The cash conversion cycle chains these three together. It's the number of days between paying for the stock and getting paid for the finished sale.

CCC=DSO+DIO−DPO=60.8+73.0−60.8=73.0 days\text{CCC} = \text{DSO} + \text{DIO} - \text{DPO} = 60.8 + 73.0 - 60.8 = 73.0 \text{ days}CCC=DSO+DIO−DPO=60.8+73.0−60.8=73.0 days

So Fenwick finances 73 days of its operating cycle out of its own pocket. Let's sanity-check that against the balances. NWC is 20.0 + 18.0 − 15.0, which gives £23.0m. Divide that by revenue, 23.0 ÷ 120.0, and you get 19.2% of revenue, which is a fairly typical level for a distributor that holds stock. Both views, days and percentage of revenue, are standard. Deal teams tend to quote NWC as a percentage of revenue for the headline, and then use the days to diagnose which component has moved.

So what looks good, and what looks bad? Good is days that stay stable, or improve gently, over time. A rising DSO means customers are paying more slowly. Worse, it can mean disputed invoices, or aggressive revenue recognition that books sales customers haven't actually accepted. A rising DIO means stock is building up, either because demand is softening, or because obsolete stock hasn't been written off. And a sudden rise in DPO looks like free cash, but it usually means the company is leaning on its suppliers. That always reverses, and you'll see it planted in this module's case study.

§2.3.3Why growth consumes cash

Here's the counter-intuitive part that catches people out: growth makes the working capital problem worse, not better. If NWC runs at a stable percentage of revenue, then every pound of new revenue drags new working capital along with it.

Let's go back to Fenwick, where NWC is 19.2% of revenue. Suppose revenue grows by 20% next year, from £120.0m to £144.0m. At a constant 19.2%, NWC grows from £23.0m to about £27.6m. That's an outflow of £4.6m, and none of it ever touches the P&L. If Fenwick's EBITDA is, say, £8.4m, which is a 7% margin, then more than half of the year's EBITDA is swallowed up by funding its own growth. Fast-growing businesses that are heavy on working capital can be profitable on paper and starved of cash in reality. "Overtrading", which means growing faster than your working capital funding allows, kills more healthy-looking companies than losses do.

Here's the multiplication to internalise:

Cash absorbed by growth≈Revenue growth (£)×NWC as % of revenue\text{Cash absorbed by growth} \approx \text{Revenue growth (£)} \times \text{NWC as \% of revenue}Cash absorbed by growth≈Revenue growth (£)×NWC as % of revenue

So £24.0m of growth, multiplied by 19.2%, gives roughly £4.6m. That's why lenders and deal models always carry a working capital line linked to revenue growth. And it's why anyone buying a growing distributor needs a revolving credit facility that's sized for it.

§2.3.4Negative working capital: growth that pays you

Now let's flip every sign. Some business models collect cash from customers before they pay their suppliers. Their NWC is negative, so the operating cycle generates cash, rather than consuming it.

Here's a worked example: a grocery retailer with revenue of £200.0m and COGS of £150.0m. Its receivables are £1.0m, because customers pay at the till, so DSO is 1.0 ÷ 200.0 × 365, which gives 1.8 days. Its inventory is £10.0m, so DIO is 10.0 ÷ 150.0 × 365, or 24.3 days. And its payables are £20.0m, so DPO is 20.0 ÷ 150.0 × 365, or 48.7 days.

CCC=1.8+24.3−48.7=−22.6 days\text{CCC} = 1.8 + 24.3 - 48.7 = -22.6 \text{ days}CCC=1.8+24.3−48.7=−22.6 days

So NWC is 1.0 + 10.0 − 20.0, which gives minus £9.0m. The retailer sells its stock about 24 days before it has to pay for it. Every new store releases cash when it opens, so growth funds itself, and then some. The classic negative-working-capital models are food retail; insurance, where premiums come in up front and claims are paid later; and any business that collects subscriptions or deposits in advance. SaaS businesses that bill annually up front carry large deferred revenue balances that work in the same way.

PE finds these models attractive for obvious reasons. Cash arrives early and reliably, and that supports more debt. But notice the sting in the tail: negative working capital reverses viciously when a business declines. If the grocer's revenue shrinks, its payables unwind faster than its stock does. The model that funded the growth now drains cash, exactly when the business can least afford it. The same goes for a subscription business that's losing customers. It still has to deliver the service for the deferred revenue it has already spent.

§2.3.5Seasonality: the year-end is not the year

Working capital breathes. A toy distributor builds up stock from June, peaks in October, and collects its cash in January. A balance sheet at a December year end catches it at close to its best-looking moment, with the stock sold and the cash in. A September balance sheet, by contrast, would show peak inventory and stretched payables. Neither single date is "the" working capital of the business.

That has some practical consequences.

  • Use monthly data, not year-end snapshots. Any serious analysis asks for 24 to 36 months of month-end working capital balances, and looks at the average and the peak, not just the year end. The gap between the average and the year-end figure is informative in itself. If a company's year end is always its low point, it may have chosen that year end for exactly that reason.
  • The peak sets the funding need. Facilities have to cover the worst month, not the average one. A business with average working capital of £15m and a seasonal peak of £26m needs about £11m of headroom, just for the cycle.
  • In deals, seasonality drives the "working capital peg". Acquisitions complete on a cash-free, debt-free basis, with an agreed normal level of working capital. Completing in the low month without an adjustment would hand the seller a windfall. You'll meet the mechanics in Module 8. For now, just know that "what is normalised working capital?" is a standard diligence question, and often a contentious one.
  • Watch out for window dressing. Companies can flatter a single date. They can delay paying suppliers for a couple of weeks, run a blitz on collections, or hold off on purchases. Monthly data makes this visible. A year-end DPO that's 15 days higher than at every other month end is a tell.

§2.3.6What deal teams actually ask

Here are the stock questions on working capital, and you can answer all of them with the tools from this lesson.

  • "What are DSO, DIO and DPO, and how have they trended over three years?" Work them out for each year. The good answer is a stable cash conversion cycle alongside growing revenue.
  • "What's NWC as a percentage of revenue, and how much cash does the growth plan absorb?" That's the calculation above, 19.2% multiplied by the growth, and it goes straight into the deal model.
  • "What does working capital look like month by month: the average, the peak and the trough?" That covers seasonality, funding needs and the peg.
  • "Has the company stretched its payables, or speeded up its collections, recently?" That's because a seller preparing for an exit can 'generate' one-off cash, and even flatter its apparent cash conversion, by squeezing working capital. And it always unwinds on the buyer's watch.

Working capital is the first place where accounting profit and cash reality part company. That's exactly why the next lesson builds the full bridge from EBITDA down to free cash flow, with working capital as its first, and most volatile, step.

Lesson 2.4/Financial Statement Analysis

Cash Conversion and Capex

24 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson builds the bridge from EBITDA to free cash flow, with a full worked table. It separates maintenance capex from growth capex, and it covers cash conversion ratios: what "good" looks like for different types of business, and why PE prizes conversion of 85% or more in asset-light businesses.

  1. 2.4.1EBITDA is where the analysis starts, not ends
  2. 2.4.2The EBITDA-to-FCF bridge: full worked table
  3. 2.4.3Maintenance vs growth capex
  4. 2.4.4Cash conversion ratios
  5. 2.4.5What "good" looks like
  6. 2.4.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.4.1EBITDA is where the analysis starts, not ends

Deals are priced off EBITDA, but debt is repaid with cash. In between the two sits a series of very real claims: working capital, capex, tax, and eventually interest. Cash conversion measures how much of each pound of EBITDA survives that journey and becomes cash you can actually spend, and it varies enormously. Two businesses with an identical £15.0m of EBITDA might throw off £13m and £6m of cash respectively, and they're worth very different amounts.

This lesson builds the standard bridge, line by line, using Marlow Instruments. It's a fictional specialist manufacturer, with £100.0m of revenue and £15.0m of EBITDA.

§2.4.2The EBITDA-to-FCF bridge: full worked table

£m FY25 Notes
EBITDA 15.0 Reported, pre any adjustments
Change in net working capital (1.2) Growth absorbing cash (Lesson 3)
Maintenance capex (2.0) Keeping existing kit running
Operating free cash flow 11.8 "Pre-tax operating FCF"
Growth capex (1.5) New capacity — discretionary
Cash exceptionals (0.3) Restructuring costs actually paid
Cash tax (2.4) Tax paid, not the P&L charge
Free cash flow (pre-financing) 7.6 Cash available to all capital providers
Cash interest (1.5)
FCF after interest 6.1 Cash available for debt paydown

Read the table from top to bottom. Of the £15.0m of EBITDA, £1.2m goes into working capital just to fund growth, £3.5m in total goes on capex, £0.3m pays for last year's restructuring commitments, and £2.4m goes to HMRC. What's left before financing is £7.6m, which is about half the headline EBITDA. After interest, £6.1m remains. That's the number that actually pays down debt in an LBO, and it's why lenders build exactly this bridge before they offer a single pound.

There are three technical notes. First, every line is the cash amount, not the P&L amount. Cash tax and the tax charge on the P&L differ, because of timing differences and instalments, and "exceptional" costs only matter here when they're actually paid. Second, the change in NWC is a flow. It's the year-on-year change in the balance, not the balance itself. And third, notice what's missing: depreciation. It isn't cash. Capex is the cash reality that depreciation approximates, and that's the whole reason the bridge swaps one for the other.

Always rebuild this bridge yourself from the audited cash flow statement, rather than accepting the version in a sale pack. The cash flow statement is the hardest of the three statements to flatter, because the cash either arrived or it didn't, so it acts as the truth serum for the other two. Suppose the pack's bridge shows £9m of free cash flow, but the cash flow statement shows net debt flat year on year. Then something in the bridge is a definition game: a "pre-exceptional" line here, perhaps, or an "underlying working capital" adjustment there. Tracing every line of the bridge back to a line in the statutory cash flow statement takes about twenty minutes, and it regularly pays for itself.

§2.4.3Maintenance vs growth capex

This is the single most argued-about split in the whole bridge. Maintenance capex keeps today's revenue running. It covers replacing worn-out machines and van fleets, routine IT refreshes, and safety work. Growth capex creates tomorrow's revenue, such as a new production line, a new warehouse, or a major new system. The distinction matters because maintenance capex is a compulsory deduction from earning power. A business that "makes" £15.0m but has to spend £2.0m every year just to stand still really makes £13.0m. Growth capex, on the other hand, is discretionary, and it should come with a return attached.

Sellers know this, so information packs habitually label as much capex as they can as "growth". Deal teams run three cross-checks.

  • First, compare capex with depreciation. Over time, maintenance capex should roughly track depreciation, because you replace assets at about the rate they wear out. Marlow's D&A is £3.5m, against a claimed maintenance capex of £2.0m, and that's a gap worth probing. If total capex stays below depreciation year after year, that's the classic sign of an under-invested business. The P&L looks fine while the asset base quietly rots, and the buyer inherits the bill for catching up.
  • Second, look at capex as a share of revenue over five years or more. The long-run average through a cycle is a better estimate of the true ongoing capex than any single year, or any label from management.
  • Third, ask for the capex register. Detail project by project makes the split auditable. A "replacement CNC machine" is maintenance, whatever the pack calls it.

A sudden drop in capex in the year or two before a sale is a standard red flag. It flatters free cash flow at the expense of the condition of the assets, and it reverses on the buyer.

Remember, too, that capex is naturally lumpy. A distributor might spend £0.8m a year for four years, and then £4m in year five, when the warehouse racking, the fleet and the ERP system all come due at once. A single low-capex year proves nothing about the ongoing requirement. That's why every capex ratio in this lesson should be worked out on an average over several years, and why "last year's capex" is never the number that goes into a model.

§2.4.4Cash conversion ratios

Several ratios compress the bridge into a single number. Be precise about which one is being quoted, because they differ a lot.

  • Lender's conversion is EBITDA minus total capex, divided by EBITDA. For Marlow, that's 15.0 minus 3.5, divided by 15.0, which gives 76.7%.
  • Underlying conversion is EBITDA minus maintenance capex, divided by EBITDA. For Marlow, that's 15.0 minus 2.0, divided by 15.0, which gives 86.7%. It's flattering, and it depends on that contestable split of capex.
  • Operating cash conversion is EBITDA minus the change in NWC and minus total capex, all divided by EBITDA. For Marlow, that's 15.0 minus 1.2 minus 3.5, which is 10.3, divided by 15.0, giving 68.7%. It's the toughest test, and the one that's closest to the cash reality from year to year.

Here's the trap to avoid: quoting the flattering ratio, and benchmarking it against the tough one. When a seller says "90% cash conversion", it usually means EBITDA minus maintenance capex, in a year when working capital happened to be flat. So always ask: which definition, and over which period? And then work it out again yourself from the cash flow statement.

§2.4.5What "good" looks like

Here are some rules of thumb for operating cash conversion, meaning EBITDA minus the change in NWC and minus capex, as a percentage of EBITDA, averaged over a few years.

Business type Typical conversion Why
Asset-light services / software 85–100%+ Minimal capex, low or negative NWC
Distribution 60–80% Modest capex, but NWC grows with revenue
Manufacturing 55–75% Real capex plus stock and debtors
Capital-intensive (plants, fleets, infra) 30–60% Heavy, lumpy, non-negotiable capex

For asset-light businesses, 85% or more is the magic number, and it's why PE gravitates towards them. The reason is mechanical, and it's worth spelling out. An LBO's returns come largely from paying down debt out of the company's own cash; Module 7 does the full maths. A business with £15.0m of EBITDA converting at 90% generates roughly £13.5m a year, before tax and interest, to service and repay debt. With the same EBITDA converting at 50%, it generates £7.5m. The first business can safely borrow far more, pays its debt down faster, and is less likely to run into trouble if trading dips, and every one of those things improves equity returns. High conversion also validates the EBITDA itself. Profit that reliably turns into cash is much harder to fake than profit that doesn't, and Lesson 6 picks up that thread.

Let's contrast Marlow with an asset-light peer, Ashworth Advisory. It has the same £15.0m of EBITDA, but its working capital absorbs only 0.5 and its capex is only 0.8. So its operating free cash flow is 15.0 − 0.5 − 0.8, which gives £13.7m. That's conversion of 91.3%, against Marlow's 68.7%. If both trade at 8× EBITDA, the buyer of Ashworth is paying 8.8 times its operating free cash flow, while the buyer of Marlow is paying 11.7 times. It's the same EBITDA multiple, but a very different cash multiple. That's the sense in which "PE loves asset-light" isn't a preference of style. It's arithmetic.

So what looks bad? Conversion that stays below about 50%. Conversion that swings wildly from year to year, which usually means working capital games or lumpy, badly managed capex. And worst of all, conversion that falls while EBITDA grows. That last pattern means each extra pound of profit brings less cash with it, and it's the signature of aggressive revenue recognition or stuffed inventory. Growing EBITDA with falling conversion is one of the most rewarding red flags to look for in all of financial analysis.

§2.4.6What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show us the bridge from EBITDA to free cash flow for the last three years." Not one year, but three, because working capital and capex are lumpy, and a single year can either flatter or slander the business.
  • "Split capex into maintenance and growth, and reconcile it to depreciation." Do it with the register, not just management's labels. Expect the maintenance number to be argued over in every deal you ever see.
  • "Why did conversion dip in FY24?" There's usually a story, such as a build-up of stock, a big debtor, or a capex project. Whether it's a one-off or structural changes the model.
  • "What's the normalised capex through the cycle?" The number that goes into the model is an estimate through the cycle, not last year's actual figure, which may well have been starved.

Here's a habit to build. Whenever someone shows you an EBITDA number, silently add, "and how much of that is cash?" Lessons 3 and 4 have given you the two big leakages: working capital and capex. The next lesson takes the output of this bridge, and asks the lender's question: how much debt can this cash flow support?

Lesson 2.5/Financial Statement Analysis

Leverage and Coverage Ratios

22 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson covers net debt to EBITDA, interest cover and fixed charge cover, each with a worked example. It includes a table of normal and stretched leverage in different contexts, and it builds the intuition for how much debt a given cash flow profile can support.

  1. 2.5.1Why leverage ratios exist
  2. 2.5.2Net debt / EBITDA: the headline leverage ratio
  3. 2.5.3What's normal vs stretched: context is everything
  4. 2.5.4Interest cover: can the P&L afford the debt?
  5. 2.5.5Fixed charge cover: the fuller test
  6. 2.5.6Debt capacity: the intuition
  7. 2.5.7What deal teams actually ask

§2.5.1Why leverage ratios exist

Debt is central to private equity; it's the "leveraged" in leveraged buyout. So you need a compact way to answer two questions about any company. First, how much debt is it carrying, relative to its size? And second, can it comfortably afford the payments? The first is answered by a leverage ratio, and the second by a coverage ratio. Between them, they tell you whether a balance sheet is conservative, efficient, or an accident waiting for a downturn.

We'll use one worked company throughout: Whitmore Group, with EBITDA of £15.0m, gross debt of £65.0m, and cash of £5.0m.

§2.5.2Net debt / EBITDA: the headline leverage ratio

Leverage=Net debtEBITDA,Net debt=Gross debt−Cash\text{Leverage} = \frac{\text{Net debt}}{\text{EBITDA}}, \qquad \text{Net debt} = \text{Gross debt} - \text{Cash}Leverage=EBITDANet debt​,Net debt=Gross debt−Cash

For Whitmore, net debt is 65.0 minus 5.0, which gives £60.0m, so leverage is 60.0 divided by 15.0, which gives 4.0×. You'd read that as "four turns of EBITDA". If every pound of EBITDA went towards repayment, it would take four years to clear the debt. In practice it can't, because tax, capex and working capital take their cut first, as Lesson 4 showed.

There are two traps in the definitions that deal teams check before quoting the ratio.

  • What counts as debt? Bank loans and bonds, obviously. But lease liabilities, unpaid earn-outs from past acquisitions, pension deficits, and supplier balances stretched beyond their terms are all claims that behave like debt. Buyers and lenders usually add them in, and sellers usually don't. The gap can be a full turn of EBITDA. These "debt-like items" come back with a vengeance in the equity bridge, in Module 4.
  • Which EBITDA? Is it reported, adjusted, run-rate, or "pro-forma with synergies"? Leverage quoted on an optimistic EBITDA understates the risk by construction, and that's a big part of why the quality-of-earnings toolkit in Lesson 6 matters. Leverage of 4.0× on EBITDA you can trust, and 4.0× on flattered EBITDA, are entirely different risks wearing the same number.

§2.5.3What's normal vs stretched: context is everything

There's no universally "safe" level of leverage. It depends on how stable and how cash-generative the EBITDA is. Here are the typical ranges.

Context Normal Stretched
Investment-grade listed corporate 1.0–2.5× above 3.0×
Cyclical / project-based business 1.5–2.5× above 3.5×
Mid-market LBO 3.5–4.5× above 5.0×
Large-cap LBO, stable sector 4.5–6.0× above 6.5×
Software / contracted recurring revenue 6.0–7.0× above 7.5×

The pattern behind the table is that the capacity for leverage tracks the stability of EBITDA and its conversion into cash. A software business with 95% recurring revenue and 90% cash conversion can carry 6.5×, because its EBITDA barely moves and most of it turns into cash. A housebuilder at the same leverage would be reckless. Its EBITDA can halve in a downturn, and at that point 6.5× becomes 13× overnight. Notice, too, that the "same" company can sit in different rows at different times. Taking on leverage at the peak of the cycle is the classic way that LBOs die.

Whitmore, at 4.0×, is normal for a mid-market buyout of a decent business, aggressive for a cyclical one, and conservative for contracted software. Once again, it's the placement that matters, not the raw number.

§2.5.4Interest cover: can the P&L afford the debt?

Interest cover=EBITDACash interest\text{Interest cover} = \frac{\text{EBITDA}}{\text{Cash interest}}Interest cover=Cash interestEBITDA​

Whitmore pays roughly 8% on its £65.0m of gross debt, so its cash interest is about £5.2m. Its cover is 15.0 divided by 5.2, which gives 2.9×. Here are some rules of thumb. Above 3× is comfortable. Between 2 and 3× is tight; that's normal in a fresh LBO, which starts tight by design and improves as the debt is paid down. Below 2× is a flashing warning light. And below 1.5× means the company is mostly working for its lenders. For capital-intensive businesses, some analysts put EBIT in the numerator instead of EBITDA. That's harsher, and arguably more honest, since depreciation foreshadows capex that will have to be spent.

There's a useful identity linking the two ratios. Interest as a share of EBITDA is roughly leverage multiplied by the interest rate. At 4.0× and 8%, interest eats about 4.0 × 8%, or 32%, of EBITDA before anything else is paid. At 6× with money costing 10%, that's 60%. That's why the appetite for leverage falls when rates rise, regardless of anyone's tolerance for risk.

§2.5.5Fixed charge cover: the fuller test

Interest isn't the only payment a business can't avoid. Rent behaves exactly like interest, because if you miss it you lose the premises, and scheduled repayments of debt are contractual too. Fixed charge cover, or FCC, widens the lens to include them.

FCC=EBITDA+RentCash interest+Rent\text{FCC} = \frac{\text{EBITDA} + \text{Rent}}{\text{Cash interest} + \text{Rent}}FCC=Cash interest+RentEBITDA+Rent​

Rent is added back on top because EBITDA is already stated after deducting it, and some versions also add the scheduled debt repayments to the denominator. Suppose Whitmore also pays £2.0m of rent. Then FCC is 15.0 plus 2.0, divided by 5.2 plus 2.0. That's 17.0 ÷ 7.2, which gives 2.4×, and it's meaningfully tighter than the 2.9× that interest cover suggested. For rent-heavy businesses, such as retail, leisure, gyms and restaurants, FCC is the ratio. A retailer can look only modestly levered on net debt to EBITDA, while an enormous rent roll, which doesn't feel like debt, makes its true fixed charges crushing. Lenders to businesses like these set their covenants on FCC, precisely because interest cover flatters them. Roughly 1.5× or more is healthy, and below 1.2× is danger territory.

§2.5.6Debt capacity: the intuition

Turn the ratios around, and you get the question every deal team actually asks: how much debt will this business support? There are two ways to triangulate the answer.

The top-down way follows market convention. Debt capacity is roughly the sustainable EBITDA multiplied by the leverage that lenders will offer for this sector and quality of business. If lenders go to 4.0 to 4.5× for mid-market businesses like Whitmore, its capacity is roughly 4.25 × 15.0, or somewhere between £60m and £68m. This is how deals are actually sized from day to day.

The bottom-up way follows the cash flow. Here, debt capacity is whatever the free cash flow can service and repay, with some headroom. Remember the Whitmore-like cash flows from Lesson 4. After working capital, capex and tax, there's roughly £7.6m of free cash flow before interest. At 8% interest, £60.0m of debt costs £4.8m a year. That leaves under £3m a year for repayment, so paying down the debt in any meaningful way takes years, and depends on EBITDA growing. Push leverage up to £75m, which is 5.0×, and the interest of £6.0m eats nearly 80% of the free cash flow, leaving nothing for bad luck.

The structure of the debt matters too. Amortising debt has a contractual repayment schedule, so the free cash flow has to cover both the interest and the instalments every year. Bullet debt is only repaid at maturity. That eases the demands on cash each year, but it bets the refinancing on market conditions years into the future. Most LBO structures mix the two. And the more the stack leans towards bullet debt, the more the deal depends on exit or refinancing markets being open when the music stops.

Then stress-test it, because the lenders certainly will. If EBITDA falls by 20%, Whitmore drops to £12.0m. Leverage becomes 60.0 divided by 12.0, which is 5.0×, and interest cover becomes 12.0 divided by 5.2, which is 2.3×. The very same balance sheet now reads as "stretched" in the table above. A structure is only sound if it survives the downside case. And the analysis of fixed and variable costs from Lesson 2 tells you how bad that downside could be. High operating leverage combined with high financial leverage is the combination that turns a 10% dip in revenue into a covenant breach.

So what looks good? Leverage in the normal band, measured on conservative EBITDA; cover above 3×; headroom in the downside case; and cash conversion strong enough to pay down a turn of leverage every 18 to 24 months. And what looks bad? Leverage that can only be justified on adjusted EBITDA; cover below 2×; FCC ignored in a rent-heavy model; or debt capacity sized off earnings at the peak of the cycle.

These same ratios live on after the deal closes, in the form of covenants. Covenants are contractual promises in the loan agreement that leverage will stay below agreed levels, and cover will stay above them, and they're usually tested every quarter. A deal levered at 4.0× might carry a leverage covenant set at 5.0×. That gives Whitmore about 20% of EBITDA headroom before a breach, because EBITDA below 60.0 divided by 5.0, which is £12.0m, would trip the test. Breaching a covenant doesn't usually mean instant insolvency. What it does mean is that the lenders gain the right to renegotiate, charge fees, raise their pricing, or in bad cases, take the keys. That's why deal teams quote "covenant headroom" as a percentage of EBITDA, and treat anything below about 15% as uncomfortable. A structure with thin headroom hands control of the company's bad quarter to its lenders. So when you read that a portfolio company has "reset its covenants", the ratios in this lesson are exactly what was reset.

§2.5.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's the leverage through the cycle?" That means net debt against EBITDA at the bottom of the cycle, not just today's. 4.0× on £15.0m becomes 5.0× if EBITDA falls back to £12.0m.
  • "What's in net debt?" This is the hunt for debt-like items: leases, earn-outs, pension deficits, factored receivables, which are debt dressed up as working capital, and payables stretched beyond their terms. The case study in this module plants exactly that last one.
  • "What does the downside case do to the covenants?" Model EBITDA falling by 15 to 20%, and check the leverage and cover against the covenant levels. The gap is the "headroom", and investment committees want it quantified.
  • "How fast does it pay down its debt?" Free cash flow after interest, divided by net debt, gives a crude annual rate of deleveraging. For Whitmore, roughly £3m on £60.0m is about 5% a year. That means the deal's returns have to lean on EBITDA growth instead, which is a genuinely different investment thesis.

You now have the full chain of statement analysis: what the P&L says, from Lessons 1 and 2; how much cash it really produces, from Lessons 3 and 4; and what obligations sit against it, from this lesson. The last step is the sceptic's question that sits underneath all of it: can you trust the EBITDA in the first place? That's Lesson 6.

Lesson 2.6/Financial Statement Analysis

First Look at Quality of Earnings

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson looks at what makes reported EBITDA trustworthy, or not. It covers run-rate versus reported earnings, one-off adjustments, customer concentration, related-party items, and the hierarchy of revenue quality: recurring, re-occurring and one-time.

  1. 2.6.1The question underneath every deal
  2. 2.6.2Run-rate vs reported: which year are you actually buying?
  3. 2.6.3One-offs: the adjusted EBITDA bridge
  4. 2.6.4Customer concentration: earnings held hostage
  5. 2.6.5Related-party items: transactions that aren't at arm's length
  6. 2.6.6Revenue quality: recurring, re-occurring, one-time
  7. 2.6.7The trustworthiness checklist

§2.6.1The question underneath every deal

Everything in this module so far, whether margins, conversion or leverage, has taken the reported numbers as its inputs. This lesson asks the question that comes before all of that: should you believe them? In deal-speak, this is called quality of earnings, or QoE. It's about how well the reported EBITDA represents the true, sustainable earning power of the business, backed by cash.

The stakes are mechanical. Deals are priced at a multiple of EBITDA, so at 8×, every £1m of overstated EBITDA means £8m of overpayment. And because the debt was sized off the same number, a deal that's been overpaid is over-levered too. Full QoE work is a specialist workstream that you'll meet in Module 9. This lesson gives you the first-pass toolkit, and it catches a surprising share of the problems.

Here's the mindset. Reported EBITDA is a claim. It's made by a seller who has every incentive to maximise it, in the one year when it matters most. Your job is to work out what the number would be if a sceptical owner were calculating it for themselves.

§2.6.2Run-rate vs reported: which year are you actually buying?

Reported EBITDA describes the last twelve months. But a buyer owns the next twelve months, so the number that matters is run-rate EBITDA. That's what the business earns going forward, taking account of everything that's already known to have changed.

Run-rate adjustments cut both ways.

  • Some adjust upwards, which is called "annualisation". A price rise brought in during month 7 only benefited half the year, so a full year of it adds the missing half. A newly signed contract that starts next quarter isn't in the reported numbers at all. And cost savings that have already been actioned, such as a closed office or completed redundancies, get credit for a full year.
  • Others adjust downwards. A customer that gave notice part-way through the year still contributed several months of profit to the reported figure, but it will contribute nothing next year. A rent review, a subsidy that's lapsed, or a rise in input costs that's locked in for next year all reduce the run-rate as well.

Sellers, unsurprisingly, present every upward annualisation and forget the downward ones. The discipline is simple. For every adjustment, ask yourself: would this survive if the same rule were applied in both directions? If mid-year price rises get annualised, then so do mid-year customer losses.

§2.6.3One-offs: the adjusted EBITDA bridge

Between reported and run-rate EBITDA lies the land of "adjustments". These are items that management argues are one-offs, non-recurring, or not part of operations. Let's take a worked example. Hollins Media reports EBITDA of £10.0m, and it presents this bridge.

£m Legitimate?
Reported EBITDA 10.0
Add back: legal settlement paid +0.6 Probably — if genuinely isolated
Add back: owner's excess salary +0.4 Yes — if a market-rate MD costs £0.4m less
Annualise: mid-year price rise +0.5 Yes — if churn didn't follow it
Deduct: customer lost in September (0.8) Required — sellers rarely volunteer it
Deduct: below-market related-party rent (0.3) Required — see next section
Adjusted run-rate EBITDA 10.4

Notice the shape. The seller's own version of this bridge would probably have shown £11.5m: the reported figure plus all of the add-backs, minus none of the deductions. The honest number is £10.4m, and at 8×, that gap is worth £8.8m of price.

Here are the tests for whether an add-back deserves to survive.

  • Frequency. "One-off" restructuring costs that appear three years running are simply costs. Add up the exceptional items over five years. If the total is large and steady, the business just has a lower margin than it claims.
  • Direction. Does the pack contain only favourable one-offs? Genuine one-offs are random, so a list where every item increases EBITDA has been curated. The mirror image is a one-off gain, such as a property sale, an insurance recovery or a provision release, sitting quietly inside EBITDA. That has to come out.
  • Cash. Was it actually paid or received, and does the cash flow statement agree?
  • Evidence. Every material add-back should trace back to invoices or contracts, not to a spreadsheet cell labelled "normalisation".

§2.6.4Customer concentration: earnings held hostage

EBITDA of £10m means something different when one customer generates £4m of it. Customer concentration is a question of quality, not just a footnote about risk. That's because concentrated earnings are, first, fragile, since they're one procurement decision away from disappearing. And second, they come with little bargaining power, because the big customer eventually learns to price accordingly.

Here are the first-pass checks, and you can do all of them from a data pack.

  • Look at the share of revenue from the top 1, 5 and 10 customers, over three years. As a rule of thumb, a top customer above about 15% of revenue needs explaining. Above 25 to 30%, it dominates the deal conversation, and usually the price as well. Watch out for the sneaky version, too: five "different" customers that all turn out to be subsidiaries of one group.
  • Look at profit concentration, which is usually worse than revenue concentration. Big customers negotiate hard, but they also absorb fixed costs. If the top customer is 30% of revenue at thin margins, losing it doesn't remove 30% of the overheads. The contribution maths from Lesson 2 says EBITDA can fall by far more than that customer's "share" of it.
  • Look at contract cover. Is the relationship contracted? For how long? And what are the notice terms, and the terms for terminating for convenience? Revenue with a 90-day notice clause is barely more secure than revenue with no contract at all.
  • And look at the trajectory. A top customer that's growing its share flatters growth while quietly concentrating the risk. The quality of growth and the quality of revenue can move in opposite directions.

§2.6.5Related-party items: transactions that aren't at arm's length

Private companies get tangled up with their owners. The founder owns the warehouse and charges the company rent; a sibling's firm supplies the logistics; family members are on the payroll. None of this is necessarily improper. But it does mean the reported costs aren't market costs, and the buyer's future costs will be.

The logic of the adjustment is always the same: restate the P&L as if every related-party transaction had happened at market rates. In the Hollins bridge above, the company pays the owner's property company £0.2m in rent for premises that would cost £0.5m on the open market. So run-rate EBITDA loses £0.3m, because the buyer will be paying market rent from day one. Owner salaries that are below market work in the same way; the £0.4m add-back only stands if a market-rate CEO genuinely costs less than the departing owner. You should also look for sales to related parties: are they real, at real prices, and actually paid? Look for assets the business uses but doesn't own. And look for services a parent provides for free, such as group IT, insurance or treasury, which a standalone buyer will have to replace. That last one is a big theme in corporate carve-outs.

There's a hierarchy of red flags here. Related-party items that are disclosed and quantified are a question of pricing. Undisclosed ones, found by accident, are a question of integrity, and questions of integrity kill deals.

§2.6.6Revenue quality: recurring, re-occurring, one-time

Not all revenue is equal, and the standard way of classifying it has three tiers.

  • Recurring revenue is contractually committed, and continues automatically. Examples are subscriptions, maintenance contracts and rent. The customer has to act in order to stop it. It's the highest quality, and it supports the highest multiples and the most debt.
  • Re-occurring revenue repeats reliably in practice, but without any contractual commitment. Think of the plumbers' merchant a builder uses every week, annual audit work, or refill purchases. The customer has to act in order to continue, but habitually does. It's good quality, but the evidence for it is behavioural, coming from retention and repeat-purchase data, rather than contractual.
  • One-time revenue comes from projects, installations and one-off sales. Every year starts from zero. It's the lowest quality, because although the revenue may come again, the customer relationship has to be won again each time.

Here's a worked example. Two consultancies each report £20.0m of revenue and £4.0m of EBITDA. Alpha's revenue is 70% multi-year retainers, 20% repeat clients and 10% one-off projects. Beta's is 10%, 30% and 60%. So Alpha starts next year with about £14m contractually in the bag, while Beta starts with £2m. The P&Ls are the same, but the risk is radically different. Alpha might trade at 10× and Beta at 6×, and the gap between them is pure revenue quality. Deal packs know this, so treat their labels sceptically. Any claim of "recurring revenue" should be tested against the contracts and against churn. Genuinely recurring revenue comes with a measurable retention rate, and if management can't produce one, the revenue is re-occurring at best.

§2.6.7The trustworthiness checklist

So, pulling the module together, reported EBITDA deserves your trust when the following things are true.

  1. It converts into cash at a rate that makes sense for the sector, as covered in Lesson 4. Profit that never becomes cash is the master red flag. Most manipulations, such as recognising revenue early, under-accruing, or capitalising costs, leave profit up but cash lagging behind.
  2. The margin can be explained. It sits within the sector's norms, or above them for a reason you can name, and there's a margin bridge that adds up, as covered in Lessons 1 and 2.
  3. The adjustments are few, evidenced, and run in both directions. A one-page bridge with items going both ways reads as honest. Three pages of favourable add-backs reads like a negotiating position.
  4. The accounting policies are stable. Changes to capitalisation, revenue recognition, depreciation or provisioning in the run-up to a sale are guilty until proven innocent, and this module's case study turns on exactly that.
  5. Working capital behaves itself. The days are stable, accruals grow with the business, and there's no stretching of payables at the year end to manufacture fake cash flow, as covered in Lesson 3.
  6. The earnings aren't held hostage by one customer, one contract, one subsidy, or one related party.

Here's the reflex to build. Whenever you see "Adjusted EBITDA", reach for three numbers: the reported EBITDA, the cash generated, and your own estimate of the run-rate. Then make the pack reconcile them. In the case study that follows, you'll do precisely that, for a distributor whose margins improved suspiciously well in the year before it was sold.
