Lesson 3.1/Business Models & Unit Economics

How Businesses Make Money — Revenue Models

22 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson covers the six revenue models you'll meet in deal work: transactional, subscription, usage, licensing, marketplace and distribution. For each one, it shows what the P&L looks like, and it explains why the revenue model, rather than the revenue number, drives the valuation multiple.

  1. 3.1.1Why the revenue model matters more than the revenue number
  2. 3.1.2Transactional revenue: sell it once, sell it again
  3. 3.1.3Recurring / subscription revenue: sell it once, get paid forever
  4. 3.1.4Usage-based revenue: the meter is running
  5. 3.1.5Licensing revenue: selling permission
  6. 3.1.6Marketplace / take-rate revenue: clipping the ticket
  7. 3.1.7Distribution / resale revenue: buy at 100, sell at 118
  8. 3.1.8Why the revenue model drives the valuation multiple

§3.1.1Why the revenue model matters more than the revenue number

Picture two companies, each reporting £20m of revenue and £5m of EBITDA. One of them might sell for £30m, and the other for £90m. The difference is almost never down to accounting. It comes down to the revenue model: how the money arrives, how predictable it is, and how much of it comes back next year without anyone having to pick up the phone.

When a deal team opens a CIM, one of the first questions it asks is, "how does this business actually make money?" That doesn't mean the sector, or the product; it means the mechanics. Does a customer pay once, or forever? Does revenue arrive in £5 increments a million times over, or in £2m increments ten times? Does the company own the customer relationship, or does it just clip a fee as the money passes through?

This lesson walks through the six models you'll meet again and again. For each one, we'll look at how it works, a realistic example, what the P&L looks like, and how buyers think about it. Learn to classify a business within the first five pages of a CIM, because everything else in this module builds on that.

§3.1.2Transactional revenue: sell it once, sell it again

This is the oldest model of all. A customer pays for a distinct product or service, and then the relationship ends, until they choose to come back. Think of a kitchen fitter, a corporate law firm billing matter by matter, an M&A boutique, or a retailer selling sofas.

Here's an example. Hartwell Kitchens sells fitted kitchens, with an average order value of £12,000. Last year it took 1,500 orders, giving £18m of revenue. Materials and installation labour cost £10.8m, which is 60%, so gross profit is £7.2m, or 40%. Marketing, showrooms and overheads eat up £5.4m, which leaves £1.8m of EBITDA, a 10% margin.

The shape of the P&L is that revenue resets to zero on 1 January. Every year, Hartwell has to find 1,500 new buyers. And since a kitchen is something people buy once a decade, there's very little repeat business. Marketing spend is high, and it's permanent. It's the engine of the business, not an investment that compounds.

So what do deal teams ask? What share of revenue comes from repeat customers or referrals? Is there an order book that gives even three to six months of visibility? And how did revenue hold up in the last downturn? Transactional businesses can be excellent. They can have a high ROCE, generate plenty of cash, and need little capex. But buyers price in the uncertainty. Their multiples typically sit well below those of recurring-revenue peers, often 4 to 7x EBITDA, where a comparable recurring business might get 10 to 15x.

§3.1.3Recurring / subscription revenue: sell it once, get paid forever

Here, the customer signs up and pays a fixed amount each period, monthly or annually, until they cancel. Software-as-a-service is the textbook case, but the model is everywhere: alarm monitoring, testing and certification contracts, gym memberships, and managed IT services.

Here's an example. Brindle HR sells payroll software at £500 per client per month. With 3,000 clients, that's £1.5m of monthly recurring revenue, or MRR, which is £18m of annual recurring revenue, or ARR. Hosting and support cost £3.6m, giving an 80% gross margin. Sales and marketing run at £5.4m, R&D at £3.6m, and general and administrative costs at £1.8m. That leaves EBITDA of £3.6m, a 20% margin.

The shape of the P&L is that most of next year's revenue has already been sold. If Brindle keeps 92% of its clients, it starts the year with £16.6m of the £18m already in the bank, before the sales team has made a single call. Costs split into serving existing customers, which is cheap, and winning new ones, which is discretionary. That split is why subscription businesses can turn their profitability up or down at will. Cut the spending on new customers, and EBITDA jumps, at the cost of growth.

So what looks good? Retention above 90%, contracts that renew automatically, and revenue billed annually in advance. That last one also means customers fund the working capital, because deferred revenue is a liability that never has to be repaid in cash. And what looks bad? "Recurring" revenue that's really re-occurring, meaning it repeats, but it isn't contracted. Deal teams always test the definition, and Lesson 3 goes deep on this.

§3.1.4Usage-based revenue: the meter is running

Here, the customer pays for each unit they consume: per API call, per kilowatt-hour, per parcel shipped, or per test processed. Cloud infrastructure, payment processors charging per transaction, and lab-testing businesses all run meters.

Here's an example. Ferrocourier charges e-commerce sellers £2.50 per parcel. A seller shipping 4,000 parcels a month generates £10,000, while one shipping 400 generates £1,000. So revenue is the sum of thousands of meters, each one tied to the customer's level of activity.

The shape of the P&L is that revenue is repeatable, but variable. It grows automatically when customers grow, which is a free tailwind that no salesperson had to earn. And it shrinks automatically in a downturn. The gross margin depends on how much marginal cost each unit carries. That's close to 100% for an API call, but perhaps 25% for a parcel with a driver behind it.

So what do deal teams ask? Is usage linked to the customers' revenue, such as payment volumes, which is resilient? Or is it linked to their discretionary spend, such as ad impressions, which is fragile? And what minimum-commitment floors are there? A usage business with contracted minimums covering 70% of revenue is priced closer to a subscription business, while one with no floors is priced closer to a transactional one. The honest classification is usually "hybrid", and the job of diligence is to size each layer.

§3.1.5Licensing revenue: selling permission

Here, the company owns some intellectual property, such as software, a brand, a patented process or content, and it sells the right to use it. There are two flavours that matter.

  • A perpetual licence is a one-off fee for using the product indefinitely, usually with a separate annual maintenance contract costing 15 to 22% of the licence price. This is old-school enterprise software.
  • A royalty, or term licence, is an ongoing fee, often a percentage of the licensee's sales. Think of a character brand licensed to a toymaker at a 10% royalty.

Here's an example. Calderbrook Systems sells factory-scheduling software, on £400k perpetual licences plus 20% annual maintenance, which is £80k per customer per year. In a good year, it closes 25 licence deals, worth £10m, on top of a £6m maintenance base from past sales. That gives £16m of revenue. And because the marginal cost of a licence is close to zero, its EBITDA margin reaches 35%.

The shape of the P&L is that the gross margin is spectacular, but the licence line is lumpy. If three deals slip from December into January, the year's revenue drops by £1.2m without any warning. The maintenance base is the genuinely valuable part, because it behaves like subscription revenue. Buyers routinely split a licensing P&L in two, pricing the maintenance like recurring revenue, and the new-licence revenue like transactional revenue. The case study for Module 3 turns on exactly this split.

§3.1.6Marketplace / take-rate revenue: clipping the ticket

Here, the company runs a platform that matches buyers with sellers, and it keeps a percentage of each transaction, known as the take rate. Think of property portals, freelance platforms, food-delivery apps and ticket exchanges.

The key distinction here is between GMV and revenue. Gross merchandise value, or GMV, is everything transacted on the platform, while revenue is only the slice that the platform keeps. A marketplace boasting "£500m of transactions" at a 6% take rate is a business with £30m of revenue. CIMs love to lead with GMV, and deal teams immediately convert it into revenue.

Here's an example. TradeYard connects builders with sellers of reclaimed materials. Its £200m of GMV, at a 7.5% take rate, gives £15m of revenue. Payment processing and support cost £3m, giving an 80% gross margin. Marketing to keep both sides of the market active costs £7m, and EBITDA is £2m.

The shape of the P&L is that the marginal cost of each transaction is tiny, so contribution margins are superb at scale. But scale is everything. A marketplace that's below scale burns cash trying to win both sides at once. And take rates are under constant pressure. If the platform adds little value, buyers and sellers meet once, and then do business off the platform, which is called "disintermediation". So deal teams ask: what stops that leakage? Is the take rate rising or falling? And does the platform hold the flow of money? Integrating payments is the strongest lock-in of all.

§3.1.7Distribution / resale revenue: buy at 100, sell at 118

Here, the company buys products from manufacturers and resells them, adding logistics, availability, credit, range and technical support along the way. Examples include pharmaceutical wholesalers, electrical distributors, food-service suppliers, and value-added resellers of IT.

Here's an example. Kembrey Electrical distributes cabling and switchgear to contractors. It has £120m of revenue at an 18% gross margin, giving £21.6m of gross profit. Warehouses, vans and salespeople cost £16.8m, so EBITDA is £4.8m. That's a 4% EBITDA margin on revenue, but a much healthier margin of 22% on gross profit.

The shape of the P&L is huge revenue, thin margins, and real working capital. Inventory and receivables soak up cash as the business grows. The revenue line is almost meaningless for comparisons; a distributor "growing revenue by 10%" might simply be passing through inflation in the price of copper. So deal teams analyse distributors on gross profit, treating that as the real top line. And they watch out for two threats: suppliers going direct, and customers consolidating their purchasing.

It isn't a glamorous model. But predictable demand, much of it for repair and maintenance rather than projects, along with fragmented customers and the economics of density, make good distributors quietly excellent LBO candidates. That's why PE keeps buying them.

§3.1.8Why the revenue model drives the valuation multiple

A multiple is shorthand for a DCF. It has growth, risk and reinvestment needs built into it. The revenue model moves all three, and that's why classifying a business is an act of valuation, not just an exercise in taxonomy.

Model Predictability Marginal economics Typical pricing attitude
Subscription Very high — revenue is contracted forward High gross margin Premium; often priced on revenue, not EBITDA
Usage (with floors) High, but cyclical with customers Varies Premium if tied to non-discretionary volumes
Marketplace at scale High Excellent Premium — if take rate and liquidity defensible
Licensing (maintenance base) High on maintenance, low on new licences Excellent Sum-of-parts: base premium, licence line discounted
Distribution Moderate — repeat but uncontracted Thin, working-capital-heavy Modest EBITDA multiple, judged on gross profit
Transactional Low — resets each year Varies Discounted; buyers cap what they'll pay for hope

Here's the same arithmetic, seen from the buyer's chair. With £5m of EBITDA, 90% of it pre-sold through contracts, next year's downside is narrow. A lender will happily lend 4 to 5x against it, and the buyer at exit in five years' time will pay up for that same predictability. Now take £5m of EBITDA that has to be won again from scratch every January. One bad year can halve it, lenders cap leverage at 2 to 3x, and the exit is harder. That means less debt, more risk and a worse exit. Every driver of the LBO return is weaker, so the entry multiple has to be lower to compensate.

Here are the practical takeaways for deal work.

  • Classify before you value. "A software company with £20m of revenue" means nothing until you know how that revenue splits between recurring, licence and services.
  • Reported revenue isn't all the same. Split every target's revenue into layers, by model and by quality, and then value the layers rather than the total.
  • Beware of relabelling. Sellers know that recurring revenue is priced higher, so CIMs stretch the definition. "Recurring and repeat revenue: 78%" is a phrase designed to blur contracted subscriptions together with habitual re-ordering. Diligence separates them, and when it does, the price moves.

Lesson 3.2/Business Models & Unit Economics

Unit Economics — Contribution Margin, CAC and LTV

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson shows how to judge a business one unit at a time, using contribution margin, customer acquisition cost, lifetime value and payback periods. It includes a full worked SaaS example, introduces cohort thinking, and covers the situations where unit economics can actively mislead you.

  1. 3.2.1Why deal teams think in units
  2. 3.2.2Contribution margin: the first cut
  3. 3.2.3CAC: what a customer costs to acquire
  4. 3.2.4LTV: what a customer is worth
  5. 3.2.5Full worked example: Brindle HR
  6. 3.2.6Payback period: the cash-flow lens
  7. 3.2.7Cohort thinking: the honest view
  8. 3.2.8When unit economics mislead

§3.2.1Why deal teams think in units

A P&L tells you what happened to the company as a whole last year. Unit economics answer a sharper question: does the business make money on each additional customer, and how quickly? If the answer is yes, then growth creates value, and today's losses may be an investment. If the answer is no, then growth destroys value, and the losses are just losses. "We lose money on every unit, but we make it up on volume" is the oldest joke in finance, precisely because people keep doing it.

What counts as a "unit" depends on the model. It could be a customer, in SaaS; an order, in e-commerce; a site, for gyms or dental practices; a vehicle, in logistics; or a project, in consulting. Pick the unit at which decisions are actually made. For most of this lesson, the unit is a customer, because that's where PE spends its time.

§3.2.2Contribution margin: the first cut

Contribution margin is the revenue per unit, minus the variable costs per unit. It's what each unit contributes towards the fixed costs and profit. The discipline lies in deciding what's truly variable. That means costs that scale one for one with the unit, such as materials, payment fees, delivery and per-seat hosting, and not allocated overheads.

Here's a worked example, for a single e-commerce order.

Per order £
Average order value 80.00
Product cost (36.00)
Packaging and delivery (8.00)
Payment fees and returns provision (4.00)
Contribution before marketing 32.00 (40%)
Marketing cost per order (18.00)
Contribution after marketing 14.00 (17.5%)

There are two ways to read the same business. At £32 of contribution before marketing, every order helps to cover the £2m of fixed costs. But if it takes £18 of paid advertising to cause each order, the real economics are £14 an order. And if a growing share of orders needs paid traffic, the business is weaker than its gross margin suggests. Deal teams always work out both lines, and ask which orders come "free", from repeat customers or organic search, and which ones have been bought.

Contribution margin also sets up the story on operating leverage. Businesses with high contribution, such as software at 80% or more, turn extra revenue into profit quickly once their fixed costs are covered. Businesses with low contribution, such as distribution at 18%, need volume and cost discipline forever.

§3.2.3CAC: what a customer costs to acquire

Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is total sales and marketing spend, divided by the number of new customers acquired in the period. Use the fully loaded sales and marketing cost, including salaries, commissions, ad spend, events and sales tools, not just the advertising budget. Sellers quote CAC on ad spend alone. Diligence rebuilds it fully loaded, and the number often doubles.

There are two subtleties that matter in practice.

  • Count new customers only. Marketing that serves existing customers, such as retention campaigns and account management, belongs in the cost of retention, not in CAC. Most companies can't split it cleanly, so make a reasonable allocation, and say what it is.
  • Allow for the time lag. In B2B businesses with long sales cycles, this quarter's spending produces next quarter's customers. For a business with a six-month cycle, divide this period's new customers into the previous period's sales and marketing spend. Otherwise, CAC looks artificially good during a slowdown, because spending falls first, and signings fall later.

§3.2.4LTV: what a customer is worth

Lifetime value, or LTV, is the contribution a customer generates over their whole life. For a subscription business with steady churn, the workhorse formula is:

LTV=ARPU×gross marginchurn rate\text{LTV} = \frac{\text{ARPU} \times \text{gross margin}}{\text{churn rate}}LTV=churn rateARPU×gross margin​

Here, ARPU and churn are measured over the same period, so both are monthly, or both are annual. The logic is that the average customer's lifetime is one divided by the churn rate. So at 2% monthly churn, the expected lifetime is 50 months.

Notice the gross margin term. Calculating LTV on revenue flatters every business, because only gross profit can repay the cost of acquisition. And strictly speaking, future contribution should be discounted. With a 50-month lifetime, an undiscounted LTV overstates the value by a meaningful amount. So simple LTV is a screening tool, not a valuation.

§3.2.5Full worked example: Brindle HR

Let's take the payroll-software business from Lesson 1, and run its unit economics from end to end.

Input (per customer, monthly) Value
Subscription price (ARPU) £500
Gross margin 80%
Monthly gross churn 1.5%
Fully loaded S&M last year £5.4m
New customers acquired 450

Step 1 is CAC. £5,400,000 divided by 450 gives £12,000 per customer.

Step 2 is monthly contribution. £500 multiplied by 80% gives £400 a month.

Step 3 is the expected lifetime. One divided by 1.5% gives 66.7 months, which is about 5.6 years.

Step 4 is LTV. £400 multiplied by 66.7 gives £26,700. You'd get the same answer from £500 × 0.80 ÷ 0.015.

Step 5 is the ratio of LTV to CAC. £26,700 divided by £12,000 gives 2.2x.

Step 6 is the CAC payback. £12,000 divided by £400 gives 30 months to recover the cost of acquisition from gross profit.

Now comes the judgement, which is the whole point of the exercise.

  • An LTV to CAC ratio of 2.2x is thin. The rule-of-thumb benchmark for a healthy SaaS business is 3x or more. Below about 1.5x, growth destroys value, once you discount and allow for doubt about the churn estimate. Brindle creates some value per customer, but without much cushion.
  • A 30-month payback is slow. Good B2B SaaS pays back in 12 to 18 months. At 30 months, every new customer is effectively a two-and-a-half-year loan that the company makes to itself, so growth consumes cash. And if churn ticks up from 1.5% to 2.5%, the lifetime drops to 40 months, LTV falls to £16,000, and the ratio falls to 1.3x. So the model is fragile to a one-point move in churn.
  • So what would fix it? Brindle could raise its price; at an ARPU of £600 with the same churn, LTV becomes £32,000, and payback falls to 25 months. It could cut CAC, through more inbound leads or channel partners. Or it could reduce churn, as covered in Lesson 3. That's by far the most powerful lever, because churn sits in the denominator.

A deal team seeing these numbers doesn't walk away. Instead, it reprices the growth story. The CIM's plan to "double the sales team and double the growth" only works if the unit economics deserve the fuel.

§3.2.6Payback period: the cash-flow lens

LTV to CAC compresses everything into one ratio, but it leans on the churn estimate, which is the softest number in the room. CAC payback, which is CAC divided by the monthly gross-profit contribution, needs no assumption about lifetime at all. That's why many investors trust it more.

  • Under 12 months is excellent. The business can grow quickly on its own cash flow.
  • Between 12 and 24 months is normal for B2B. Growth needs funding, but the maths works.
  • Over 24 months, growth is expensive. The company is betting heavily on retention, and the balance sheet has to carry that bet.

Payback also frames the classic PE conversation with a SaaS company that's loss-making but healthy. Losses equal to this year's sales and marketing spend are a choice. If payback is 14 months and retention is strong, cutting the growth spend would reveal a profitable core. That's exactly the value-creation case that some software deals are built on.

§3.2.7Cohort thinking: the honest view

Blended averages hide everything that's interesting. A cohort is the group of customers acquired in the same period, tracked over time. Cohort tables answer the questions that averages dodge. Do customers actually stay as long as the churn rate implies? Do they spend more over time, or less? And are recent vintages better or worse than the older ones?

Here's an example, showing the annual revenue retained by each cohort, with each row indexed to 100 in the year it was acquired.

Cohort Yr 0 Yr 1 Yr 2 Yr 3
2022 100 88 82 79
2023 100 84 76 —
2024 100 78 — —

Blended churn might still look stable, because a growing base of young customers masks the decay. But read down the Year 1 column: 88, then 84, then 78. Each vintage is worse than the one before. Perhaps the company has used up its best-fit market, and the newer customers are poorer matches. This is one of the most valuable patterns diligence can uncover, because it tells you that the future unit economics are worse than the historic ones the CIM is selling. The reverse pattern, where vintages improve, is a genuine buy signal.

Deal teams ask for cohort data in every diligence on a subscription business. A seller who "can't produce it" either has weak systems, which is an operational finding, or unflattering cohorts, which is a pricing finding. Either way, you've learned something.

§3.2.8When unit economics mislead

Unit economics are a lens, not the truth. Here are the classic ways they fail.

1. Averages mask mix. A blended LTV to CAC of 3x might really be one segment at 8x and another at 0.5x. If the growth plan pours money into the second segment, the blended history is irrelevant. So always segment, by size, channel, product and geography, before you trust a ratio.

2. The churn assumption does all the work. LTV divides by churn, so small errors explode. Moving the assumed monthly churn from 1.5% to 1.0% inflates LTV by 50%, with a single keystroke. Young companies have little history of churn, and the LTVs in CIMs routinely assume that the best-ever retention will continue for a decade. Prefer payback, which assumes nothing.

3. Marginal CAC isn't average CAC. The first customers came cheaply, through the founders' networks, early adopters and free press. The next 1,000 will cost more, because channels saturate and each new audience converts less well. Historic CAC understates the CAC that's built into the growth plan, so look at the trend quarter by quarter, rather than the average.

4. Fixed costs exist. Units with a positive contribution can still add up to a loss-making company, if the fixed base is too big for any realistic volume. Unit economics tell you whether growth is worth buying, but they say nothing about whether the overheads are affordable. A business that's been "profitable on a unit basis" for ten years in a row is running at a scale it can't support.

5. Some units aren't repeatable. In lumpy project businesses, an "average project margin" isn't really a unit economic. The projects are all different, and one bad fixed-price contract can wipe out twenty good ones. Unit economics need lots of similar units before they mean anything.

6. Loyalty can be bought. Discounts, free months and paid incentives make cohorts look sticky during the acquisition period, while they're being paid to stay. Check what retention looks like after the promotional pricing ends, because that step down is where the truth lives.

Here's the deal-team habit. Work out the unit economics, and then attack your own calculation with these six questions. Whatever survives is usually the real investment case.

Lesson 3.3/Business Models & Unit Economics

Recurring Revenue and Retention

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson defines ARR and MRR properly, and explains gross and net revenue retention with a worked cohort table. It shows why small monthly churn numbers compound into catastrophe, what actually makes revenue sticky, and how PE prices recurring revenue compared with transactional revenue.

  1. 3.3.1ARR and MRR: the vocabulary, precisely
  2. 3.3.2Gross versus net revenue retention
  3. 3.3.3Churn maths: why 2% monthly churn is catastrophic
  4. 3.3.4What actually makes revenue sticky
  5. 3.3.5How PE prices recurring versus transactional revenue

§3.3.1ARR and MRR: the vocabulary, precisely

MRR, or monthly recurring revenue, is the total of all contracted subscription revenue, expressed as a monthly figure. ARR, or annual recurring revenue, is MRR multiplied by 12, or equivalently the total of the annual contract values. Both of them are run-rate snapshots. They answer the question, "if nothing changed, what would we bill over the next year?" They are not accounting revenue. A company can have £12m of ARR on 31 December, but only £10.5m of recognised subscription revenue for the year, because the ARR was added along the way, and only earned for part of the year.

So what belongs in ARR? Contracted subscription fees, committed minimums on usage contracts, and maintenance contracts with renewal terms. And what doesn't? One-off implementation fees, billing for usage above the committed minimums, "customers who always come back" but have no contract, and licence sales that are non-refundable but one-time. Sellers stretch this all the time. The single most common diligence adjustment in software deals is redefining ARR downwards, by stripping out re-occurring services and uncommitted usage. And the price adjusts along with it, because buyers only pay recurring-revenue multiples for revenue that is genuinely contracted to recur.

You'll meet some related vocabulary too. Bookings is the value of new contracts signed in a period. Billings is what was invoiced. And recognised revenue is what the accounting rules let you count. They differ because of timing, and bridging between them is a standard quality-of-earnings exercise.

§3.3.2Gross versus net revenue retention

Take all the customers who existed at the start of the period, and ask what their revenue looks like a year later. There are two answers.

  • Gross revenue retention, or GRR, only counts the losses, meaning cancellations and downgrades, so it can never be more than 100%. GRR isolates one question: how leaky is the bucket?
  • Net revenue retention, or NRR, adds back the expansion from those same customers, such as upsells, price rises and extra seats. So it can be more than 100%. NRR asks: does the existing customer book grow on its own?

Crucially, neither metric includes new customers. That's the whole point. They measure the quality of the installed base, without any contamination from sales effort.

Here's a worked cohort table, following one customer book through FY25, in thousands of pounds of ARR.

Movement in the FY24 customer base £000
Opening ARR (1 Jan) 10,000
Churned customers (full losses) (700)
Downgrades (kept customers, smaller contracts) (300)
Retained ARR 9,000
Upsell and cross-sell to retained customers 900
Price increases on renewal 300
Closing ARR from the opening cohort 10,200
GRR=10,000−700−30010,000=90%NRR=10,20010,000=102%\text{GRR} = \frac{10{,}000 - 700 - 300}{10{,}000} = 90\% \qquad \text{NRR} = \frac{10{,}200}{10{,}000} = 102\%GRR=10,00010,000−700−300​=90%NRR=10,00010,200​=102%

If the company also signed £1.3m of ARR from new customers, total closing ARR is £11.5m. But that £1.3m appears in neither of the retention metrics.

The skill lies in reading the two together.

  • NRR of 102% with GRR of 90%, as in this table, means the base grows, but only by patching a real leak with expansion. You need to ask whether expansion can keep outrunning churn forever.
  • NRR of 115% with GRR of 95% is elite. Growth is almost free, and the sales team is a bonus.
  • NRR of 105% with GRR of 78% is a red flag dressed up as a green one. A third of customers leave within eighteen months, while a few whales expand hard. Concentration risk is building up inside a healthy-looking NRR, so always ask how much of the expansion comes from the top five accounts.
  • NRR of 88% with GRR of 85% means the bucket leaks, and nobody upgrades. The company has to sprint, with new sales, just to stand still.

So what do deal teams actually ask for? The GRR and NRR calculations by cohort and by segment; the definition being used, whether by logo or by revenue, and annualised or monthly; and whether price rises are doing all of the work in NRR. Pricing-led NRR is real money, but it tests customers' goodwill, and it can't repeat forever.

§3.3.3Churn maths: why 2% monthly churn is catastrophic

Small monthly percentages hide some brutal compounding. Monthly churn of ccc gives annual retention of (1−c)12(1-c)^{12}(1−c)12.

Monthly churn Annual retention Annual churn Implied avg. customer life
0.5% 94.2% 5.8% 200 months (~17 yrs)
1.0% 88.6% 11.4% 100 months (~8 yrs)
2.0% 78.5% 21.5% 50 months (~4 yrs)
3.0% 69.4% 30.6% 33 months (~3 yrs)
5.0% 54.0% 46.0% 20 months

"Only 2% a month" means losing more than a fifth of the customer book every year. A company with £10m of ARR and 2% monthly churn has to sign £2.15m of new ARR each year before it grows at all. Over a five-year PE hold, the original book shrinks to 0.7855≈30%0.785^5 \approx 30\%0.7855≈30% of its starting size. The company you bought has mostly evaporated and been replaced, at full acquisition cost, more than twice over.

Now run the flywheel in reverse. Cut monthly churn from 2% to 1%, and the average customer's life doubles, from 50 months to 100. LTV doubles with it, every pound spent on acquisition buys twice as much value, and the treadmill of new sales slows by half. That's why reducing churn is the single most powerful operating initiative in any subscription portfolio company. It's worth more than most growth plans, and it's much cheaper.

There's one more trap: churn compounds off a growing denominator. Fast-growing companies quote low blended churn, because the base is full of new customers who haven't had time to leave yet. So always ask for churn by tenure. If customers churn heavily at month 13, their first renewal, then a company that doubled in size last year hasn't yet met its own true churn rate.

§3.3.4What actually makes revenue sticky

Retention is an output. The inputs are what drive stickiness, and they're what diligence tests, because they predict whether historic retention will hold up under new ownership and higher prices.

  • Being embedded in the workflow. The product is where the work happens every day, as with payroll, practice management or ERP. Ripping it out means retraining everyone and migrating the data. Contrast that with a reporting tool that one analyst opens once a month.
  • Data gravity. Years of records live in the system, and they don't export well. Switching means either losing that history or paying for a painful migration.
  • Depth of integration. The product is wired into five other systems through APIs. Each of those integrations is a switching cost that someone else would have to rebuild.
  • Use across many stakeholders. Ten departments use it, so no single person can decide to leave. Products with a single internal champion die when that champion changes jobs.
  • Mission criticality, and the pain of failure. Software that runs a factory or a payroll simply can't be allowed to fail, and a 3% price rise isn't worth the risk of changing it. That's why boring, critical software has GRR of 95% or more, and commands premium prices.
  • The mechanics of the contract. Multi-year terms, auto-renewal, annual billing in advance, and contractual price escalators, such as clauses linking prices to inflation plus 2%, all harden the revenue. They're cheap to add, valuable at exit, and a standard item in the 100-day plan.

So what looks bad? Products that are discretionary "nice-to-haves"; sales that depend on a single champion; month-to-month terms; heavy discounting at renewal, which means retention is being bought; and support tickets trending upwards, which is the leading indicator of churn, six to twelve months ahead.

§3.3.5How PE prices recurring versus transactional revenue

The market pays radically different prices for the same pound of profit, depending on how it recurs. Here's a stylised view, for a decent mid-market business.

Revenue type Typical pricing lens
Contracted recurring (GRR 90%+) 10–15x EBITDA, or 3–6x+ revenue for growers
Repeat / re-occurring (uncontracted) 7–9x EBITDA
Transactional / project 4–7x EBITDA
One-off licences in a software mix Often valued near 1x revenue — barely more than this year's sales

And here's why the gap is rational, rather than a matter of fashion.

  1. Debt capacity. Lenders size leverage off cash flow in the downside case. Contracted revenue supports 4 to 5x leverage, while lumpy revenue might support 2 to 3x. More cheap debt mechanically lifts the equity IRR, so buyers can pay more and still hit the same return.
  2. The shape of the downside. A book with 90% GRR has a hard floor, while a project book can halve. Equity in a leveraged structure is effectively an option on the downside, and a narrower downside is worth paying for.
  3. Reliability at exit. The next buyer applies the same logic, so the multiple is more likely to hold up, or even expand. The risk to the multiple is lower, even if the level of the multiple were the same.
  4. Compounding without effort. A base with NRR of 105% grows by 5% a year at no sales cost at all. Embedded growth is the cheapest growth there is.

There are two practical consequences for deal work. First, mixed businesses get sum-of-the-parts pricing. Take a software company with £20m of revenue, of which £12m is maintenance and £8m is licences and services. It gets priced at a premium multiple on the first part, and a modest one on the second. That's why sellers fight to reclassify revenue upwards, and buyers fight back. Second, shifting the mix is a value-creation lever in its own right. Converting licence customers to subscriptions, putting contracts around handshake relationships, or attaching monitoring contracts to equipment sales can re-rate the whole company at exit, even with flat EBITDA. Some buy-and-build theses essentially boil down to "buy at transactional multiples, and sell at recurring ones".

Here's a quick sanity check you can run on any target in five minutes. Take the reported "recurring" revenue, multiply it by GRR, and compare the result with next year's budgeted revenue from existing customers. If the budget assumes more than ARR×NRR\text{ARR} \times \text{NRR}ARR×NRR from the installed base, someone is planning on retention improving, so ask why. And if reported recurring revenue with 93% GRR somehow fell by 15% last year, then the "recurring" label is doing more work than the contracts are. These are thirty-second calculations, and they regularly reprice deals.

Here's the one-line summary a deal partner would give you: it's the quality of revenue that gets priced, not just the quantity, and retention is the single best proxy for quality.

Lesson 3.4/Business Models & Unit Economics

Moats and Competitive Position

24 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson covers the five types of moat: switching costs, network effects, scale economies, brand, and regulatory barriers. It shows how to use Porter's five forces as a practical checklist, rather than a diagram, and explains why fragmented market structures attract buy-and-build strategies.

  1. 3.4.1Why moats are a pricing question
  2. 3.4.2Switching costs: the PE favourite
  3. 3.4.3Network effects, scale economies, brand, regulation
  4. 3.4.4Porter's five forces, used practically
  5. 3.4.5Market structure: fragmented versus consolidated
  6. 3.4.6Why fragmentation attracts buy-and-build

§3.4.1Why moats are a pricing question

A moat is anything that lets a company keep earning above-normal returns without competitors wearing them away. In public-market investing, moats are about compounding over decades. In PE, the horizon is a hold of four to six years, so the question is sharper and more practical: will this company's margins and retention survive the hold period, and last long enough for the next buyer to believe in them too?

That matters because the price of an LBO capitalises today's EBITDA at a multiple. If competition can squeeze margins from 25% down to 18% over five years, the buyer overpaid, however good the diligence spreadsheets looked. Every commercial due diligence report is, at heart, an assessment of the moat wearing a suit.

The test for any claimed moat is always the same: what specifically happens when a competitor cuts its price by 20%, or a customer threatens to leave? If the answer involves real costs, lost data, retraining, regulatory approval or an inferior alternative, then there's a moat. If the answer is "our service is great", there isn't one.

§3.4.2Switching costs: the PE favourite

Switching costs make leaving painful, even when the alternatives are cheaper. They come in several flavours.

  • Procedural switching costs mean retraining staff, migrating data, and re-integrating systems. A management system for a vet practice touches bookings, clinical records, billing and stock, so replacing it disrupts the whole practice for months.
  • Financial switching costs include set-up fees that haven't yet been recouped, lost volume discounts, and early-termination clauses.
  • Relational switching costs come from things like an account manager who knows all the client's quirks, or a supplier certification that took 18 months of audits, which is common in aerospace and pharma supply chains.
  • Risk-based switching costs are the strongest of all. If the current product works, and failure would be catastrophic, as with payroll, parts for air-traffic systems, or lab accreditation, then the risk of switching outweighs any saving. Nobody gets fired for renewing.

Here's a small worked example. A customer pays £40k a year for some software, and a rival offers it for £30k. But switching would cost £25k for migration, £15k of internal project time, and six months of disruption risk. It would take more than four years of savings to pay back the cost of switching. So the incumbent keeps the customer, and it can push through a 5% price rise every year. That pricing headroom, discovered in diligence, is a value-creation lever. PE loves businesses with switching costs precisely because modest price increases drop straight through to EBITDA, at a margin of close to 100%.

So what looks bad? Switching costs that cut the other way, where the target's suppliers or sales channel hold the relationship. Or low switching costs masked by long contracts. When those contracts roll over, the truth arrives.

§3.4.3Network effects, scale economies, brand, regulation

Network effects mean the product gets better as more people use it. Think of marketplaces, where more buyers attract more sellers; exchanges; social platforms; and data networks, where each customer's data improves the product for everyone. They're powerful, but rare in mid-market PE, and they're often local. A freelancer marketplace can dominate one vertical while being irrelevant in the next one along. The diligence question is: does liquidity actually concentrate, or do users spread themselves across two or three platforms? That "multi-homing", like drivers on two apps or sellers on three marketplaces, guts the effect.

Scale economies mean unit costs fall as volume grows. They come from purchasing power, route density in distribution, spreading fixed costs, such as one R&D budget over more customers, and scale in data. In the mid-market, the version that matters is usually density rather than size. A waste collector with 80% of the bins on a street earns structurally more per bin than a rival with 20%, whatever the national market shares say. This is the quiet engine behind many buy-and-build strategies. Bolt-ons buy density, and density buys margin.

Brand is only a moat when it changes behaviour. That means it commands a price premium, wins the default choice, or reduces the perceived risk, as in "no one ever got fired for buying" a particular name. In B2B, "brand" is usually better described as reputation and accreditation, such as a testing house whose certificates its customers' own clients insist on. Be sceptical of consumer brand moats in diligence. Ask for evidence of a price premium over peers, and for repeat-purchase rates, rather than awareness surveys. A brand that's nothing more than a marketing budget is a cost, not a moat.

Regulatory and licence moats come from permits, accreditations and compliance regimes that take years to obtain, or simply aren't granted any more, such as landfill permits, certain care licences and aviation approvals. They create hard limits on supply, and positions protected by being grandfathered in. The flip side is regulatory risk. The same state that grants the moat can reprice it. Pharmacy reimbursement rates, energy tariffs and government-funded care fees can all move against you in a single budget statement. A moat granted by the payer is also a dependency on that payer, so diligence treats exposure to a single payer as concentration risk.

§3.4.4Porter's five forces, used practically

Porter's framework earns its keep as a checklist of questions about who captures the value in an industry, not as a diagram for page 4 of the investment committee deck. Here's the practical version a deal team runs on every target.

  1. Supplier power. Who does the business buy from, and could those suppliers squeeze it or bypass it? Distributors that depend on a single brand die when that brand goes direct. So check the concentration of suppliers, the exclusivity terms, and how gross margin has trended. If it's drifting down, someone upstream is winning.
  2. Customer power. Can the buyers squeeze? Check the concentration of the top 10 customers, whether customers run formal procurement or tender processes, the length of contracts, and the price increases actually achieved over five years. A company that hasn't raised its prices since 2019 either has no power, or power it isn't using. Diligence has to find out which, because one is a red flag and the other is the upside case.
  3. Rivalry. How do competitors actually behave? Count them, but more importantly, ask how they compete. If they compete on price, that's bad, because someone is always desperate. If they compete on service, specification and relationships, that's survivable. Win and loss data, and the rate at which quotes turn into wins, tell you more than charts of market share.
  4. New entrants. What does it cost to enter the market credibly? Think about capital, accreditation, reference customers and density. If a competent team with £2m could take share within 18 months, the margins are living on borrowed time. If entering needs ten years of certifications, you can sleep well.
  5. Substitutes. These aren't rival vendors, but different ways of solving the problem: in-house teams instead of outsourcing, software instead of services, or simply doing nothing at all. Substitutes are the force that CIMs never mention, and they're the one that kills whole industries, rather than individual companies.

The output that matters isn't five scores, but one sentence: where does the value settle in this chain, and is the target on the right side of it? A business can grow its revenue for a decade while its suppliers and customers capture every pound of that growth.

§3.4.5Market structure: fragmented versus consolidated

Beyond the moats of individual firms, the shape of the market drives PE strategy.

  • Consolidated markets, where the top three players hold 60% or more, offer stable pricing and fat margins, as long as everyone behaves rationally. But the targets are big and expensive, and often already efficient. The moat question is whether the oligopoly will hold.
  • Fragmented markets have hundreds of local operators, and no player above about 5%. Think of dental practices, vet clinics, accountancy firms, heating and ventilation services, and testing labs. The businesses are individually small, and often run by their owners, and they're priced cheaply, because small businesses trade at small multiples.

Fragmentation usually persists for a reason. Local relationships matter, the service is physical and local, and owner-operators accept low returns. The PE insight is that some of those reasons dissolve under shared ownership. The back office, procurement, systems and compliance can all be centralised, even when the service itself is still delivered locally.

§3.4.6Why fragmentation attracts buy-and-build

Buy-and-build means buying a "platform" business and then following it with many "bolt-on" acquisitions. It's the single most common playbook in mid-market PE, and fragmented markets are its natural habitat. The value creation stacks up in four layers.

  1. Multiple arbitrage. Small businesses trade cheaply, and big ones trade dearly. Say you buy a platform with £3m of EBITDA at 7x, then buy ten bolt-ons with £1m of EBITDA each at 4x, and the combined group, with £13m of EBITDA, exits at 9x. The bolt-on EBITDA was bought at 4x and sold at 9x. That's £5 of value for every £1 of EBITDA, before any operational improvement at all. In numbers, the total invested is £21m plus 10 × £4m, which is £61m, and the exit is £13m × 9, which is £117m. That's before any synergies, and it ignores leverage, which amplifies it further.
  2. Synergies. These come from central procurement, a single finance function, shared systems, and cross-selling. Even one or two points of margin across the group compounds the arbitrage.
  3. Moats of density and scale. Each local bolt-on adds route density, purchasing power, and reach when recruiting. So the group builds the scale moat that the fragments never had.
  4. The exit story. A professionalised, systemised group of 30 sites can be bought by a larger fund or a trade buyer, in a way that no individual site ever could. Liquidity itself is manufactured.

So what do deal teams check before they believe a buy-and-build thesis? Is there a real pipeline of willing sellers at sensible prices? Bolt-on multiples inflate quickly once two or three sponsors are working the same space. Does integration actually work here, or does the value walk out of the door with the selling owner-operator and their client relationships? And is the platform's own operating model strong enough to absorb ten acquisitions? A mediocre platform plus ten bolt-ons is just a bigger mediocre business, with a backlog of integration work.

The link back to moats closes the loop. The end state of a good buy-and-build is a company with moats, such as density, brand, accreditation and systems, in a market that used to have none. You're not just buying EBITDA cheaply; you're constructing the competitive position that justifies the exit multiple. When the investment committee asks, "why will the exit buyer pay 9x for something you bought at 4x?", the answer had better be a moat, not a spreadsheet.

Lesson 3.5/Business Models & Unit Economics

Sector Archetypes PE Loves (and Avoids)

25 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson covers the six sectors that dominate mid-market PE: business services, software, healthcare services, industrials, distribution and consumer. For each one, it gives typical margins, capex intensity, cyclicality and key KPIs. It finishes with the classic value traps that catch new analysts out.

  1. 3.5.1Reading a sector like a deal team
  2. 3.5.2Business services: the workhorse of mid-market PE
  3. 3.5.3Software: the multiple champion
  4. 3.5.4Healthcare services: demographics with a payer problem
  5. 3.5.5Industrials and niche manufacturing: cash flow with a cycle
  6. 3.5.6Distribution: unglamorous, dense, and quietly excellent
  7. 3.5.7Consumer: brands, baskets, and fashion risk
  8. 3.5.8The classic value traps

§3.5.1Reading a sector like a deal team

By the end of this module, you can classify a revenue model, run the unit economics, judge retention, and assess a moat. Sectors are where all of that lands. Each sector that PE favours is really a bundle of recurring characteristics: a typical margin structure, an appetite for capex, a degree of cyclicality, and a short list of KPIs that the deal team lives in.

Knowing the archetypes does two things for you. The first is speed. When a teaser describes "a tech-enabled compliance services business, with 60% recurring revenue", you should already have a prior view on its margins, its likely multiple range, and the three risks to probe. The second is calibration. You can spot deviations from the archetype. A distributor with 30% EBITDA margins, or a software company with 60% churn, is either a gem or a fiction, and either way it deserves immediate attention.

The margins below are typical EBITDA ranges in the mid-market. Treat them as starting assumptions to be updated, not as laws.

§3.5.2Business services: the workhorse of mid-market PE

This sector covers testing and inspection, facilities management, compliance services, managed IT services, professional training and waste. These are companies paid to do something that businesses have to do, but don't want to do themselves.

  • Margins vary widely, from 10 to 25% EBITDA. Niches built on accreditation sit at the top, while contract cleaning and generic outsourcing sit at the bottom.
  • Capex is low, because these are people businesses, and capex is often under 2% of revenue. Cash conversion is excellent, as long as working capital is well managed.
  • Cyclicality is low for services driven by compliance, because regulation doesn't check the FTSE. It's moderate for discretionary services, such as consulting and marketing.
  • The key KPIs are the contract retention rate, revenue per employee, staff attrition, which is the real constraint on capacity, the share of revenue under contract, and the net pricing achieved compared with wage inflation.

Why does PE love it? Recurring or repeat revenue from spending that has to happen, low capex, fragmented markets that are ripe for buy-and-build, and margins that respond quickly to work on pricing and mix. The classic risk is that the assets go home at night. If margins depend on paying people less than the market rate, then wage inflation and attrition will catch up with the business eventually, so diligence always tests whether pricing can outrun wages. And avoid the sub-type where "services" means putting people on client sites at thin mark-ups, with no contract. That's staffing, and it's priced like staffing, which means low.

§3.5.3Software: the multiple champion

Software was covered in depth in Lessons 1 to 3, so here's a brief look through the lens of the sector.

  • Margins are 25 to 40% EBITDA or more at maturity, with gross margins of 70 to 85%. Companies at the growth stage show lower EBITDA by choice, because they're spending on sales and marketing.
  • Capex is minimal, but watch out for capitalised development costs. They shift R&D from the P&L onto the balance sheet, which flatters EBITDA. Quality-of-earnings work always looks at EBITDA minus capitalised development.
  • Cyclicality is low for mission-critical vertical software. It's higher for discretionary tools bought seat by seat, where downturns bring seat reductions, known as "downgrade churn".
  • The key KPIs are ARR growth, GRR and NRR, CAC payback, the Rule of 40, meaning revenue growth plus EBITDA margin should add up to at least 40%, concentration of customers, and the share of revenue that's truly contracted.

Why does PE love it? It offers the best quality of revenue money can buy: contracted, compounding, with gross retention of 90% or more, plus pricing power that comes from switching costs. And why does PE hesitate? Entry multiples are the highest in the market, often 12 to 20x EBITDA, or multiples of revenue for fast growers, so the margin for error is thin. And product and technology risk is real. A platform that's one architectural generation behind needs reinvestment, and the CIM won't volunteer that. The sweet spot in the mid-market is boring vertical market software, such as pharmacy systems, plant maintenance and legal practice management. These are small markets that big tech ignores, where a company can hold a dominant local share, with brutal switching costs.

§3.5.4Healthcare services: demographics with a payer problem

This sector covers dental and vet groups, care homes, clinics, pharmacies, staffing, and care at home.

  • Margins are 15 to 25% EBITDA at the level of each site, and lower for the group as a whole, once central costs are included.
  • Capex is moderate to high. Sites need fit-outs and clinical equipment, and their maintenance capex genuinely can't be deferred. Care homes are close to being real-estate businesses.
  • Cyclicality is very low, because demand barely moves with the economy; teeth and pets ignore GDP. The volatility comes from the payer, not the patient.
  • The key KPIs are occupancy or utilisation, fee rates compared with cost inflation, the mix of payers, meaning self-pay versus government versus insurers, clinician vacancies and the use of agency staff, and regulatory ratings.

Why does PE love it? Demographic tailwinds, fragmented supply and demand that ignores the cycle. It's the classic habitat for buy-and-build, and vets and dentistry were the textbook examples. And why does PE get burned? First, reimbursement risk. Where the government sets the fee, one budget decision can squeeze every site's margin at the same time. Second, staff costs rising while fee rates lag behind. And third, regulatory or reputational blow-ups that damage the whole platform. The payer-mix line in the CIM is the single most important table in a healthcare services deal. A dental business that's 80% self-pay, and a care business that's 80% government-funded, are different asset classes wearing the same scrubs.

§3.5.5Industrials and niche manufacturing: cash flow with a cycle

This sector covers specialty components, engineered products, flow control, packaging, and the aerospace supply chain.

  • Margins are 10 to 20% EBITDA for decent niche players, and 25% or more for genuine monopolies, where the part is specified into the customer's design.
  • Capex is the real cost here. Maintenance capex runs at 3 to 6% of revenue, and there are "one-off" machine purchases that recur suspiciously often. PE analyses these businesses on EBITDA minus capex, not EBITDA. A manufacturer with a 15% margin and capex of 5% of revenue is really a 10% business.
  • Cyclicality is the defining risk. Exposure to end markets decides everything. Aftermarket parts and consumables are resilient, while sales of original equipment into construction or cars swing hard.
  • The key KPIs are the order book or backlog, and the ratio of orders booked to revenue billed; the split of revenue between aftermarket and original equipment; capacity utilisation; the ability to pass through the cost of raw materials; and concentration of customers or platforms.

Why does PE like the right ones? Niche leaders with "spec-in" positions, where the part is designed into the customer's product and re-qualifying a replacement is painful, have quiet moats and pricing power, plus a valuable annuity from the aftermarket. The discipline is this: never pay a mid-cycle multiple on peak-cycle EBITDA. The classic way industrial deals fail is buying at the top of the cycle, at 7x "current" EBITDA, when that was really 10x the normalised EBITDA. So diligence builds a view through the cycle. What did FY09 or FY20 look like? And what would this cost base do to the covenants in a year when volumes fall by 20%?

§3.5.6Distribution: unglamorous, dense, and quietly excellent

We covered distribution as a revenue model in Lesson 1. Here it is as a sector.

  • Margins: gross margins are 15 to 30%, and EBITDA margins are only 3 to 8% of revenue. But judge EBITDA as a percentage of gross profit instead, where 20 to 30% is healthy.
  • Capex is low, because warehouses are often leased and fleets can be leased too. But working capital is the real capital. Inventory plus receivables can amount to 15 to 25% of revenue, so growth consumes cash.
  • Cyclicality follows the end markets, but it's softened where revenue comes from repair and maintenance, known as "break-fix", rather than new projects. Distributors weighted towards maintenance, repair and operations, or MRO, are prized for exactly this reason.
  • The key KPIs are gross margin percentage, gross profit per employee, inventory turns, the share of own-brand products, which is a margin lever, the concentration of customers and suppliers, and the share of revenue from MRO compared with projects.

Why does PE love it? Repeat purchasing from fragmented customers, the economics of density, buy-and-build maths that's been proven many times, and self-help levers, such as pricing discipline, more own-brand products and consolidating warehouses, which reliably add 100 to 200 basis points of margin. There are two existential questions. Will the internet, or manufacturers selling direct, erode the value the distributor adds? And could a key supplier terminate the relationship? A distributor is structurally a middleman, so diligence has to prove that some value genuinely settles in the middle, through technical advice, availability, credit or range. Otherwise, the margin is on loan from the supply chain.

§3.5.7Consumer: brands, baskets, and fashion risk

This sector covers food and drink brands, personal care, leisure operators, e-commerce, and roll-outs of multi-site restaurants or gyms.

  • Margins are 10 to 20% EBITDA for brands, and 8 to 15% for retail and leisure operators. For operators, the economics before rent matter, so always check whether "EBITDA" is quoted before or after rent, under IFRS 16.
  • Capex is high for site roll-outs, where each new site is a mini-project with its own payback case. It's low for asset-light brands that outsource their manufacturing.
  • Cyclicality: discretionary spending is the first thing households cut, and premium and big-ticket segments swing the hardest. Staples, and businesses positioned on value, are more resilient.
  • The key KPIs are like-for-like, or same-store, sales growth; the repeat purchase rate; the payback period on new sites; the mix of channels and the concentration of retailers; marketing as a percentage of sales; and the split of growth between price and volume.

Why is PE selective here? The winners are spectacular, combining a compounding brand with the maths of a roll-out. But the sector carries fashion risk and channel power; a grocer delisting a single product line can wipe out 15% of a brand's revenue. And there's the perennial trap of mistaking a trend for a franchise. The roll-out question is always the same: are the new sites as good as the old ones? Imagine a concept whose most recent sites pay back in four years, while the CIM quotes a two-year average across all vintages. That concept is slowing down in plain sight. It's the same cohort logic as in Lesson 2, applied to buildings.

§3.5.8The classic value traps

These traps catch analysts out because each one looks like a marker of quality at first glance.

1. Project-based revenue dressed up as growth. Three years of 20% growth built on ever-larger projects isn't a growth business. It's a business that has to replace all of its revenue every year, and is currently enjoying a hot streak. The tells are revenue growth alongside a shrinking or missing order book, language about "flagship contracts", and lumpy quarterly phasing. Price it on the sustainable base of repeat revenue, not on the headline.

2. Customer concentration. A business that gets 40% of its revenue from one customer is partly a subsidiary of that customer, whatever the margin says. Concentration caps leverage, chills buyers at exit, and hands the customer pricing power at every renewal, because they know their own weight. Deal teams carry some rules of thumb. A top customer above 20% needs explaining, and above 35% it reshapes the whole deal, through earn-outs, price reductions, or walking away. Check contract concentration too. Five contracts with one framework body, all renewing in the same year, are one risk, not five.

3. Earnings at the peak of the cycle. This is the most expensive mistake in PE, because leverage magnifies it. It means paying a full multiple on EBITDA that's been lifted by the cycle, such as surges in demand after COVID, windfalls from commodity prices, or one-off regulatory deadlines that pull demand forward. The tells are record margins that the company can't fully explain, capacity that's sold out, and competitors also at record levels. The discipline is to normalise the earnings first, and then apply the multiple to that figure.

There are some honourable mentions. Regulatory dependency is the moat that the payer can reprice. Founder dependency is the moat that retires on completion. And there's "recurring" revenue that diligence reclassifies, as in Lesson 3. The common thread running through every trap is the same: an earnings number that won't repeat, priced as if it will. The whole discipline of this module, from revenue models to unit economics, retention and moats, exists to answer one question: which parts of this year's EBITDA are permanent? Pay for those, and only those.

Module 4 of 12

Multiples and comps, DCF, enterprise vs equity value, and the bridges between them — when each method fits.

Lesson 4.1/Valuation

Enterprise Value vs Equity Value: The Bridge

25 min read
In brief

This lesson explains why every deal has two prices: enterprise value and equity value. It shows how the bridge between them works, item by item, covering net debt, pensions, leases, earn-outs and minority interests. And it explains what "cash-free, debt-free" actually means in an SPA.

  1. 4.1.1Two prices for the same company
  2. 4.1.2Net debt: the core of the bridge
  3. 4.1.3Debt-like items: where the arguments live
  4. 4.1.4A worked bridge
  5. 4.1.5Cash-free, debt-free
  6. 4.1.6Why deals price on EV but shareholders receive equity value
  7. 4.1.7What deal teams actually ask

§4.1.1Two prices for the same company

Every deal has two headline numbers, and mixing them up is the quickest way to look junior in a deal-team meeting.

Enterprise value, or EV, is the value of the business. That means the operating assets that generate cash flow, regardless of how they happen to be financed today. Equity value is what the shareholders actually receive when they sell. The difference between the two is everyone else who has a claim on the business's cash flows: lenders, pension trustees, lessors, minority shareholders, and the seller of a business that was bought last year on an earn-out.

Think of a house. Say the house is "worth" £500k; that's the enterprise value. But if there's a £300k mortgage outstanding, the seller walks away with £200k, and that's the equity value. Nobody would say the seller "got £500k for the house", and nobody sensible compares houses by what their sellers pocketed after paying off their mortgages. You compare houses on the £500k figure, and you pay the sellers the £200k figure. Companies work in exactly the same way.

The two are linked by the bridge from EV to equity value:

Equity value=EV−Net debt−Debt-like items−Minority interests\text{Equity value} = \text{EV} - \text{Net debt} - \text{Debt-like items} - \text{Minority interests}Equity value=EV−Net debt−Debt-like items−Minority interests

Here, net debt is gross debt minus cash. Everything in this lesson is about what belongs in that bridge, and why deal teams argue about it for weeks.

§4.1.2Net debt: the core of the bridge

The simplest version of the bridge subtracts gross debt, meaning bank loans, bonds, drawn revolving credit facilities, and shareholder loans owed to the outgoing owners. Then it adds back cash. So a company with £100m of EV, £40m of debt and £8m of cash has net debt of £32m, and an equity value of £68m.

Why does cash add to equity value? Because the buyer receives it. If you buy the business and there's £8m sitting in the bank account on day one, you could in principle pay yourself an £8m dividend the very next morning. The seller knows that, so they charge you for it. In the same way, you inherit the obligation to repay the £40m of debt, so you pay the seller £40m less than the business is worth.

There are two practical wrinkles that deal teams always probe.

  • Is the cash really free? Some cash can't be freely distributed. That includes cash trapped in overseas subsidiaries, where bringing it home has a cost; regulated or ring-fenced cash, such as client money or insurance reserves; and the minimum level of operating cash needed to fill the tills and pay wages. Buyers argue that trapped and operating cash should be treated as not being cash, which reduces what they pay for it. A retailer that "has £10m of cash", but needs £6m of it in tills and in transit, really has £4m.
  • Is the debt really all of the debt? The audited balance sheet is a starting point, not the answer, and that's what the rest of the bridge is for.

§4.1.3Debt-like items: where the arguments live

Between clean bank debt and clean cash sits a long list of items that behave like debt. They're fixed, or nearly fixed, claims that the buyer will have to settle with cash that would otherwise belong to the shareholders. Here are the most common ones.

  • Pension deficits. An underfunded defined-benefit pension scheme is a promise to pay cash into the scheme over future years. Buyers treat the deficit as debt, usually after tax, because the contributions are tax-deductible. So a £10m deficit with 25% tax relief is roughly a £7.5m debt-like item. Sellers argue for the lower "technical provisions" figure, while buyers argue for the higher cost of a full buy-out. The gap can be enormous. This is a whole diligence workstream in itself, not a footnote.
  • Leases. Under IFRS 16, lease liabilities sit on the balance sheet, and EBITDA excludes rent, which flatters EBITDA. You have to be consistent. Either you use an EV that includes the lease liabilities, against IFRS 16 EBITDA, or you strip leases out of both sides, and use pre-IFRS 16 EBITDA, sometimes called "frozen GAAP", with rent deducted. Mixing the conventions, for instance by multiplying IFRS 16 EBITDA by a multiple from comparables built on pre-IFRS 16 numbers, quietly misprices the deal. Finance leases on equipment that's genuinely debt-financed are almost always treated as debt either way.
  • Earn-outs and deferred consideration. Suppose the target bought a business last year, and still owes the seller £5m, depending on performance. That £5m, or its probability-weighted value, is a debt-like item, because the buyer inherits the obligation.
  • Tax liabilities. These include overdue corporation tax, disputed tax assessments, and deferred payroll taxes.
  • Other favourites include provisions for dilapidations, legal settlements, and customer prepayments that are well above their normal level, because you've been paid for work you still have to do. There are also bonuses accrued but not yet paid, dividends declared but not yet paid, and liabilities on derivatives.

Minority interests, also called non-controlling interests, are subtracted for a different reason, which is consistency. If the target owns 80% of a subsidiary, its consolidated EBITDA includes 100% of that subsidiary's earnings. So the EV you calculate from that EBITDA includes some value that belongs to the 20% of outside shareholders. You subtract their share to get to the equity value that belongs to your shareholders. By the same logic, stakes in associates, where you own, say, 30% and don't consolidate, are added, because they're value that the EBITDA doesn't capture.

§4.1.4A worked bridge

Suppose we've agreed to buy Brindley Engineering at an enterprise value of £100m. Diligence finds the following, in millions of pounds.

EV-to-equity bridge £m
Enterprise value 100.0
Less: bank debt (40.0)
Less: finance leases (5.0)
Less: pension deficit (post-tax) (6.0)
Less: minority interest (3.0)
Plus: cash 8.0
Equity value 54.0

The headline in the press release will say "a £100m deal". But the sellers' bank accounts will show £54m between them. Both numbers are true; they just answer different questions.

Notice the leverage in this arithmetic. It's not financial leverage, but negotiating leverage. The EV was agreed at "8x EBITDA of £12.5m", and nobody moves that headline now, because it was set during the competitive phase of the auction. But every £1m that the buyer's diligence adds to the debt-like items comes straight out of the sellers' £54m. A pension actuary who moves the deficit from £6m to £10m has just cost the sellers £4m. That's a 7.4% haircut to their proceeds, from a 4% quibble on a £100m deal. That's why the items in the bridge are fought over line by line in the SPA, and why "what's in net debt" is a defined term that runs to several pages.

§4.1.5Cash-free, debt-free

Most private M&A is done on a cash-free, debt-free, or CFDF, basis. The price is quoted as an enterprise value, and the mechanism effectively says: "the sellers keep or repay the cash and the debt, and we're only buying the operating business." At completion, the EV is adjusted by the actual net debt and debt-like items on the completion date, to work out the cash that changes hands.

CFDF almost always comes with a second adjustment, for normalised working capital. The buyer needs the business to arrive with a normal level of stock, debtors and creditors. Otherwise, a seller could quietly harvest cash before completion, either by not paying suppliers, which pushes creditors and cash up, or by collecting receivables aggressively. So the SPA sets a target level of working capital, usually a 12-month average, which is itself heavily negotiated. It then adjusts the price pound for pound for any difference at completion. If normal working capital is £10m and the business completes with £7m, the buyer pays £3m less, because they'll have to fund that £3m themselves in the first weeks of ownership.

The alternative mechanism is called a locked box. It fixes the equity price off a balance sheet at a historical date, and prohibits any "leakage", such as dividends or fees paid to the sellers, between that date and completion. It's simpler and faster, and it favours the seller, which is why sellers in competitive auctions increasingly insist on it. Either way, the intellectual structure is the same: you agree the value on EV, and you deliver the equity value through a bridge.

§4.1.6Why deals price on EV but shareholders receive equity value

So why not just negotiate the equity number directly? There are three reasons, and they're all worth being able to recite.

  1. Comparability. EV is neutral to the capital structure. Two identical businesses, one financed with 60% debt and the other with no debt at all, are worth the same EV, but they have wildly different equity values. Multiples of EBITDA or EBIT, which are measured before interest, only make sense against EV. Pairing an equity value with a measure of earnings before interest is a category error. That's why comparables, precedent transactions and headline deal announcements all speak in terms of EV.
  2. The capital structure changes at completion anyway. In a buyout, the buyer repays the existing debt and puts in a new structure. The seller's financing choices make no difference to what the business is worth to the buyer. They only determine how the EV gets split between the seller's lenders and the seller's shareholders.
  3. Timing. Cash and debt balances move every day, but the value of the operating business doesn't. So you agree the stable number, the EV, early on, and you true up the volatile parts, net debt and working capital, at completion.

But shareholders can only ever receive equity value. The rest of the EV goes on repaying lenders and settling debt-like claims. So when a founder says "I sold my company for £100m", the deal team's first question is always: "was that EV, or equity?" In the Brindley example, the answer changes the story by nearly half.

§4.1.7What deal teams actually ask

When a bridge lands on the table, experienced eyes go straight to a few places.

  • "What's in 'cash'?" That means trapped cash, client money, till floats, and cheques that haven't cleared. What looks good is clean, onshore, unrestricted cash. What looks bad is a third of the "cash" sitting in a Chinese subsidiary, or held against customer deposits.
  • "Is that the full pension picture?" Which measure of the deficit is being used, with which discount rate, and what will the trustees demand on a change of control? A change-of-control clause can let the trustees reopen the funding schedule at the worst possible moment.
  • "On IFRS 16, are the multiple and the EBITDA on the same basis?" This is the single most common technical error in junior models. Putting leases in the bridge and adding rent back to EBITDA is double counting in the buyer's favour, while leaving leases out altogether is a gift to the seller.
  • "Are any debt-like items hiding in working capital?" Look for stretched creditors, factored receivables, which are debt dressed up as a movement in working capital, and deferred capex.
  • "Who gets the equity value?" With institutional sellers, there's usually a waterfall of loan notes, preference shares and sweet equity, so even the equity value isn't shared out pro rata. That's for a later module, but the bridge is where it starts.

The bridge itself is arithmetic that a spreadsheet does in a single column. The judgement, about what counts as debt, what cash is real, and which measure of a pension deficit is fair, is where deals are won, lost and repriced. So get fluent in it. Every later lesson in this module quotes multiples of EV, and every multiple is only as good as the bridge behind it.
