Lesson 4.2/Valuation

Valuation Multiples: What Each One Really Tells You

25 min read
In brief

This lesson covers EV to EBITDA, EV to EBIT, EV to sales, and the P/E ratio: what each one captures and distorts, and when each one fits. It explains the LTM and NTM conventions, how to adjust multiples for differences in growth, margin and capex, and how multiple arbitrage generates PE returns, and sometimes flatters them.

  1. 4.2.1A multiple is a compressed DCF
  2. 4.2.2The four workhorses
  3. 4.2.3LTM vs NTM: which year's earnings?
  4. 4.2.4Adjusting multiples for growth, margin and capex
  5. 4.2.5Multiple arbitrage
  6. 4.2.6What deal teams actually ask

§4.2.1A multiple is a compressed DCF

A valuation multiple looks like the opposite of a discounted cash flow. It seems quick and crude, with no forecasts at all. But it isn't the opposite. A multiple is a DCF, just with the assumptions hidden. If you pay 8x EBITDA, you're implicitly making claims about growth, margins, capex needs and risk; you just haven't written them down. The perpetuity maths makes this explicit. If free cash flow is a stable proportion of EBITDA, and grows at ggg forever, then:

EVEBITDA=FCF/EBITDAWACC−g\frac{EV}{EBITDA} = \frac{FCF/EBITDA}{WACC - g}EBITDAEV​=WACC−gFCF/EBITDA​

So a business converting 50% of its EBITDA into free cash flow, with a 10% discount rate and 2% growth, is "worth" 0.5/0.08=6.25x0.5 / 0.08 = 6.25x0.5/0.08=6.25x. Raise the conversion to 70%, through low capex and negative working capital, and the same formula gives 8.75x. Nothing about the business has changed except the quality of its cash conversion, and yet the "fair" multiple has moved by 40%. Keep this formula in your head. Every argument about why one company deserves a higher multiple than another is really an argument about one of those three inputs.

It follows that multiples from companies with different cash conversion, growth or risk can't be compared without adjusting them. "The sector trades at 10x" is the beginning of an analysis, not the end of one.

§4.2.2The four workhorses

EV to EBITDA is the default currency of private markets. Both the numerator and the denominator are neutral to the capital structure, because EBITDA is before interest and EV is before the bridge. So it lets you compare companies regardless of their leverage, and it also neutralises differences in depreciation policy. What it distorts is capex, because it treats capex as free. Two businesses with £20m of EBITDA look identical at 8x, even if one has to spend £10m a year on machinery and the other spends £1m on laptops. EBITDA isn't cash. Module 2 made that point, and here it turns into a pricing error worth millions.

EV to EBIT partly fixes that. Depreciation is a rough long-run proxy for capex, so EBIT gets you closer to the sustainable operating cash flow before tax. It suits capital-intensive sectors, such as manufacturing, transport and rental businesses, where EBITDA flatters aggressively. It has weaknesses, though. Depreciation is an accounting estimate, muddied by useful lives, revaluations and the amortisation of acquired intangibles. And it diverges from capex whenever a company is growing or shrinking its asset base.

Here's a worked contrast, in millions of pounds. Alpha and Beta both have EBITDA of 20, and both are offered at an EV of 160, which is 8.0x EBITDA. Alpha depreciates 10, because it has heavy equipment, with capex to match. Beta depreciates just 2. So Alpha's EBIT is 10, and Beta's is 18. On EV to EBIT, Alpha is at 16.0x, while Beta is at 8.9x. So Beta is dramatically cheaper for the same headline multiple, because more of its EBITDA survives contact with the capex line. Whenever two comparable companies show similar EV to EBITDA but very different EV to EBIT, capital intensity is the reason, and EBITDA is the wrong lens to use.

EV to sales ignores profitability altogether, and that's precisely when you need it. It's for businesses that are loss-making or below scale, such as early-stage SaaS or turnarounds, where EBITDA is negative or meaningless. But it only works between companies with similar margin potential. Two times sales for a business that can reach 30% EBITDA margins is cheap; two times sales for one that's structurally stuck at 5% is ruinous. Here's a useful bridge: EV to sales equals EV to EBITDA multiplied by the EBITDA margin. So a business on 10x EBITDA, with a 20% margin, trades at 2.0x sales, and with a 10% margin, it trades at 1.0x sales. Quoting EV to sales without the margin is quoting half a number.

The P/E ratio, or price to earnings, which is equity value divided by net income, is the odd one out. It's an equity multiple, measured after interest and tax. That makes it the natural tool for banks and insurers, where leverage is the business itself, rather than its financing, and for public-market investors buying shares. In M&A, it's dangerous, because it tangles operating performance up with the capital structure. Load a business up with debt, and its P/E falls, with no change at all in the enterprise. Never pair an equity-side numerator with an enterprise-side denominator, or the other way round. EV to earnings, and price to EBITDA, are both category errors, and both turn up depressingly often in first drafts.

Here's a rule of thumb for choosing. Use EBITDA for most PE deals and for services businesses; EBIT where capex is structural; sales where the profits haven't arrived yet; and P/E where the analysis is genuinely about equity, as with listed shares and financial companies.

§4.2.3LTM vs NTM: which year's earnings?

A multiple needs a time period, and there are two standard ones.

  • LTM, or the last twelve months, is actual, more or less audited, and real. But it looks backwards, and you're buying the future, not the past.
  • NTM, or the next twelve months, also called forward, matches the price to what you'll actually own. But it relies on forecasts, and management forecasts in a sale process have a well-documented problem with optimism.

For a growing company, NTM EBITDA is bigger than LTM EBITDA, so the NTM multiple is lower. An EV of £200m on LTM EBITDA of £20m is 10.0x. If EBITDA grows by 25% to £25m, the same price is 8.0x on an NTM basis. So sellers quote NTM, saying "only 8x!", buyers quote LTM, saying "a full 10x!", and both are describing the same deal. In comparables work, the cardinal rule is consistency. Every company in the set should be on the same basis, and the multiple you apply to your target should be on the same basis as the comparables that produced it. Applying an NTM multiple from a comparables set to your target's LTM EBITDA understates the value of a growing business, and doing the reverse overstates it. It sounds too obvious to mention, until you see it in a live investment committee paper.

Precedent transactions bring a third basis: EBITDA as disclosed when the deal was announced, which is usually LTM at signing. That's worth remembering when precedent multiples look rich compared with today's trading comparables.

§4.2.4Adjusting multiples for growth, margin and capex

The compressed DCF formula tells you what to adjust for. In practice, there are three moves.

Growth. Faster growth justifies a higher multiple, but how much higher? A quick tool is the growth-adjusted multiple, which is EV to EBITDA divided by the expected growth in EBITDA. It's similar to the PEG ratio in equity markets. Two comparables at 12x and 8x look far apart. But if the first grows EBITDA at 15% and the second at 5%, the growth-adjusted picture, 0.8 against 1.6, reverses the ranking. A cruder but effective approach is to run the comparables on next year's numbers, or the year after, which lets growth "catch up" in the denominator.

Margin. For EV to sales especially, plot EV to sales against EBITDA margin across the comparables set, or run a regression. The relationship is usually strong, and your target should be priced on the line, not at the median of the set. A business with a 25% margin, priced at the median EV to sales of a set with 15% margins, is being given away.

Capex. Where capital intensity varies across the set, switch to EV to EBIT. Or better still, work out EV divided by EBITDA minus maintenance capex for each comparable. That's as close as a multiple gets to a cash flow lens, and it's what many PE investment committees actually want to see. In the Alpha and Beta example above, Alpha is at EV divided by 20 minus 10, which is 16.0x, and Beta is at EV divided by 20 minus 2, which is 8.9x. That's the same answer as EV to EBIT here, but this measure keeps working even when depreciation and capex diverge.

So what looks bad on a comparables page? A single median multiple applied to a target that sits at the extreme of the set on growth, margin or capex. And what looks good? An explicit argument for "why our target deserves a premium, or a discount, to the median", tied to those three drivers.

§4.2.5Multiple arbitrage

Multiple arbitrage, also called multiple expansion, means selling at a higher multiple than you paid. Say you buy at 8x EBITDA of £20m, an EV of £160m, and sell five years later at 10x EBITDA of £25m, an EV of £250m. Of the £90m gain in EV, £40m came from growing EBITDA at the entry multiple, that's 5 times 8, and £50m came purely from the multiple moving. That's the arbitrage. With leverage amplifying the returns to equity, multiple expansion has historically made up a very large share of the value PE creates. That's exactly why investment committees treat it with suspicion.

So where does legitimate expansion come from?

  • Size. Bigger businesses trade at higher multiples, as Lesson 6 explains. Growing a business from £10m of EBITDA to £25m can move it into a different universe of buyers.
  • Buy-and-build. Buying bolt-ons at 5 to 6x, and selling the assembled group at 9x. Here, the arbitrage is earned through the work of integration.
  • Improving quality. Shifting the revenue mix towards recurring contracts, diversifying the customer base, and professionalising the finance function.
  • The sector or the market being re-rated. That's luck, dressed up as skill.

The discipline that follows at investment committee is this. Base cases generally assume that the exit multiple equals the entry multiple, or allow a modest step down to be conservative. That way, the underwritten return depends on EBITDA growth and paying down debt, which are things the fund controls. Multiple expansion is upside, not the plan. When a deal only reaches its target return if it exits at 11x, against an entry at 9x, the model is telling you the price is too high, and that someone has hidden the problem in the last row of the assumptions page.

§4.2.6What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's the multiple of?" Is it reported EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, or run-rate EBITDA including synergies? A "7x deal" on aggressively adjusted EBITDA can be a 9x deal on real earnings. The denominator is negotiated just as fiercely as the multiple, and Lesson 6 and Module 9 pick this up as quality of earnings.
  • "Is it LTM or NTM, and is the basis consistent with the comparables?"
  • "Is it before or after IFRS 16?" That's Lesson 1's warning, applied here. For rent-heavy businesses, the two bases can differ by a full turn of EBITDA.
  • "What does the multiple imply?" Turn the compressed DCF around. At 12x, with 50% cash conversion and a 10% discount rate, the implied perpetual growth rate is 10%−0.5/12=5.8%10\% - 0.5/12 = 5.8\%10%−0.5/12=5.8%, forever. Is that believable for this business? Checks on implied assumptions kill more bad deals than any page of comparables.
  • "Would we be happy holding at this multiple if we can't sell any higher?" That's the multiple arbitrage question, asked honestly.

Multiples are how the market talks, so you need to be fluent in them. Just remember what fluency means here. It isn't reciting the sector median. It's knowing what any given multiple assumes, what it hides, and when it's the wrong tool altogether. The next lesson puts all this to work, building a set of comparables properly.

Lesson 4.3/Valuation

Comparable Companies and Precedent Transactions

25 min read
In brief

This lesson shows how to build a set of comparables properly, covering screening, calendarisation, spreading and how to handle outliers. It explains the difference between trading comparables and precedent transactions, where control premiums come from, and why "the comps say 10x" always deserves some scepticism.

  1. 4.3.1What comps are actually for
  2. 4.3.2Screening: choosing the set
  3. 4.3.3Spreading and calendarisation
  4. 4.3.4A worked mini comps set
  5. 4.3.5Trading comps vs precedent transactions
  6. 4.3.6Why "the comps say 10x" deserves scepticism
  7. 4.3.7What deal teams actually ask

§4.3.1What comps are actually for

Comparable company analysis, known as "trading comps", answers a simple question: what is the market paying today for businesses like this one? You take a set of listed companies that resemble your target, work out their multiples, and apply a chosen multiple to your target's earnings. Precedent transaction analysis, known as "deal comps", does the same thing, using the prices actually paid in M&A deals.

Both methods are relative valuation. They tell you what something is worth compared with what similar things fetch, not what it's worth intrinsically. That's both a feature and a bug. The feature is that markets pull together enormous amounts of information, and any buyer who ignores what the market pays will systematically lose auctions, or overpay. The bug is that if the market is wrong, because of a bubble, a panic, or a sector that's temporarily in fashion, the comparables import that error straight into your valuation, with a false air of objectivity. Comparables tell you the price of similar assets. Whether that price reflects value is your problem, not the spreadsheet's.

The craft lies almost entirely in building the set. The multiplication at the end takes seconds, but a set you can defend takes days.

§4.3.2Screening: choosing the set

Start wide, and then cut it down with explicit criteria. Deal teams screen on the following.

  • The business model, not the industry code. Industry classifications lump together companies that make their money in completely different ways. A "software" screen will return old licence-and-maintenance dinosaurs alongside SaaS businesses with 130% net retention, and their multiples differ by a factor of three for good reason. So read the annual reports, and screen on how the revenue is actually earned: recurring or project-based, asset-light or asset-heavy, business-to-business or business-to-consumer.
  • Size. A £2bn company isn't a comparable for a £100m company, however similar the product. Scale changes margins, customer concentration and funding costs, and crucially, it changes the multiple itself, as Lesson 6 explains. Common practice is to stay within roughly a third of, and three times, the target's revenue or EBITDA, where the universe allows.
  • Geography and end markets. A UK contractor exposed to public-sector spending isn't priced like a US peer exposed to capex on data centres.
  • The profile of growth and margin. This is Lesson 2's point. A comparable growing at three times your target's rate belongs in the appendix, not in the median.
  • Liquidity and coverage. Illiquid micro-caps that no analysts cover produce stale, noisy multiples.

Expect to end up with five to ten names. With fewer than five, the median is fragile, and with more than a dozen, you've stopped screening. There's never a perfect comparable. The honest output is a set where, for each name, you can explain how it differs from the target, and which way that difference should push the multiple.

§4.3.3Spreading and calendarisation

"Spreading comps" means building each company's numbers to a common standard, because the reported figures can't be compared straight off the shelf.

  • Build the EV properly. Start with the market capitalisation, on a fully diluted basis, including any options and convertibles that are in the money. Then add the full bridge from Lesson 1: debt, leases on a consistent basis, pensions and minority interests, less cash and associates. An EV taken lazily from a data vendor can be wrong by a full turn of EBITDA.
  • Clean the earnings. Strip the one-offs out of each comparable's EBITDA, such as restructuring charges, disposals and impairments, in the same way you'd want your target's EBITDA cleaned. And treat IFRS 16 consistently across every comparable.
  • Calendarise. Companies have different year ends, but the multiples need to cover the same twelve months. The standard fix is a weighted blend. Take a comparable with a June year end, EBITDA of £28m for the year to June 2024, and a forecast of £32m for the year to June 2025. Its EBITDA for calendar 2024 is 0.5×28+0.5×32=£30m0.5 \times 28 + 0.5 \times 32 = £30m0.5×28+0.5×32=£30m. A March year end blends three twelfths and nine twelfths. If you skip calendarisation in a growing sector, you'll systematically misstate every comparable whose year end is out of step.

§4.3.4A worked mini comps set

Our target is Tarn Instruments, a UK testing and certification business with LTM EBITDA of £25m. Here's the screened set, all in millions of pounds, calendarised to the last twelve months.

Company EV EBITDA EV/EBITDA Net debt/EBITDA EBITDA growth
Halden Testing plc 450 50 9.0x 1.8x +6%
Wrekin Labs plc 240 30 8.0x 2.0x +4%
Girton Analytics plc 1,800 150 12.0x 1.5x +15%
Pennine Inspection plc 130 20 6.5x 5.5x +2%
Solent Certification plc 285 30 9.5x 2.2x +7%
Mean 9.0x
Median 9.0x

The mean and the median both say 9.0x. Case closed? Let's look more closely.

  • Girton, at 12.0x, is six times the size of the next-largest name, and it's growing at twice the rate of the set. Its multiple has scale and growth built into it that your target, with £25m of EBITDA, doesn't have. Including it drags the mean up, for reasons that don't carry across.
  • Pennine, at 6.5x, carries net debt of 5.5 times EBITDA. Its equity is a sliver of its EV, its shares trade like an option, and its depressed multiple reflects distress and the dynamics of a forced seller, not the value of testing businesses. Its 6.5x drags the mean down, again for reasons that don't carry across.

If you exclude both, the core set of Halden, Wrekin and Solent runs from 8.0 to 9.5x, with a median of 9.0x. The answer didn't move much this time, but the reasoning did, and next time the outliers won't happen to cancel each other out. Handling outliers should be explicit and symmetrical. State the rule for exclusion, such as distress, scale, a pending takeover, or an accounting restatement, apply it in both directions, and show the set both with and without the outliers. Quietly deleting the names that hurt your answer is the oldest trick in the book, and an investment committee that catches it once will re-check your work forever.

For Tarn, a range of 8.5 to 9.5x on £25m gives an EV range of £212.5m to £237.5m. There's a case for the lower half of that range, because Tarn is the smallest name in the peer group, and its growth is in line with the slower names.

§4.3.5Trading comps vs precedent transactions

Precedent transactions apply the same machinery to M&A deals: the EV paid, over the target's EBITDA when the deal was announced. They answer a different question. Rather than "what does the market pay for minority stakes in listed peers?", they ask, "what have buyers paid for control of whole companies?"

Precedents usually come out higher than trading comparables, and the reasons are worth separating.

  • The control premium. Buying control lets you replace management, change strategy, put new debt on the business, and capture the whole of the benefit, and that's worth paying for. Premiums paid to take public companies private have historically averaged around 25 to 40% over the undisturbed share price.
  • Synergies. Strategic buyers can pay for overlaps in cost that a financial buyer can't. A deal at 11x by a trade consolidator that takes out £5m of duplicated overheads may only be 8x after synergies. That multiple isn't available to you unless you have the same synergies.
  • Competitive dynamics. The heat of the auction is built into every precedent by construction. The recorded price is the winning bid, which means it's the most optimistic buyer's number.

Precedents also have data problems that trading comparables don't. The terms of private deals are patchily disclosed, so the EBITDA behind a rumoured multiple might be adjusted, run-rate, or simply invented. Deal structures muddy the headline, through earn-outs, rollover and vendor loans. And deals go stale. A 2021 deal at 12x tells you about the debt markets of 2021, not today's. Standard practice is to look at the last three to five years, flag the context of the cycle for each deal, and never let one trophy deal set your range.

Use both, for what each one tells you. Trading comparables show today's market level, and precedents show what control of the whole business has cost. A PE buyer paying "trading comparables plus a control premium", with no synergies, should hear alarm bells. That premium has to be earned back by someone, and that someone is them.

§4.3.6Why "the comps say 10x" deserves scepticism

When someone quotes a single comparables number in a meeting, run through this checklist in your head.

  1. Ten times what? Is it LTM or NTM? Reported or adjusted EBITDA? Before or after IFRS 16? Each of these choices moves the answer, and combinations of them move it a lot.
  2. Whose set is it? The seller's banker built a set to maximise the number, and the buyer's adviser built one to minimise it. Both of them will describe theirs as "the comps".
  3. Is it a mean, a median, or a cherry-pick? With five names, one outlier can move the mean by a full turn. So always use the median, with the policy on outliers disclosed.
  4. Is the target actually in the middle of the set? Applying the median assumes the target is a median business. If it's smaller, slower-growing, or more concentrated than the set, it belongs below the median. And a private company usually deserves a further discount for illiquidity compared with listed peers.
  5. A multiple of which metric? If the set's range of EV to EBITDA is tight, but EV to EBIT is all over the place, then capital intensity differs across the set, and EBITDA is hiding it, as Lesson 2 explained.
  6. When? Comparables are a snapshot. Sector re-ratings of two turns, up or down, within a single year are routine.

None of this makes comparables useless. It makes the headline useless without the workings behind it. So what looks good on a comparables page? An explicit screen, calendarised numbers, both bases shown, outliers handled openly, and a recommended multiple with a stated premium or discount to the median, linked to the target's characteristics. And what looks bad? A bare median, a set of four names, and a footnote saying "source: broker research".

§4.3.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "Walk me from the raw set to your number." They're testing whether the set was screened properly, or reverse-engineered from the answer.
  • "Why is [obvious name] not in the set?" Have a one-line reason ready for every exclusion.
  • "What were these names trading at a year ago?" The current level compared with history matters. 9x might be the set's lowest point in five years, which could mean a market-wide de-rating and an opportunity, or it could be an all-time high.
  • "Which precedent is most like our deal, and what did that buyer achieve?" One deeply understood precedent beats ten rows of multiples from a vendor's database.
  • "If we paid the comparables median, what would the LBO return?" This is the PE punchline: the comparables propose, but the LBO model decides. Lesson 6 takes this up properly.

Comparables are the most-used, and most-abused, tool in valuation. Used well, they discipline a valuation with evidence from the market. Used lazily, they launder a single number through five ticker symbols. The difference lies in the workings.

Lesson 4.4/Valuation

DCF Fundamentals: Cash Flows, WACC and Terminal Value

30 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the mechanics of a discounted cash flow. It shows how to project unlevered free cash flow, and how to build a WACC from its parts: the risk-free rate, the equity risk premium, beta, a size premium, and the cost of debt. It explains terminal value, using both Gordon growth and an exit multiple, and finishes with a full worked mini-DCF for a fictional company and a sensitivity table for WACC and growth.

  1. 4.4.1The idea, stripped bare
  2. 4.4.2Projecting free cash flow
  3. 4.4.3Building a WACC from parts
  4. 4.4.4Terminal value
  5. 4.4.5The full mini-DCF
  6. 4.4.6The sensitivity table
  7. 4.4.7What deal teams actually ask

§4.4.1The idea, stripped bare

A business is worth the cash it will hand to its providers of capital over its lifetime, discounted back to today at a rate that reflects the risk of actually receiving that cash. That's the whole theory of a DCF. Everything else, the tabs, the betas and the terminal value formulas, is implementation.

EV=∑t=1nFCFt(1+WACC)t+TV(1+WACC)nEV = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{FCF_t}{(1+WACC)^t} + \frac{TV}{(1+WACC)^n}EV=t=1∑n​(1+WACC)tFCFt​​+(1+WACC)nTV​

Two design choices define the standard version. First, we discount unlevered free cash flow, which is the cash generated by the operations before any financing. That means the answer is an enterprise value, independent of the capital structure, exactly in parallel with Lesson 1. You get to equity value through the bridge, as always. Second, because we can't forecast forever, we project explicitly for five to ten years, and collapse everything after that into a single terminal value.

A DCF is the only mainstream method that values a business from its own economics, rather than from other people's prices. That independence is the whole point of it. But, as Lesson 5 will show, it's also its danger, because nothing outside the model disciplines the inputs.

§4.4.2Projecting free cash flow

Here's how unlevered free cash flow is calculated for each forecast year.

FCF=EBIT×(1−tax)+D&A−Capex−ΔNWCFCF = EBIT \times (1 - tax) + D\&A - Capex - \Delta NWCFCF=EBIT×(1−tax)+D&A−Capex−ΔNWC

We start from EBIT rather than EBITDA, so that tax is calculated on the right base. Then we add back the non-cash D&A, and subtract the two real drains on cash that earnings ignore: capex, and growth in net working capital. Notice what's missing. Interest is left out, because it's financing rather than operations, and so are dividends, because they're a distribution of cash rather than a way of generating it.

Let's build year 1 for Kestrel Foods, a fictional producer of ambient foods, in millions of pounds.

Year 1 build £m
Revenue 100.0
EBITDA (20% margin) 20.0
Less: D&A (6.0)
EBIT 14.0
Less: tax at 25% (3.5)
NOPAT 10.5
Add back: D&A 6.0
Less: capex (6.0)
Less: increase in NWC (0.5)
Unlevered FCF 10.0

Run the same logic across a five-year plan, with revenue growing at about 5%, a stable margin, capex tracking D&A, and working capital absorbing about 10% of each year's revenue growth. Rounded, that gives free cash flows of 10.0, 11.0, 12.0, 13.0 and 14.0.

The projection is where the value really lives, so that's where the quality checks live too. Does the revenue growth imply a believable share of the market? Does the margin expand for a reason, such as mix, pricing or operating leverage, or just because the spreadsheet formulas were dragged to the right? Is the capex consistent with the growth? You can't grow volumes by 5% a year on maintenance capex alone. And does working capital scale with revenue? A DCF inherits every sin of its forecast, and Lesson 5 catalogues them.

§4.4.3Building a WACC from parts

The discount rate is the weighted average cost of capital, or WACC. It's the blended return that the company's investors require.

WACC=EE+D×ke+DE+D×kd×(1−tax)WACC = \frac{E}{E+D} \times k_e + \frac{D}{E+D} \times k_d \times (1 - tax)WACC=E+DE​×ke​+E+DD​×kd​×(1−tax)

Debt is cheaper than equity, because lenders get paid first and so bear less risk, and interest is tax-deductible, which gives the (1−tax)(1-tax)(1−tax) shield. The weights should be the target long-run weights, at market values, rather than whatever today's balance sheet happens to show.

The cost of equity comes from the capital asset pricing model, or CAPM, plus some adjustments in practice.

ke=rf+β×ERP+size premiumk_e = r_f + \beta \times ERP + \text{size premium}ke​=rf​+β×ERP+size premium

Let's build one for Kestrel.

Component Value Where it comes from
Risk-free rate rfr_frf​ 4.0% Long-dated government bond yield (10–20yr gilt)
Equity risk premium 5.0% Long-run excess return of equities over bonds; practitioner consensus ~4.5–6%
Beta β\betaβ 1.2 Sector betas from listed comps, unlevered then re-levered to the target structure
CAPM cost of equity 10.0% 4.0%+1.2×5.0%4.0\% + 1.2 \times 5.0\%4.0%+1.2×5.0%
Size premium 2.0% Empirically, small companies return more / are riskier; ~1–3% for mid-market
Cost of equity 12.0%

Beta measures how the sector's returns move with the market. Food producers sit below 1, because they're defensive, while housebuilders sit above it, because they're cyclical. The figure of 1.2 here reflects Kestrel's exposure to supermarket own-label products. The size premium is the practitioner's patch for CAPM's best-documented failure. It covers the risks of small companies, such as illiquidity, dependence on key people, and concentration, which beta doesn't capture. Frankly, it's also a judgement dial, and Lesson 5 comes back to that.

The cost of debt is what the company would pay to borrow today. Let's say that's 7.0% before tax, or 7.0%×(1−0.25)=5.25%7.0\% \times (1-0.25) = 5.25\%7.0%×(1−0.25)=5.25% after tax.

The weights are a target of 70% equity and 30% debt.

WACC=0.70×12.0%+0.30×5.25%=8.4%+1.6%≈10.0%WACC = 0.70 \times 12.0\% + 0.30 \times 5.25\% = 8.4\% + 1.6\% \approx 10.0\%WACC=0.70×12.0%+0.30×5.25%=8.4%+1.6%≈10.0%

A mid-market UK company in 2026 typically lands somewhere between 9 and 13%. Hold on to the intuition, not just the formula. WACC is the return the money could earn elsewhere, at the same level of risk. Discounting at 10% says that "£1 of Kestrel's cash next year is worth 91p today, because 10% is what this level of risk has to pay."

§4.4.4Terminal value

The explicit forecast stops at year 5, but the business, we hope, doesn't. There are two standard ways to value everything beyond that point.

Gordon growth treats year 5's free cash flow as growing at a constant rate, ggg, forever:

TV=FCF5×(1+g)WACC−gTV = \frac{FCF_5 \times (1+g)}{WACC - g}TV=WACC−gFCF5​×(1+g)​

For Kestrel, with g=2%g = 2\%g=2%, that gives TV=14.0×1.020.10−0.02=14.280.08=178.5TV = \frac{14.0 \times 1.02}{0.10 - 0.02} = \frac{14.28}{0.08} = 178.5TV=0.10−0.0214.0×1.02​=0.0814.28​=178.5.

You need discipline on ggg. It's perpetual growth, so it can't be higher than long-run nominal GDP growth, which is about 3.5 to 4%. A company that grows faster than the economy forever eventually becomes the economy. The typical range is 1.5 to 2.5%. Notice, too, how the denominator works. As ggg gets closer to WACC, the terminal value explodes towards infinity. Small changes in either input move the terminal value violently, and that matters, because the terminal value is most of the answer.

The exit multiple method asks instead what the business would sell for in year 5, at a multiple like those in the comparables. Terminal-year EBITDA of £24.3m at, say, 7.5x gives a terminal value of about £182m. This feels more intuitive to deal people, but it smuggles relative valuation into your "intrinsic" method. Your DCF is now partly a comparables page in disguise.

Best practice is to use one method, and cross-check it with the other. Our Gordon terminal value of £178.5m, against year-5 EBITDA of £24.3m, implies an exit multiple of 178.5/24.3=7.3x178.5 / 24.3 = 7.3x178.5/24.3=7.3x. That's below today's sector multiples, so it's mildly conservative. If your Gordon terminal value had implied 14x, the terminal assumptions would be doing something that the market doesn't believe.

§4.4.5The full mini-DCF

Now we discount at a WACC of 10%.

£m Y1 Y2 Y3 Y4 Y5
Unlevered FCF 10.0 11.0 12.0 13.0 14.0
Discount factor @10% 0.909 0.826 0.751 0.683 0.621
PV of FCF 9.1 9.1 9.0 8.9 8.7
Valuation build £m
Sum of PV of explicit FCF (Y1–Y5) 44.8
Terminal value at Y5 (Gordon, g = 2%) 178.5
PV of terminal value (× 0.621) 110.8
Enterprise value 155.6

Before anyone gets excited about the precision, there are two observations to make. First, an EV of £155.6m on year-1 EBITDA of £20m is an implied multiple of about 7.8x. That's a number you can now sanity-check against the comparables, which is exactly how the methods should talk to each other. Second, the terminal value contributes 110.8/155.6=71%110.8 / 155.6 = 71\%110.8/155.6=71% of the entire answer. Five carefully built forecast years drive less than a third of the value, and a two-line perpetuity formula drives the rest. Sit with that for a moment. It's the central fact about DCFs, and it's the subject of the next lesson.

To get to equity value, apply Lesson 1. If Kestrel carries net debt and debt-like items of £35m, its equity value is £120.6m.

§4.4.6The sensitivity table

Because the terminal value dominates, and its formula is on a hair trigger, no DCF should ever be presented as a single number. The standard exhibit is a two-way sensitivity table, showing EV against WACC and terminal growth.

EV (£m) g = 1.5% g = 2.0% g = 2.5%
WACC 9% 169.1 178.6 189.5
WACC 10% 148.6 155.6 163.6
WACC 11% 132.4 137.7 143.8

Read what it's telling you. Across combinations of inputs that are all entirely defensible, because nobody can prove that 10% is right and 9% is wrong, or that 2.0% is right and 2.5% is wrong, the valuation spans £132m to £190m. That's a 43% range. The DCF hasn't given you a number; it's given you a map from assumptions to numbers. That's genuinely useful, because it shows which assumptions matter and puts a price on them. But it's only useful if you present the whole map, rather than pointing at your favourite cell.

§4.4.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's the terminal value as a percentage of EV?" Above about 75%, the explicit forecast is just decoration.
  • "What exit multiple does your Gordon terminal value imply?" It's the single fastest sanity check.
  • "Why is your WACC 10%, and not 9%?" If you can't defend each component, the table above says that's a £23m question.
  • "Does the capex support the growth?" Growth in the revenue line, alongside maintenance-only capex in the cash flow line, is the most common way that DCFs flatter.
  • "What does the DCF say on management's case, compared with ours?" A DCF always runs on somebody's forecast, so always know whose.

You now have the machine. The next lesson is about judgement: where the machine misleads, and how experienced teams use it anyway.

Lesson 4.5/Valuation

DCF Judgement and Pitfalls

25 min read
In brief

This lesson looks at where DCFs go wrong, and how professionals use them anyway. It covers the dominance of terminal value, hockey-stick forecasts, the false precision of WACC, and the mid-year convention. It explains when a DCF beats multiples, and when it's the other way round, and how to triangulate methods on a football-field chart.

  1. 4.5.1The uncomfortable truth about DCFs
  2. 4.5.2Terminal value dominance: what to do about it
  3. 4.5.3Hockey sticks: the forecast pathology
  4. 4.5.4WACC: precise, and false
  5. 4.5.5The mid-year convention
  6. 4.5.6When DCF beats multiples — and vice versa
  7. 4.5.7Football fields and triangulation
  8. 4.5.8What deal teams actually ask

§4.5.1The uncomfortable truth about DCFs

Lesson 4 ended on a number that should change how you see every DCF. In a completely standard model, the terminal value made up 71% of the enterprise value. That's typical; with a five-year explicit period, 60 to 80% is the normal range. The implication is blunt: a DCF is mostly a perpetuity formula, wearing a five-year forecast as a disguise. The forecast tab gets weeks of work and all of the investment committee's attention, while two cells, WACC and terminal growth, quietly decide the answer.

That doesn't make DCFs useless. It makes them a different kind of tool from the one they appear to be. A DCF is at its best not as a valuation oracle, but as an X-ray of the assumptions. It forces every belief about growth, margins, capex and risk out into the open, puts a price on each one, and shows you which of those beliefs the valuation actually depends on. Teams that use DCFs well spend their time interrogating the map, which is the sensitivity table, rather than defending their favourite cell in it. Teams that use them badly present EV to one decimal place. Kestrel is "worth £155.6m" only in the sense that a dart is "in the treble twenty" while it's still in your hand.

§4.5.2Terminal value dominance: what to do about it

You can't get rid of the dominance of terminal value. It's mathematics, not sloppiness, because most of the value of any long-lived asset genuinely lies beyond year 5. What you can do is stop it hiding.

  • Report the terminal value as a percentage of EV on the face of the output. If it's above about 75%, say so, and treat the DCF as a supporting method rather than the lead one.
  • Cross-check the implied exit multiple, which is the habit from Lesson 4. If a Gordon terminal value implies 12x for a business whose peers trade at 8x, then your terminal assumptions, not your forecast, are the entire investment thesis.
  • Check that the terminal year is a steady state. The perpetuity extends year 5 forever, so year 5 has to be a representative year. That means margins at sustainable levels rather than peak ones, capex roughly equal to D&A plus an allowance for growth, working capital growing in line with revenue, and no one-offs that are about to expire. Capitalising a peak year into perpetuity is the single most expensive error a DCF can make. At a capitalisation rate of 8%, every £1m of overstated terminal free cash flow adds £12.5m to the terminal value.
  • Lengthen the explicit period for businesses that are in the middle of a transition. Use ten years, with growth and margins fading towards a steady state, rather than asking the perpetuity to do transition work it can't do.

§4.5.3Hockey sticks: the forecast pathology

Every sell-side plan you'll ever see has the same shape. There's a flat or bumpy history, followed by a smooth upward sweep that always starts next year. That's the hockey stick. Management forecasts in sale processes are systematically optimistic, because everyone's incentives point the same way. The seller wants a high price, management often has bonuses tied to the sale, and the CIM is a marketing document.

Here are the concrete tells, with the kind of numbers you'd actually see.

  • Margins that ramp up without a mechanism. The EBITDA margin has been 12% for five years of history, and then the plan takes it from 12% to 20%. On £100m of revenue, that ramp manufactures £8m of EBITDA. Capitalise that into the terminal value at 12.5x, which is an 8% capitalisation rate, and you've fabricated about £100m of DCF value. So demand the bridge: which contracts, which price rises, and which cost lines?
  • Growth that costs nothing. Revenue grows by 8% a year, while headcount, marketing and capex are all held flat. Operating leverage is real, but it has limits. Operating leverage without limits is a typo.
  • "Year 1 is already secured." Check that the order book actually covers it. And check what last year's plan said about this year. The single most powerful diligence question is to compare plan against actual for the last three plans. A management team that has missed three budgets in a row by 20% has told you exactly what discount to apply to this one.
  • A flattered base year. The stick starts from an adjusted, run-rate base that's been made pro-forma for everything, which is Module 9's territory. A hockey stick that starts from an inflated base compounds two frauds.

The professional response isn't cynicism, but re-underwriting. You build your own case, usually a "management minus" case, with a haircut to growth, a slower ramp in margins, and realistic capex. Then you run the DCF on both cases, and you make sure you know which case you're being asked to pay for.

§4.5.4WACC: precise, and false

Open any valuation textbook, and WACC arrives complete with decimal places. Now remember its parts, each one a judgement wearing a formula. Which risk-free rate should you use: the spot rate or an average, and 10-year or 20-year? Respectable sources put the equity risk premium anywhere from 4% to 6.5%. Beta is estimated by regression, so over what period, against which index, and unlevered how? Its standard error is often half its value. And the size premium is anywhere from 0 to 3%, depending on which study you cite. Stack up all the defensible high choices, and you get 9%; stack up all the defensible low ones, and you get 12.5%, for the same company. On Kestrel's sensitivity table, that spread is worth roughly £60m of EV, and it comes entirely from methodology, before anyone has formed an opinion about the business.

So treat WACC honestly.

  • Use a range, not a point. Present 9 to 11%, with sensitivities, and be suspicious of any output whose sign or verdict flips within that band.
  • Consistency beats precision. Use nominal cash flows with nominal rates, and the same currency in the flows and the rate. Put tax either in the flows or in the shield, but don't count it twice. And make sure the leverage in the re-levered beta matches the weights. Most real-world errors in WACC are errors of consistency, not of estimation.
  • Watch for the dial being used as a dial. When a deal's DCF "works" at a 9.0% WACC and 2.75% terminal growth, and in no neighbouring cell, then someone has solved for the answer. Investment committees know this move, and so do auditors. You should be able to spot it at fifty paces.

§4.5.5The mid-year convention

Here's one genuine mechanical refinement. It's worth knowing because it's standard, and because it shows up when you compare models. Discounting year 1's free cash flow by a full year assumes that all the cash arrives on 31 December. In reality, it arrives roughly evenly through the year, so on average it arrives in the middle. The mid-year convention discounts year ttt at (1+WACC)t−0.5(1+WACC)^{t-0.5}(1+WACC)t−0.5, instead of at (1+WACC)t(1+WACC)^t(1+WACC)t.

The effect is that every discount factor shrinks by half a year, which scales the whole valuation up by (1+WACC)0.5(1+WACC)^{0.5}(1+WACC)0.5. At a 10% WACC, that's a factor of 1.049, so Kestrel's £155.6m becomes about £163.2m. Call it an uplift of about 5%. It's more accurate for cash flows that are evenly spread, but in practice it's also a small button that favours the seller. There are three things to check. Is it applied consistently to the terminal value, as it should be? Is it disclosed? And does it match reality? A business that collects all its cash in a single season at the year end shouldn't use it. If a banker's model comes out 5% above yours for no visible reason, look here first.

§4.5.6When DCF beats multiples — and vice versa

Neither method is "better". They just fail in different situations.

A DCF earns its keep in four situations.

  • When there are no good comparables. Think of unusual business models, hybrid companies and niche infrastructure. Relative valuation needs relatives.
  • When cash flows are contracted, or highly visible. Think of concessions, power purchase agreements, long-term leases, and subscription books with known churn. Here the forecast genuinely can be known, the dominance of the terminal value shrinks, and the asset may even have a finite life, which removes the terminal value altogether. In these cases, the DCF is close to the answer.
  • When the business is changing shape, with heavy investment now and the payoff later. Applying multiples to today's depressed earnings punishes the transition, whereas a DCF can price it, if you believe the plan.
  • When you suspect the whole market is mispriced. Comparables import the market's mood, and only an intrinsic method can disagree with it. The buyers of 2007, who "validated" their prices against each other's deals, learned this lesson expensively.

Multiples win in four situations too.

  • When there's plenty to compare against. In mature sectors with many traded peers and frequent transactions, the market's pooled judgement beats your spreadsheet's.
  • When the forecasts are unreliable. That covers cyclicals, early-stage businesses, and anything where year 3 is a guess. A DCF built on rubbish forecasts is just rubbish with more steps.
  • When you need to transact. Deals clear at market prices. A DCF that says a business is worth 6x, when every auction clears at 9x, is an interesting essay, but it isn't a bidding strategy.
  • When speed and communication matter. "8x EBITDA" travels through an investment committee, a bank and an SPA in a way that a 40-tab model doesn't.

§4.5.7Football fields and triangulation

Since every method is flawed in a different way, professionals run several, and look for where they overlap. The standard exhibit is the football field. It's a chart with one horizontal bar for each method, each bar spanning that method's range of values, all on a common EV axis.

Here's a typical football field for a UK mid-market target.

Method Low (£m) High (£m)
Trading comps (8.0–9.0x LTM EBITDA) 160 180
Precedent transactions (9.0–10.5x) 180 210
DCF (WACC 9–11%, g 1.5–2.5%) 165 215
LBO ability-to-pay (target 2.5x MoM) 150 175

The skill is in reading it. Where do the bars overlap? Here, roughly between £165m and £180m, which gives a credible central range. Which bar is the outlier, and why? The precedents sit high, because of control premiums and synergy-rich strategic deals, so do those conditions apply to us? The LBO bar sits low, as it usually does, because it's a constraint, not an opinion, as Lesson 6 explains. And what would you have to believe to pay £200m? Only the optimistic half of the DCF, and the precedents set by strategic buyers, support that figure. If you're a financial buyer with no synergies, the football field is telling you that £200m is someone else's price.

Triangulation isn't averaging. Averaging four numbers launders judgement into arithmetic. The football field is an argument. Each bar is a piece of evidence with known biases, and the valuation conclusion is the range you can defend once you've weighed them up, written down, with the weighing shown.

§4.5.8What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's the terminal value percentage, and what's the implied exit multiple?" That's the two-question audit of any DCF, every time.
  • "Whose forecast is it, and what's their record of plan against actual?"
  • "Show me the deal with WACC up 1%, and growth down 0.5%." If the recommendation dies, it was never really alive.
  • "Is the mid-year convention on or off, and is theirs?" You'll ask this when reconciling your number to a counterparty's.
  • "Where do the methods disagree, and why?" Disagreement between the bars is information, usually about control, synergies or the mood of the market. It's not noise to be averaged away.

Carry Lesson 4's machine and this lesson's scepticism together, and a DCF becomes what it should be: the most honest way of having an argument about assumptions. The final lesson turns to how PE actually sets the number it's willing to pay.

dcfterminal-valuefootball-fieldtriangulation
↑ Module 4

Lesson 4.6/Valuation

Valuation in a PE Context: What Can We Pay?

25 min read
In brief

This lesson shows how PE actually sets its price. It covers LBO ability to pay, which asks "what can we pay and still make 2.5x?", discipline on the entry multiple, and how quality-of-earnings adjustments change the base the multiple is applied to. It compares the outputs of the different methods, and gives rule-of-thumb multiple ranges by sector and size, including why small companies trade more cheaply.

  1. 4.6.1PE asks a different question
  2. 4.6.2LBO ability-to-pay: the reverse valuation
  3. 4.6.3Entry multiple discipline
  4. 4.6.4Quality of earnings: fighting over the multiple base
  5. 4.6.5Comparing the methods' outputs
  6. 4.6.6Rule-of-thumb ranges by sector and size
  7. 4.6.7Why small companies trade cheaper
  8. 4.6.8What deal teams actually ask

§4.6.1PE asks a different question

Everything so far has answered the question "what is this business worth?" A PE fund asks something subtly, but importantly, different: "what can we pay, and still make our return?" The fund has promised its LPs a target, say 2.5 times their money and an IRR of 20% or more over a hold of about five years, and every deal has to be underwritten to that target. So valuation in PE is really an exercise in satisfying a constraint. Comparables and DCFs describe the market's price and the business's intrinsic worth, but the number that decides the bid comes out of the LBO model, run backwards.

That's why PE professionals can seem strangely uninterested in DCFs. It isn't that intrinsic value doesn't matter. It's that the fund's economics impose a harder test. A business can genuinely be worth 10x, and still be a bad PE deal at 10x, if the leverage, growth and exit assumptions can't turn that 10x into 2.5 times the money.

§4.6.2LBO ability-to-pay: the reverse valuation

Here's how the mechanics work; Module 7 has the full detail. You fix the things you can defend, and then solve for the entry price.

Here's a worked example, in millions of pounds. The target is an industrial services business, with EBITDA today of £15.0.

  1. First, the exit assumptions. A credible plan grows EBITDA to £20.0 by year 5. The exit multiple is disciplined to the entry multiple, so we assume 8.0x, with no expansion, following Lesson 2's rule. That gives an exit EV of £160.0.
  2. Next, the debt. Lenders will provide 4.0x EBITDA at entry, which is £60.0. The cash the business generates pays this down to £40.0 by exit. So the equity at exit is 160.0 minus 40.0, which gives £120.0.
  3. Then, the required return. The fund's target is 2.5 times its money. So the maximum equity it can put in at entry is 120.0 divided by 2.5, which gives £48.0.
  4. Finally, the ability to pay. The maximum entry EV is the entry equity plus the entry debt, so 48.0 plus 60.0, which gives £108.0. That's 7.2x today's EBITDA.

If the auction is clearing at 8.5x, which is £127.5m, then this fund is £19.5m short. It has exactly four options, and every live deal discussion is some mix of them. It can believe in more growth, taking EBITDA to £23m or more; but can the plan really support that? It can pay up and accept a return of about 2.2x; but will the investment committee bend? It can find more leverage, or cheaper capital, through structuring, which is Module 8. Or it can walk away. What it mustn't do is discover, in week six, that the multiple was never achievable with an LBO. Running the ability-to-pay calculation before the first bid is the whole point.

Notice what this machine really is. It's a DCF where the discount rate is the fund's required return, and the terminal value is the exit. All of Lesson 5's scepticism applies. The two assumptions doing the heavy lifting are EBITDA growth and the exit multiple, and the model rewards optimism in both. The discipline lives in the investment committee's standard challenges: the exit multiple should be no higher than the entry multiple, the leverage should be what the debt market will actually provide, and the base case should assume no multiple expansion.

§4.6.3Entry multiple discipline

Returns break down into EBITDA growth, paying down debt, and changes in the multiple, as Module 7 explains. Of those, the entry multiple is the one lever that gets fixed, irreversibly, on day one. Overpay by a single turn, and you spend the whole hold running just to stand still. With £15m of EBITDA, one turn is £15m, which is roughly a third of the equity cheque in the example above.

So what does discipline look like in practice?

  • A house view on the multiple that's independent of the auction. The range from the comparables, in Lesson 3, and the ability to pay together set a ceiling before the process of price discovery begins. After that, the auction tests your willpower, not your analysis.
  • Underwriting the base, not the story. The multiple applies to adjusted EBITDA, which we'll come to below, and to this year's figure, not a run-rate for a year you're hoping for.
  • Paying for what exists, and treating what doesn't as an option. The upside cases, such as entering a new market or winning the big contract, are why you do the deal, not what you pay for. If the seller insists on being paid for the plan, structure it. Earn-outs move part of the price into a contingent future, as Module 8 explains.
  • Knowing when discipline says walk away. Funds are remembered for the deals they didn't do in 2007 and 2021. "We were outbid" is a perfectly good sentence at an annual meeting. "We won it at 13x" often isn't.

§4.6.4Quality of earnings: fighting over the multiple base

At 8x, every £1m of EBITDA is worth £8m of price. So the definition of EBITDA is worth exactly eight times as much argument as you'd naively expect. This is the battleground of quality of earnings, or QoE. We're previewing it here, and it's fought properly in Module 9.

The seller presents "Adjusted EBITDA". That's the reported earnings, plus add-backs for everything that's supposedly a one-off, and, strangely enough, the adjustments almost always point upwards. The buyer's QoE work then re-cuts the base. Here's a typical exchange, in millions of pounds.

EBITDA bridge £m
Reported EBITDA (LTM) 15.0
Seller add-back: "one-off" legal costs +0.6
Seller add-back: pro-forma new contract at full run-rate +0.9
Seller's Adjusted EBITDA 16.5
Buyer: legal costs recur every year of the last three (0.6)
Buyer: run-rate contract not yet delivered a full quarter (0.9)
Buyer: one-off grant income in the base (0.8)
Buyer: under-market owner salary normalised (0.2)
Buyer's QoE-adjusted EBITDA 14.0

It's the same business, but the two bases are 18% apart. At 8.0x, that's the difference between £132m and £112m. That £20m is probably more than the fees of every adviser on the deal combined. There are some practical rules. Every add-back needs evidence, and three years of history for a "one-off" is a contradiction in terms. Credit for a run-rate needs delivery, not just a signature. And adjustments have to be symmetrical. A seller who normalises costs upwards must also normalise windfalls downwards. When you hear "7.5x" and "8.5x" quoted for the same deal, the two sides are usually quoting the same price over different denominators.

§4.6.5Comparing the methods' outputs

From the PE seat, the football field from Lesson 5 gets read in a particular way.

Method Range (£m) What it means to a PE buyer
Trading comps 8.0–9.0x on £14.0m QoE EBITDA 112–126 Where the market prices peers — context, and the seller's anchor
Precedent transactions 9.0–10.0x 126–140 What control has cost others — mostly strategics with synergies; a warning about the auction, not a target
DCF (9–11% WACC) 110–140 Sanity check on intrinsic worth; wide, TV-dominated
LBO ability-to-pay at 2.5x 100–115 The bid range

The LBO bar sits lowest, as it almost always does. A financial buyer with no synergies, paying with expensive equity and disciplined leverage, should have the lowest willingness to pay in the room. The deal can be done where the LBO bar overlaps the price at which the auction will clear. Here, that's only at the bottom of the comparables range, which tells you this deal will be won on an angle, such as a bolt-on thesis, an operational plan or a proprietary relationship, or not at all. When the LBO bar sits above the comparables, either you've found genuine mispricing, or, far more often, your model believes something the market doesn't. So check the model again first.

§4.6.6Rule-of-thumb ranges by sector and size

Calibration matters. You should flinch at "14x for a contractor" before you've even opened a spreadsheet. Here are some indicative ranges of EV to EBITDA for decent mid-market assets in the UK and Europe. The mood shifts with the cycle, so treat these as anchors, not gospel.

Sector archetype Typical EV/EBITDA Why
Contract-backed software / SaaS 12–20x+ (often EV/ARR) Recurring revenue, ~90%+ retention, low capex
Healthcare services, pharma services 10–15x Non-cyclical demand, regulatory moats
Tech-enabled / professional services 8–12x Sticky clients, people risk
Industrial / testing / route-based services 7–10x Contracted but competitive, some cyclicality
Manufacturing / distribution 5–8x Capex-hungry, cyclical, low differentiation
Construction / project contracting 3–6x Lumpy, low-margin, working-capital sinks, tail risk

Within every sector, there's a gradient by size. A business with £3m of EBITDA might fetch 5 to 6x, while a peer in the same trade with £30m of EBITDA fetches 9x. This is the size discount, and it's the engine behind buy-and-build. You acquire at small-company multiples, and sell the combined group at mid-market ones. That's the earned arbitrage from Lesson 2, and the playbook of Module 10.

§4.6.7Why small companies trade cheaper

The size discount is rational. It isn't a market inefficiency waiting to be naively "captured". Small companies carry more of everything that's bad.

  • Key-person risk. The founder is the sales team, the CFO is really a bookkeeper, and the customer relationships live in two people's heads, and those two people may leave on completion.
  • Concentration. Three customers making up 60% of revenue is normal for a business with £3m of EBITDA, but it would be a scandal at £30m. Lose one, and the equity story is over.
  • Data and controls. The accounts may be unaudited, there may be no monthly management pack, and the number of QoE surprises tends to grow the longer you look.
  • Financing. Lenders offer smaller businesses less leverage, at wider margins. That mechanically reduces every buyer's ability to pay; it's the £108m machine above, with worse inputs.
  • The universe of buyers, and liquidity. Fewer funds cover businesses of this size, and the routes to exit are thinner. So the eventual exit multiple carries the same discount, unless the business has grown out of it.
  • Resilience. One bad quarter, one lost contract, or one departed rainmaker can do real damage, because small businesses have no shock absorbers.

The professional summary is that small companies are cheaper because their earnings deserve a lower multiple. They're riskier pounds, and they're capitalised accordingly. The magic of buy-and-build only works when integration genuinely fixes those risks, through diversified customers, professional management and proper reporting, so that the combined group has earned the bigger multiple. Stapling five key-person businesses together and calling the bundle institutional is the version that ends badly.

§4.6.8What deal teams actually ask

  • "What does the LBO say we can pay, and on what assumptions for leverage and exit?" That's the first question on any new opportunity, and it's usually answered on a single page, before an NDA has even been signed.
  • "What's the real EBITDA?" The answer should show the reported, seller-adjusted and QoE views, with the multiple quoted on each one.
  • "Where does our number sit against the comparables and the precedents? And if we're below the market, what's our angle for winning anyway?"
  • "Are we paying for the plan, or for the actual results?" If the price only works on the forecast, structure the gap.
  • "What has to be true?" This is the investment committee's favourite. Turn the model inside out, and list the beliefs that the price requires, such as EBITDA reaching £20m, an 8x exit and 4x leverage. Then ask which of them you'd bet the fund's money on.

That question, what has to be true, is where this module lands. Bridges, multiples, comparables, DCFs and LBO models are all machines for turning beliefs into prices, and prices back into beliefs. The valuation skill PE actually pays for is running them in both directions. Given a price, extract the beliefs it implies; then judge, with evidence, whether those are beliefs you'd be willing to own.

Lesson 5.1/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

What Private Equity Is

20 min readPrimer
In brief

This lesson explains what the private equity asset class is, and walks through the spectrum of strategies, from venture capital through growth equity to buyouts and special situations. It looks at why the model exists at all, and how a PE firm is actually organised, from the partners right down to the operations and data teams.

  1. 5.1.1The asset class in one paragraph
  2. 5.1.2The strategy spectrum
  3. 5.1.3Why private equity exists
  4. 5.1.4How a PE firm is organised
  5. 5.1.5What looks good, what looks bad
  6. 5.1.6Where this module goes next

§5.1.1The asset class in one paragraph

Private equity means investing in companies whose shares don't trade on a public exchange, through funds that lock investors' money up for around ten years. A PE firm raises a pool of capital from institutions, buys stakes in companies, which are usually private, works on those companies for three to seven years, sells them, and returns the proceeds. The firm is paid a management fee for running the fund, and a share of the profits, called carried interest, for performing well. That's the whole model. Everything else in this module is the machinery that makes it work.

The word "private" does the heavy lifting. Because the shares are illiquid, PE funds can take control, replace management, change strategy, and load the company with debt, without a share price punishing them every quarter. And because investors can't redeem their money, the fund can hold on through a downturn, rather than being forced to sell at the bottom. Illiquidity isn't a bug that the industry puts up with. It's the feature that the returns are built on.

To give you a sense of scale, the global PE industry manages several trillion pounds of assets. Buyout funds alone hold well over £1 trillion of capital that's been committed but not yet invested, known as "dry powder", which lesson 3 covers. A single large-cap fund can be more than £15bn, while a UK lower-mid-market fund might be £150m. The mechanics in this module apply to both; only the number of zeros changes.

§5.1.2The strategy spectrum

"Private equity" covers a spectrum of strategies, and they differ along three axes: how mature the company is, the size of the ownership stake, and how much leverage is used. Deal teams place any fund on this spectrum within seconds of hearing its name, and you should be able to do the same.

Strategy Company stage Typical stake Leverage Return driver Loss rate
Venture capital Pre-profit, often pre-revenue 10–25% minority None A few huge winners (power law) High — many zeros
Growth equity Revenue £10m+, growing 20%+ 20–40% minority Little or none Revenue growth Low-moderate
Buyout (LBO) Profitable, cash-generative 51–100% control 3–6x EBITDA of debt EBITDA growth, debt paydown, multiple Low, but each loss hurts
Special situations / distressed Stressed or broken Varies — often via debt Complex Buying below intrinsic value, fixing Moderate

Venture capital buys minority stakes in early-stage companies. The maths follows a power law. A fund makes 25 investments, expecting 15 of them to fail, 7 to return roughly what they cost, and 2 or 3 to return 10 to 50 times their cost and carry the whole fund. There's no leverage, because the companies have no cash flow to service debt.

Growth equity sits in the middle. It buys minority stakes in fast-growing companies that are profitable, or nearly so, where the cheque funds expansion rather than buying out the existing shareholders. Protection on the downside often comes from preference structures, covered in module 8, rather than from control.

Buyouts are the centre of gravity of this course. A buyout fund acquires control of a profitable, cash-generative business, and funds a large slice of the price with debt secured on the company itself. It then improves earnings, repays debt, and sells. Here's a typical worked shape. You buy a company making £20m of EBITDA for 10x, which is an enterprise value of £200m, and fund it with £110m of debt and £90m of equity. Over five years, you grow EBITDA to £28m, and repay £50m of debt. Then you sell at 10x, an EV of £280m. So the equity is worth £280m minus the £60m of remaining debt, which is £220m. That's roughly 2.4x the £90m invested, since 220 ÷ 90 = 2.44. Module 7 unpacks that arithmetic properly. Here, the point is the shape: control, leverage, operational improvement, and exit.

Special situations funds buy where something is broken: over-levered balance sheets, distressed sellers, carve-outs that nobody wants, and assets weighed down by litigation. Their returns come from buying well below intrinsic value, and fixing the specific problem.

So what do deal teams actually ask when they hear a fund's name? Where is it on the spectrum, how big is the fund, how big are its cheques, and does it take control or minority stakes? Those four facts predict almost everything about how a firm will behave in a process.

§5.1.3Why private equity exists

Here's a fair question. Public markets are cheaper to access, and they're liquid, so why would anyone accept a ten-year lock-up and fat fees? There are four reasons, listed here in descending order of how much deal teams believe them.

1. Governance and alignment. A PE owner holds a concentrated, controlling stake, sits on the board, and can change the CEO within a week. Management is given meaningful equity, typically 5 to 15% of the upside through a management incentive plan, so a mediocre outcome hurts them, and a great one makes them rich. Compare that with a FTSE 250 company whose largest shareholder owns 4%, and whose board meets eight times a year. Concentrated ownership, combined with real incentives, is the most defensible source of PE's outperformance.

2. Leverage. Debt amplifies the returns on equity, and the losses too. Suppose a company is bought for £100m, with £60m of debt and £40m of equity. If the enterprise value rises by just 20%, to £120m, with the debt unchanged, the equity is now worth £60m. That's up 50%, on a 20% move in the value of the assets. Leverage also imposes discipline, because cash has to go on interest and repayments, not on empire-building.

3. Access and information. PE buyers do months of due diligence, with full access to the data room, the management team and the customers. That's far more than a public investor can legally obtain. They can also buy businesses that simply aren't available on an exchange, such as family successions, corporate carve-outs and founder exits.

4. Time arbitrage. A five-year hold lets an owner make investments that depress earnings in the first year, such as new systems, building out a sales force, or consolidating factories. A company that reports every quarter struggles to justify those.

Be honest about the counter-argument, because sophisticated LPs certainly are. After fees, the average PE fund has delivered returns close to those of leveraged public equity, and the illiquidity is real. The industry's pitch survives because top-quartile funds keep on outperforming, and because the gap between good and bad managers is far wider than it is in public equities. That's exactly why choosing the right fund matters so much, along with everything in lessons 4 to 6 about fees and measuring performance.

§5.1.4How a PE firm is organised

A PE firm is a surprisingly small business. A firm managing more than £1bn might employ just 40 to 80 people. The hierarchy is steep, and the titles are consistent across the industry.

  • Founding or Managing Partners own the management company, sit on the investment committee, or IC, and hold the relationships with the LPs. They decide what gets bought, and who gets carry.
  • Partners or Managing Directors lead deals from end to end. They originate them, negotiate them, and chair the boards of portfolio companies. They're typically 8 to 15 years into their careers.
  • Principals or Directors run the execution of deals day to day, and are being tested for partnership.
  • Vice Presidents, or VPs, manage the workstreams. They coordinate the advisers, run the model reviews, and draft the IC papers.
  • Associates, who are usually former bankers or consultants with two to four years' experience, build the models, crunch through the data room, and write the first draft of everything.
  • Analysts exist at larger firms. At smaller ones, the associate is the bottom rung of the ladder.

Around the deal ladder sit the functions that have grown fastest over the last decade.

  • Operating partners, or the portfolio team. These are former CEOs and functional experts who work inside portfolio companies on pricing, procurement and 100-day plans, as covered in module 10.
  • Investor relations, or IR, runs fundraising and reporting to the LPs.
  • Finance, or fund operations, calculates capital calls, distributions, management fees and the waterfall. Lessons 2, 4 and 5 describe their day job.
  • Data and digital teams are increasingly central. They work on signals for sourcing deals, pipelines of portfolio KPIs, automating board packs, and analytics for due diligence. If you work in a PE data team, your customers are the deal teams and the portfolio team, and your raw material is everything in module 12.

Here's a worked example of the economics that pay for all this. Take a firm managing two funds. Fund I is £500m, now in year 7, with £300m of invested cost remaining, on a 1.5% fee. Fund II is £700m, in year 2, paying 2.0% on its commitments. So the annual fee income is 1.5% of £300m, plus 2.0% of £700m. That's £4.5m plus £14m, which is £18.5m a year. That pays the salaries, the rent and the costs of deals that die for perhaps 50 people. The real prize, though, is carried interest. If Fund II returns 2.0x on its £700m, the profit is £700m, and the 20% carry pool is £140m. That's split among perhaps 15 to 25 people who hold carry, and paid out over years 6 to 10. Lesson 4 does this arithmetic properly.

§5.1.5What looks good, what looks bad

You can tell a lot about a firm before you've seen a single deal, and deal teams and LPs read the same signals.

Here's what looks good.

  • A stated strategy that the track record actually matches. For example, a firm describing itself as "UK lower-mid-market buyouts", whose last ten deals were UK companies, with cheques sized for businesses making £5 to £15m of EBITDA.
  • Fund sizes that grow steadily, say from £150m to £250m to £400m, rather than quadrupling. That shows discipline about staying where the returns were earned.
  • Low turnover in the senior team, and carry shared beyond the founders. The departure of the people who built the old track record is the classic hidden red flag.
  • Genuine operating capability, rather than two "senior advisers" listed on the website.

And here's what looks bad.

  • Strategy drift. A buyout firm doing minority growth deals, or a £300m fund suddenly writing £80m cheques, usually means the fund was raised bigger than the set of opportunities.
  • A track record that was built by two partners who have since left.
  • "Spray" portfolios, with 25 or more deals run by a small team. Nobody is really minding the companies.
  • Vague answers about who sits on the IC, and how decisions are made.

§5.1.6Where this module goes next

You now have the map. There's an illiquid asset class, a spectrum of strategies with buyouts at the centre, a rationale built on governance, leverage, access and time, and a small firm with a steep hierarchy running the show. The next five lessons follow the money. Lesson 2 covers who supplies the capital, and on what terms. Lesson 3 covers how a fund lives and dies over ten years or more. Lesson 4 covers how the GP gets paid. Lesson 5 covers exactly how the profits are split when cash comes back. And lesson 6 covers how anyone can tell whether the fund was any good. Keep the £500m fund from this lesson in mind, because we'll reuse it as the running example.
