Lesson 5.2/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

LPs and GPs: Who Funds Private Equity and How

25 min read
In brief

This lesson explains who the limited partners are, and why they allocate to PE. It covers the difference between committed and called capital, how capital calls and distributions actually work, and the J-curve, with a full worked table of cash flows. It also sets out the legal architecture: the limited partnership, the GP entity, and the management company.

  1. 5.2.1The two parties: LP and GP
  2. 5.2.2Who the LPs are and why they bother
  3. 5.2.3Commitments, capital calls, and distributions
  4. 5.2.4The J-curve: a worked example
  5. 5.2.5The legal architecture: LP, GP entity, management company
  6. 5.2.6What looks good, what looks bad

§5.2.1The two parties: LP and GP

Every PE fund has exactly two kinds of participant. The limited partners, or LPs, supply almost all of the capital. They have limited liability, and, crucially, they have essentially no say in investment decisions. The general partner, or GP, supplies a small sliver of the capital, makes every decision, and bears unlimited liability. That's in theory, anyway; in practice, the GP is a shell entity, as we'll see. "LP" and "GP" are legal terms from the law on limited partnerships, but the industry uses them as shorthand for "the investors" and "the PE firm".

The relationship is governed by the Limited Partnership Agreement, or LPA. It's a contract of 150 pages or more, and it sets the life of the fund, the fee rate, the hurdle, the waterfall, what the GP is and isn't allowed to buy, and what happens if things go wrong. Most of lessons 3 to 5 is really a tour of the LPA's key clauses. Side letters give large LPs bespoke extras, such as fee discounts, rights to co-invest, and extra reporting, which is a perennial governance grumble for smaller LPs.

The GP also invests its own money, which is called the GP commitment, and it's typically 1 to 5% of the fund. On a £500m fund, a 2% GP commitment is £10m of the partners' own cash. LPs read this closely. A 1% commitment financed by a loan against future fees says one thing; a 4% commitment in cash, from the partners' personal balance sheets, says quite another. Having skin in the game is the cheapest diligence signal an LP gets.

§5.2.2Who the LPs are and why they bother

The capital comes overwhelmingly from institutions that manage other people's long-term liabilities.

LP type Why PE fits Typical PE allocation
Public & corporate pension funds 30-year liabilities; can harvest the illiquidity premium 5–15% of assets
Sovereign wealth funds Effectively permanent capital; huge cheques 5–20%
University endowments & foundations Perpetual horizon; pioneered the model (Yale) 15–40%
Insurance companies Long liabilities, though regulation constrains them 2–8%
Funds of funds Aggregate small investors into diversified PE portfolios 100% (it's their product)
Family offices & wealthy individuals Return-seeking, flexible, faster decisions Varies widely

So why accept a ten-year lock-up? Because these investors don't need the money any time soon. And they believe that PE returns beat public equities by a few hundred basis points after fees. There's fair evidence for that among top-quartile managers, though weaker evidence on average. A pension fund that's paying out benefits in 2050 gives up very little by holding illiquid assets. In exchange, it collects the illiquidity premium, plus access to the engine of governance and leverage from lesson 1. Boards also appreciate that PE valuations move smoothly once a quarter, rather than every day. Economists call this "volatility laundering"; allocators call it convenient.

So what does an LP diligence before it commits? The track record, meaning net returns, how much is realised and how much unrealised, and whether the people who generated it are still there. Discipline on strategy. The stability of the team, and how the carry is allocated. The terms, meaning fees, the hurdle and the waterfall, covered in lessons 4 and 5. And operations, meaning fund administration, the valuation policy, and the quality of reporting to LPs.

§5.2.3Commitments, capital calls, and distributions

Here's the mechanic that surprises everyone who's new to the industry: when an LP commits £10m to a fund, no money moves. A commitment is a contractual promise to wire cash when asked. The GP then draws the money down in instalments, called capital calls, or "drawdowns", as it needs it, deal by deal, and fee payment by fee payment. The notice period is typically 10 business days.

  • Committed capital is the total promise, which here is £10m.
  • Called, or paid-in, capital is the cumulative amount actually drawn so far.
  • The uncalled commitment, which the LP calls its "unfunded" commitment, is committed capital minus called capital. It's what's still owed.

Here's a worked example. An LP commits £10m. In year 1, the fund calls 25%, which is £2.5m, across three deals and a call for fees. In year 2, it calls another £3.0m. So the called capital is now £5.5m, and the unfunded commitment is £4.5m. If the fund sells a company in year 3 and sends the LP £0.5m, that's a distribution. And notice that, unless the fund recycles capital, which lesson 3 covers, the distribution does not reduce the £4.5m that can still be called. Distributions and commitments run on separate tracks.

This structure has teeth. An LP that fails to meet a capital call is in default, and LPAs impose brutal remedies, up to forfeiting the LP's entire existing stake in the fund. So LPs have to hold their unfunded commitments in reasonably liquid form, which drags on their overall returns. And in a crisis, as in 2008 and 2009, some LPs found themselves facing calls at exactly the moment everything else in their portfolio was underwater. Managing "commitment pacing", meaning how much to commit each year so that calls and distributions roughly offset each other, is a real job in every LP organisation.

For the GP, uncalled capital is firepower. For the LP, the practical question about returns isn't "what did the fund earn on my commitment?" It's "what did it earn on my paid-in capital, and when?" That's exactly what the metrics in lesson 6, DPI, TVPI and IRR, measure.

§5.2.4The J-curve: a worked example

If you plot an LP's cumulative net cash flow, meaning distributions minus calls, over a fund's life, you get the industry's most famous shape. It goes down for years, and then, hopefully, it comes back up. That's the J-curve.

Let's take our LP's £10m commitment through the full life of a decent fund.

Year Calls (£m) Distributions (£m) Net flow (£m) Cumulative net (£m) NAV (£m)
1 (2.5) – (2.5) (2.5) 2.2
2 (3.0) – (3.0) (5.5) 5.0
3 (2.5) 0.5 (2.0) (7.5) 7.6
4 (1.5) 1.5 0.0 (7.5) 9.0
5 (0.5) 2.5 2.0 (5.5) 8.5
6 – 3.5 3.5 (2.0) 6.5
7 – 4.0 4.0 2.0 3.5
8 – 3.0 3.0 5.0 1.5
9 – 1.5 1.5 6.5 0.5
10 – 1.0 1.0 7.5 –

The total called is £10.0m, and the total distributed is £17.5m, which is a net multiple of 1.75x on paid-in capital. But look at the path. The LP is out of pocket until year 7, reaches its maximum exposure of £7.5m in years 3 and 4, and only breaks even in cash terms when the fund is seven years old.

Early on, the J-curve is steepest in the reported returns, and there are two mechanical reasons for that. First, management fees are drawn from day one. In year 1, our LP paid £0.2m of fees inside that £2.5m call, while the investments were still held at cost. So the NAV, at £2.2m, sits below the paid-in capital, and the interim IRR is sharply negative. Second, conservative valuation practice holds new deals at cost, while any problems are written down promptly, so the early valuations skew negative. A three-year-old fund with an IRR of minus 5% may be doing perfectly well, and lesson 6 comes back to why interim IRRs mislead.

So what do LPs do about the J-curve? They commit steadily across different vintage years, so that the distributions from older funds pay for the calls from younger ones. That's called a "self-financing" programme. They buy stakes in mature funds on the secondaries market, which also prices the J-curve; buying in at year 5 skips the worst of it. And they tolerate GPs using subscription credit lines, which flatten the early part of the curve cosmetically. Lesson 6 covers that controversy.

§5.2.5The legal architecture: LP, GP entity, management company

"The fund" isn't a company. It's a limited partnership, and it's chosen for two properties. First, it's transparent for tax purposes, meaning profits flow through to the investors and are taxed in their hands, which is vital for pension funds and international LPs. Second, it hard-wires the split between passive LPs and an active GP. Common places to set them up include England, Scotland, Delaware, Luxembourg, the Channel Islands and the Cayman Islands. Scottish limited partnerships are popular because they have a separate legal personality.

Three entities matter here, and it's worth keeping them straight, because fees, carry and liability each flow to a different one.

  1. The fund, which is the limited partnership, holds the investments. The LPs are its limited partners.
  2. The GP entity is a special-purpose company that acts as the fund's general partner. It carries the theoretically unlimited liability, and it usually receives the carried interest. A fresh GP entity is created for each fund, which ring-fences the liability fund by fund.
  3. The management company, also called "the manager" or "the adviser", is the PE firm itself. It employs the people, pays the rent, and receives the management fee, under an advisory agreement with the fund. This is the entity the partners own, and it's the one that carries on from fund to fund.

So when we say "the GP earns two and twenty", which lesson 4 covers, here's what that means. The 2% management fee is revenue for the management company, and it pays the salaries. The 20% carry builds up in the GP entity, usually through a "carry partnership", whose members are the individual partners and, at better firms, the wider team. Carry is typically structured to be taxed as a capital gain rather than as income. That's a large part of why the structure looks the way it does, and it's a recurring political football in both the UK and the US.

There's one more layer you'll meet in practice. Funds often hold each portfolio company through a stack of holding companies, known as Topco, Midco and Bidco, which module 8 covers. And large LPs may invest through feeder vehicles or parallel funds, for their own tax or regulatory reasons. The economics are as described here; the organisation chart on the structure slide is just plumbing.

§5.2.6What looks good, what looks bad

So what looks good, through an LP's eyes? A GP commitment of 2% or more, in cash. A diversified, stable base of LPs, with high re-up rates from existing investors. That's the single strongest external signal, because the people with the most information chose to come back. A clean, steady pace of capital calls. LPA terms close to market standard, in line with the guidelines from ILPA, the industry body for LPs. And an experienced, independent fund administrator.

And what looks bad? A GP commitment funded entirely by fee waivers or loans. One LP making up 40% of the fund, which is concentration risk, because if they wobble, the fund fails. Heavy reliance on new LPs because past investors have quietly declined to re-up. LP defaults in the previous fund. And capital-call notices that are opaque or chronically late. Sloppy fund operations are a leading indicator of sloppiness everywhere else.

Next comes the fund's timeline: fundraising, the investment period, the harvest, and how a GP decides how many deals to do, and at what size.

Lesson 5.3/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

The Fund Lifecycle

25 min read
In brief

This lesson follows the ten-plus-year life of a fund: fundraising, the investment period, the harvest, and extensions. It covers vintage years, dry powder and recycling, and how a GP constructs a portfolio, meaning the number of deals, the size of the cheques, and the reserves, with a worked example of a £500m fund.

  1. 5.3.1The shape of a fund's life
  2. 5.3.2Fundraising and closings
  3. 5.3.3The investment period
  4. 5.3.4Portfolio construction: a worked £500m fund
  5. 5.3.5Harvest, extensions, and the end of life
  6. 5.3.6What looks good, what looks bad

§5.3.1The shape of a fund's life

A buyout fund is a machine with a timer. The LPA typically sets a ten-year term. Roughly years 1 to 5 are for buying companies, which is the investment period. Years 4 to 10 are for improving them and selling them, which is the harvest period. The two overlap, because early deals exit while late ones are still being made. On top of that, there's the option of extensions, usually two one-year extensions, where the first is at the GP's discretion, and the second needs the LPs' consent. In practice, the average fund takes 12 to 14 years to wind up completely, and LPs grumble about that constantly.

Lay the fundraising cycle on top, and a GP's decade looks like this. It raises Fund II while it's investing Fund I. Then, when Fund II is around 70 to 80% invested, which is often the LPA's own threshold before a successor fund can be raised, it goes to market with Fund III. So a healthy firm has two or three funds alive at once, each at a different stage. That's exactly the two-fund fee arithmetic we did in lesson 1. The flywheel only keeps spinning if exits from the old fund arrive in time to sell the track record for the new one. When exit markets freeze, fundraising freezes about eighteen months later. The whole industry's rhythm follows the exit environment, which module 11 covers.

§5.3.2Fundraising and closings

Fundraising is a sales process lasting 12 to 24 months, run by the IR team and placement agents. The GP issues a private placement memorandum, or PPM, the LPs run their due diligence, and commitments are gathered in stages called closings. At the first close, the fund can legally start doing deals. More LPs join at later closes, until the final close, which is capped by the LPA's hard cap. LPs who join late pay an equalisation adjustment, plus interest, so that everyone is treated as if they'd invested from day one.

There are three terms that deal teams use loosely, but that you should use precisely.

  • The target is the number on the cover of the PPM, say £500m.
  • The hard cap is the contractual maximum, say £600m. "Raised at the hard cap in a single close" is the industry's way of showing off. "Extended fundraising, with a final close below target" is the euphemism for a struggle.
  • The vintage year is the year the fund starts deploying capital. Conventions vary; it might be the year of the final close, the first close, or the first capital call. But a fund is benchmarked only against funds of the same vintage, as lesson 6 explains. Comparing a 2019-vintage fund with a 2021-vintage one tells you about the markets, not about the managers.

Diversifying across vintages matters, because the year you enter dominates the outcome. Funds that deployed at the prices of 2006 and 2007 mostly limped along, while funds from the 2009 and 2010 vintages, which bought cheaply into the recovery, were among the best ever. Since nobody can time this, disciplined LPs commit similar amounts every year, and let the vintages average out.

§5.3.3The investment period

During the investment period, which is typically five years, though sometimes four or six, the GP can call capital for new platform deals. When the period ends, or earlier if the fund becomes fully invested, investing in new deals stops. After that, capital can usually only be called for follow-on investments in existing companies, and for fees and expenses. Two consequences follow from this clock.

The pace of deployment. A £500m fund with a five-year investment period needs to invest roughly £85m to £100m a year. If it goes too slowly, the fund risks expiring with capital still unspent, while the IRR clock ticks on nothing. If it goes too fast, the fund concentrates its money into a single price environment; the frantic deployment of 2021, at peak multiples, is the cautionary tale. LPs scrutinise the pace in every quarterly report. A GP that suddenly does four deals in the final six months of its investment period is chasing the clock, and everyone knows it.

Dry powder. At any moment, the capital that's been committed but not yet called is the fund's dry powder. If our £500m fund has called £280m so far, its dry powder is £220m. That's true regardless of any distributions it's paid out, because, as lesson 2 established, distributions don't refill the uncalled pot. Dry powder across the industry runs into the trillions, and that's why competitive auctions stay competitive even in downturns. The money is contractually committed, and it's paying fees, so it will be spent.

Recycling. LPAs usually let the GP reinvest, or "recycle", some of its early proceeds, rather than distributing them. That's commonly capped at 10 to 25% of commitments, and often limited to proceeds from investments realised within, say, 18 months, or to recouping amounts used for fees. Here's the point. On a £500m fund paying £68m of fees over its life, only £432m would otherwise ever reach the companies. Recycling lets the GP get closer to putting the full £500m to work. That's good for the LPs' money multiple, because more capital is earning a return, at the price of getting cash back slightly later.

§5.3.4Portfolio construction: a worked £500m fund

Before the first deal is done, the GP has already decided the shape of the portfolio, and pitched it to the LPs. Let's construct our running £500m buyout fund properly.

Step 1 is the investable capital. Lesson 4 derives the lifetime fees and expenses. They're 2.0% on £500m for five years, which is £50m, then 1.5% on the declining invested cost, which is about £18m, making £68m in total. Add about £7m of partnership expenses, and assume recycling recovers about £25m of that. Call the investable capital £450m.

Step 2 is the reserves. The GP holds back capital for follow-on investments. Those might be equity injections to fund add-on acquisitions, which is module 10's buy-and-build, or defensive top-ups for companies in trouble with their covenants. Buyout funds typically reserve 10 to 20% of their investable capital. VC funds reserve far more, often about half, because their winners raise several rounds. Let's take 15%. That makes reserves of £68m, which leaves £382m for platform deals.

Step 3 is the number of deals, and the size of the cheques.

Design Platforms Avg equity cheque Implication
Concentrated 8 £48m Each deal ~10% of fund; one zero forfeits ~0.25x of expected TVPI
Chosen 12 £32m Each deal ~6–7% of fund; two failures survivable
Diffuse 20 £19m No deal moves the fund; team of 10 can't govern 20 boards

Twelve platforms, with an average equity cheque of £32m, since £382m ÷ 12 ≈ £31.8m, is a classic mid-market shape. It's concentrated enough that good deals matter, and diversified enough that one failure doesn't sink the fund. Sanity-check the cheque against the strategy. £32m of equity, at a loan-to-value of about 50%, buys an enterprise value of around £65m. That's a company making roughly £8m of EBITDA, at 8x. If the firm's pipeline is actually made up of businesses with £3m of EBITDA, then the fund is too big for its strategy. That mismatch is the strategy drift red flag from lesson 1.

Step 4 is the pace. Twelve platforms over five years means two or three deals a year. That's comfortably achievable for a team of, say, four partners, each leading roughly one deal every 18 months.

Here's the arithmetic that LPs run on how much failure a fund can tolerate. For the fund to return 2.0x gross, the £450m invested has to become £900m. If two of the £32m deals go to zero, that's £64m lost, and the remaining £386m of cost has to generate the whole £900m. That's 2.33x on everything else, which is feasible. In the concentrated design, two £48m deals going to zero would leave £354m of cost needing to produce the £900m. That's 2.5x on every survivor, which is heroic. That's why "how many deals, what size of cheque, and what reserves?" is the first page of every LP's underwriting.

§5.3.5Harvest, extensions, and the end of life

From roughly year 4, the exits begin. The GP's job flips from buying to selling, which means getting companies ready for exit, timing the sale, and choosing the route, whether a trade sale, a secondary buyout or an IPO, as module 11 covers. As each deal is realised, the distributions flow through the waterfall, which is lesson 5. A well-run fund is largely realised by year 10.

Then reality sets in. There are nearly always stragglers: the two companies that missed their plan, and won't fetch an acceptable price. Here are the options, in rising order of how difficult they are for relations with the LPs.

  • Extensions. Use the one- or two-year extensions. Fees during extensions are typically reduced, or waived altogether.
  • Sell anyway. Take the disappointing price and return the cash. It's often the right answer, but GPs find it chronically hard, because it crystallises the bad valuation.
  • Continuation vehicles. Sell the asset or assets from the old fund into a new vehicle, managed by the same GP and funded by secondaries investors, which gives the old LPs the option to cash out. This is now mainstream, but it's full of conflicts, because the GP sits on both sides of the price. So expect fairness opinions, and votes by the LP advisory committee.
  • Liquidating the tail. Distribute the remaining assets in kind, or sell what's left of the portfolio to a secondaries buyer.

A "zombie fund" is one that's past year 10, with unsold assets, no successor fund coming, and fees still trickling in. It's the worst outcome short of actual losses. The team has no carry incentive left, and the LPs have no way out. LPs diligence the tail end of a GP's previous funds for exactly this pattern.

§5.3.6What looks good, what looks bad

So what looks good? Steady deployment, with roughly level annual investment across the period. Cheque sizes consistent with the stated strategy, and with the previous fund, allowing for growth in fund size. Reserves actually used for follow-ons that add value. Funds largely realised by year 10 to 12. And successor funds raised on a realised track record, not a paper one.

And what looks bad? A cliff of deployment at the end of the investment period. A fund size up 2.5 times, with the same team and strategy, which suggests the motive is fees. Repeated extensions, with full fees. A continuation vehicle for the good assets, priced by the GP itself without any competitive tension. Dry powder still above 40% in year 4, which means either the market or the team isn't working. And recycling used aggressively to inflate the story on invested capital.

Next, we'll look at precisely how the GP gets paid: the mechanics of the management fee, offsets, the hurdle and catch-up, and the full economics of a two-and-twenty fund.

Lesson 5.4/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

Fees and Carried Interest

30 min read
In brief

This lesson explains how the GP gets paid. It covers the mechanics of the management fee, including the step-down from committed to invested capital, fee offsets, the 8% preferred return, and the catch-up. It finishes with the full worked economics of two and twenty for a £500m fund, showing exactly how 2.5x gross becomes 1.93x net.

  1. 5.4.1Two-and-twenty: the headline and the reality
  2. 5.4.2Management fee mechanics: the step-down
  3. 5.4.3Fee offsets and the other fee streams
  4. 5.4.4The hurdle: 8% preferred return
  5. 5.4.5The catch-up
  6. 5.4.6Full worked example: 2-and-20 on the £500m fund
  7. 5.4.7What looks good, what looks bad

§5.4.1Two-and-twenty: the headline and the reality

Here's the famous formula. The GP charges a management fee of around 2% a year, and keeps 20% of the profits as carried interest, usually above an 8% preferred return to the LPs. "Two and twenty" is a fine first approximation, but it's wrong in every detail. The base for the fee changes over the fund's life, and parts of it get offset. The 20% only switches on after a hurdle-and-catch-up mechanism. And market rates vary with the size of the fund and its negotiating power. Large buyout funds often charge 1.5 to 1.75%, while sought-after mid-market funds still get 2%, and some GPs now offer 25 to 30% carry in exchange for a higher hurdle. This lesson builds each piece in turn, and then assembles the full economics of our £500m fund.

Keep the map of entities from lesson 2 in mind. The management fee is revenue for the management company, and it pays salaries whether or not the fund performs. Carry is a share of profit that flows to the GP entity, and it only pays out on success, usually years after the work was done. The fee pays the mortgage; the carry builds the house.

§5.4.2Management fee mechanics: the step-down

The fee works in two regimes, split at the end of the investment period.

  • During the investment period, which is years 1 to 5, it's a percentage of committed capital. That's the whole £500m, however little has actually been invested. The rationale is that the team's cost of finding and executing deals scales with the size of the mandate, not with the capital deployed so far. The effect is that the fee is at its highest precisely when the fund has done the least, and that's the engine of the J-curve from lesson 2.
  • After the investment period, the base steps down to invested capital. That's usually the cost of the investments still held, sometimes called net invested capital, so deals that have been realised or written off drop out of the base. Often the rate drops too, from 2.0% to between 1.5 and 1.75%. The rationale is that the job is now looking after a shrinking portfolio.

Here's a worked example for our £500m fund, at 2.0%, stepping down to 1.5% on invested cost.

Years Basis Amount (£m) Rate Fee (£m)
1–5 Committed capital 500 2.0% 10.0 × 5 = 50.0
6 Invested cost 400 1.5% 6.00
7 Invested cost 350 1.5% 5.25
8 Invested cost 250 1.5% 3.75
9 Invested cost 150 1.5% 2.25
10 Invested cost 50 1.5% 0.75
Lifetime 68.0

£68m, which is 13.6% of commitments, goes on fees over the life of the fund. That's capital the LPs pay in that never buys a company, so only £432m of the £500m reaches deals, although recycling can claw some back, as lesson 3 explained. When LPs talk about "fee drag", this is the number they mean. And it's the reason the step-down exists at all. Without it, 2% of £500m for ten years would be £100m, a fifth of the fund, and the economics would be indefensible. A fund that charges on committed capital for its whole term, or whose definition of "invested capital" quietly includes realised deals, is taking £10m to £30m that market-standard terms wouldn't allow. So read the definition in the LPA, not just the headline rate.

§5.4.3Fee offsets and the other fee streams

Historically, GPs double-dipped. As well as the management fee, they charged the portfolio companies a range of fees: transaction fees of 1 to 2% of the deal value for doing the deal, annual "advisory" monitoring fees, directors' fees, and break fees on deals that died. Since the LPs ultimately own those companies, these fees came out of the LPs' pockets and went into the management company.

The fix is the management fee offset. A percentage of those fees is credited against the management fee. The market standard is now a 100% offset, or 80% among the laggards. Here's a worked example. Our GP charges a portfolio company a £2.0m transaction fee at closing. With a 100% offset, the next £2.0m of management fee that the LPs would otherwise owe is cancelled. The GP is left exactly indifferent, and that's the point, because offsets kill the incentive to milk portfolio companies. With an 80% offset, the GP keeps £0.4m and offsets £1.6m.

Some costs are still borne by the LPs, outside the fee. There are organisational expenses, meaning the legal costs of setting up the fund, typically capped at around £1m to £2m. There are partnership expenses, such as audit, administration and valuation. And there are broken-deal costs, for transactions the fund pursued and lost. These can be material, at £5m or more over a fund's life, and LPs increasingly demand that they're disclosed. When you see a "Total Expense Ratio" in an LP report, it's trying to capture all of this, not just the 2%.

§5.4.4The hurdle: 8% preferred return

Carry doesn't switch on with the first pound of profit. First, the LPs have to get their capital back, plus a preferred return, known as the hurdle. That's almost always 8% a year, compounded, building up on each drawdown from the date the cash left the LP until the date it comes back. The logic is that 8% roughly matched what LPs could earn in liquid markets, so the GP should only be paid for performance above that opportunity cost. And yes, the number has survived every interest-rate regime since the 1980s. It's a convention everyone has settled on, not a calculation. Credit funds use 6 to 7%, and some VC funds have no hurdle at all.

There are two flavours that matter.

  • A soft hurdle, with a catch-up, is overwhelmingly the standard, and it's described below. Once the hurdle has been cleared, the GP catches up, so that its carry ends up as 20% of all the profits.
  • A hard hurdle means the GP only earns carry on the profits above the hurdle, with no catch-up. It's much friendlier to LPs, and much rarer.

Because the preferred return compounds day by day on the actual drawdowns, the entitlement in pounds depends on the timing of the fund's cash flows. A fund that returns capital quickly builds up a smaller preferred return. In our worked examples, we'll state the calculated entitlement as an assumption, and just note the shape. £500m drawn over five years, and returned over years 5 to 10, builds up a preferred return somewhere in the region of £150m to £200m.

§5.4.5The catch-up

After the preferred return, the standard waterfall inserts a GP catch-up tier. The GP receives all of the distributions, which is called a "100% catch-up", until it has received 20% of the cumulative profits distributed so far. Some funds use a 50% catch-up instead, which just stretches the tier out. After that, the split settles at 80 to 20.

Here's the arithmetic that everyone gets wrong the first time. If the LPs have received a preferred return of £24m, the catch-up is not 20% of £24m, which would be £4.8m. The GP catches up until its receipts are 20% of the total profit distributions. Let the catch-up be ccc. We need c=0.20×(24+c)c = 0.20 \times (24 + c)c=0.20×(24+c), so 0.8c=4.80.8c = 4.80.8c=4.8, and c=£6.0mc = £6.0mc=£6.0m. To check: the total profits distributed are £30m, and the GP has £6m, which is exactly 20%. The general shortcut for a 100% catch-up is that the catch-up equals the preferred return divided by 4, because it's the preferred return divided by 0.8, multiplied by 0.2.

Here's the effect of the whole mechanism of preferred return plus catch-up. For a fund that comfortably clears the hurdle, the GP ends up with a straight 20% of the total profits. So the hurdle only protects LPs in mediocre outcomes, but there it bites hard. A fund returning just above capital plus the preferred return generates almost no carry. This pattern of a "dead zone, then a cliff" is worth internalising. Around the hurdle, small changes in the fund's outcome swing the carry violently, and that's exactly when GPs get creative about valuations and the timing of exits.

§5.4.6Full worked example: 2-and-20 on the £500m fund

Let's put everything together. Here are the assumptions. £500m is committed and fully drawn. The fees are as we calculated, £68m, so £432m is invested, with no recycling. The portfolio returns 2.5x gross on invested capital. The preferred return entitlement works out at £180m. There's a 100% catch-up, 20% carry, and a whole-fund, or European, waterfall; lesson 5 contrasts the alternative.

The gross proceeds are 2.5 times £432m, which gives £1,080m. So the fund's profit over contributions is £1,080m minus £500m, which gives £580m.

Tier Rule Amount (£m) To LPs (£m) To GP (£m)
1. Return of capital 100% to LPs until £500m returned 500.0 500.0 –
2. Preferred return 100% to LPs until 8% pref paid 180.0 180.0 –
3. GP catch-up 100% to GP until GP has 20% of profits 45.0 – 45.0
4. 80/20 split Remaining proceeds 355.0 284.0 71.0
Total 1,080.0 964.0 116.0

Here are the checks worth doing by hand, every time. The catch-up is 180 ÷ 4, which is £45m, and after tier 3, the GP holds £45m of the £225m of profits distributed, which is 20% ✓. The residual is 1,080 − 500 − 180 − 45, which is £355m, split £284m and £71m ✓. The total carry of £116m is 20% of the £580m total profit ✓. And the distributions total 964 + 116, which is £1,080m ✓.

Now for the scoreboard.

Measure Calculation Result
Gross multiple on invested capital 1,080 ÷ 432 2.50x
Gross multiple on committed capital 1,080 ÷ 500 2.16x
Net multiple to LPs (TVPI) 964 ÷ 500 1.93x
GP: lifetime management fee £68m
GP: carried interest 20% × 580 £116m
GP: total take 68 + 116 £184m

Here's the one-line summary that deal teams carry around: a 2.5x gross became a 1.93x net. Roughly 0.6x of multiple, or about a quarter of the LPs' profit, was absorbed by fees and carry. In terms of IRR, the same fund might be about 24% gross, and 17 to 18% net. The GP's total take of £184m on a £500m fund also explains lesson 3's warning about fees motivating bigger funds. Doubling the size of the fund roughly doubles the fee stream, whatever the performance.

§5.4.7What looks good, what looks bad

So what looks good, through an LP's lens? Terms of 2%, 20% and 8%, with a step-down to invested cost and 100% offsets. In other words, boring, market-standard terms. Carry spread across the team, which helps retention. A GP commitment of 2% or more, in cash. And a GP that's willing to show its track record net of everything, without being asked.

And what looks bad? Fees charged on committed capital for the whole term. "Invested capital" defined to include realised investments. Offsets below 100%, combined with actively charging monitoring fees. Management fee waivers recharacterised as the GP commitment, where the GP contributes fees it has given up instead of cash, which means less skin in the game, plus some tax games. No hurdle, or carry above 20% without a matching increase in the hurdle. And heavy, undisclosed broken-deal and travel expenses pushed onto the fund.

Lesson 5.5/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

Distribution Waterfalls

30 min read
In brief

This lesson explains how exit proceeds are split between the LPs and the GP. It covers the four-tier waterfall, and works through the European, or whole-fund, and American, or deal-by-deal, mechanics, with full numerical tables on the same £100m fund. It shows why the two arrive at the same totals, but differ in timing and risk, and how clawback and escrow protect the LPs.

  1. 5.5.1What a waterfall is
  2. 5.5.2European (whole-fund) waterfall: worked example
  3. 5.5.3American (deal-by-deal) waterfall: worked example
  4. 5.5.4Clawback: the true-up, with numbers
  5. 5.5.5Escrow and other protections
  6. 5.5.6What looks good, what looks bad

§5.5.1What a waterfall is

When a portfolio company is sold, cash arrives at the fund, and it has to be divided between the LPs and the GP. The LPA prescribes how, as a sequence of tiers. Each tier has to fill up completely before a single drop reaches the next one, which is why it's called a waterfall. Here are the four standard tiers, which we assembled in lesson 4.

  1. First, return of capital. All of it goes to the LPs, until their contributed capital is back.
  2. Second, the preferred return. All of it goes to the LPs, until the 8% compounded preferred return has been paid.
  3. Third, the GP catch-up. All of it goes to the GP, until the GP holds 20% of the profits distributed so far. With a 100% catch-up, the catch-up equals the preferred return divided by 4.
  4. Fourth, the carry split. Everything after that is split 80% to the LPs and 20% to the GP.

The tiers themselves are settled ground. The fight is over scope. Is the waterfall applied to the fund as a whole, or deal by deal? That single choice, between a European, or whole-fund, waterfall and an American, or deal-by-deal, one, decides when the GP first sees carry, and who bears the risk of losses that come late. The names are conventions rather than geography, though European funds do mostly use the whole-fund version, and US funds historically used deal-by-deal.

§5.5.2European (whole-fund) waterfall: worked example

Under a whole-fund waterfall, tiers 1 and 2 apply to the entire fund's capital. The GP receives no carry until the LPs have got back all of their contributed capital, for every deal and for the fees, and the full preferred return. So the proceeds from early exits all go to the LPs.

Here's a worked example. A £100m fund, all of it called, distributes £250m over its life. Let's assume that the compounded 8% preferred return entitlement works out at £40m.

Tier Rule Amount (£m) To LPs (£m) To GP (£m)
1. Return of capital 100% LP until £100m 100.0 100.0 –
2. Preferred return 100% LP until pref paid 40.0 40.0 –
3. GP catch-up 100% GP until 20% of profits 10.0 – 10.0
4. 80/20 Balance 100.0 80.0 20.0
Total 250.0 220.0 30.0

Here are the checks. The catch-up is 40 ÷ 4, which is £10m. After tier 3, the GP holds £10m of the £50m of profits distributed, which is 20% ✓. The balance is 250 − 100 − 40 − 10, which is £100m ✓. The total carry of £30m is 20% of the fund's £150m profit ✓. And the LPs' 220 plus the GP's 30 makes 250 ✓.

The defining feature is when tier 3 arrives. Suppose this fund's exits came in at £75m in year 3, £15m in year 4, £50m in year 5, and £40m or more across years 6 to 8. Then the first £140m of proceeds, which is all of the first two exits and most of the third, belongs entirely to the LPs. The GP's first pound of carry arrives around year 5, more than six years after work began on the first deal. LPs love this, because it gives maximum protection, with no risk of over-distributing. GPs point out the human consequence. Associates and principals who've been promised carry may wait a decade to see any of it, and that's a genuine retention problem at younger firms.

§5.5.3American (deal-by-deal) waterfall: worked example

Under a deal-by-deal waterfall, the four tiers apply to each realised investment separately. When deal A exits, the LPs get back deal A's capital plus a preferred return on it, and the GP takes carry on deal A's profit, even though deals B, C and D haven't been realised yet. Some protections are bolted on to stop this from being a one-way bet. First, realised losses are carried forward. A loss on any realised deal has to be netted against later profits before more carry is paid, and earlier carry is recalculated. Second, fees and expenses that haven't been returned are usually included in the capital tier. And third, the whole thing is trued up at the end by the clawback, which is the next section.

Let's take the same £100m fund, now split into four deals of £25m each. To keep the table readable, we'll assume each profitable deal's preferred return is met within the figures shown, and focus on how losses are netted off.

Exit Cost (£m) Proceeds (£m) Profit/(loss) (£m) Loss b/f applied (£m) Carry basis (£m) GP carry @20% (£m) To LPs (£m)
Yr 3: Deal A 25 75 50 – 50.0 10.0 65.0
Yr 4: Deal B 25 15 (10) – – – 15.0
Yr 5: Deal C 25 50 25 (10) 15.0 3.0 47.0
Yr 7: Deal D 25 40 15 – 15.0 3.0 37.0
Total 100 180 80 80.0 16.0 164.0

Let's walk through it. Deal A pays the GP £10m of carry in year 3. Deal B's £10m loss earns no carry, and it's carried forward. Deal C's £25m profit is first reduced by B's loss, so its carry is 20% of £15m, which is £3m. Deal D works the same way. The total carry is £16m. That's exactly 20% of the fund's total profit of £80m, which is the same as a whole-fund waterfall would eventually pay on these cash flows. You can run it yourself: capital of 100, a preferred return of, say, 30, a catch-up of 7.5, and a balance of 42.5, which gives the GP 7.5 plus 8.5, or £16m.

So in a fund that ends up comfortably successful, the two waterfalls arrive at the same total, because the loss carry-forward and the final true-up force them to. What differs is the timing. Here, under the American waterfall, the GP has £10m in year 3, while under the European one, its first carry arrives around year 5. In present-value terms, that's worth millions to the GP. And the risk differs too. Under the American waterfall, the GP is holding LP money whenever early winners come before late losers. Which brings us to the clawback.

§5.5.4Clawback: the true-up, with numbers

Let's run the American fund again, with a worse ending. This time, deals C and D each limp out at cost, with £25m of proceeds apiece.

  • The proceeds are 75 + 15 + 25 + 25, which gives £140m on £100m, so the fund's profit is £40m.
  • The carry actually paid along the way was £10m on deal A, in year 3, and nothing on B, C or D.
  • Now comes the final whole-fund test, which every American LPA includes. Let's assume the fund-level preferred return entitlement is £35m. So the LPs are entitled to 100 + 35, which is £135m, before any carry, and above that, the catch-up tier applies. Total distributions were £140m, so the GP's true entitlement is the £5m above £135m. That's a partial catch-up. A full catch-up would have been 35 ÷ 4, or £8.75m, but there's only £5m of headroom.
  • The GP holds £10m, but it's only entitled to £5m. So the clawback is £5m, which has to be repaid to the LPs.

In the end state, the LPs have £135m and the GP has £5m, making £140m in total ✓. Notice how much real work the preferred return did here. Without it, the GP's entitlement would have been 20% of £40m, which is £8m, and the clawback would only have been £2m. Around mediocre outcomes, the hurdle bites; that's lesson 4's "dead zone".

Here's why clawbacks are hated in practice, and why they're only partly effective.

  • Tax leakage. Clawback obligations are almost always calculated net of the tax that the carry-holders paid. If the GP's partners paid around £2.8m of tax on the £10m they received, the amount that can be recovered shrinks towards £7.2m, before anyone even starts arguing. So LPs may recover less than the gross amount that was over-distributed.
  • Collection risk. By year 12, the individuals who received the carry may have left, retired, divorced, or spent it. LPAs require personal guarantees from the carry-holders, sometimes on a joint basis. But chasing former partners through the courts is nobody's plan A.
  • Timing. If the clawback is only tested at final liquidation, LPs can be left out of pocket for years. Better LPAs add interim clawback tests, for example at the end of the investment period, or whenever the coverage from NAV deteriorates.

§5.5.5Escrow and other protections

Because a clawback is a remedy that looks a lot like a lawsuit, LPs prefer prevention.

  • Escrow, or holdback. A slice of each carry distribution, commonly 20 to 50% under deal-by-deal waterfalls, is held in an escrow account until the fund's final numbers are safe. In our clawback example, a 50% escrow would have held back £5m of the carry from deal A, exactly covering the shortfall, without touching anyone's bank account.
  • NAV coverage tests. Carry can only be distributed if the remaining NAV exceeds some multiple, say 125%, of the capital that hasn't yet been returned. It's a live solvency check before each carry payment.
  • The European waterfall itself. This is the bluntest protection of all. If carry only flows after all the capital and the preferred return are back, over-distribution is nearly impossible. That's why ILPA, the LPs' trade body, recommends whole-fund waterfalls as best practice, and why the market has drifted in that direction since 2008.

Here's the negotiating logic to internalise. The GP wants early carry, which means an American waterfall, low escrow, and a clawback that's net of tax. The LPs want certainty, which means a European waterfall, or an American one with a fat escrow, interim tests, and guarantees from each individual. Where a fund lands on this spectrum tells you precisely how much bargaining power the GP had when it raised the fund. Funds that are in high demand get waterfalls that favour the GP.

§5.5.6What looks good, what looks bad

So what looks good, through an LP's lens? A whole-fund waterfall; an 8% compounded preferred return; a 100% catch-up only after all the capital and the preferred return are back; escrow on any early carry; interim clawback tests; joint and several guarantees; and, where it can be achieved, which is rare, a clawback that's gross of tax. For the GP's own team, it's good to see the vesting and allocation of carry documented, so that mid-level staff genuinely benefit. That's good for the LPs too, because it helps retention.

And what looks bad? Deal-by-deal carry, with no carry-forward of losses from unrealised write-downs. That means paper losses are ignored until they're crystallised, and GPs can delay crystallising them. Low escrow, or none. A clawback that's net of a generously assumed tax rate. Carry paid out while NAV coverage is thin. And provisions for "recycled" carry, which let the GP earn again on the same profits. In diligence, LPs ask one killer question: "Have any of your previous funds had a clawback situation, and how was it resolved?" Both the answer, and the willingness to answer, tell you something.

Next, we'll look at how to measure whether any of this was worth it: IRR, the family of multiples, PME, and the tricks that flatter the numbers, subscription lines included.

Lesson 5.6/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

Fund Performance Measurement

30 min read
In brief

This lesson covers how fund performance is measured, and how it's gamed. It compares IRR with the family of multiples, TVPI, DPI, RVPI and MOIC, and explains why interim IRRs mislead. It introduces the basics of the public market equivalent, or PME, shows how LPs benchmark funds by vintage and quartile, and works through the effect of subscription credit lines on IRR, with numbers.

  1. 5.6.1Two families of metric
  2. 5.6.2The multiple family: TVPI, DPI, RVPI, MOIC
  3. 5.6.3Why interim IRRs mislead
  4. 5.6.4PME: benchmarking against public markets
  5. 5.6.5How LPs benchmark funds
  6. 5.6.6Subscription credit lines and the IRR effect
  7. 5.6.7What looks good, what looks bad

§5.6.1Two families of metric

Every question about fund performance is answered with one of two families of metric.

  • Multiples answer "how many times my money?" They're simple ratios of cash and value to the cash invested, and they ignore time completely.
  • IRR answers "at what annual rate?" It's the discount rate that sets the net present value of the fund's dated cash flows to zero, with calls as negatives, distributions as positives, and the closing NAV treated as a final inflow. It's all about time.

Neither one is enough on its own. Doubling your money over four years is excellent, an IRR of 18.9%, since 21/4=1.1892^{1/4} = 1.18921/4=1.189. But doubling it over ten years is pedestrian, at 7.2%. And the other way round, a 40% IRR on a deal held for eight months that returned 1.25x barely moved the fund. So LPs always quote the pair: "net TVPI and net IRR". And deal teams keep the doubling table in their heads: doubling in 3 years is about 26%, in 4 years about 19%, and in 5 years about 15%.

Always check whether a figure is gross or net. Gross is before management fees, expenses and carry, so it measures performance at the level of the deals. Net is what the LPs actually got. The fund in lesson 4 ran at 2.5x gross and 1.93x net, which is roughly a 24% gross IRR, landing at 17 to 18% net. Any track-record slide that doesn't say which one it's quoting is quoting gross.

§5.6.2The multiple family: TVPI, DPI, RVPI, MOIC

All of these multiples are anchored on paid-in capital, which is the cumulative capital called, including fees. Here's a worked example. A fund in year 8 has called £400m, distributed £520m, and holds a remaining portfolio with a NAV of £280m.

Metric Formula Calculation Result
DPI ("distributions to paid-in") Cumulative distributions ÷ paid-in 520 ÷ 400 1.30x
RVPI ("residual value to paid-in") NAV ÷ paid-in 280 ÷ 400 0.70x
TVPI ("total value to paid-in") (Distributions + NAV) ÷ paid-in 800 ÷ 400 2.00x

TVPI always equals DPI plus RVPI, and that breakdown is the whole point. This fund claims 2.0x, but only 1.3x has been realised, as cash in the LPs' bank accounts. The other 0.7x rests on the GP's own valuations. The older the fund, the more DPI should dominate. LPs have a shorthand for this: "DPI is truth, RVPI is opinion, and TVPI is the pitch." A nine-year-old fund boasting a TVPI of 2.2x, with a DPI of only 0.4x, is telling you that its winners haven't been sold, or can't be.

MOIC, the multiple of invested capital, is the same idea, but calculated on invested cost rather than paid-in capital, and it's usually gross. Deal teams use MOIC for individual deals, as in "a 3.1x MOIC on Project Falcon", while LPs use TVPI and DPI for funds. Because paid-in capital includes the fees, the net TVPI is lower than the gross MOIC for the same portfolio. Sloppy decks blur this line, so always ask which denominator is being used.

§5.6.3Why interim IRRs mislead

Here's the industry's dirty secret: a fund's IRR in years 1 to 5 is close to meaningless, and yet that's precisely when the GP is fundraising on it. There are four mechanical reasons.

  1. The J-curve, from lesson 2. Early fees on committed capital, plus assets held at cost, push the early IRR negative. That reveals nothing about the fund's eventual quality.
  2. Unrealised valuations. An interim IRR treats the current NAV as if it were a cash inflow today. But NAV is an estimate of fair value produced by the GP. It's audited, but there's genuine latitude, in which comparable multiples are chosen, and which budgets are believed. The IRR inherits every one of those assumptions.
  3. Explosive results on a small base. A single early win annualises absurdly. A fund that returns 1.3x on its first small deal within 18 months prints an IRR of around 19%, from 1.31/1.5=1.191.3^{1/1.5} = 1.191.31/1.5=1.19, on a tiny amount of capital, and that number will drift down for a decade. An early top-quartile IRR has almost no power to predict where the fund will finally rank. Funds routinely swing two quartiles between years 3 and 10.
  4. The quirks of money-weighting. IRR implicitly assumes that interim distributions are reinvested at the IRR itself. So a fund that returns capital quickly can post a stellar IRR on a modest total profit. But you can't eat IRR. A fund with a 30% IRR and a DPI of 1.5x made its LPs less money than a fund with a 17% IRR at 2.1x.

So here's the discipline LPs apply. They judge funds younger than about six years mainly on deployment, discipline at entry, and the health of the portfolio, rather than on IRR. From year 6 onwards, they watch DPI converge on TVPI. And they treat any IRR quoted to one decimal place as false precision.

§5.6.4PME: benchmarking against public markets

An LP's real alternative was an index fund. So the sharpest question is: did this fund beat the public market, on exactly the same cash flows? Public Market Equivalent, or PME, analysis answers that by replaying the fund's calls and distributions into a public index.

The cleanest version is the Kaplan–Schoar PME. You roll every cash flow forward to today using the index's return, and then calculate KS-PME=FV(distributions)+NAVFV(contributions)\text{KS-PME} = \frac{FV(\text{distributions}) + \text{NAV}}{FV(\text{contributions})}KS-PME=FV(contributions)FV(distributions)+NAV​ A result above 1.0 means the fund beat the index. Below 1.0, the LP paid fees for underperformance.

Here's a worked example. An LP pays £100m into a fund at the start, and the fund distributes £250m at year 5, with nothing else left. Over the same five years, the chosen index returned 2.0x. So if the £100m had gone into the index instead, it would be worth £200m at year 5. The Kaplan–Schoar PME is 250 ÷ 200, which is 1.25. The fund delivered 25% more wealth than the index, with identical timing. But if the index had returned 2.6x, the PME would be 250 ÷ 260, which is 0.96. So a fund that proudly reported a TVPI of 2.5x and an IRR of about 20% would still have destroyed value compared with indexing. That's entirely possible in a strong bull market, and it's exactly why LPs run PME.

There are some practical notes. The choice of index moves the answer. Small-cap or sector indices are fairer than the FTSE 100 for mid-market funds, and choosing a flattering index is a classic GP trick. Variants such as PME+ and direct alpha fix some technical quirks. And PME on young funds inherits the same dependence on NAV as an interim IRR.

§5.6.5How LPs benchmark funds

Here's the standard machinery.

  • Peer groups by vintage year. A fund is ranked against funds of the same vintage, strategy and geography, using databases such as Burgiss, Cambridge Associates, Preqin or PitchBook. Quartile boundaries on net IRR and net TVPI are the common language. "Top quartile" means above the 25th-percentile boundary of that group.
  • Beware of quartile arbitrage. There are several benchmark providers, several metrics, IRR or TVPI, and several ways of assigning the vintage, first close or first call. So a middling fund can usually find some cut on which it's "top quartile", and that's why a comfortable majority of funds in the market claim to be. Diligent LPs recalculate the quartiles themselves on a consistent benchmark, and ask for the full tape of cash flows, rather than summary numbers.
  • Persistence. The evidence is that performance does persist across a GP's successive funds, but less than it used to, and it's stronger at the bottom than at the top; bad managers stay bad. Hence the LP mantra. Decisions to re-up weigh the continuity of the team and the discipline of the strategy as heavily as the raw track record, because the numbers were earned by specific people, at a specific fund size.
  • Attribution. Sophisticated LPs break returns down. How much came from leverage, from multiple expansion, and from EBITDA growth? That's module 7's value-creation bridge. How concentrated were the returns in one or two deals? As in, "take out your best deal, and what does the fund look like?" And how do they split between realised and unrealised?

§5.6.6Subscription credit lines and the IRR effect

A subscription credit line, or "sub line", is a bank facility that's secured not on the portfolio companies, but on the LPs' uncalled commitments. The bank is lending against the enforceability of the capital calls. Its original purpose was operational convenience. It would bridge a deal closing for a few weeks, so the GP could call capital once a quarter, rather than pestering the LPs deal by deal.

The modern controversy is that GPs leave sub lines outstanding for 6 to 24 months. So the LPs' capital goes in later, and the measured IRR clock starts later. Here's a worked example.

  • A deal costs £50m, is held for five years, and returns £100m, so it's a 2.0x. If LP capital funds it on day one, the LP IRR is 21/5−1=14.9%2^{1/5} - 1 = 14.9\%21/5−1=14.9%.
  • Now take the same deal, but with a sub line funding the first 12 months, and the LP capital called at the end of year 1. The LPs' money is out for four years, so the LP IRR is 21/4−1=18.9%2^{1/4} - 1 = 18.9\%21/4−1=18.9%.

That's four points of IRR conjured up from financing mechanics, while the underlying deal is identical. Meanwhile, the interest cost, say 2 to 3% on the drawn line for a year, or about £1.2m here, comes out of the proceeds. So the multiple falls slightly: the LPs receive about £98.8m, which is 1.98x. Sub lines trade TVPI down in exchange for IRR up. And since the headline league tables run on IRR, GPs are happy to make that trade.

There are some second-order effects worth knowing. The 8% preferred return builds up from the capital call dates, so delaying calls shrinks the preferred return entitlement, and gets the GP to its carry sooner. That's a genuine conflict of interest, not just cosmetics. Early fund IRRs become spectacular, and meaningless; they can even be briefly infinite, if distributions come before any call at all. And in a crisis, a levered fund still has to call the capital, right into the teeth of the LPs' own liquidity stress. So ILPA's guidance asks GPs to report IRR both with and without the facility, to cap its size, typically at 15 to 25% of commitments, and its duration, and to disclose its costs. When you compare two funds' IRRs, the first diligence question is now: "how much do you use your sub line?" An unlevered 16% can be better than a levered 18%.

§5.6.7What looks good, what looks bad

So what looks good? Net numbers volunteered alongside the gross ones. A DPI of at least 1.0x by around year 7 or 8, converging towards TVPI after that. Returns spread broadly across the portfolio, rather than coming from one hero deal. A Kaplan–Schoar PME comfortably above 1.0, against a fair index. Conservative valuations, with exits consistently at or above the last carrying value, which is the cleanest single test of honest valuation. And use of the sub line disclosed, with IRRs shown both with and without it.

And what looks bad? "Performance" that's heavy on TVPI and light on DPI, late in the fund's life. An IRR quoted gross, with leverage, and to one decimal place. Claims to be top quartile that only survive on one metric, from one provider. Exits repeatedly below carrying value, which means the valuations were marketing. A track record whose authors have left. A refusal to share the tape of cash flows. And the perennial one: a GP fundraising on the 28% IRR of a three-year-old fund. You now know all four reasons why that number is a placeholder, not a result.

That completes the toolkit for fund mechanics. You can now read the economic terms of an LPA, trace a pound all the way from capital call to clawback, and interrogate any claim about performance that a GP makes.

Lesson 6.1/The Deal Lifecycle

Sourcing and Origination

22 min read
In brief

This lesson looks at where deals come from. It compares proprietary origination with deals brought by intermediaries, explains how sell-side advisers bring auctions to market, and covers what teasers and CIMs contain, and how to read them sceptically. It also covers NDAs, and explains why the quality of a fund's origination engine drives its returns.

  1. 6.1.1Where deals actually come from
  2. 6.1.2Proprietary vs intermediated: what the difference is worth
  3. 6.1.3Sell-side advisors and how auctions come to market
  4. 6.1.4The teaser: one page, no name
  5. 6.1.5NDAs: what you're actually agreeing to
  6. 6.1.6The CIM: what's in one
  7. 6.1.7How to read a CIM sceptically
  8. 6.1.8Why origination quality drives fund returns

§6.1.1Where deals actually come from

Before a deal team ever builds a model, someone has to find the deal. Origination is the top of the funnel, and it shapes everything that follows: the price you pay, the information you get, and the competition you face. Deals reach a PE fund through a handful of channels.

  • Intermediated, or auction, deals. A sell-side adviser, which might be an investment bank or an M&A boutique, runs a structured sale process and invites several buyers to take part. Most mid-market and large-cap deals arrive this way.
  • Limited, or targeted, processes. Here the adviser approaches only three to six carefully chosen buyers, trading a little competitive tension for speed and confidentiality.
  • Proprietary deals. Here, the fund finds the company itself. That might be through a partner's relationship with a founder, a programme of outreach driven by an investment thesis, a buy-and-build platform approaching bolt-on targets directly, or an introduction from an operating partner or the CEO of a portfolio company.

The word "proprietary" gets abused. A deal that a banker showed you first isn't proprietary; it's just early. A genuinely proprietary deal is one where no other buyer is at the table, and no adviser is running a process to discover the price. These are rare, perhaps 10 to 20% of completed mid-market deals, depending on the market. And they're prized, because in an auction it's competition, not cleverness, that sets the price.

§6.1.2Proprietary vs intermediated: what the difference is worth

The economics are simple and brutal. In a competitive auction, the clearing price is set by the most optimistic, or the most desperate, credible bidder. In a proprietary deal, the price is a negotiation, anchored on what alternatives the seller has.

Here's a worked example. Take a target with £10m of EBITDA. In a well-run auction, comparable businesses clear at 9.0x, so you'd pay an EV of £90m. Sourced proprietarily, the same business might be agreed at 7.5x, which is an EV of £75m. That's because the founder values certainty, speed and the relationship, and there's no rival bid to push the price up.

Let's assume both deals are funded with 50% debt and 50% equity, that EBITDA grows to £13m over five years, and that you exit at 9.0x in both cases, which gives an exit EV of £117m. For simplicity, we'll ignore any cash sweep.

Auction entry Proprietary entry
Entry EV £90.0m £75.0m
Entry equity £45.0m £37.5m
Debt (constant) £45.0m £37.5m
Exit EV (9.0x × £13m) £117.0m £117.0m
Exit equity £72.0m £79.5m
MOIC 1.6x 2.1x

It's the same company, with the same operating performance, and yet the proprietary entry adds half a turn of MOIC. That half turn is why funds invest so heavily in origination. They have sector teams that publish thought pieces to attract founders, dedicated business-development professionals who track thousands of companies, and CRM systems that log every meeting with a banker. It's also why "angle" matters, even inside auctions. A fund with a genuine reason to pay more, such as synergies with a portfolio company, or sector insight that takes risk out of the plan, wins better deals. So does a fund with a reason to be chosen at the same price, such as credibility with management, or certainty of funding.

So what do deal teams actually ask when a new opportunity lands? How did this reach us? Who else is seeing it? And why do we have an advantage here? If the honest answers are "a broad auction, everyone, and we don't", the bar for spending money on diligence should be high.

§6.1.3Sell-side advisors and how auctions come to market

When an owner decides to sell, whether that's a founder retiring, a corporate selling off a division, or another PE fund exiting, they usually hire a sell-side adviser through a pitch, which is a "bake-off" between banks. The adviser's job is to maximise the price and the certainty of the deal. Its fee, typically 1 to 2% of the deal value in the mid-market, with incentive ratchets above a target price, aligns it with the seller, not with you.

Before launch, the adviser spends six to twelve weeks on preparation. It builds the financial model and drafts the marketing materials. It often commissions vendor due diligence, or VDD, which is a quality of earnings report on the sell side, and sometimes commercial and legal VDD as well. And it grooms the numbers, as we'll see when we come to scepticism below. It also assembles a buyer list of trade buyers, PE funds, and sometimes infrastructure investors or family offices. For a broad process, that's usually 30 to 80 names.

The process then launches in a deliberate sequence. The teaser goes out under a codename, NDAs are signed, the CIM is distributed, and first-round bids come in, and so on; Lesson 2 has the full timetable. Everything about the choreography, from simultaneous deadlines and controlled information to codenames like "Project Falcon", exists to create competitive tension, and to keep the seller's options open for as long as possible.

§6.1.4The teaser: one page, no name

The teaser is a one- or two-page anonymous summary, sent to the long list of buyers before any NDA is signed. It gives you just enough to decide whether to engage. It covers the sector, the rough geography, a description that doesn't name the company, such as "a leading UK provider of mission-critical compliance software", the headline financials, such as revenue of about £40m, EBITDA of about £10m and growth of about 15%, and the rationale for the deal.

Read teasers with a translator's eye. "Leading" means "we found one league table that it tops". "Highly cash generative" is doing a lot of heavy lifting if the capex is capitalised development spend. "Significant white-space opportunity" often means that growth has already slowed. The real information in a teaser is the sector, the size, and the fact that this business is for sale now. The timing itself is a signal worth interrogating.

§6.1.5NDAs: what you're actually agreeing to

To get past the teaser, you sign a non-disclosure agreement, or NDA, also called a confidentiality agreement. The standard terms say you'll keep the information confidential, use it only to evaluate the transaction, and destroy or return it if you withdraw. Three clauses deserve real attention, because they constrain your fund beyond this one deal.

  • Non-solicitation of employees, typically for 12 to 24 months. That's fine in principle, but push for carve-outs for general recruitment advertising. Otherwise, you've restricted hiring across your whole firm, for the sake of a company you may never buy.
  • Standstill provisions. These mostly matter for listed targets. They bar you from buying shares, or from making unsolicited approaches.
  • Team separation, or no-club, clauses. Sellers increasingly prohibit bidders from teaming up into consortia, or from talking to financing banks assigned to other bidders without consent. The aim is precisely to preserve competitive tension.

NDAs are negotiated by the lawyers, but the deal team scans them, and the practical question is always: "what does this stop us from doing later, and for how long?"

§6.1.6The CIM: what's in one

Once the NDA is signed, you receive the Confidential Information Memorandum, or CIM, which is also called the IM, or in Europe, the "info memo". It's a marketing document of 60 to 150 pages, and it typically has the following structure.

  1. The executive summary. That's the deal in ten pages, and it's always the most polished section.
  2. The investment highlights. Six to eight bullet points giving reasons to buy.
  3. The market overview. The size of the market, its growth and its drivers, usually quoting a commissioned market study.
  4. The business description. Products, customers, operations, technology and sites.
  5. Organisation and management. The organisation chart, and biographies of the leadership.
  6. The financials. The historical P&L, usually for three years; the budget or forecast for the current year; management's projections, known as "the business plan"; and an adjusted EBITDA bridge, reconciling the statutory numbers to the headline figure.
  7. The transaction overview. What exactly is being sold, and contact details for the process.

Alongside the CIM, you may get a financial fact book, or the VDD report, though sometimes that only comes in round 2. For larger processes, there may also be a model or a data pack.

§6.1.7How to read a CIM sceptically

A CIM is an advocacy document. Usually, nothing in it is false; it's just that everything in it has been selected. Your job is to reconstruct the unvarnished business from a varnished text. Here are the places deal teams probe first.

The adjusted EBITDA bridge. Here's a worked example. The CIM leads with "£12.0m of adjusted EBITDA", for a business whose statutory accounts show £9.2m.

Bridge item £m
Statutory EBITDA 9.2
One-off legal dispute +0.8
Owner remuneration above market +0.6
"Run-rate" of price increases implemented in Q4 +0.9
Pro-forma synergies from a recent bolt-on +0.5
Adjusted EBITDA 12.0

At a 9.0x multiple, every £1m of add-backs is worth £9m of price. The legal cost may genuinely be a one-off, and the owner's pay can be checked against a market salary. But the run-rate price increase assumes no loss of volume at all, and the pro-forma synergies are a plan, not a result. A sceptical reader would bank perhaps £10.0m to £10.6m of that bridge, not £12.0m, and note each weak add-back as a point for negotiating the price later on.

Here are some other classic tells.

  • Games with definitions. Revenue that includes pass-through costs; "recurring revenue" defined to include purchases that repeat, but aren't contracted; and gross margin flattered by moving costs below the line.
  • The hockey-stick forecast. Three years of 6% growth, followed by a plan showing 15%. Ask what changed, and check whether the current year is tracking its budget. Ask for trading so far this year, compared with budget, which is the single most revealing early request you can make.
  • Customer concentration buried in an appendix. If the chart of the top 10 customers shows percentages but no names or contract terms, assume the biggest one is the problem.
  • What's missing. No mention of churn in a subscription business, no history of capex in an industrial one, or no named competitors in a supposedly "fragmented market". Silence is data.
  • Why now? Sellers time their exits. Selling just after two record years, ahead of a contract renewal, or before a regulatory change is rational for them, and dangerous for you.

So what looks good in a CIM? Reconciliations that tie exactly to the audited accounts, add-backs that are few and boring, a forecast the business is already beating, and disclosure of its warts, such as a lost customer or a failed product. Sellers who disclose bad news early usually have less of it hidden.

§6.1.8Why origination quality drives fund returns

Now zoom out from the single deal to the whole fund. A fund's gross return is roughly the average of its deals' MOICs, and the entry price is the one lever that's fully in the fund's control at the moment of investment. Remember the worked example. Saving 1.5 times EBITDA at entry, 7.5x rather than 9.0x, turned a 1.6x deal into a 2.1x deal. Across a ten-deal fund, sourcing even three deals away from auctions at that kind of discount moves the fund's gross MOIC by roughly 0.15x. That's often the difference between a second-quartile fund and a first-quartile one, and so between raising the next fund easily, or not.

The quality of origination also improves the information you're buying with. Proprietary and early-look deals give you months with management, rather than four hours, while auction deals give you a data room curated by the other side. Funds systematise this. They build coverage models for each sector, keep lists of "priority targets" that they review every quarter, run programmes of banker relationships so they see auction deals early, and hold post-mortems on deals they lose. For a data team, origination is one of the most valuable places to work. That means screening company databases, monitoring trigger events, such as a founder's age, how long PE-owned targets have been held, or stress on covenants, and measuring conversion through the funnel.

Here's the judgement to carry into the next lesson: how a deal reached you tells you how to price it. A broad auction means paying close to full value, so the returns have to come from the plan rather than the price, and that raises the bar for everything the process now has to prove.
