Lesson 6.2/The Deal Lifecycle

The Auction Process End-to-End

24 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the mechanics of a two-round auction: process letters, indicative offers, or IOIs, and how binding they are, management presentations, data rooms, final offers and LOIs, and exclusivity. It includes the timeline of a typical four-month process, and the tactics the seller deploys at each stage.

  1. 6.2.1The shape of an auction
  2. 6.2.2Process letters: the rules of the game
  3. 6.2.3Round 1: the IOI
  4. 6.2.4The shortlist and round 2 access
  5. 6.2.5The data room and Q&A
  6. 6.2.6Round 2: final offers and the LOI
  7. 6.2.7Exclusivity: the buyer's prize, the seller's last card
  8. 6.2.8A typical four-month timetable — and the seller's tactics at each stage
  9. 6.2.9Pre-emption and process judo

§6.2.1The shape of an auction

A standard mid-market sale is run as a two-round auction. Round 1 filters a long list of interested parties down to a shortlist, using cheap, indicative bids. Round 2 gives the shortlist expensive access, to management, the data room and adviser sessions, and demands final offers that are close to binding. The seller then picks a winner, grants it exclusivity, or refuses to, and negotiates through to signing.

Everything in the design serves one goal: keeping several credible buyers competing for as long as possible, while revealing as little as possible. Understanding the choreography from the seller's side is how a buyer avoids being played by it.

§6.2.2Process letters: the rules of the game

At each round, the sell-side adviser issues a process letter. It's a formal letter setting out what bidders have to submit, in what form, and by when. A first-round process letter typically requires your indicative offer to state the following.

  • Value. That's the enterprise value, or a range, plus the key assumptions behind it, such as a cash-free, debt-free basis, normalised working capital, and the EBITDA figure you priced on.
  • Funding. How you'll finance the deal: the fund equity available, the amount of debt you expect, and whether financing is a condition.
  • Approvals. Your internal process, meaning the stage you've reached at investment committee and what approvals remain, and any regulatory approvals your bid would trigger.
  • The diligence plan. What confirmatory work you'd need, and how long it would take.
  • The contact protocol. All contact goes through the adviser. Approaching management or employees directly is grounds for being excluded.

The second-round letter adds the heavier asks. It wants a mark-up of the seller's draft SPA, commitment letters for the debt from the financing banks, confirmation that the equity is committed, and confirmation that diligence is complete, or nearly so.

Process letters aren't contracts. The seller almost always reserves the right to change the process, let in late bidders, or sell to anyone at any time. Read that reservation literally, because it does get used.

§6.2.3Round 1: the IOI

The first-round submission is an indicative offer, or IOI, which stands for indication of interest. It's usually a letter of three to eight pages, and here's its core content.

Element What good looks like (from the seller's side)
Headline value A tight range, e.g. "£95–105m EV", not "£80–120m"
Basis Cash-free debt-free; states the EBITDA it capitalises, e.g. "9.5x FY25E EBITDA of £10.5m"
Funding Named debt providers already engaged; equity from a fund with dry powder
Conditionality Few conditions; diligence scope defined and short
Approvals "Fully approved by our Investment Committee to submit this offer"
Speed Ability to complete round 2 in 4–6 weeks

So how binding is an IOI? It isn't. It's expressly non-binding. It's a statement of intent, subject to diligence, financing, documentation and internal approvals, and no court will make you pay it. Its force is reputational and procedural. Bid £105m in round 1, and then cut to £88m in round 2 without any new facts, and you'll be dropped, and remembered by that adviser in future processes. A habit of "bidding high and chipping late" genuinely damages a fund's deal flow.

That creates the dilemma of pricing in round 1. Bid your true maximum, and you've nowhere left to go, and may be overpaying just to get in. Bid low, and you won't make the shortlist. The standard play is to bid at the top of the range that your early work genuinely supports, and to state your EBITDA basis precisely. That way, any later reduction can be put down to their numbers disappointing, rather than your gamesmanship. And you flag the two or three diligence items that your price depends on. That paper trail is what makes a later price chip defensible.

§6.2.4The shortlist and round 2 access

The adviser scores the round-1 bids on price, certainty and credibility, and typically admits three to six parties to round 2. Now the seller starts spending real resources on you, and you on them. The round-2 budget for a £100m deal can easily reach £1.5m to £2.5m in adviser fees, covering financial, commercial, legal, tax and insurance diligence, plus the costs of financing. Most of that is lost if you don't win. The cost of aborted deals is why funds are selective about which auctions they enter at all.

Management presentations, or MPs, are the set piece. They're a half-day or full-day session where the CEO and CFO present the business and take questions. So what do deal teams actually do with an MP? It's less about gathering facts, which are in the data room, and more about calibration. Does the CFO know the numbers cold, or defer to the adviser? Do the answers to questions on margin match the CIM? And how does the team respond when it's challenged? A well-rehearsed CEO alongside a shaky CFO is a classic warning sign, because the numbers in the plan live with the CFO. You'll typically also get expert sessions, such as product demonstrations and site visits, and later on, if you're a favoured bidder, access in smaller groups.

Remember that the seller coached this team for weeks. The MP is theatre, with a layer of information in it. So treat anything disclosed without prompting as significant, and treat the polished sections as rehearsed.

§6.2.5The data room and Q&A

The virtual data room, or VDR, opens with round 2. It holds thousands of documents: statutory accounts, management accounts, contracts, employment terms, IP, litigation and tax. Access is logged. Sellers literally monitor which bidders open which documents, and read effort as interest. Alongside it runs a formal Q&A process, where written questions are submitted through a portal and answered in batches, often with a limit on the number of questions each bidder can ask, say 50 a week.

Here's some practical craft for the buy side.

  • Prioritise ruthlessly. With a limit on questions, each one has to earn its place. Ask for data, such as monthly revenue by customer for 36 months, rather than opinions, such as "how sticky are your customers?"
  • Triangulate. The data room only shows what the seller chose to upload. So cross-check the terms of contracts against how revenue is recognised in the accounts, and check the list of top 10 customers against the debtors ledger.
  • Watch the gaps. A missing major contract, thin board minutes, or an empty "disputes" folder that later turns out not to be empty. The absence of documents is a finding in itself, and it's worth a direct question in the Q&A, such as "please confirm that no other material litigation exists".

§6.2.6Round 2: final offers and the LOI

The round-2 submission is the final offer. In US practice, it's often wrapped in an LOI, or letter of intent. It has to be capable of being accepted with very little further negotiation, so it contains the following.

  • A single number, not a range, on a stated cash-free, debt-free basis, with an assumption about normalised working capital.
  • A marked-up SPA. The seller circulated its draft sale and purchase agreement, and your mark-up shows how much legal risk you're asking it to keep. A light mark-up is a pricing tool, because fewer changes read as more certainty.
  • Debt commitment letters. These show the financing banks are committed on agreed terms, which is known as "certain funds" in UK and European practice, so that financing isn't a condition.
  • The equity commitment, plus evidence of full approval from the investment committee.
  • Any remaining conditions, which ideally means only regulatory or antitrust ones.

Final offers are still formally non-binding until the SPA is signed, unless a process demands executable "sign here" offers with the SPA already agreed. But the room for walking away has narrowed to almost nothing that won't cost you your reputation. The real bid now has three dimensions: price, certainty and speed. Sellers routinely take a slightly lower price from a bidder with no financing risk and a clean mark-up. Certainty has a price, usually reckoned at a low single-digit percentage of EV.

§6.2.7Exclusivity: the buyer's prize, the seller's last card

After the final offers, the seller picks a preferred bidder, and usually grants exclusivity. That's a contractual promise not to negotiate with anyone else for a fixed window, typically two to six weeks, so that the winner can finish its confirmatory work and sign. This is the single biggest shift of leverage in the whole process, because competitive tension, which is the seller's only real weapon, has been switched off.

So sellers ration it. They grant short windows, with extensions only for demonstrated progress. Sometimes they offer "soft" exclusivity, which is a comfort letter rather than a binding lock-up. And occasionally they keep a dual track warm, with a second bidder, or an IPO, ready if you falter. Buyers push the other way: no exclusivity, no final spending on lawyers and warranty and indemnity insurance. Once a buyer is inside exclusivity, its leverage grows every day, because the seller's process has gone cold, and restarting it is costly and stigmatising. That's precisely why late, unjustified price chips, known as "re-trading", happen. It's also why sellers hate them, and remember the funds that do it.

§6.2.8A typical four-month timetable — and the seller's tactics at each stage

Week Stage Seller-side tactic to watch
−8 to 0 Preparation: VDD, CIM drafting, buyer list Numbers groomed; adjusted EBITDA maximised; process timed just after strong results
0–2 Teaser out, NDAs negotiated Broad list creates the impression of deep interest; NDA terms tightened while you have least leverage
2–5 CIM distributed; early Q&A Advisor "guides" bidders on value expectations to anchor round-1 bids upward
5–6 Round 1: IOIs due Deadline pressure; hints that "the round is very competitive" (true or not — you cannot verify)
6–7 Shortlist chosen Ambiguity about how many are through ("a small number of parties") to keep tension
7–11 Round 2: MPs, data room, expert sessions Staged disclosure — sensitive data (customer names, pipeline detail) held back to the end; access rationed to favoured bidders
11–12 Draft SPA issued; W&I process started Seller-friendly draft plus stapled W&I sets the negotiating baseline
12–13 Final offers with SPA markups due "Best and final" that may not be final — a top-two bid-off ("we need you to sharpen your number") is common
13–14 Preferred bidder; exclusivity negotiated Exclusivity kept short; runner-up kept warm as leverage
14–17 Confirmatory diligence, SPA negotiation Time pressure inverted onto buyer: "sign by month-end or we go back to the market"
17 Signing —

Timelines stretch in practice. Slippage of two to six weeks is normal, and a process that speeds up usually means a pre-emptive bid is in play, which we'll come to next.

§6.2.9Pre-emption and process judo

The auction structure can be attacked. A confident buyer may make a pre-emptive bid. That's a knock-out price, with full financing and an SPA ready to sign, on condition of immediate exclusivity. The buyer pays up, to avoid a bidding war at the end. Sellers accept when the price clears their expectations and the certainty is real. The buyer's calculation is that the premium it pays is less than the price inflation that a full round 2 would generate.

Conversely, when you don't have an angle, the honest move is to withdraw early. Round 2 costs £1.5m or more, and a fund that enters every auction "to learn" burns through money and credibility. The questions a deal team asks before committing to round 2 are always the same. Can we win this at a price that works? What's our angle compared with the other likely bidders? What would need to be true, and can round 2 actually prove it? The next lesson covers the internal machine, the Investment Committee, that forces those questions to be answered in writing.

Lesson 6.3/The Deal Lifecycle

Inside the PE Firm — the IC Process

22 min read
In brief

This lesson explains how deals are approved inside a PE firm. It covers screening memos and early looks, and the structure of a full investment committee paper, with its thesis, market, financials, returns and risks. It shows how investment committees challenge deals, how capital approval is staged in step with spending, and why most deals die, with the numbers from the funnel showing where.

  1. 6.3.1Why the IC exists
  2. 6.3.2Screening memos and early looks
  3. 6.3.3Staged capital approval: permission to spend, not just to buy
  4. 6.3.4Anatomy of an IC paper
  5. 6.3.5The returns section: what the IC actually stares at
  6. 6.3.6How ICs challenge deals
  7. 6.3.7Why most deals die — and where

§6.3.1Why the IC exists

While the auction runs on the outside, a parallel process runs inside the fund: the Investment Committee, or IC. The IC is typically made up of the firm's senior partners, sometimes with a rotating seat or an independent member. It's the body that approves spending the LPs' money, both the budget for diligence and the equity cheque itself.

The IC exists because deal teams fall in love. After three months on a deal, a team has sunk costs, personal relationships with management, and a carry incentive to get money deployed. The IC is the institutional antidote. Its members have no time invested in this deal, they recognise patterns from hundreds of others, and they have a mandate to ask the questions that the team has stopped asking itself. LPs diligence a fund's IC process precisely because it's the firm's system of quality control. A fund where the founder can push deals through a rubber-stamp IC is one bad vintage away from trouble.

The IC also has to keep pace with the auction clock. Round-1 process letters ask what internal approvals you have, and round-2 letters demand proof of full approval. A firm whose IC can't produce a real approval within a four-month auction simply can't compete for good deals.

§6.3.2Screening memos and early looks

Not every teaser deserves a meeting. The first internal document is the screening memo, also called a "one-pager" or an "early look memo". It runs to two to five pages, and it's produced within days, from the teaser, the executive summary of the CIM, and desk research. It covers the following.

  • What the business does, and roughly how big it is, in terms of revenue, EBITDA and growth.
  • How it fits the fund's mandate, in terms of sector, cheque size, geography and control.
  • The two or three reasons why it could be interesting, which is the thesis in embryo.
  • The two or three things most likely to kill it, such as concentration, cyclicality, structural decline, or a price expectation that the maths can't reach.
  • A back-of-the-envelope return. At the guided multiple, with plausible growth and standard leverage, is there anything like a gross MOIC of 2.5x here?
  • And a recommendation: pass, watch, or work it up.

The matching meeting is the early look, which is often a weekly pipeline meeting rather than the formal IC. Its purpose is to kill deals quickly and cheaply. The most valuable output of a good screening process is a quick, well-reasoned "no". Every deal that survives screening will consume partners' time, and before long, real money.

So what looks good at screening? A thesis you could state in two sentences, and test with specific diligence. And what looks bad? "An attractive market, strong management, and multiple levers." That thesis is so generic that it fits every CIM ever written, which means the team hasn't yet found the actual reason to own this business.

§6.3.3Staged capital approval: permission to spend, not just to buy

The IC doesn't make a single decision. It makes a sequence of escalating commitments, each one unlocking the spending needed to reach the next stage. Here's a typical sequence for an auction deal.

Stage Auction moment What the IC approves Rough spend at risk
Screening / early look Teaser–CIM Team time to work it up Internal time only
First-round IC Before IOI Submit indicative offer in a price range; small advisor budget £50–150k
Second-round IC Entering round 2 Full diligence budget; engage advisors and financing banks £1.5–2.5m
Final IC Before binding offer Submit final offer up to a price ceiling; approve deal structure The equity cheque
Sign-off / closing approval Before signing Confirm no material adverse findings since final IC; execute —

Two design features matter here. First, price discipline is set as a ceiling. The IC approves something like "up to 9.25x FY25 EBITDA of £10.5m, with a maximum EV of £97m", and any bid above that means going back to the IC. That stops the endgame of the auction, the "sharpen your pencil" call at 11pm, from being decided by an adrenalised deal team on its own. Second, spending is staged in line with information. The £2m diligence budget is only committed once the cheap questions have been survived, and that's what makes a wide funnel affordable.

§6.3.4Anatomy of an IC paper

The full IC paper for a final decision runs to 30 to 80 pages, plus appendices. The structure varies from firm to firm, but here's the classic skeleton.

  1. The executive summary and thesis. One page that states the deal, along the lines of "acquire X at up to £97m EV, or 9.25x, because of A, B and C", along with the two or three beliefs that the returns depend on. The best papers state the thesis in a way that could be proved wrong. For example: "we believe churn is structurally below 5%, because the contracts build in switching costs; commercial due diligence tested this with 25 customer interviews."
  2. The transaction and the process. How the deal arose, the dynamics of the auction, who else is bidding, as far as anyone knows, the timetable, and the position on exclusivity.
  3. The market. Its size, growth, structure, and the target's competitive position, now grounded in the findings of commercial due diligence rather than the CIM's commissioned study.
  4. The business and the financials. The historical figures, with the team's own view of the quality of earnings, meaning which of the CIM's add-backs were accepted and which were rejected. Then the management plan, set against the IC base case, which is the team's more conservative operating model, plus a downside case.
  5. Returns. The entry assumptions, sources and uses, leverage, and the returns under each case, usually with a sensitivity grid, which we'll come to below.
  6. Risks and mitigants. The honest list, with each risk paired with a mitigant, and with what diligence did to size it. ICs read this section first, and they judge the whole paper by whether the risks are real ones or straw men.
  7. The recommendation and conditions. This is the ask: approve up to so many million pounds, subject to the named confirmations that are still outstanding.
  8. Appendices. Summaries of the due diligence reports, outputs from the model, structure charts, and an outline of the 100-day plan.

§6.3.5The returns section: what the IC actually stares at

Here's a worked example of the core exhibit. The deal has an entry EV of £90m, which is 9.0x EBITDA of £10.0m, funded with £45m of debt and £45m of equity. The IC base case grows EBITDA to £13.0m by year 5, and repays £20m of debt, so net debt at exit is £25m. The management case reaches £15.0m.

The exit equity equals the exit multiple times the exit EBITDA, minus net debt. At a 9.0x exit, the base case gives 9.0 × 13.0 − 25, which is £92m of equity on £45m invested. That's a MOIC of 2.0x, and an IRR of about 15% over five years. The sensitivity grid shows how that result holds up against the two big uncertainties.

MOIC on £45m equity Exit 8.0x Exit 9.0x Exit 10.0x
Exit EBITDA £11.0m 1.4x 1.6x 1.9x
Exit EBITDA £13.0m 1.8x 2.0x 2.3x
Exit EBITDA £15.0m 2.1x 2.4x 2.8x

Let's check one cell. 8.0 × 11.0 gives an EV of £88m; take away £25m of net debt, and you get £63m, which divided by £45m is 1.4x. Here's how the IC reads it. The plan has to work, reaching £13m, just to hit 2.0x at a flat exit multiple, and the downside cell on the left still returns the capital. If the base case had already assumed multiple expansion to reach 2.0x, expect the paper to be sent back. Paying 9.0x and underwriting a 10.0x exit is buying the return from the market, not from the business.

§6.3.6How ICs challenge deals

Good ICs attack the assumptions that bear the weight of the paper, not its typos. Here are the questions that come up again and again. They're worth internalising, because they're also your checklist, whether you're writing the paper or working on it as an analyst.

  • "Why do we win?" In a broad auction, what do we know, or bring, that the underbidders don't? "We like it" isn't an angle; the winner's curse is the default.
  • "What must be true?" Which two or three assumptions carry the returns, and what evidence, not assertion, supports each one?
  • "Why is the base case only 8% below the management plan?" Haircuts should be justified line by line, not applied as a cosmetic percentage.
  • "What kills it?" Walk through the downside: a recession in year 2, the biggest customer lost, the covenants. Does the structure survive, and do we still get our money back?
  • "What did diligence change?" If £2m of diligence confirmed everything the team already believed, then either the deal is unusually clean, or the diligence was scoped to confirm rather than to test.
  • "Are we the forced buyer?" That might mean pressure to deploy at the end of a fund's life, or a sector team that needs a deal. The IC polices the incentive problems the firm knows it has.

In terms of mechanics, ICs manage dissent in different ways. Some require unanimity. Some use a majority, with the chief investment officer holding a veto. And some assign a devil's advocate, or take written votes in advance, to stop everyone anchoring on the senior partner's view. The output is rarely a flat yes. It's usually "yes, subject to" something: a price ceiling, a structural requirement, such as a cap on the locked-box ticker or a specific indemnity, or a list of named confirmatory items.

§6.3.7Why most deals die — and where

The numbers from the funnel are stark. Here's a representative year for a mid-market fund.

Stage Deals Survival to next stage
Opportunities logged (teasers, intros) 500 20%
Screened seriously (memo written) 100 30%
First-round bid submitted 30 40%
Round 2 entered 12 ~42%
Final binding offer made 5 40%
Deals closed 2 —

So roughly 0.4% of the opportunities logged actually close. And even after the fund has spent seven figures in round 2, most of those deals still die. Here's where they die, and why.

  • Most deaths happen at screening. The causes are a misfit with the mandate, a business facing structural challenges, or price guidance that the maths can't reach. These are cheap deaths, and they show the system working.
  • After round 1, deals die because the fund is outbid, or because early findings, such as a red flag in the quality of earnings or a problem with a customer, break the thesis. The cost so far is small.
  • In round 2, the deaths are expensive. Diligence contradicts the CIM. Churn turns out to be 12%, not 5%; the "run-rate" price rises lost volume; or the margin bridge in the plan doesn't reconcile. Or the IC caps the price below the level that round 2 reveals is needed to win. Losing a final bidding war after spending the full budget is the worst routine outcome in the business.
  • After becoming preferred bidder, or during exclusivity, deaths are rare, and ugly. Confirmatory diligence finds something material, the financing markets move, or the SPA negotiations break down over how risk should be allocated. Late deaths burn the most money, and the most reputation, on both sides.

Here's the discipline to notice. In a healthy fund, the dead deals die early, and for stated reasons. Post-mortems on each deal, asking "what did we believe at the IOI stage that turned out to be false?", feed back into the quality of screening. And a fund that closes every deal it takes to a final IC isn't disciplined. It's either brilliant at screening, or, more likely, its IC has stopped saying no. In the next lesson, we'll see what happens when the IC says yes, and the deal sprints from preferred bidder to a signed SPA.

Lesson 6.4/The Deal Lifecycle

From Offer to Signing

26 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the sprint from preferred bidder to a signed deal. It explains how the confirmatory diligence workstreams run in parallel, compares staple financing with debt the buyer arranges itself, and sets out the fundamentals of the SPA. That includes a worked example of both the locked box and completion accounts, as well as warranties and indemnities, W&I insurance, MAC clauses, and the split between signing and closing.

  1. 6.4.1The sprint: everything in parallel
  2. 6.4.2Debt financing: staple vs self-arranged
  3. 6.4.3The SPA: what it actually does
  4. 6.4.4Pricing mechanism 1: the locked box
  5. 6.4.5Pricing mechanism 2: completion accounts
  6. 6.4.6Warranties, indemnities, and W&I insurance
  7. 6.4.7MAC clauses and the signing–closing gap
  8. 6.4.8Signing vs closing, and conditions precedent

§6.4.1The sprint: everything in parallel

Winning preferred bidder status starts the most intense phase of the whole deal. It's typically four to six weeks in which every workstream runs at the same time, because exclusivity is short, and every week inside it costs money and goodwill. The deal team turns into a project manager for a crowd of advisers.

Workstream Who runs it Typical output Indicative cost (£100m deal)
Financial / QofE (confirmatory) Accounting firm Confirmed adjusted EBITDA, net debt and working capital analysis £300–500k
Commercial DD (confirmatory) Strategy consultancy Market model, customer references, plan validation £300–600k
Legal DD + SPA Law firm DD report, negotiated SPA and ancillaries £400–800k
Tax structuring Tax advisor Acquisition structure, tax DD report £100–250k
Debt financing Debt advisor + lenders Committed facilities, term sheets to full docs Fees mostly in debt pricing/OID
Insurance / W&I Broker + insurer W&I policy bound at signing Premium £0.5–1.5m
Management terms Deal team + lawyers Rollover and incentive package agreed —

The key word is "confirmatory". Round 2 diligence built the thesis from material in the data room; this phase verifies it. Now there's access to the auditors' files, customer calls that were previously off limits, and a detailed review of tax and legal matters. The findings feed straight into the SPA. Each diligence issue either changes the price, becomes a warranty or an indemnity, or is accepted as a risk. That triangle, price, protection or acceptance, is the whole logic of the documentation phase.

§6.4.2Debt financing: staple vs self-arranged

An LBO needs committed debt at signing. In UK and European practice, that's called "certain funds", because the seller won't sign against financing that could still fall away. There are two routes to getting it.

Staple financing. The sell-side bank, or a lender it organises, offers a pre-packaged debt facility that's "stapled" to the deal, so any winning bidder can use it. Indicative staple terms might be 4.5x EBITDA of senior debt, at SONIA plus 5.5%, with a 2% arrangement fee. The staple serves the seller. It sets a floor on the leverage that every bidder can access, which supports the price, it signals the debt market's appetite, and it speeds up the process. For a buyer, it's a useful benchmark and a fallback. But it rarely offers the best terms available, and using the seller's bank as your lender leaks information about the economics of your bid.

Self-arranged financing. Here, the buyer runs its own process. A debt adviser, or the fund's own capital markets team, sends a financing pack to banks and private credit funds, collects term sheets, and negotiates. A competitive private credit process on the same deal might produce 5.0x at SONIA plus 5.25%, on covenant-lite terms. That's half a turn more leverage, and a cheaper margin, than the staple, because the lenders are competing for you, rather than being handed the deal. The cost is management time, and the risk that the commitment comes more slowly.

In practice, buyers do both. They engage with the staple to keep it honest, run their own track alongside it, and choose when it's time to sign commitment letters. Here's what the deal team watches: total leverage, the margin and fees, the package of covenants, the flex terms, which give the arranger the right to worsen the pricing in order to syndicate the debt, and conditionality. The fewer conditions there are in the commitment letter, the stronger your "certain funds" position, and the stronger your bid.

§6.4.3The SPA: what it actually does

The sale and purchase agreement, or SPA, is the contract that transfers the shares. At its economic core, it answers three questions.

  1. What exactly is the price, and how does it adjust? That's the pricing mechanism: either a locked box or completion accounts.
  2. Who bears which risks about the past? That's covered by warranties, indemnities, limitations, and W&I insurance.
  3. What has to happen between signing and closing, and who bears the risk in that gap? That's covered by conditions precedent, covenants, and MAC clauses.

Everything else, all 150 pages of it, is machinery for answering those three questions.

§6.4.4Pricing mechanism 1: the locked box

Offers are made on a cash-free, debt-free basis, with a normal level of working capital. You bid an enterprise value, and the equity price is the EV minus net debt, adjusted for any deviation in working capital. The two mechanisms differ in when that calculation is fixed.

Under a locked box, the price is fixed off a historical balance sheet, at what's called the locked-box date, and it doesn't adjust afterwards. Here's a worked example.

  • The agreed EV is £100m. The locked-box date is 31 December, using the audited balance sheet.
  • Net debt at 31 December is £30m, and working capital is at its normal level.
  • So the equity price is £70m, and it's fixed. Completion happens on 30 June, six months later.

From the locked-box date onwards, the business is run for the buyer's economic benefit, so the profits belong to the buyer, even before completion. That has two consequences.

  • The value ticker. Because the buyer gets the profits, but the seller has to wait for its money, the seller charges interest on the equity price. That's called a "ticker", at, say, 8% a year. Here, that's £70m × 8% × 6/12, which is £2.8m, so the buyer pays £72.8m at completion. Deal teams run a sanity check here: the ticker rate should roughly match the cash the business generates. If the company will generate £4m of free cash in those six months, then a £2.8m ticker still leaves the buyer ahead. A 12% ticker, at £4.2m, wouldn't.
  • Leakage. Since the price can't adjust, the seller has to promise that no value has left the box since the locked-box date, other than agreed items. Leakage, such as dividends, above-market fees paid to the seller, or assets transferred to affiliates, has to be repaid pound for pound. Permitted leakage is the negotiated list of items that are allowed, such as a £0.4m monitoring fee to the departing sponsor, and the buyer prices those in.

A locked box gives certainty on price, with no true-up after closing, and no argument. It favours sellers, because they fix the price on numbers they prepared themselves, and PE sellers love distributing clean proceeds without any escrow held back. It works best with a recent, audited balance sheet. Its risk to buyers grows with the gap. A stale locked-box date means months of unverified trading between the numbers you priced on and the business you actually receive, plus more ticker. That's why buyers scrutinise current trading right up to signing, and resist boxes that are more than about six to nine months old.

§6.4.5Pricing mechanism 2: completion accounts

Under completion accounts, the price adjusts to the actual balance sheet at completion. Here's a worked example, using the same deal.

  • The EV is £100m. At completion, the seller delivers an estimate: net debt of £30m, and working capital at the agreed target. That target is known as the "peg", and it's set at a normalised level, say £12m.
  • The buyer pays the estimated equity price at completion, which is £70m.
  • Then, 60 to 90 days later, the completion accounts are drawn up, and if they're disputed, they're settled by an independent expert. The actual net debt turns out to be £32m, because a supplier payment was accelerated, or so the buyer argues. And the actual working capital is £11m, which is £1m below the peg.
  • So here's the adjustment. The buyer overpaid by £2m on net debt, and received £1m less working capital, so the seller repays £3m, and the final equity price is £67m.

Completion accounts price the business you actually receive. That protects you against deterioration, and manipulation, in the gap. But the cost is a second negotiation after closing. The definitions become the battleground. Is that customer prepayment "debt-like"? Are overdue creditors "working capital", or "debt"? Deal teams and their accountants fight line by line over the schedule of net debt and debt-like items, and over the working capital peg, which is typically set off a 12-month average to neutralise seasonality. So what looks bad? A seller that pushes for completion accounts, and controls the first draft, and proposes loose definitions. That's an invitation to a £5m argument next quarter.

So how do you choose between them? PE sellers in the UK and Europe strongly prefer a locked box, for its certainty and clean exit. US practice, and corporate carve-outs, lean towards completion accounts, because no clean historical balance sheet exists for a carve-out. Buyers accept a locked box when the accounts are audited, recent and diligenced. They demand completion accounts when the box would be stale, or when the business is being carved out.

§6.4.6Warranties, indemnities, and W&I insurance

Warranties are statements of fact about the business, such as "the accounts give a true and fair view", or "there's no litigation, except as disclosed". If a warranty turns out to be false, and the buyer suffers a loss, the buyer can claim damages. But that's subject to negotiated limitations. There's a cap, often 10 to 30% of the price for business warranties in a deal without insurance. There's a time limit, typically 18 to 24 months, and longer for tax. There are minimum thresholds, both per claim and in total. And there's the disclosure letter: anything fairly disclosed against a warranty can't be claimed on. Warranties do a double job. They allocate risk, and they flush out information, because sellers scrub through the business so they can disclose against them.

Indemnities are stronger. They're a promise to repay a specific, identified loss, pound for pound, if it materialises, such as "the ongoing HMRC enquiry". They're usually not capped by the general limits, and the buyer doesn't need to prove that a warranty was breached. Diligence findings that are real, but can't be quantified, become indemnities; ones that can be quantified become price reductions.

Warranty and indemnity insurance, or W&I insurance, has transformed this market. With a buy-side W&I policy, the buyer claims against an insurer, rather than the seller, for breaches of warranty. Here's a typical shape on a £100m deal. The policy limit is 10 to 30% of EV, say £20m. The premium is about 1 to 1.5% of the limit, which is £200k to £300k. There's an excess, or retention, of around 0.5% of EV. And the seller's own liability is capped at a nominal £1. Sellers, especially PE funds, can't hold contingent liabilities against a fund they want to wind up, so they increasingly staple a W&I policy to the process. But the buyer needs to be cautious. W&I excludes known issues, meaning anything in the due diligence reports or the disclosure letter, so it's never a substitute for diligence. It typically also excludes forward-looking statements, some tax matters, and fraud. And with the seller's liability capped at a nominal amount, the warranties may be negotiated lazily, which is known as "warranty-light", since the seller no longer stands behind them. A thin policy limit with a £1 cap for the seller shifts essentially all the remaining risk onto the buyer. That's a price point, and it's negotiable.

§6.4.7MAC clauses and the signing–closing gap

A material adverse change, or MAC, clause lets the buyer walk away, or renegotiate, if something severe happens to the business between signing and closing. Sellers resist it fiercely, and the courts set a very high bar. That's especially true in Delaware, but the logic travels. A genuine MAC has to be significant in duration and specific to the company, and events affecting the whole market or sector are usually carved out. In practice, a MAC clause is a nuclear option, not a tool for adjusting the price. In UK private deals, a true MAC condition is relatively rare. Instead, buyers protect the gap through pre-completion covenants. These require the seller to run the business in the ordinary course, not to pay dividends, which locked-box leakage covers too, and not to lose key contracts without consultation, and so on.

§6.4.8Signing vs closing, and conditions precedent

Signing, also called exchange, is when the SPA becomes binding. Closing, also called completion, is when the shares and the money actually move. The two separate whenever something has to happen in between. Those things are called conditions precedent, or CPs.

  • Regulatory conditions include merger control clearance, approvals for foreign direct investment, such as under the UK's National Security and Investment Act, and consents from sector regulators to a change of control, such as the FCA for financial firms.
  • Occasionally, there are others, such as shareholder approvals, consent from the counterparty to a key contract, or a step in separating a carve-out.

Notice what's missing from a well-negotiated PE deal: financing conditions, because of certain funds, and diligence conditions, because diligence is finished before signing. UK practice keeps CPs to a minimum, and when no approvals are needed, the deal signs and closes at the same time.

Between signing and closing, the buyer holds a binding contract, but not the company. That's typically for 4 to 12 weeks, and longer with complex antitrust issues. The risk in that gap is allocated by the CPs, the covenants on conduct, any MAC, and sometimes break fees, which are reverse termination fees payable if the buyer's approvals fail. Once the last CP has been satisfied, a completion date is set, and the deal moves on to the mechanics of actually moving the money, which is the next lesson.

Here's the judgement that sums up this lesson. Every diligence finding has to land somewhere. It goes into price, through a price chip or the mechanism; into protection, through a warranty, an indemnity or W&I; or into accepted risk, with the IC told explicitly. Deals go wrong when findings land nowhere.

Lesson 6.5/The Deal Lifecycle

Close and Beyond

20 min read
In brief

This lesson covers what happens at completion and afterwards. It explains how the regulatory conditions are satisfied, walks through the flow of funds on completion day with a worked sources-and-uses table, and covers readiness for day 1. It finishes with the handover from the deal team to ownership, which sets up value creation.

  1. 6.5.1Between signing and closing: clearing the conditions
  2. 6.5.2Completion day: the funds flow
  3. 6.5.3Day-1 readiness
  4. 6.5.4The post-completion tail
  5. 6.5.5The handover into ownership
  6. 6.5.6The deal lifecycle, seen whole

§6.5.1Between signing and closing: clearing the conditions

The SPA is signed and the press release is out, but nobody owns anything yet. The weeks between signing and completion are about satisfying the conditions precedent, and almost all of the risk to the timetable sits with the regulators.

  • Merger control. Most regimes are triggered by thresholds of turnover or market share. A UK mid-market deal may need to be considered by the CMA. Deals with an EU dimension go to the European Commission. And a connection to the US triggers a filing under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, the HSR, with its waiting period. A straightforward "Phase 1" clearance takes roughly four to eight weeks from filing, while a referral to Phase 2 adds months, and real risk to the deal. PE deals are usually clean, because funds rarely own direct competitors. Buy-and-build platforms increasingly do, though, and regulators have noticed these roll-ups.
  • Foreign direct investment and national security. The UK's National Security and Investment Act, the NSIA, makes notification mandatory in 17 sensitive sectors, including defence, energy, data infrastructure and AI. If notification was mandatory, closing without clearance makes the transaction void. Equivalent regimes exist almost everywhere, such as CFIUS in the US. Deal teams screen for this early, because it catches deals that feel nowhere near "national security".
  • Sector regulators. This means consent to a change of control from bodies such as the FCA for regulated financial firms, Ofgem, Ofcom, or the CQC in healthcare. It's often the slowest condition of all.

While the lawyers chase the clearances, the deal team runs the completion machine. It agrees the completion steps paper, which is a numbered choreography of every signature and payment. It finalises the funds flow statement. It works through the lenders' checklist of conditions precedent, such as board resolutions, security documents and insurance certificates. And in a deal using completion accounts, it receives the seller's estimates of net debt and working capital, which set the completion payment.

§6.5.2Completion day: the funds flow

Mechanically, completion is a series of simultaneous payments, executed against a pre-agreed funds flow statement. That's the single page that every party's lawyers check to the penny. Let's continue the running example from Lesson 4. The EV is £100m, with a locked box giving an equity value of £70m, plus a £2.8m ticker. The target has £32m of gross bank debt, which gave net debt of £30m at the locked-box date, after £2m of cash. Management rolls £4.0m of its proceeds into the new structure. And new senior facilities of £45m are drawn at closing.

Funds flow at completion £m
Sources
Senior term loan (drawn at close) 45.0
Sponsor equity (fund) 60.3
Management rollover (applied to equity, non-cash) 4.0
Total sources 109.3
Uses
Cash to selling shareholders (£72.8m less £4.0m rolled) 68.8
Management rollover into NewCo equity (non-cash) 4.0
Repay existing bank debt (£32.0m) incl. break costs £0.5m 32.5
Debt arrangement fees (2% of £45m) 0.9
Advisory fees (financial, legal, tax, commercial DD) 2.4
W&I insurance premium 0.7
Total uses 109.3

Here are the points that a deal team checks, along with its data team, which often builds and checks this table.

  • It balances. Sources equal uses, exactly. The sponsor equity line is the balancing figure, here £60.3m, and it's what the fund actually draws from its LPs. So getting it wrong means an embarrassing correction to the capital call on the same day.
  • The rollover isn't cash. Management's £4.0m never moves. It nets off what they're owed as sellers against what they're subscribing as buyers. It appears on both sides of the table, so that the economics are visible.
  • The existing debt is repaid at completion, through payoff letters from the incumbent lenders, who release their security the moment they're paid. The target's £2m of cash stays in the business, because the buyer has paid for it through the deduction for net debt.
  • Fees are real uses of equity. Roughly £4.0m of this table, made up of £0.9m, £2.4m and £0.7m, buys nothing except the deal itself. That's nearly 7% of the sponsor's cheque, and it's why aborted processes hurt, and why fee budgets are approved by the IC.

The day itself is anticlimactic and tense in equal measure. There's a completion call, with lawyers confirming receipt of each wire. Board resignations and appointments are signed in sequence, following the steps paper. And then, often hours later than planned, because a wire is stuck in an intermediary bank, there's confirmation that completion has taken place. The share transfers are registered, and the fund owns a company.

§6.5.3Day-1 readiness

At 9 o'clock the next morning, employees want to know whether they still have jobs, customers are reading the press release, and suppliers are wondering about their terms. Day-1 readiness is the workstream, planned during the window between signing and closing, that makes the first day boring.

  • Communications. These are announcements in a set sequence, to employees first, and then to customers, suppliers and the press. There's the CEO's town hall meeting, and scripts of frequently asked questions for account managers facing customers' questions.
  • The basics of control. New bank mandates and authorities for making payments, the composition of the board, and limits on delegated authority. Those limits set out what management can now spend without the sponsor's consent, and they're typically formalised in a matrix in the shareholders' agreement. Insurance gets switched over too.
  • The mechanics of a carve-out, where relevant. Transitional services agreements, or TSAs, go live from day 1. These mean that payroll, IT and invoicing are still run by the seller for 6 to 18 months, at an agreed price and for a limited time.
  • Reporting goes live. The clock on reporting to lenders starts straight away, with covenant reporting every month or quarter, and the fund's own monitoring cycle begins. For a data team, this is the sharpest deadline. The KPI pack that the deal team promised the IC has to exist within weeks, built from systems you first saw in a data room.

So what looks bad on day 1? Silence. A change of ownership that isn't communicated breeds rumours, and the best employees and the most nervous customers move first. And what looks good? Management announcing the deal together with the sponsor; a concrete message that "nothing changes today, and here's the plan for the next 90 days"; and the first meeting between sponsor and management already in the diary.

§6.5.4The post-completion tail

Completion doesn't quite end the transaction. Three tails run on for months afterwards, and someone has to own each one.

  • The true-up of the completion accounts, where that mechanism was used. The buyer, who now controls the books, prepares the completion accounts within 60 to 90 days. The seller reviews them, and any disputes go to an independent expert, whose decision is final. The arguments are always about definitions that were agreed months earlier. Remember the example from Lesson 4, where £2m of extra net debt and a £1m shortfall in working capital moved £3m back from the seller to the buyer. Under a locked box there's no true-up, but the buyer's finance team still checks that no leakage has occurred. Any dividend, or any payment to the seller that wasn't permitted, since the locked-box date can be claimed back pound for pound. The window for claims, often 6 to 12 months, is short enough that the check has to happen at the first close of the accounts.
  • The windows for warranty and W&I claims. General warranty claims typically expire 18 to 24 months after completion, and tax warranties after four to seven years. Issues that surface in the first two audits, such as a misstated debtor or an undisclosed dispute, need to be assessed against the disclosure letter and the W&I policy before the clock runs out. In practice, most W&I claims are notified in the first year, and the most common categories are warranties on the accounts, and tax.
  • The mechanics of the fund. The equity cheque was drawn from the LPs through a capital call shortly before completion. The deal now enters the fund's quarterly valuation cycle at cost, and the deal team writes the first quarterly report that the LPs will see. Any amounts that were under-drawn or over-drawn, from that balancing figure in the funds flow again, are trued up in the next call.

§6.5.5The handover into ownership

The deal team that fought the auction now hands over to the ownership team, or becomes part of it. The centre of gravity of the deal shifts from buying well to running well. Here are the documents that form the bridge.

  • The IC paper becomes the value creation plan. The thesis, the base case and the risk register were promises made to the IC. The 100-day plan turns them into actions with owners and dates: a review of pricing, quick wins in procurement, an upgrade of the finance function, and the first pipeline of bolt-ons.
  • The diligence reports become the first draft of the operating manual. The customer interviews from commercial due diligence seed the sales strategy. The working capital analysis from the quality of earnings work becomes the agenda for managing cash. And every risk that the SPA couldn't price is now an action for management.
  • The model becomes the budget. The IC base case is cut into the format of the monthly board pack, with covenant headroom, a KPI dashboard, and a 13-week cash flow if leverage is high.

Two governance documents formalise the new world. The first is the shareholders' agreement, which covers board seats, reserved matters, and the terms for management leavers. The second is the board calendar, with monthly packs and quarterly deep dives. The habits set in the first 100 days, such as discipline in reporting, honesty about misses, and the working relationship between the CEO and the sponsor, last for the whole hold.

§6.5.6The deal lifecycle, seen whole

Let's step back and look across the whole module. A deal is a funnel of decisions, made under escalating commitment.

Phase Core question Money at risk
Sourcing Is this worth our time — and do we have an angle? Time
Round 1 What is it plausibly worth to us? Tens of £k
Round 2 / IC What must be true, and can we prove it? £1.5–2.5m
Exclusivity to signing Price, protection, or acceptance for every finding? Fees + reputation
Signing to close Clear the CPs, prepare day 1 The equity cheque
Ownership Deliver the plan the IC bought The fund's returns

The discipline that recurs at every stage is the same: write down what you believe, attach the evidence, and make the price and the contract reflect it. Funds that do this lose the auctions they should lose, and win deals that work. The next module, on Value Creation, picks up exactly where the funds flow ends. You own the company, the 100-day plan is on the table, and now the return has to be built, rather than bought.

Lesson 7.1/LBOs & Returns Math

The LBO Idea: Buying With Borrowed Money

22 min read
In brief

This lesson explains why buying a business with borrowed money amplifies the returns to equity. It does the house-purchase analogy properly, works through a comparison of the same business bought with no leverage and with 4x leverage, explains why leverage cuts both ways, and sets out the checklist that makes a business "LBO-able".

  1. 7.1.1The house analogy, done properly
  2. 7.1.2Same business, two capital structures
  3. 7.1.3Where the extra return comes from — and the mirror image
  4. 7.1.4Why targets need stable cash flows
  5. 7.1.5What makes a business "LBO-able"
  6. 7.1.6What deal teams actually ask

§7.1.1The house analogy, done properly

Everyone reaches for the house analogy, so let's do it properly, with numbers, and then be honest about where it breaks down.

Say you buy a house for £500k, with a £400k mortgage and £100k of your own money. Five years later, you sell it for £600k. The house went up by 20%, but you didn't make 20%. After repaying the £400k mortgage, you walk away with £200k, on the £100k you put in, so you've doubled your money. A 20% return on the asset became a 100% return on your equity, because the lender's claim was fixed, and every pound of upside above it belonged to you.

Now for the honest part. The analogy breaks down in two ways, and both of them matter for LBOs.

  1. You paid the mortgage out of your salary. The house didn't generate the cash to service its own debt. In an LBO, the business itself has to produce the cash that pays the interest and repays the principal. That's the single most important difference, and it's why LBO targets are screened on cash generation above almost everything else.
  2. The bank could repossess. If the house had fallen to £380k, your £100k would have gone completely, before the lender lost a penny. Leverage amplifies losses exactly as efficiently as it amplifies gains. Equity is the piece that takes the first loss.

A leveraged buyout applies precisely this structure to a company. A private equity fund buys a business using a large slug of debt, historically 50 to 70% of the price, which is secured on the business itself, and serviced by the business's own cash flows. The fund's equity cheque covers the rest. At exit, typically three to seven years later, the outstanding debt is repaid out of the proceeds, and the equity keeps everything above it.

§7.1.2Same business, two capital structures

Let's take one business and buy it twice, once with no debt and once with leverage, and watch what happens to the return on equity. The business has £10m of EBITDA, and it's bought at 8.0x, so the enterprise value is £80m. Over five years, EBITDA grows to £13m, and the exit multiple stays at 8.0x, so the exit EV is £104m. It's the same business, with the same operational outcome and the same discipline on price.

In Case A, there's no debt at all, so you write an £80m cheque. In Case B, there's 4x leverage. You borrow £40m, which is 4.0x EBITDA, and write a £40m cheque.

On the first pass, let's ignore cash generation entirely, and assume the £40m of debt is still outstanding at exit. The interest is paid out of free cash flow, but nothing is repaid.

Case A: 0x leverage Case B: 4x leverage, no paydown
Entry EV £80m £80m
Debt — £40m
Equity invested £80m £40m
Exit EV (8.0x × £13m) £104m £104m
Less: debt at exit — (£40m)
Exit equity £104m £64m
MOIC 1.3x 1.6x
IRR (5 years) ~5% ~10%

The EV grew by 30% in both cases. But in Case B, that £24m of growth in EV went to an equity base of £40m, rather than £80m. The fixed claim of the debt concentrated the gain.

On the second pass, let's let the business's cash flow repay some debt. Say the business generates roughly £5m a year of free cash flow after interest, and all of it is swept into repaying principal. That's £25m over the hold, so the debt at exit is £15m.

Case B with debt paydown
Exit EV £104m
Less: debt at exit (£15m)
Exit equity £89m
MOIC (on £40m) 2.2x
IRR (5 years) ~17%

It's the same business, at the same exit price. With no debt, it returns 1.3x. Levered, with debt paydown, it returns 2.2x. That difference is the whole thesis of the asset class. In Case A, the cash the business generated would pile up on the balance sheet, or be paid out as dividends, which lifts the all-equity return somewhat. But it's nowhere near enough to close the gap, because that cash isn't being applied against a fixed claim that ranks ahead of the equity.

§7.1.3Where the extra return comes from — and the mirror image

It's worth being precise about why Case B wins. "Leverage juices returns" is the kind of phrase people repeat without being able to defend it in an interview.

  • A fixed claim concentrates the upside. The lender's return is capped at the interest. So every pound of growth in EV above the debt belongs to a smaller base of equity.
  • Paying down debt transfers value to the equity. Each pound of principal repaid out of the company's cash flow converts enterprise value into equity value, pound for pound, even if the EV never moves. This is the "forced saving" effect, and you'll meet it again as deleveraging, when we come to attributing returns.
  • Interest is partly tax-deductible, so the government subsidises a slice of the cost of the debt. That's a real effect, but a second-order one, and tax rules such as the UK's corporate interest restriction now cap it.

And now for the mirror image. Run the deal again with a bad outcome. EBITDA falls to £8m, and the buyer at exit only pays 7.0x, so the exit EV is £56m. With no debt, that's £56m on £80m, which is 0.7x, a 30% loss. That's painful, but survivable. With leverage, and assuming weak cash flow meant no debt was paid down, the equity is £56m minus £40m, which is £16m on £40m invested. That's 0.4x, a 60% loss. And if the EV had fallen below £40m, the equity would have been worth nothing at all. Leverage doesn't create value. It amplifies whatever happens, in both directions. And it adds a way to fail that the unlevered buyer doesn't have: running out of cash to service the debt before you ever get to exit.

§7.1.4Why targets need stable cash flows

Servicing debt is a contractual obligation. EBITDA is not.

A business levered at 4 to 5 times might pay 8 to 10% interest on its debt. On our £40m package, that's £3m to £4m a year of interest, before a pound of capex, tax or working capital. If EBITDA is £10m and steady, that's comfortable. But if EBITDA swings between £4m and £16m across a cycle, with the same average, there will be years when the business can't cover its interest. Then it's the lenders, not the fund, who control what happens next. At best, that means covenants waived in return for a fee. At worst, it means the security is enforced, and the equity cheque is wiped out.

That's why the LBO screen cares less about growth than about predictability.

  • Recurring or repeat revenue, from contracts, subscriptions, maintenance or regulated income, beats project-based or cyclical revenue at the same margin.
  • High cash conversion means EBITDA that turns into cash, with low capex needs and little cash absorbed by working capital. A business that converts 80% or more of its EBITDA into free cash flow before interest can carry far more debt than one that converts 40%.
  • Demonstrated resilience. What actually happened to revenue in the last downturn is worth more than anything management asserts about how defensive the business is.

§7.1.5What makes a business "LBO-able"

Here's the classic checklist that a deal team runs, in rough order of importance.

  1. Stable, predictable cash flows, as above. This is the criterion that bears the weight.
  2. A strong market position, or moat. Pricing power and a defensible market share protect margins over a five-year hold. And lenders read the same CIM that the fund does.
  3. Low intensity of capex and working capital. The cash has to be free to service debt, not trapped in machines and inventory.
  4. A believable angle for creating value, such as cost-cutting, pricing, buy-and-build, or professionalising the business. Leverage amplifies the plan, but it isn't the plan.
  5. The capacity to deleverage. Can the business plausibly repay a meaningful slug of debt over the hold? Lenders size the package on exactly this.
  6. Being sellable. Will there be a buyer at a sensible multiple in five years' time, whether that's a trade buyer, another sponsor, or an IPO? A business that nobody wants to own next is a bad LBO, however cheap it is.
  7. A management team worth backing, or a clear plan to upgrade it.

So what looks bad? Heavy cyclicality. Customer concentration; one customer making up 40% of revenue is a lender's veto. End markets in structural decline. Big, lumpy capex programmes. Businesses whose assets walk out of the door at night; pure people businesses carry less debt for a reason. And heavy existing lease or pension obligations, which already behave like debt.

§7.1.6What deal teams actually ask

When a deal team first screens a target for leverage, the questions are concrete.

  • "What's the cash conversion?" That's free cash flow before interest, divided by EBITDA. Above about 70 to 80% is attractive, and below about 50% caps the debt the deal can carry.
  • "What did FY09, or FY20, look like?" That's the downturn test. A business whose revenue fell 5% in the global financial crisis, and recovered within a year, can support far more leverage than one that fell 40%.
  • "How much debt will this carry?" The answer comes in turns of EBITDA, such as 4x or 5x, and it's driven by the two questions above, plus the mood of the credit market that quarter.
  • "Can we underwrite 2x on conservative assumptions?" In other words, does the deal work with no multiple expansion, and sensible growth, with leverage doing its share?

Keep the two-sided intuition from this lesson in your head permanently. Leverage multiplies the consequences for the equity of everything else in the deal. The next lesson gives you the two numbers that measure those consequences: MOIC and IRR.

Lesson 7.2/LBOs & Returns Math

MOIC and IRR: The Two Numbers That Rule Everything

24 min read
In brief

This lesson gives the definitions and formulas for MOIC and IRR, and sets out the triangle linking MOIC, IRR and the holding period, with a full conversion table. It explains why IRR rewards speed, how IRR can be manipulated with early recaps and subscription lines, and when to trust MOIC over IRR.

  1. 7.2.1MOIC: the honest multiple
  2. 7.2.2IRR: the time-weighted answer
  3. 7.2.3The MOIC–IRR–hold triangle
  4. 7.2.4Why IRR rewards speed
  5. 7.2.5How IRR gets manipulated
  6. 7.2.6When to trust MOIC over IRR

§7.2.1MOIC: the honest multiple

MOIC stands for multiple of invested capital. It's also called the money multiple, MoM, or just "the multiple", and it's the simplest measure of returns in finance:

MOIC=Total value returned (realised + unrealised)Total capital invested\text{MOIC} = \frac{\text{Total value returned (realised + unrealised)}}{\text{Total capital invested}}MOIC=Total capital investedTotal value returned (realised + unrealised)​

Put £40m in, and get £89m back, and the MOIC is 2.2x. That's all there is to it. There's no discounting, no timing, and no assumptions. Gross MOIC is measured at the level of the deal, before the fund's fees and carry. Net MOIC is what the LP actually experiences after them. Always check which one you're looking at, because the gap between them is routinely 0.3 to 0.5x.

MOIC's great virtue is that timing can't game it. Its great weakness is the mirror image: it's blind to timing. Doubling your money in two years, and doubling it in ten years, are both "2.0x", and they're emphatically not the same investment outcome. A fund could have recycled the fast double twice more in the same decade.

§7.2.2IRR: the time-weighted answer

IRR, or internal rate of return, is the annual rate that makes the deal's cash flows worth zero in present-value terms. Formally, it's the discount rate rrr that solves:

∑t=0TCFt(1+r)t=0\sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} = 0t=0∑T​(1+r)tCFt​​=0

Here, the initial equity cheque is a negative cash flow, and every distribution back is a positive one. Intuitively, it's the constant interest rate that a bank account would have needed to pay in order to replicate these exact cash flows.

For the common shape of an LBO, with one cheque going in at t=0t=0t=0, and one lump sum coming out at exit in year nnn, IRR collapses into a neat formula:

IRR=MOIC1/n−1\text{IRR} = \text{MOIC}^{1/n} - 1IRR=MOIC1/n−1

So with £40m going in, and £89m coming out after five years, we get (2.225)1/5−1=17.3%(2.225)^{1/5} - 1 = 17.3\%(2.225)1/5−1=17.3%. When there are cash flows in between, such as a dividend in year 3 or a partial sale in year 4, there's no neat formula, and you solve it numerically, with Excel's XIRR. But the single-cheque approximation is the workhorse of mental maths in the industry, and it's what "paper LBO" interview questions expect.

There are two properties worth internalising.

  • IRR isn't the return on your money over the whole period. It's the return on the capital while it was deployed. A 40% IRR on money returned after 14 months is a great number, but a modest amount of actual profit.
  • IRR assumes nothing about reinvestment. But comparing IRRs across deals implicitly assumes that you could redeploy the early proceeds at similar rates. That assumption is where most misuse of IRR hides.

§7.2.3The MOIC–IRR–hold triangle

MOIC, IRR and the holding period lock each other in place. Fix any two, and the third follows. The conversion table below is genuinely worth memorising, because deal teams quote these numbers from memory in investment committees and interviews.

MOIC 3-year hold 5-year hold 7-year hold
2.0x 26.0% 14.9% 10.4%
2.5x 35.7% 20.1% 14.0%
3.0x 44.2% 24.6% 17.0%

Each cell is MOIC1/n−1\text{MOIC}^{1/n}-1MOIC1/n−1. Here are some anchors to keep in your head for sanity checks.

  • Doubling your money in 5 years is about 15%. That's the classic "base case" underwriting for a buyout.
  • Doubling it in 3 years is about 26%. It's the same money multiple, but an IRR that looks top-decile.
  • Tripling it in 5 years is about 25%. That's a genuinely excellent deal.
  • Doubling every 5 years or so is about 15%, every 4 years about 19%, and every 3 years about 26%. The rule of 72 works here: 72 divided by the IRR percentage gives you roughly the number of years it takes to double.

Funds typically underwrite deals at a gross IRR of about 20 to 25%, and a multiple of 2.0 to 2.5x, hoping to deliver LPs about 15% or more net, and about 1.7 to 2.0x, after fees. Read the table along the rows and down the columns until both directions feel automatic.

§7.2.4Why IRR rewards speed

Look at the 2.0x row again. The identical profit, £1 returned for every £1 invested, is worth 26% a year over three years, and 10% over seven. IRR compounds the multiple over time, so time is the exponent in the denominator. That means shortening the hold does more for IRR than improving the multiple does.

That creates real behavioural incentives, some of them healthy, and some not.

  • Here's the healthy one: return capital when the plan is finished. If the work of creating value is complete by year 3, holding on until year 5 just dilutes the annual return down towards the market's.
  • And here's the unhealthy one: selling a compounding asset early to flatter the IRR, when the LPs would have preferred the extra multiple. Making 4.0x over 8 years, an IRR of 19%, creates far more actual wealth than making 1.8x over 2 years, an IRR of 34%. Yet the second one "wins" on IRR. LPs eat multiples, not IRRs, because they can't reliably reinvest early distributions at 34%.

The tension is structural. GPs raise their next fund on the strength of IRR league tables, while LPs pay pensions out of multiples. So sophisticated investment committees and LPs always look at the pair, as in "2.3x and 24%", and never at either number on its own.

§7.2.5How IRR gets manipulated

Because IRR is so sensitive to when cash moves, it can be engineered without creating a single extra pound of value. There are two classic mechanisms.

1. Early recapitalisations, or "dividend recaps". Two years in, the company borrows more against its EBITDA, which has hopefully improved, and pays the fund a dividend. Suppose a £40m cheque gets £20m back through a recap in year 2, and £69m at the exit in year 5, instead of £89m all at exit. The total returned is £89m either way. The MOIC barely moves; in fact, it goes slightly down, after the extra interest the company now pays. But the IRR jumps by several points, because half the cheque was only "at risk" for two years. The recap also put more debt back on the company, so the risk went up, while the headline return metric improved. That asymmetry is exactly why you should treat IRRs driven by recaps with suspicion, and why lenders and LPs scrutinise them.

2. Subscription credit lines, or "sub lines". This is a tool at the level of the fund, rather than the deal. The fund borrows against the LPs' undrawn commitments to pay for deals, and only calls the LPs' capital months or years later. The LP's clock, which drives the fund's reported IRR, starts at the capital call, not at the deal. Delay the call by 18 months on a deal that returns 2.0x, and you can turn an IRR of about 15% into one of 20% or more, with no change at all in the underlying investment. Sub lines do have legitimate uses for managing cash, such as batching capital calls and bridging closings. But using them for extended periods is cosmetic surgery on IRR. It costs the fund interest, and it makes the net MOIC slightly worse. ILPA's guidance now pushes funds to disclose IRRs both with and without the line. If a GP only shows you one of them, ask why.

To see the effect of a recap concretely, let's run the numbers on lesson 1's deal: £40m in, £89m out after five years, which is an IRR of 17.3%. Now restructure the flows. A recap in year 2 returns £20m, and the exit in year 5 delivers the remaining £69m. The total returned is still £89m, so the MOIC is unchanged at 2.2x. But solve the IRR equation with the new timing:

−40+20(1+r)2+69(1+r)5=0  ⟹  r≈21%-40 + \frac{20}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{69}{(1+r)^5} = 0 \implies r \approx 21\%−40+(1+r)220​+(1+r)569​=0⟹r≈21%

Four points of IRR have appeared out of thin air. Nothing about the business has changed, except that it now carries the recap debt. The risk-adjusted position got worse, while the league-table number got better. Whenever a track record's IRRs look oddly high compared with its multiples, this is usually the mechanism.

There are softer flavours of the same game. They include timing exits to fall just inside reporting dates, holding unrealised valuations high late in a fund's life, and quoting gross returns when net would be the fair comparison.

§7.2.6When to trust MOIC over IRR

Neither number is "the right one", because they answer different questions. IRR asks how hard the capital worked while it was deployed. MOIC asks how much money we actually made. Trust MOIC more in the following situations.

  • When holds are short, or cash came back early. IRRs annualised over periods of less than two years are close to meaningless. A 1.5x return in 12 months "is" a 50% IRR, but nobody can compound that.
  • When recaps or sub lines are involved. MOIC is immune to both.
  • When comparing funds with different styles of pacing. A fund that calls capital late and recaps early will beat a plain-vanilla fund on IRR, at identical multiples.
  • When the number is mostly unrealised. Interim IRRs lean on valuations. A MOIC split into its realised part, DPI, and its unrealised part, RVPI, tells you how much is actually in the bank.

Trust IRR more when holds are long and comparable, and when you genuinely care about opportunity cost. A 1.9x that took nine years should be penalised against a 1.9x that took four.

So what do deal teams actually ask when someone quotes a return at them? "What's the multiple, and what's the hold?", so they can rebuild the triangle. "Is it gross or net?" "Is there a recap in there?" And "how much of it has been realised?" If you ask those four questions of every headline IRR you ever see, you'll rarely be fooled. From here, the module builds the machinery that produces these numbers: the funding of the deal, through sources and uses, the debt stack, and the model that links the entry price to the equity at exit.
