Lesson 8.3/Deal Structuring

Management Rollover and Incentives

25 min read
In brief

This lesson explains why sellers and managers roll equity into the new deal, and covers market norms for rollover percentages. It then looks at good and bad leaver provisions, vesting, drag and tag rights, and ratchets, with a worked example of a ratchet kicking in once the fund's return clears a hurdle of 2.5x.

  1. 8.3.1Why anyone rolls money back into the deal
  2. 8.3.2Leaver provisions: what you keep when you leave
  3. 8.3.3Drag, tag, and who controls the exit
  4. 8.3.4Ratchets: performance-linked equity splits
  5. 8.3.5What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

§8.3.1Why anyone rolls money back into the deal

A rollover is when a seller takes part of their sale proceeds not in cash, but in shares and loan notes of the new acquisition vehicle. The seller might be a founder, a management team in a secondary buyout, or the managers of a sponsor that's exiting. On paper it looks odd, because they've just achieved liquidity, and they're immediately putting it back at risk. But in practice, rollover is close to universal wherever the sellers carry on running the business, and there are four reasons.

  1. Alignment the buyer can believe in. A founder who takes all of their proceeds in cash, and stays on as CEO, is a walking red flag. Rolling 20 to 40% of the proceeds says, "I believe in the plan I've just sold you." Funds routinely make rollover a condition of the deal, not an option.
  2. The second bite of the cherry. Rolled equity takes part in the next exit. A founder who rolls £16m into a deal that returns 2.5x turns that £16m into £40m, which is often comparable to the original cash-out. Sellers who have watched a buyer double the business they built once tend not to want to miss out a second time.
  3. Bridging gaps on price. Rollover reduces the cash the fund needs at closing, which can support a higher headline price. A headline of £80m, with £16m rolled over, costs the fund £16m less in equity than £80m paid all in cash.
  4. Deferring tax. In the UK, a properly structured exchange of shares for shares lets the seller defer capital gains tax on the rolled portion until the eventual exit. That's only the high-level picture; this is territory for specialist advice.

So what are the market norms? Founders selling a majority stake typically roll 10 to 30% of their gross proceeds. Management teams in secondary buyouts often roll 50% or more of their net proceeds, after tax. Funds push hard here, because these managers are the plan. Below about 10%, the signalling value evaporates. Above about 50% of net proceeds, you start hearing legitimate complaints about concentration and personal risk.

The rolled money normally subscribes for the same institutional strip as the fund: loan notes and ordinaries in a 90 to 10 split, ranking equally, as Lesson 2 explained. Watch out for exceptions. A rollover into ordinaries only, or into a junior class of notes, quietly subordinates the seller.

§8.3.2Leaver provisions: what you keep when you leave

Management's equity isn't just an investment. It's tied to their employment through leaver provisions, which force a departing manager to sell their shares back, and set the price. Here's the standard way they're classified.

  • A good leaver leaves because of death, serious illness, planned retirement, or sometimes redundancy, or departure "through no fault of their own". They typically receive fair market value for their vested shares.
  • A bad leaver has been dismissed for cause, has resigned to join a competitor, or has breached their restrictive covenants. They typically receive the lower of cost and fair market value. In other words, at best they get their money back, and less if the equity is underwater.
  • An intermediate leaver, which is increasingly common, has resigned voluntarily, without any aggravating factors. They often get fair value on their vested shares, and cost on the unvested ones.

The battleground is where plain resignation sits. Documents that favour the fund make any resignation before the exit a bad-leaver event. So a manager who serves four years, builds the value, and then leaves for family reasons forfeits the upside. Documents that favour management move resignation into the intermediate category after a qualifying period. When you review a structure, read the leaver matrix before you read the ratchet, because it decides whether the equity is really owned, or just dangled.

Vesting interacts with all of this. Sweet equity commonly vests over three to five years, on a straight line, sometimes with a one-year cliff, or it simply vests "at exit". Unvested shares go back at cost, whatever the leaver's status. Cliff-vesting everything at exit maximises retention, but it's brutal in year four. Straight-line vesting is fairer, but it loosens the handcuffs. Notice the asymmetry with the fund. The fund's strip never vests. Vesting is a discipline applied only to the sweet equity.

§8.3.3Drag, tag, and who controls the exit

Two provisions on transferring shares appear in every institutional shareholders' agreement.

  • Drag-along. If the fund accepts an offer for the company, it can compel all the other shareholders to sell on the same terms. The fund usually needs more than 50% of the shares to do this, sometimes defined as an "investor majority". Without drag, a management holdout with 5% could block a sale, or extract a price for allowing it. For the fund, this is non-negotiable, because it has to be able to deliver 100% of the company to a buyer.
  • Tag-along. This is the mirror image. If the fund sells its stake, the minorities have the right to sell alongside it, on the same terms. That protects management and the sellers who rolled over from waking up with a new controlling shareholder they never chose, while the fund has cashed out.

Here are the points of judgement. What are the thresholds for drag? Can the fund drag at a price where the sweet equity gets nothing? Usually it can, because the protection comes from the waterfall, not the drag. Does the drag require the same form of payment for everyone? Cash for the fund, and paper for management, is a classic squeeze. And do the tag rights cover partial sales?

§8.3.4Ratchets: performance-linked equity splits

A ratchet adjusts management's share of the ordinary equity according to the fund's realised return. An upside ratchet says: "if the fund clears a hurdle, management's percentage of the ordinaries steps up." It lets a fund concede more of the upside only in outcomes where it's already winning. That's a cheap concession at signing, and it's valuable to management precisely in the scenarios they're aiming for.

Here's a worked example. A fund invests £50m in the institutional strip. Management hold 15% of the ordinary shares, ratcheting up to 20% if the fund's total return, from its loan notes plus its ordinary proceeds, reaches at least 2.5x. At exit, the loan notes, including the accrued PIK, are worth £65m. Let's run two exits.

In Exit 1, the equity proceeds are £125m. The notes are repaid at £65m, leaving a pool of £60m for the ordinaries. Test the hurdle at the split before the ratchet, with the fund on 85%. The fund's total is 65 plus 0.85 × 60, which is 65 plus 51, or £116m. That's 2.32x on £50m. It's below 2.5x, so there's no ratchet. Management take 15% of 60, which is £9m, and the fund takes £116m. As a check, 116 + 9 = 125 ✓.

In Exit 2, the equity proceeds are £145m. The pool for the ordinaries is 145 minus 65, which is £80m. Before the ratchet, the fund's total is 65 plus 0.85 × 80, which is 65 plus 68, or £133m. That's 2.66x, which is above 2.5x, so the ratchet is triggered. Management's share steps up to 20%, so management take 0.20 × 80, which is £16m instead of £12m. The fund takes 65 plus 0.80 × 80, which is £129m, or 2.58x, still comfortably over the hurdle. As a check, 129 + 16 = 145 ✓. The ratchet moved £4m from the fund to management, and the fund barely felt it. That's the design.

There are two technical points that deal teams always probe. The first is circularity. If the hurdle is tested on the fund's return after the ratchet, the ratchet itself can pull the fund back below its own trigger. Documents handle this by testing before the ratchet, as above, or by saying that the ratchet only applies to the extent that the fund stays at or above the hurdle. The second is cliff edges. A single-step ratchet creates a discontinuity. Here, at the trigger point, management's proceeds jump by a third for £1 of extra price. Around that cliff, management and the fund have distorted incentives on when to exit, and which price to accept. Sliding-scale ratchets, such as 15% at 2.0x, rising in a straight line to 20% at 3.0x, take more drafting, but they behave far better.

Reverse ratchets exist too, where management's percentage falls if performance disappoints. But they're rarer. Taking equity away from a struggling team part-way through the hold is usually counterproductive, and the option-like payoff of the sweet equity already punishes underperformance.

§8.3.5What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

So what looks good? Rollover of 20 to 40% of proceeds by sellers who stay involved in running the business, invested on equal terms with the fund. A leaver matrix with a genuine intermediate category. Vesting that's mostly earned by the expected exit date. Drag and tag rights that are both present, with language requiring the same terms and the same form of payment. And ratchets on a sliding scale, tested without circularity.

And what looks bad? A departing founder rolling over nothing, while urging the buyer on. Resignation treated as bad leaving, with shares bought back at cost after year four. Drag rights that can be exercised with non-cash payment for the minorities only. Single-cliff ratchets set exactly at the fund's base case, which maximises the distortion of incentives at the most likely outcome. And sellers who've rolled over holding a different, more junior instrument from the fund's.

So what do deal teams actually ask? "How much of the seller's net proceeds are going back in, and in what instrument?" And, "show me management's outcome if the CFO resigns in year three." The first question separates signalling from substance. The second forces you to read the leaver matrix, the vesting schedule and the valuation mechanics together, which is the only way they ever work in real life.

Next, we'll zoom in on the management incentive plan itself: how big the pot of sweet equity should be, the envy ratio, option pools compared with direct equity, and the tax framework that shapes all of it.

Lesson 8.4/Deal Structuring

Management Incentive Plans in Detail

25 min read
In brief

This lesson covers how to size sweet equity, defines the envy ratio and shows how to calculate it, and compares option pools with direct equity. It gives a high-level picture of UK tax, meaning capital versus income, and explains what separates a management incentive plan that motivates from the classic design mistakes that quietly demotivate a team.

  1. 8.4.1What a MIP is actually for
  2. 8.4.2Sizing the sweet pot
  3. 8.4.3The envy ratio: definition and worked computation
  4. 8.4.4Direct equity vs option pools
  5. 8.4.5Tax framing, at a high level
  6. 8.4.6What a well-designed MIP achieves — and the classic mistakes

§8.4.1What a MIP is actually for

A management incentive plan, or MIP, is the package of equity instruments, prices and terms through which the operating team shares in the outcome of the deal. Strip away the legal machinery, and it has exactly three jobs.

  1. To motivate. It should make the difference between an average exit and a great one worth life-changing money to the people who decide which one happens.
  2. To retain. It should make leaving before the exit expensive, through vesting and leaver terms, as covered in Lesson 3.
  3. To align. It should make sure management get rich in the same scenarios as the fund does, not in different ones, and not in none.

Everything else, whether envy ratios, hurdle instruments or the size of the pool, is engineering in service of those three jobs. A MIP that's generous, but pays out in scenarios the fund doesn't care about, has failed. So has one that's beautifully aligned, but so stingy, or so far underwater, that the team mentally writes it off in year two. The most expensive MIP is the one nobody believes in.

§8.4.2Sizing the sweet pot

Remember the architecture from Lesson 2. About 90% of the fund's money goes into loan notes, and the ordinary shares, the sweet equity, form a small pool that management buys into. Two dials set what management get.

  • The percentage of the pool. That's management's share of the ordinary equity. The norm in the UK mid-market is 10 to 20% of the ordinaries for the whole team, with the CEO commonly taking between a third and a half of management's allocation, and the fund holding the rest.
  • The price. Management subscribe at, or close to, the market value of the shares at completion. Because the ordinaries sit beneath a large claim from the loan notes, that market value is low, and that's exactly what makes the equity "sweet". The cheque should still hurt a little. Somewhere between half and one and a half times each participant's annual salary is the customary range for a sanity check. Free equity aligns nobody, and it creates tax problems. Equity that costs three years' salary creates resentment and the risk of personal borrowing, rather than motivation.

§8.4.3The envy ratio: definition and worked computation

The envy ratio is the standard single-number summary of how sweet the sweet equity is. Here's the definition:

Envy ratio=institutional investment/institutional % of ordinary equitymanagement investment/management % of ordinary equity\text{Envy ratio} = \frac{\text{institutional investment} / \text{institutional \% of ordinary equity}}{\text{management investment} / \text{management \% of ordinary equity}}Envy ratio=management investment/management % of ordinary equityinstitutional investment/institutional % of ordinary equity​

In words, it's how much the fund pays for each percentage point of the upside instrument, divided by how much management pay for each percentage point. An envy ratio of 1 means management got no structural favour at all. Higher numbers mean a sweeter deal for management, because the fund "envies" their entry price.

Here's a worked calculation. A fund invests £36m in total, made up of £34.8m of loan notes and £1.2m of ordinary shares, and ends up with 80% of the ordinaries. Management invest £1.2m of their own cash for the other 20%.

  • For the fund, £36m divided by 80 is £0.45m per point of ordinary equity.
  • For management, £1.2m divided by 20 is £0.06m per point.
  • So the envy ratio is 0.45 divided by 0.06, which is 7.5.

Management are buying a share of the upside at a price per point that's seven and a half times lower than the fund's effective price. That discount isn't charity. The fund's £34.8m of notes rank ahead and accrue a coupon, so the fund has bought protection, while management have bought pure risk. The envy ratio simply measures how that trade nets out.

So what are the market norms? In the UK mid-market, envy ratios typically land between 4 and 8. Competitive processes for strong teams push them higher; 10 or more happens when a fund is desperate to win a management team's backing. Proprietary deals, or nervous credit markets, push them lower. A ratio below about 3 will strike any experienced adviser to management as mean, and anything in double figures will make the fund's investment committee ask who negotiated it.

A word of caution, though. The envy ratio compresses a whole structure into a single number, and it can be gamed. A high envy ratio, alongside a 12% PIK coupon and a seven-year hold, can leave management worse off than a modest ratio with an 8% coupon. So always run the waterfall from Lesson 2 in the base case, and never judge a MIP on the envy ratio alone.

§8.4.4Direct equity vs option pools

UK buyouts overwhelmingly use direct equity, where managers buy real shares at completion, with real money. US deals, and companies at an earlier stage, lean more on options, or profits interests. Here are the trade-offs.

Direct sweet equity Option pool
Cash from managers Yes — skin in the game No (strike paid at exercise, often net-settled)
UK tax character Capital gains on growth (if structured properly) Unapproved options: gains taxed as income at exercise
Downside for managers Real — can lose the cheque None beyond opportunity cost
Flexibility for joiners Harder — new shares need valuing each time Easy — grant from the pool
Dilution mechanics Fixed at completion Pool overhang, top-ups possible

The UK preference for direct equity is largely driven by tax, which is the next section, but it's also philosophical. Funds want managers to have written a cheque that they can lose. The practical weakness of direct equity is hiring people part-way through the hold. A CFO joining in year three has to buy shares at their current market value, which, after two good years, may be many times the entry price. Well-designed MIPs hold back an unallocated reserve of sweet equity, often 2 to 5% of the ordinaries, held by the fund or by an employee benefit trust, so that new joiners can be brought in without renegotiating the whole structure.

§8.4.5Tax framing, at a high level

There's no detailed tax advice here, because every real MIP is structured with specialist advisers. But you can't read UK structures without knowing the shape of the incentive.

  • Capital versus income is the whole game. Growth on shares that a manager genuinely bought at market value is taxed as capital gains. UK rates of capital gains tax are materially lower than the top combined rates of income tax plus employee and employer National Insurance. The same economic gain, recharacterised as employment income, can lose roughly half its value, and create a cost in employer's National Insurance on top. That single distinction explains why UK MIPs are built from shares that managers buy, rather than from options or bonuses that they're granted.
  • The entry price has to be defensible. Because the managers are employees, shares they acquire cheaply relative to market value count as "employment-related securities", and the discount is taxable as income. Hence the ritual of valuing the sweet equity at completion. The thin slice of ordinaries under a big stack of loan notes genuinely is worth very little, and the valuation evidences that. Standard practice includes making elections, in the UK under section 431, to pay any small income-tax cost up front, so that all future growth counts as capital.
  • The structure is doing tax work everywhere. The coupon on the loan notes, the split of the rollover between notes and shares, and the mechanics of valuing leavers' shares all have tax consequences. When a term looks economically pointless, the explanation is usually tax.

For a deal team, the point of judgement isn't the tax detail. It's noticing when a MIP's tax position is fragile, such as aggressive entry valuations, or ratchets that HMRC might read as disguised bonuses. Fragile tax positions blow up at exit, in the middle of negotiations with a buyer, at the worst possible moment.

§8.4.6What a well-designed MIP achieves — and the classic mistakes

A good MIP produces sentences like this from the CEO, unprompted, in year two: "If we hit the plan, my equity's worth about £4m, and I check that maths every quarter." More concretely, a well-designed plan has the following features.

  • Sweet equity that's in the money in the fund's base case, by a meaningful margin, so that the team's realistic effort changes their outcome now, not just in dreamland.
  • Cheques that are real, but survivable, for each participant.
  • An envy ratio and a coupon that are within market norms, so that the plan survives a review by management's adviser without poisoning the relationship.
  • A reserve pool for future hires.
  • Leaver and vesting terms that the team accepts as fair, as covered in Lesson 3.
  • And simplicity, so that the CFO can reproduce the maths of the payoff on a single page.

And here are the classic design mistakes, all of them tested in the field as ways to destroy value.

  1. Underwater by construction. A PIK coupon of 10 to 12% on a big stack of notes, plus a timetable for exit that slips, and by year five the ordinaries need a stretch-case exit to be worth anything at all. The team knows it before the fund admits it, and effort quietly shifts towards updating CVs.
  2. Putting everything on a cliff. Vesting everything at exit, plus treating resignation as bad leaving, reads as distrust. And by year four, it retains bodies, not minds.
  3. A pool sized for the organisation chart, not the plan. Spreading 15% across twenty-five managers gives nobody a stake that motivates them. Concentrating it on three people leaves the next tier, who are often the operators that actually deliver, with nothing.
  4. No reserve, so that every senior hire triggers a renegotiation with all the existing holders.
  5. Complexity used as a weapon. Multiple ratchets, catch-ups and hurdle instruments that only the fund's lawyers can model. If management need an adviser to tell them what they'd make at 2.5x, then alignment has already failed.

So what do deal teams actually ask? "What does the CFO personally make in the base case, at 1.5x, and at zero, and do they know those numbers?" If the answers are, respectively, "something meaningful", "something", and "they lose their cheque", and the CFO knows them cold, then the MIP is doing its job. The case study for this module puts you on the other side of exactly that conversation.

Lesson 8.5/Deal Structuring

Earnouts, Deferred Consideration and Vendor Instruments

24 min read
In brief

This lesson covers when earn-outs can bridge a gap in valuation, and how to choose the metrics and the periods. It explains why earn-outs go wrong, through disputes over measurement and over control. It also covers vendor loan notes and contingent structures in carve-outs, with a worked earn-out example across three scenarios.

  1. 8.5.1Not all consideration arrives at completion
  2. 8.5.2Earnouts: bridging the valuation gap
  3. 8.5.3A worked earnout
  4. 8.5.4Why earnouts go wrong
  5. 8.5.5Vendor loan notes and deferred consideration
  6. 8.5.6Contingent structures in carve-outs
  7. 8.5.7What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

§8.5.1Not all consideration arrives at completion

So far, the seller has been paid in two currencies: cash at closing, and rollover equity. There's a third family. This is consideration that's promised rather than paid, and sometimes conditional rather than certain.

  • Deferred consideration is a fixed amount payable later, such as "£10m on the second anniversary". The amount is certain; the only uncertainty is about credit, because the seller is now an unsecured creditor of the buyer.
  • An earn-out is a variable amount payable later, depending on the business hitting defined targets. Both the amount and the credit are uncertain.
  • Vendor loan notes mean the seller formally lends part of the price back to the buyer, on documented terms, with a coupon. It's deferred consideration, with paperwork and interest.

All three exist for the same underlying reason: the buyer and the seller disagree about the future, or the buyer can't, or won't, fund the full price today. Structure lets the disagreement be priced, instead of being argued to a standstill.

§8.5.2Earnouts: bridging the valuation gap

Here's the classic situation for an earn-out. The seller says, "we'll make £10m of EBITDA next year, so pay me for it." The buyer says, "you made £7m last year, and that's what I'll pay for." An earn-out turns the argument into a bet that both sides can accept: the buyer pays for the £10m, but only if it turns up. Earn-outs appear most often where the uncertainty is concentrated and close at hand. That means founder-led businesses with concentrated customers, businesses part-way through winning a big contract, pharma and services businesses with risk in their pipeline, and, critically for PE, carve-outs whose economics as a standalone business are unproven.

The choice of metric is the central design decision. Revenue is hard to manipulate downwards, but it rewards unprofitable growth. EBITDA measures what the buyer actually bought, but it's riddled with judgements about definitions. Which overheads count? Whose accounting policies apply? And what about the integration costs that the buyer chooses to incur? Gross profit sits usefully between the two. Non-financial milestones, such as a regulatory approval or a contract renewal, work when they're genuinely all-or-nothing. The rule is to pick the metric that the seller can still influence, and that the buyer can't easily distort, and to define it in an appendix with worked examples, not in a single line.

The period is normally one to three years. Shorter periods keep the numbers attributable to the seller's business. With anything longer, the result reflects the buyer's ownership more than the seller's machine, and the seller is taking on equity-like risk without equity-like upside.

§8.5.3A worked earnout

Fernway Ltd is sold for £50m at completion, plus an earn-out of £2 for every £1 of EBITDA in the second year above £8m, capped at £10m. Second-year EBITDA is as defined in the schedule to the SPA, using the same accounting policies as the locked-box accounts, and before any of the buyer's integration costs. Here are three outcomes.

Scenario FY2 EBITDA Excess over £8m Earnout (2x excess, cap £10m) Total consideration
Miss 7.5 — 0.0 50.0
Partial 9.5 1.5 3.0 53.0
Beat 13.5 5.5 10.0 (11.0 capped) 60.0

Read it from both chairs. The seller's story was "this is a business with £10m of EBITDA, worth £60m". The buyer's was "it's £8m, and worth £50m". The earn-out pays the seller's price only on the seller's numbers. At £9.5m of EBITDA, the total lands in between. And the marginal price, of 2 pounds for each extra pound of EBITDA, is far below the multiple of about 6x that the headline implies. That's why buyers concede earn-out formulas more readily than headline price. Notice the cap, too. Without it, the blow-out year of £13.5m would cost the buyer £11m, and open-ended earn-outs make lenders and investment committees equally nervous.

Here's a modelling habit. Always express the expected cost of the earn-out across the scenarios, not just the cap. A buyer who weights these three scenarios at 30%, 50% and 20% is really paying 50+0.3(0)+0.5(3)+0.2(10)=£53.5m50 + 0.3(0) + 0.5(3) + 0.2(10) = £53.5m50+0.3(0)+0.5(3)+0.2(10)=£53.5m. That's the number to compare against other bids, not £50m or £60m.

§8.5.4Why earnouts go wrong

Earn-outs have a deserved reputation as machines for generating litigation. There are two root causes.

Measurement. The seller's £9.6m and the buyer's £8.9m can both be "second-year EBITDA", separated by choices of accounting policy, management charges from the new parent, accruals for bonuses, and the way group overheads are allocated. Every one of those is decided after completion, mostly by the buyer. Here are the mitigations. Freeze the accounting policies, by reference to a worked schedule. Exclude costs that the buyer controls, such as integration costs and management fees, from the definition. Give the seller rights to information and audit. And appoint an independent expert, rather than a court, to settle disputes.

Control. The buyer runs the business during the earn-out period, and it can depress the metric through entirely defensible commercial decisions. It might delay a product launch, merge the sales force, move a big customer onto a group contract, or load the entity with group costs. Sellers negotiate conduct covenants, along the lines of "operate the business in line with past practice, and don't divert customers or opportunities". But these sit awkwardly against the buyer's need to actually integrate and run the company. This tension is structural, not a drafting error. That's why the best earn-outs are short, simple, and sized so that neither side is tempted to burn the relationship over them. A deal where the earn-out is 40% of the total consideration, and the seller-CEO reports to an integration director, is a dispute with a completion date.

For the fund, there's a quieter problem. An earn-out is effectively debt-like consideration, ranking ahead of the value the equity hopes to create in the future. And lenders treat the expected earn-out payments as calls on cash flow when they size the debt, as Lesson 6 explains. So model it in the waterfall, just like any other claim.

§8.5.5Vendor loan notes and deferred consideration

A vendor loan note, or VLN, turns part of the price into a loan from the seller. For example, in a £70m deal, there might be £58m of cash at closing, and a £12m VLN paying 8%, often as PIK. It's repayable at exit, or on a fixed maturity, and it's usually subordinated to the bank debt, and often to the institutional loan notes too. Here's why each side agrees to it.

  • For the buyer, it fills a funding gap without needing more bank debt or equity. It's cheap compared with mezzanine, and it signals the seller's confidence to the credit committee.
  • For the seller, it achieves the headline price, and earns a coupon while they wait. It ranks ahead of the ordinary equity, unlike a rollover. And unlike an earn-out, the amount is fixed.

The seller's real risks are subordination and credit. A VLN that sits behind 4x of senior debt, in a deal that goes sideways, is worth pennies. When you see a large VLN, ask why the institutional money didn't fill the gap. Sometimes the answer is benign, such as the fund being at its limit for concentration. Sometimes, though, it's the fund quietly capping its exposure to a deal it only half believes in.

Plain deferred consideration, meaning fixed sums on fixed dates, usually without interest and without documentation beyond the SPA, is common in smaller deals, and for founder-sellers who stay on through a transition. There are two disciplines here. Treat it as debt in the structure table, because that's what it is. And check what security or rights of set-off are attached to it. Buyers love setting warranty claims off against deferred payments, which turns the seller's "guaranteed" £10m into a contingent one.

§8.5.6Contingent structures in carve-outs

Carve-outs, meaning buying a division out of a corporate parent, are where contingent consideration really earns its keep. The core problem is that nobody, including the parent, knows the division's true cost base as a standalone business. The P&L you diligence is an exercise in allocation. Group costs for IT, HR, insurance and property are spread by formulas that won't survive separation. And transitional service agreements, or TSAs, price the interim period, not the steady state.

So carve-out structures push the price into contingent forms. These include earn-outs on the first one or two standalone years, which price the actual cost base rather than the allocated one; deferred amounts that depend on milestones for exiting the TSAs, or on key contracts being transferred; price adjustments for stranded costs above an agreed cap; and occasionally anti-embarrassment clauses, which protect the parent if the buyer quickly flips the asset at a profit. The theme is consistent with the whole module: when a number can't be agreed, structure turns it from an argument into a formula. And the quality of the deal depends on how cleanly that formula is drafted.

§8.5.7What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

So what looks good? Earn-outs of modest size, around 10 to 25% of the total consideration, over one or two years, on a metric defined by worked example, with determination by an expert, and conduct covenants that both sides can live with. VLNs with sensible coupons, and explicit subordination. And deferred consideration counted as debt in every returns model.

And what looks bad? An earn-out that's the seller's main upside, while the buyer controls the metric. Definitions of EBITDA that fit on a single line. Earn-outs stretching beyond three years. Deferred consideration ignored in the sources and uses. And a seller-CEO whose earn-out maximises second-year EBITDA, while the fund's plan front-loads investment that depresses it. Those are perfectly opposed incentives, installed on purpose, by accident.

So what do deal teams actually ask? "Who controls the metric, and what will each side rationally do in the final quarter of the earn-out period?" If the honest answer is "the buyer defers revenue and accelerates costs, while the seller does the opposite", then size your provision for the dispute now. And always ask, "what's the expected total consideration, weighted across the scenarios?" Because that's the real price of the deal, whatever the press release says.

Next comes the other side of the balance sheet: how much debt to take on, the covenants that come with it, and the moves part-way through the hold, such as cures, toggles, recaps and refinancings, that reshape a deal after completion.

Lesson 8.6/Deal Structuring

Debt-Side Structuring and Covenants

26 min read
In brief

This lesson covers how to choose how much leverage to take, and why not to take the maximum. It explains maintenance covenants, with a worked example of headroom, along with equity cures and PIK toggles. It covers dividend recaps, with a worked example of their effect on IRR and a test for telling sensible recaps from abusive ones, and finishes with refinancing during the hold.

  1. 8.6.1How much leverage — and why not the maximum
  2. 8.6.2Maintenance covenants and headroom: a worked example
  3. 8.6.3Equity cures and PIK toggles
  4. 8.6.4Dividend recaps: mechanics, a worked IRR effect, and the smell test
  5. 8.6.5Refinancing through the hold
  6. 8.6.6What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

§8.6.1How much leverage — and why not the maximum

Lenders will quote a maximum. For a solid mid-market business, that might be 4.5x EBITDA of senior debt, and more when credit markets are hot. The naive model says take all of it, because every pound of debt is a pound less of equity, and leverage amplifies the return on equity, as Module 7 showed. But deal teams routinely take less than the maximum, and the reasons are the substance of this lesson.

  1. Volatility. Leverage is sized against expected EBITDA, but covenants are breached by actual EBITDA. A services business based on contracts, with 30% of its revenue from concentrated customers, shouldn't be levered like a subscription software company, whatever the lender offers this quarter.
  2. Flexibility with cash. Servicing debt, meaning cash interest plus repayments, is the first claim on cash flow. Every pound of it is a pound that isn't available for the capex, bolt-ons and hires in the value-creation plan. Buying a company in order to grow it, and then starving the growth plan to pay interest, is self-defeating, and it's common.
  3. Keeping options open. Headroom against the covenants, and against the ceiling on debt capacity, is what lets the company survive a bad year, fund an opportunistic acquisition, or refinance on its own timetable rather than the market's.
  4. The lender's price for the last turn. The final turn of leverage carries the highest margin and the tightest terms. The blended cost of going from 3.5x to 4.5x is often poor value compared with the equity it saves.

Here's the working answer most teams arrive at. Lever up to the point where the business can comfortably service its debt in the downside case, not the base case, and let the equity cheque flex instead.

§8.6.2Maintenance covenants and headroom: a worked example

Mid-market loan agreements typically carry maintenance covenants. These are ratios tested every quarter, and breaching one is an event of default, even if every payment has been made on time. Large-cap "covenant-lite" deals replace these with incurrence covenants, which are only tested when the borrower does something, such as paying a dividend or raising more debt. Know the difference, because it decides how early the lenders get a seat at the table. There are two workhorse covenants.

  • The leverage covenant says that net debt divided by EBITDA must not exceed a scheduled level.
  • The interest cover covenant says that EBITDA divided by net cash interest must not fall below a set level.

Covenants are set off the lender's base case, with some headroom, typically a cushion of 25 to 35% on EBITDA. They usually tighten, or step down, over time, because the plan assumes the debt is being paid down.

Here's a worked example. At the test date in year 2, Halton Group plc has net debt of £70m, forecast EBITDA of £20m, and net cash interest of £7m. The covenants say leverage must be no more than 4.5x, and interest cover must be at least 2.0x.

  • For leverage, there's a breach when EBITDA falls below 70 divided by 4.5, which is £15.6m. So the cushion is 20 minus 15.6, divided by 20, which gives 22% headroom on EBITDA.
  • For interest cover, there's a breach when EBITDA falls below 2.0 times 7, which is £14.0m. So the cushion is 20 minus 14, divided by 20, which gives 30% headroom.

The leverage covenant is the binding one, because it trips first, at a 22% fall in EBITDA. That's the single number the CFO and the sponsor watch. Notice too that leverage covenants bite twice. Both EBITDA falling, and net debt failing to come down, through weak cash conversion or a blowout in working capital, push the ratio up. A business can hit its EBITDA budget, and still breach because its debt didn't come down.

The consequences of a breach are rarely an instant catastrophe. The realistic sequence is default, then negotiation, then a waiver fee, a higher margin, tighter terms, and perhaps an injection of equity. But the lender now has leverage over the deal, and that's exactly what covenants are for. From the sponsor's side, the whole game is buying enough headroom at signing that a normal bad year is a conversation with the board, not with the lender.

§8.6.3Equity cures and PIK toggles

Two structural pressure valves come up constantly.

An equity cure is a contractual right for the sponsor to inject equity after a covenant test, and have it counted towards the ratio, so that the breach is cured. It's usually counted as a reduction in net debt, and occasionally, much more generously, as if it were EBITDA. In the Halton example, suppose EBITDA comes in at £15.0m. Leverage is then 70 divided by 15, which is 4.67x, a breach. An equity cure of £2.5m, applied to net debt, gives 67.5 divided by 15, which is 4.5x, cured exactly. Loan agreements ration cures, perhaps to no more than two quarters in a row, and four over the life of the loan, sometimes with a cap on each cure. That's because a sponsor who cures every quarter is paying away the lender's risk, rather than fixing the business.

A PIK toggle is a feature of some junior debt. It lets the borrower choose, period by period, to pay interest in kind, rolling it into the principal, usually at a premium of 75 to 100 basis points, rather than paying it in cash. It turns a liquidity problem into a bigger claim in the future. That's valuable flexibility in a squeeze that's genuinely temporary. But it's corrosive if the toggle is used routinely, because the compounding balance eats the equity from above, just as the institutional loan notes eat the sweet equity from within.

§8.6.4Dividend recaps: mechanics, a worked IRR effect, and the smell test

A dividend recapitalisation puts more debt on the business part-way through the hold, in order to pay the proceeds out to the shareholders. The company borrows more, because it has paid down debt and grown into some spare debt capacity, and the new debt funds a distribution. That typically repays part of the institutional loan notes first, and then pays dividends up the waterfall.

Here's a worked example of the effect on IRR. A fund invests £40m of equity at completion. The base plan is to exit at the end of year 5, with £100m of proceeds for the equity.

  • Without a recap, the cash flows are minus 40, then four zeros, then plus 100. The MOIC is 2.50x, and the IRR is (100/40)1/5−1(100/40)^{1/5}-1(100/40)1/5−1, which is 20.1%.
  • With a recap, at the end of year 3, the company raises £20m of new debt at 10% cash interest, and distributes it to the fund. The extra debt is still outstanding at exit. And two years of interest, 2 × £2m, which is £4m, uses up cash that would otherwise have built up in the business. So the equity proceeds in year 5 fall to 100 minus 20 minus 4, which is £76m. The cash flows are minus 40, zero, zero, plus 20, zero, and plus 76. The MOIC is 96 divided by 40, which is 2.40x, and the IRR is about 21.4%.

The recap traded 0.10x of money multiple for 1.3 points of IRR, because £20m came home two years earlier. That's the general shape: recaps raise the IRR, lower the MOIC, and raise the risk. The business carries more debt for the rest of the hold, with its covenant headroom reset more tightly. Recaps also take risk off the fund. After the recap, the fund has only £20m of net capital at risk, and its downside scenarios improve, even as the company's get worse.

So when is a recap sensible? When the business has structurally outperformed, with EBITDA up materially and leverage well below the level at entry, and the recap simply restores a prudent capital structure while returning capital early to the LPs. When debt markets are cheap. And when the operating plan is still fully funded after the distribution. In that world, a recap is just disciplined management of capital.

And when is it abusive? When the recap takes leverage above the level at entry, on flat performance. When it strips out the buffer of cash that a cyclical business will need. When it gets ahead of a known deterioration. Or when it turns a struggling deal into a trade of "give the fund its money back, and let the lenders own the tail risk". The tell is simple. Ask whether the pro-forma capital structure would have been a responsible way to buy the business today, at today's level of performance. If it wouldn't, then the recap is extracting value, not managing capital.

§8.6.5Refinancing through the hold

Debt isn't something you set and forget. Over a hold of five to seven years, expect the capital structure to be revisited at least once.

  • Repricing, or amend and extend. When credit markets tighten their spreads, or the wall of maturities gets close, borrowers reprice their margins downwards, or push their maturities out. It's cheap if it's done from strength, and expensive if it's done at the market's convenience.
  • Refinancing into looser documents. A business that has paid down its debt can often replace its amortising, covenanted club loan with a covenant-lite unitranche, or an institutional term loan. That releases the cash flow that was going on repayments, and the risk from the covenants, in exchange for a higher margin.
  • Add-on facilities. These are committed lines for acquisitions or capex, or incremental "accordion" facilities, pre-negotiated at signing, so that the buy-and-build plan doesn't need a separate lender process for every bolt-on. Structuring these at entry is far cheaper than asking for them part-way through the hold.
  • Repaying the institutional loan notes. The proceeds of a refinancing often go first towards redeeming part of the fund's loan notes, which is called a "soft recap". The IRR logic is the same as above. It also takes risk off the sweet equity's position, by stopping some of the PIK from compounding, and that's why management teams are often quietly enthusiastic about it.

The thread running through all of this is that a deal's debt structure at exit rarely looks like its debt structure at entry. And the flexibility to make these moves, through baskets, accordions, portability and cure rights, is negotiated on day one, when the sponsor has competitive tension to spend.

§8.6.6What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

So what looks good? Leverage sized to the downside case, with 25 to 35% headroom on the covenants. A covenant schedule that tracks a credible path of paying down debt, rather than a hockey stick. Equity cures that are available, but unused. Recaps done on the back of outperformance, which keep pro-forma leverage below the level at entry. And options for refinancing, such as accordions and baskets, bought at signing.

And what looks bad? Debt at the top of what was offered, "because it was available". Covenant headroom below 15% at signing, which means the plan has no permission to wobble. Repeated equity cures, or a PIK toggle used for three periods in a row, which means the structure is eating itself. A recap that returns the fund's whole cheque on flat EBITDA. And a wall of maturities that falls inside the intended window for exit, with no plan for refinancing.

So what do deal teams actually ask? "How far can EBITDA fall before we're talking to the banks, and in which quarter?" That's the binding covenant, and its tightest test date. And, "what has to be true for the recap?" They insist that the answer is given in terms of performance, not in terms of the market. Debt structured with those two questions in mind is debt that the deal can live with for five years. That judgement, matching the claims to the business, rather than the business to the claims, is where this module started, and it's the whole craft of structuring.

Lesson 9.1/Due Diligence

The Diligence Machine

25 min read
In brief

This lesson explains how a diligence exercise is actually organised. It covers the seven workstreams and who runs them, and how the scope is phased against cost and exclusivity. It then shows how the findings turn into price chips, structural fixes, protections in the SPA, or a decision to walk away.

  1. 9.1.1Why diligence exists
  2. 9.1.2The seven workstreams
  3. 9.1.3Phasing: scope against cost and exclusivity
  4. 9.1.4From finding to consequence: the four outcomes
  5. 9.1.5The deal team's job: synthesis
  6. 9.1.6What looks good and what looks bad in the process itself

§9.1.1Why diligence exists

By the time a fund enters exclusivity, it has typically seen a CIM, a management presentation, and a data room curated by advisers whose fee depends on the deal completing. Everything the buyer "knows" has been arranged by the seller. Due diligence is the buyer's organised attempt to replace that curated picture with one that's been independently verified, before the money moves, and while there's still leverage in the negotiation.

The economics are brutal and simple. In a deal priced at 9.0× EBITDA, every £1m of EBITDA that turns out not to exist has cost £9m of enterprise value. And because the debt was sized off the same number, a deal that's been overpaid is over-levered at the same time. Spending £2m to £4m on diligence for a £200m deal is cheap insurance against mispricing it by £15m to £20m. The reverse matters too. Diligence that confirms quality lets a fund bid with conviction, and win auctions it would otherwise have lost to braver bidders.

Here's one mental model to carry through this whole module. Diligence doesn't exist to produce reports. It exists to answer four questions: is the EBITDA real, will it last, what could kill it, and what do we do about each finding? Each of the workstreams below is a different lens on those questions.

§9.1.2The seven workstreams

A full buyout diligence exercise typically runs seven workstreams in parallel. Each has a natural owner, a natural output, and a natural way of failing.

Workstream Typical owner Core question Headline output
Financial (FDD) Big 4 / large accounting firm Is the EBITDA and cash flow real? Quality of earnings report; NWC and net debt analysis
Commercial (CDD) Strategy house (Bain, EY-Parthenon, OC&C, LEK) or specialist Will revenue and margin persist and grow? Market model, customer references, forecast view
Legal Law firm What obligations, disputes, and change-of-control traps exist? Legal DD report; feeds directly into SPA drafting
Tax Big 4 tax practice What are the historic exposures and the efficient structure? Tax DD report; structuring memo
Operational Ops consultants, sometimes the fund's own operating partners Can the business actually deliver the plan? Capacity, supply chain, systems assessment
Management Specialist assessors (e.g. psychometric + referencing firms) Is this the team to back? Individual assessments, referencing
Insurance / ESG / IT Brokers, specialists Anything uninsurable, unfundable, or unfixable? Gap analyses, W&I feasibility

There are three practical notes on who does what. First, financial due diligence is almost always done by a Big 4 firm, or a large challenger, because the work is forensic accounting. It means rebuilding EBITDA from the ledger, testing how revenue is recognised, and tracing the cash. Second, commercial due diligence needs a different skill set: sizing markets, interviewing competitors, and taking references from customers. That's bought from strategy consultancies. A common junior mistake is to treat financial and commercial due diligence as substitutes for each other. Financial due diligence tells you what the earnings were, while commercial due diligence tells you whether they'll continue. Third, the fund's deal team owns none of the workstreams, but all of the synthesis, and there's more on that below.

§9.1.3Phasing: scope against cost and exclusivity

Diligence is expensive, often £2m to £5m in total on a mid-market deal, and much of it is wasted if the deal dies. So the scope is phased in line with the probability of the deal happening.

Phase Deal stage Spend profile What actually happens
Desktop / red-flag Pre-IOI Minimal; mostly deal-team time Public information, CIM interrogation, sector experts, a "red flag" review from advisers
Confirmatory scoping Post-IOI, pre-exclusivity Moderate Advisers engaged on limited scope; focus on the 3–4 issues that would change the price
Full / confirmatory Exclusivity Full fees committed Complete FDD/CDD/legal/tax reports, management sessions, site visits

There are two points of judgement here. A fund that spends £3m in a five-party auction, where it has a 20% chance of winning, is burning £2.4m in the expected cost of dead deals. On the other hand, a fund that spends nothing until exclusivity may win exclusivity at a price it then can't support. Sophisticated funds solve this by doing the work that's critical to price early, and cheaply. That might be a red-flag financial review focused only on the adjusted EBITDA bridge, or calls with sector experts instead of full commercial due diligence. Then they save the breadth of confirmatory work for exclusivity. The second point is about a vendor due diligence process, where the seller commissions its own financial and commercial reports, and shares them with all the bidders. Read them carefully, but remember who paid for them. Vendor due diligence is reliable on facts, because advisers won't put their name to false numbers. But it's systematically generous on judgement calls, such as which add-backs are "one-off", or how big the market is. The buyer's own "top-up" diligence should target exactly those judgement calls.

§9.1.4From finding to consequence: the four outcomes

This is the most important section in this lesson. A diligence finding is worthless until it has been turned into one of four outcomes.

1. A price chip. If the finding permanently reduces the sustainable EBITDA, the price moves. Here's a worked example. Financial due diligence concludes that £0.8m of a claimed £12.0m of adjusted EBITDA is actually a recurring cost dressed up as a one-off. At the deal multiple of 9.0×, the buyer's offer falls from £108.0m to £100.8m. That's a £7.2m chip, from a £0.8m finding. Price chips are for findings that are certain, and can be quantified.

2. A structural fix. If the finding is a risk, rather than a certainty, you don't chip the price. Instead, you restructure the deal so that the seller bears the risk. The classic tools are an earn-out, where part of the price depends on the disputed forecast being achieved; deferred consideration; a specific escrow, or retention, against a known dispute; or making completion conditional on the customer contract in question being renewed. Here's an example. Management forecast a £3m uplift in EBITDA from a contract that's been signed, but hasn't gone live. Rather than pay 9.0× on £3m of hope, which would be £27m, or pay nothing and lose the deal, the buyer offers a £13.5m earn-out, payable when the contract delivers its first full year.

3. Protection in the SPA. Findings about historic exposures, such as a tax position that might be challenged, or a dispute that hasn't been resolved, are handled in the sale and purchase agreement. There are warranties, which are the seller's statements of fact, where a breach gives the buyer a claim for damages. There are indemnities, which are pound-for-pound promises against a specific, identified risk. And there's increasingly W&I insurance, which transfers the warranty risk to an insurer, for a premium of roughly 1 to 2% of the policy limit. Here's the rule of judgement: a known, identified risk gets an indemnity or a price adjustment, not a warranty. Warranties protect against the unknown, and W&I insurers exclude anything the diligence reports flagged. So the diligence findings directly shape what protection is even available.

4. Walking away. Some findings can't be priced. Think of fraud, a broken relationship with a customer that represents 40% of gross profit, or a market in structural decline that the whole thesis denied. The discipline here is cultural. Deal teams suffer from deal momentum, after months of work, adviser fees spent, and career capital invested. The investment committee's job is to make walking away respectable. Here's a useful test: if we'd seen this finding on day one, would we have started work at all? If the answer is no, the sunk costs don't change it.

§9.1.5The deal team's job: synthesis

Advisers produce hundreds of pages, and nobody pays a fund's fees for forwarding PDFs. The deal team's distinctive job is synthesis: forcing the findings from every workstream into a single view of price, structure and risk that an investment committee can act on.

In practice, that means three things. First, cross-referencing. The most dangerous findings are the ones that no single adviser can see. Financial due diligence notes that revenue was pulled forward in the fourth quarter. Commercial due diligence notes that the top distributor complained about being "encouraged" to take stock. Neither report says "channel stuffing"; the deal team has to connect them. Second, maintaining the issues list. That's a live table of every finding, with its impact on EBITDA or value, its proposed treatment, whether that's a chip, a structure, a protection in the SPA, or acceptance, and its owner. This document is the negotiation. Third, updating the model. Every accepted finding flows into the LBO model, as a revised EBITDA, a revised peg for working capital, a debt-like item, or a downside case. That way, the investment committee sees returns on numbers that have been diligenced, rather than the numbers from the CIM.

§9.1.6What looks good and what looks bad in the process itself

The way diligence is conducted is itself evidence about the target.

Signal What it suggests
Data room complete, questions answered in days, monthly management accounts reconcile to audit Well-run business with nothing to hide — quality assets diligence easily
Key data "not tracked" (churn, margin by customer), answers routed through advisers only, management access rationed Either weak systems or something to hide — both are findings
Vendor pushes to compress exclusivity and resists FDD scope Ask why the seller fears daylight
Management privately more conservative than the CIM Normal and mildly reassuring — the CIM is the bankers' document
A finding you raise gets a fast, evidenced rebuttal Healthy; management knows its business
A finding gets a new story each time you ask Escalate — inconsistent explanations are a flag in themselves

Here's a closing rule of thumb for the whole module: diligence rarely uncovers a single fatal document. Deals die, or get repriced, through the build-up of a dozen medium-sized findings, each of which shaves away some conviction. Your job in the coming lessons is to learn what those findings look like in the numbers, and what each one is worth.

Lesson 9.2/Due Diligence

Financial DD & Quality of Earnings

30 min read
In brief

This lesson takes apart a quality of earnings report. It works through a full adjusted EBITDA bridge with eight adjustments of varying legitimacy, explains run-rate and pro-forma treatments, and shows why the peg for normalised working capital matters, with a worked example. It finishes with the hunt for net debt and debt-like items.

  1. 9.2.1What a QoE report actually is
  2. 9.2.2The adjusted EBITDA bridge: a worked example
  3. 9.2.3Run-rate and pro-forma adjustments done properly
  4. 9.2.4Normalised working capital: why the peg matters
  5. 9.2.5The net debt hunt: debt-like items
  6. 9.2.6What deal teams actually ask of FDD

§9.2.1What a QoE report actually is

Financial due diligence produces one central document: the quality of earnings, or QoE, report. Its job is to answer, line by line, whether the reported EBITDA represents the sustainable earning power of the business, backed by cash. That matters because that number drives both the price, which is the multiple times EBITDA, and the debt package, which is leverage times EBITDA.

A QoE report has a standard anatomy. There's an adjusted EBITDA bridge, from reported to adjusted, with every adjustment evidenced and given an opinion. There's analysis of revenue and margin, by customer, product and geography, looking for concentration, one-offs and problems with recognition. There's normalised working capital, which sets the peg. There's net debt and debt-like items. And there's cash conversion: does EBITDA turn into cash? This lesson walks through the three that most often move the price: the bridge, the peg, and net debt.

Here's the stance to take throughout. The seller's adviser prepared the adjusted EBITDA number to be as high as could be defended. Your job isn't to assume fraud. It's to re-underwrite each adjustment against a simple test: would this cost, or this revenue, genuinely not recur under our ownership?

§9.2.2The adjusted EBITDA bridge: a worked example

The target is a distribution business, with reported EBITDA of £10.0m for the financial year. The vendor's financial due diligence pack presents adjusted EBITDA of £13.5m, through eight adjustments.

# Adjustment £m Vendor's rationale
Reported EBITDA 10.0
1 Excess founder remuneration +0.4 Two founder-directors paid £0.9m; market cost of replacements £0.5m
2 Legal settlement +0.6 One-off dispute with former supplier, settled this year
3 Aborted transaction costs +0.3 Fees from a sale process that collapsed last year
4 "One-off" recruitment fees +0.2 Exceptional hiring campaign
5 Run-rate of January price increase +0.9 4% price rise effective month 10; full-year effect added
6 Bolt-on synergies +0.5 Acquired competitor in month 7; identified cost synergies
7 FX gains −0.2 Non-recurring translation gains removed
8 Signed contract not yet live +0.8 Three-year contract signed, service starts next quarter
Adjusted EBITDA 13.5

Now let's re-underwrite each one.

1. Excess pay for the founders, plus 0.4. This is legitimate, but verify the number. Under new ownership, the founders either leave, or take market salaries, so the excess genuinely won't recur. But test the assumption about the cost of replacing them. If you actually need a CEO and CFO costing £0.7m between them, the add-back is £0.2m, not £0.4m. This is the add-back that's most commonly accepted, and also the one most commonly overstated.

2. A legal settlement, plus 0.6. This is only legitimate if it's genuinely isolated. Pull three to five years of history. If legal and settlement costs appear in most years, say £0.3m, then £0.1m, then £0.6m, the business has a recurring level of dispute costs. The add-back should then be the excess over that run-rate, not the whole amount. One-offs that happen every year are called operating costs.

3. Costs of an aborted transaction, plus 0.3. This is legitimate. The costs of the sale process itself won't recur under your ownership. It's usually accepted with little argument, and that's exactly why sellers like to put as much as possible under this heading. So check that the invoices really relate to the process.

4. Recruitment fees, plus 0.2. This is aggressive. A business that has grown its headcount every year for five years will keep on hiring. Recruitment is a cost of growth, not a one-off. Reject it, unless a specific, abnormal event is evidenced, such as replacing an entire finance team in one go. And even then, only accept the abnormal part.

5. The run-rate of a price increase, plus 0.9. This is aggressive, because it's only half the story. Annualising a price rise brought in late in the year is a legitimate category of adjustment, because run-rate adjustments capture the full-year effect of changes that are already in place. But this one assumes no loss of volume at all. The diligence question is: what churn followed the rise? If 2% of customers left, the net effect might be plus 0.5m. Also check that the rise wasn't a manoeuvre before the sale that will unwind. At best, it gets partial credit.

6. Synergies from a bolt-on, plus 0.5. This is aggressive. "Identified" synergies are a plan, not a result. The standard is that they've been delivered, and are in the ledger. What is legitimate is the pro-forma adjustment for the bolt-on itself, which the next section covers. Buyers may pay for the potential of synergies in competitive processes, but they should do it knowingly, in the multiple, rather than having it hidden inside the EBITDA that the multiple is applied to.

7. Gains on foreign exchange, minus 0.2. This is legitimate, and notice the direction. A downward adjustment is a small signal of credibility, because an honest bridge removes non-recurring gains too. A bridge where all eight adjustments point upwards deserves extra suspicion.

8. A signed contract that isn't live yet, plus 0.8. As an add-back, this is aggressive. No revenue has been delivered, the assumptions about margin haven't been tested, and the costs of mobilising are real. This belongs in the forecast, where commercial due diligence can test it, or in an earn-out, rather than in historical adjusted EBITDA. Reject it from the bridge, and consider paying for it through the structure instead.

Here's a view a buyer could defend. Accept number 1, say at plus 0.3, after challenging the replacement cost. Accept number 2 in part, at plus 0.3 over the recurring level. Accept number 3, at plus 0.3, and number 7, at minus 0.2. Give partial credit to number 5, at plus 0.5. And reject numbers 4, 6 and 8. That gives the buyer an adjusted EBITDA of about £11.2m, against the vendor's £13.5m. At 9.0×, that gap is worth £20.7m of enterprise value. That's why it's the bridge, not the model, where mid-market deals are really negotiated.

§9.2.3Run-rate and pro-forma adjustments done properly

Two families of adjustment deserve their own discipline, because they're legitimate in principle, and abused in practice.

Run-rate adjustments restate the year as if changes that have already been made had been in force throughout. That might be a price rise, an exit from a lease that's been signed, or a redundancy programme that's been completed. The test is that they're implemented, and evidenced. The cheque has been signed, the people have left, or the new price is being invoiced. Savings that are "planned", "identified" or "targeted" fail the test.

Pro-forma adjustments for acquisitions arise when the target bought a business part-way through the year. If a bolt-on that contributes £1.2m of EBITDA a year was bought in month 7, the reported year only includes about £0.5m of it, since five twelfths of 1.2 is about 0.5. Adding the missing £0.7m is legitimate, because you're buying the combined group, and the debt will be sized on the combined group. But diligence the bolt-on's own numbers to the same standard, because its EBITDA may itself be "adjusted". Check for revenue dis-synergies, such as shared customers who'll consolidate their suppliers. And confirm that the integration costs still to come are reflected. A vendor bridge that makes the EBITDA pro-forma, but not the spending on integration, is only telling half the story.

§9.2.4Normalised working capital: why the peg matters

Deals are done on a cash-free, debt-free basis, with a normal level of working capital. That "normal level", known as the working capital peg, matters because working capital is the easiest number in the business to manipulate in the short term, and because without a peg, the seller gets paid twice.

Here's how it works. The buyer and the seller agree a peg. That's typically the average working capital that the business needs, often the monthly average over the last twelve months, adjusted for seasonality and distortions. At completion, the actual working capital is measured. If it's below the peg, the price falls pound for pound; if it's above, the price rises.

Here's a worked example. The target's working capital at the last twelve month-ends averages £8.0m. In the three months before completion, the seller quietly stretches its creditors, and runs a blitz on collecting from debtors, so working capital at closing is £6.5m. Without a peg, the buyer pays the full price, and then has to inject £1.5m of cash in the first quarter, as the creditors are paid down and the terms for debtors return to normal. The seller has effectively extracted £1.5m of extra proceeds. With a peg at £8.0m, the completion accounts show a £1.5m shortfall, and the price drops by exactly £1.5m. The peg turns a manipulation into nothing.

So what does financial due diligence do about the peg? It builds the monthly profile of working capital, and never relies on year ends, because they're the most managed balance-sheet dates of the year. It strips out distortions, such as a one-off prepayment from a customer, or an unusually large build-up of stock. And it evidences seasonality. A retailer's "normal" working capital in November isn't its normal level in February, so the peg may need to be set with reference to the month in which completion is expected. Deal teams fight hard over pegs for a reason. On a seasonal business, where the peg is set can be worth several million pounds, completely separately from any view of what the business is worth.

§9.2.5The net debt hunt: debt-like items

"Cash-free, debt-free" sounds clean, until you ask what counts as debt. Bank borrowings are obvious. The value in financial due diligence lies in the hunt for debt-like items. These are obligations that will consume the buyer's cash after completion just as surely as repaying a loan, without being labelled as debt.

Here's a worked example. The headline figures are bank debt of £20.0m and cash of £3.0m, which gives net debt of £17.0m. Then financial due diligence finds the following.

Item £m Why it's debt-like
Finance lease obligations 0.8 Contractual future payments; economically borrowing
Accrued bonuses (pre-completion year) 0.5 Earned under seller's ownership, paid under buyer's
Overdue corporation tax 0.4 Deferred payments the buyer must fund
Dilapidations provision 0.3 Committed property reinstatement cost
Declared unpaid dividend 0.5 Cash leaving the business at completion
Adjusted net debt 19.5

Adjusted net debt of £19.5m, against the headline figure of £17.0m, moves the equity value by £2.5m. That's often more than the entire fee for financial due diligence, and it was found in the footnotes. There are other regulars on the hunt list. Customer deposits and deferred income are contentious, because they're cash received for work that hasn't been done yet; sellers argue that they're working capital, and buyers argue that they're an obligation. Then there are pension deficits, deferred consideration on the target's own past acquisitions, accruals for holiday pay that hasn't been taken, and "trapped" cash that isn't freely available, such as regulatory capital, cash in subsidiaries with minority owners, and cash in the tills of stores. The arguments over classification, such as whether deferred income is debt-like or working capital, are genuinely negotiable, which is why they appear on every issues list. Here's the buyer's rule: anything that consumes cash after completion, without generating EBITDA after completion, should reduce the price somewhere, either in net debt or in the peg. But it should do so exactly once: not twice, and not zero times.

§9.2.6What deal teams actually ask of FDD

When the deal team reads a QoE report, its checklist is short. Which adjustments does the financial due diligence firm positively support, which does it merely note, and which does it challenge? These firms grade their language carefully, and "we note management's adjustment" is not an endorsement. Does EBITDA convert to cash at 85 to 90% or more, and if not, where is it leaking: into a build-up of working capital, capitalised costs, or provisions? Is the monthly profile of working capital consistent with the proposed peg? And what's on the list of debt-like items that the definitions in the SPA have to capture? A QoE report that you can't turn into a price, a peg and a definition of debt hasn't finished its job.
