Lesson 9.3/Due Diligence

Commercial Due Diligence

30 min read
In brief

This lesson explains how commercial due diligence tests whether revenue will last and grow. It covers discipline on the total addressable market, the hierarchy of evidence for competitive position, what customer references actually reveal, analysis of churn and retention, and tests of pricing power. It finishes with a worked bridge from management's hockey-stick forecast to the view from commercial due diligence.

  1. 9.3.1What CDD is for
  2. 9.3.2Market sizing sanity: TAM discipline
  3. 9.3.3Competitive position: the evidence hierarchy
  4. 9.3.4Customer references: what they actually reveal
  5. 9.3.5Churn and retention: reading the revenue engine
  6. 9.3.6Pricing power: the cleanest quality test
  7. 9.3.7Forecast credibility: bridging the hockey stick
  8. 9.3.8What looks good and what looks bad

§9.3.1What CDD is for

Financial due diligence looks backwards, and asks whether the EBITDA was real. Commercial due diligence looks forwards, and asks whether the revenue and margin will last, and grow. The two complement each other; they aren't substitutes. A business can have immaculate historic earnings, in a market that's about to fall off a cliff, and the QoE report will never tell you.

Commercial due diligence is bought from strategy houses, because the raw material is different. It's built from market models, interviews with experts, analysis of competitors, and, most valuable of all, direct conversations with the target's customers. The output is a view on three questions: how big and how healthy is the market, how strong is the target's position in it, and how credible is the forecast? Every deal thesis rests on those three legs, and the commercial due diligence report is where each leg gets tested under load.

Here's a framing to carry through this lesson. Management's plan is a claim. The job of commercial due diligence is to rebuild that claim from the bottom up, using evidence, and report the gap. A gap is normal, because almost every plan is optimistic. But its size and structure tell you whether you're looking at ambition, or fiction.

§9.3.2Market sizing sanity: TAM discipline

Every CIM contains a chart of the market, and most of them are propaganda. The classic move is to quote an enormous TAM, or total addressable market, so that the target's share looks tiny, and its runway infinite. For example: "a £6bn market growing at 8%, in which the company holds less than 1%".

The discipline is to force the market through a funnel, from the total market, to the part the target actually serves, to the part it can realistically win.

Level Question Worked example
TAM Everyone who could conceivably buy this category UK facilities services: £6.0bn
SAM The segment the target actually serves (geography, size band, spec) Specialist compliance maintenance for regulated sites: £450m
SOM What the target can realistically win given channels and capacity Sites within its three-region footprint: £180m

A target with £45m of revenue holds 0.75% of the total addressable market, or 25% of the market it can realistically win. Those imply opposite theses. The first says there's endless headroom. The second says the easy growth is done, and that any further share has to be taken from entrenched competitors. Deal teams have overpaid for stories about "1% of a huge market" many times, when the ceiling on growth was three postcodes away all along.

Two tests keep the sizing honest. First, triangulate the top-down view against the bottom-up one. If the top-down model says £450m, but multiplying the number of regulated sites by the average spend per site gives £210m, then the market model is broken. Find out which assumption is doing the lying. Second, reconcile the market's growth with the target's history. If the market "grows at 8%", but the target grew at 3% for three years, then either the market number is wrong, or the target is losing share. And a business that's losing share, priced as if it's gaining share, is one of the most expensive mistakes in PE.

§9.3.3Competitive position: the evidence hierarchy

Everyone claims to be differentiated. The job of commercial due diligence is to rank the evidence, from strong to weak.

  1. Revealed behaviour. That means records of wins and losses against named competitors, retention rates through a price rise, and customers who tried to leave and came back. Behaviour is the gold standard, because it can't be talked into existence.
  2. Testimony from third parties. That means customers and channel partners describing why they chose the target, and what would make them switch. It's good evidence, but filter it for selection bias, which we'll come to below.
  3. Structural analysis. That means switching costs, barriers from accreditation, network effects and proprietary data. These are arguments about why an advantage should exist.
  4. Management's assertion. As in, "we're the quality player". It's worth precisely nothing until it's backed up by the first three kinds of evidence.

So what looks good? A documented win rate of 60% or more in competitive tenders. A stable or rising share of wallet within existing customers. And competitors who, in expert interviews, describe the target with grudging respect, and can name what it does better. And what looks bad? "We have no direct competitors." Nobody has no competitors; it usually means the market is too small to attract any. Wins that are explained mostly by price. And a market where a credible player is currently buying share with venture money.

§9.3.4Customer references: what they actually reveal

The programme of customer references, typically 15 to 30 structured interviews, is the single most valuable part of commercial due diligence, because customers have no incentive to flatter. But the sample is poisoned at the source: management supplies the list, and no management team nominates its angriest customer. Good commercial due diligence firms push for the full list of customers, and pick their own sample, including accounts that have lapsed or are declining.

Here's what the interviews reveal, beyond the satisfaction scores, which nobody should take at face value.

  • The reality of switching. Ask, "if they raised their prices by 10%, what would you do?" A customer who laughs and says, "pay it; requalifying a supplier takes us nine months", is telling you that the moat is real. A customer who says, "I'd get two quotes by Friday", is telling you that the target is a commodity with good account managers.
  • Share of wallet, and dual sourcing. A customer that spends £2m with the target, out of £10m in the category, and deliberately splits its spending across three suppliers, will behave very differently from a customer that uses the target as its only source.
  • Where the relationship lives. If three interviews name the same salesperson as "the reason we stay", then key-person risk has just moved off the organisation chart and into the revenue line.
  • Early warnings. Customers mention a competitor's new product, a slip in service since the last reorganisation, or their own plans to bring the work in-house, quarters before any of it reaches the numbers.

Here's the rule of judgement. One grumpy customer is noise. But the same specific complaint, appearing unprompted in five interviews, is a finding, and it goes on the issues list.

§9.3.5Churn and retention: reading the revenue engine

For any business with repeat customers, retention analysis is where commercial due diligence gets quantitative. Two measures do most of the work.

Gross revenue retention, or GRR, asks how much of last year's revenue base survived, counting only losses and downgrades, and ignoring growth. Net revenue retention, or NRR, asks the same thing, but includes upselling and price increases to the customers who stayed.

Here's a worked example. Revenue from existing customers in FY23 was £40.0m. During FY24, customers representing £4.0m left altogether, and the customers who stayed reduced their spending by £1.0m. But other continuing customers expanded their spending by £3.0m. So GRR is 40.0 minus 4.0 minus 1.0, divided by 40.0, which gives 87.5%. And NRR is 40.0 minus 5.0 plus 3.0, divided by 40.0, which gives 95%. Headline revenue still grew, because new customers added £7.0m. So the CIM shows growth of 5%, and never mentions that the engine leaks 12.5% a year.

Here's why this matters. A business with GRR of 87.5% has to replace an eighth of its revenue every year before it grows at all. Its growth is being bought with spending on sales and marketing, and the moment that spending pauses, revenue shrinks. Compare that with a business with GRR of 97% and NRR of 108%, which grows by 8% just by standing still. These two businesses can show identical lines of historic revenue, and yet deserve wildly different multiples.

So what do deal teams ask for? Churn by cohort: do customers acquired recently churn faster? That would be a sign that the quality of new business is falling. Churn by value, not just by count, because losing ten tiny customers isn't the same as losing one anchor customer. And reasons coded from the exit data, rather than from management's memory. What looks bad is churn defined generously, such as only counting customers lost at the end of their contracts, and not downgrades, or annualising a lucky quarter. Or, worse still, "we don't track churn". A business with repeat revenue that can't produce an analysis of retention has either weak systems, or an answer it doesn't like.

§9.3.6Pricing power: the cleanest quality test

Pricing power is the quickest single read on competitive position, and it leaves fingerprints in the data.

  • Realised price compared with list price. Pull the last three years of like-for-like price changes, and what was actually achieved. A business that pushed through rises of 5%, 6% and 5%, with churn never exceeding 2%, has demonstrated pricing power. A business whose "5% rise" eroded to 1.5% net, through discounts and "commercial gestures", has demonstrated the opposite.
  • The spread of discounts. If the prices actually achieved for the same product vary by 40% across similar customers, then pricing is a negotiation, and the customer usually wins it.
  • Margin through shocks in input costs. When input costs spiked, did gross margin hold, which means the costs were passed through? Or did it compress for six quarters, which means they weren't?

The question of pricing matters doubly in PE, because "pricing" is the value-creation lever most commonly claimed in models. If the evidence from commercial due diligence says the last three price rises were fought to a standstill, then the model's assumption of "2% a year of price above inflation" isn't a lever. It's a hope.

§9.3.7Forecast credibility: bridging the hockey stick

Management plans take the shape of a hockey stick for structural reasons. The plan is a sales document, and the MIP is usually set off it. The most useful output from commercial due diligence is a forecast bridge. It breaks the plan down into named drivers, and re-underwrites each one with evidence.

Here's a worked example. Management's plan takes revenue from £50.0m in FY24 to £68.0m in FY27, an uplift of £18.0m. Here's the commercial due diligence bridge.

Driver Management (£m) CDD view (£m) Evidence
Market growth on existing base +6.0 (4%/yr) +6.0 Market model supports 4%; base assumed retained
Churn on existing base 0.0 −4.5 GRR of 97% claimed; cohort data shows 94% → 3%/yr attrition
Share gains / new logos +5.0 +2.5 Requires win rate of 55%; last 2 yrs actual = 40%
Price +3.0 (2%/yr) +1.5 Last 3 rises realised at ~1% net of discounts
New product launch +4.0 +1.0 Product 6 months late; pipeline covers £1m; no reference customers yet
Total uplift +18.0 +6.5
FY27 revenue 68.0 56.5

The plan says revenue will grow at a CAGR of 10.8%, but the evidence supports about 4.2%. Notice what the bridge achieves that "we've haircut the plan by 20%" never can: each driver has a named piece of evidence attached. That lets the negotiation and the model engage with specific disagreements. Management can rebut the churn line with better cohort data, but nobody can rebut a blanket haircut.

The deal team then decides which case to underwrite. Common practice is to base the price and the sizing of the debt on the commercial due diligence case, and to treat the gap to management's plan as upside owned by the buyer. And if the seller insists on being paid for the plan, the difference moves into an earn-out, so the seller is paid for the hockey stick if, and only if, it actually happens.

§9.3.8What looks good and what looks bad

Signal Read
Bottom-up SOM reconciles to top-down market model within ~20% Sizing is honest
Target's growth ≥ market growth for 3+ years Share gainer — position claims are credible
GRR ≥ 95%, NRR ≥ 100%, stable by cohort Revenue base compounds by itself
Price rises realised in full, churn unmoved Genuine pricing power
Plan drivers each tie to named evidence; management concedes weak ones gracefully Team is honest with itself — the plan may even be beatable
TAM quoted, SAM unquantifiable; "no competitors"; churn "not tracked" The commercial story is decoration, not analysis
Growth entirely from new logos over a leaking base The engine is a treadmill — value the treadmill, not the speed
Forecast back-half loaded: years 1–2 flat, years 3–5 explosive The plan's author does not believe it either

Commercial due diligence rarely kills deals outright. Its value lies in calibration. It turns "we believe in the growth story" into "we underwrite 4%, and structure the rest", and that's the difference between a thesis and a wish.

Lesson 9.4/Due Diligence

Operational, Management & Other Workstreams

25 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the workstreams beyond financial and commercial due diligence. It looks at operational due diligence on capacity, the supply chain and systems debt, which is where data teams plug in, and at how management is actually assessed. It gives a high-level view of red flags in legal and tax, covers insurance due diligence, and treats ESG as a lens for diligence rather than a compliance exercise.

  1. 9.4.1Operational DD: can the business deliver the plan?
  2. 9.4.2Systems debt: where the data team plugs in
  3. 9.4.3Management DD: assessing the team you are backing
  4. 9.4.4Legal and tax DD: the red-flag view
  5. 9.4.5Insurance DD and W&I
  6. 9.4.6ESG as a diligence lens
  7. 9.4.7Pulling the workstreams together

§9.4.1Operational DD: can the business deliver the plan?

Financial due diligence tells you what the earnings were, and commercial due diligence tells you whether the demand will last. Operational due diligence asks the question in between: can the business physically and organisationally deliver the plan that the price assumes? A plan that needs 30% more volume through a plant that's already running at 92% utilisation isn't a plan. It's a requirement for capex that nobody has costed.

Operational due diligence typically covers four areas.

Capacity and capex. Map the current utilisation against the volumes in the plan. Here's a worked example. A manufacturer runs at 85% of its practical capacity, and the plan assumes volumes grow by 40% by year 3. The missing 25% or more needs either a second shift, which raises questions about whether labour is available and at what premium, or a £6.0m extension to the line, with a lead time of 15 months. If the model shows "maintenance capex" of £1.5m a year throughout, then the plan and the capex line contradict each other. And pricing based on EBITDA quietly ignores the contradiction, because capex sits below EBITDA. This is one of the most common ways a deal model flatters itself: growth in the revenue line, and maintenance only in the capex line.

The supply chain. This covers concentration, where any supplier making up more than 20% of the cost of goods sold gets diligenced like a top customer; critical components that come from a single source; the terms of contracts, and the right to pass costs through; and exposure to particular geographies. The question is resilience, priced against cost. Sourcing everything from two suppliers is expensive. But relying on a single source for the one component that takes eight months to requalify is a risk to the thesis.

Operational maturity. Is performance managed, or is it accidental? The evidence lies in whether the business measures things like on-time-in-full delivery, scrap, and labour productivity, and whether there are KPIs for each site that the managers actually know. A business that measures nothing can be a positive finding for a value-creation thesis, because the room for improvement is real and hasn't been priced in. But that's only true if the management problem underneath it can be fixed.

§9.4.2Systems debt: where the data team plugs in

Due diligence on technology and data has grown from an afterthought into a workstream that changes prices, and it's where a PE data team touches diligence most directly. Here are the questions.

  • Can the business produce its own numbers? If monthly reporting takes 15 working days, and three spreadsheets that only the financial controller understands, then the reporting the fund needs after closing, for lender covenants, board packs and 100-day KPIs, doesn't exist yet. Budget for building it.
  • The inventory of systems, and systems debt. A 20-year-old ERP system that "works fine", but has no support from its vendor and a single 61-year-old administrator, is a deferred liability, just as real as a pension deficit. So is a business running on 40 spreadsheets that don't reconcile.
  • Is the data an asset or a liability? Is the data on customers and transactions clean, owned and usable, so that it's an asset the thesis can build on, through pricing analytics or cross-selling? Or is it fragmented, held without proper consent, or sitting in a system that the target doesn't control?
  • Entanglement in a carve-out. If the target is being carved out of a parent, every shared system, such as ERP, payroll and email, becomes a line item in a TSA, and a migration project. Underestimating the IT costs of a carve-out is a classic source of pain in the first year. Spending £2m to £5m, over 18 months, is routine for a mid-market carve-out that supposedly "just needs separating".

So what does the data team specifically bring to diligence? It rebuilds analyses from the raw transaction data, rather than from management's summaries, covering things like churn by cohort, bridges of price and volume, and margin by customer. It tests whether the KPIs in the CIM can be reproduced from the ledger. And it scopes the data stack needed after closing, while there's still time to price it in. A KPI in the CIM that can't be reproduced from the underlying data is a finding.

§9.4.3Management DD: assessing the team you are backing

In a buyout, the fund backs a plan and the people who'll deliver it, often with the same CEO for five years. Management due diligence is the least numerical workstream, and one of the most decisive.

Here's how it's actually done.

  • Structured assessment by specialist firms. That means competency-based interviews and psychometric tests, measured against the specific demands of the plan. A founder who's brilliant at running a £20m business may be wrong for a buy-and-build to £100m.
  • Referencing, which is the part that moves investment committees. That doesn't mean the referees the CEO nominates. It means references off the list, from former colleagues, former employees, customers and other investors. Patterns matter more than anecdotes. Three independent references all saying "brilliant commercially, but burns through CFOs" is a finding with a structural answer: hire a strong CFO before closing, and adjust the MIP.
  • Depth, and dependence. What breaks if the CEO is hit by a bus? Is there a layer below the founders that actually runs the business, or is it hub-and-spoke, with every decision routed through one person? You can spot it in meetings. A CEO who answers every question personally, while the finance director stares at the table, is showing you the real shape of the organisation chart.
  • Alignment, and intent. Who's rolling over equity, how much, and who's quietly retiring? A CFO rolling over 60% of their proceeds is making a statement. A CEO trying to roll over 5%, while negotiating a big cash-out, is making a different one. Diligence the shape of the conversation about the MIP, not just its size.

So what looks bad? Dodging references, as in "we'd rather you didn't speak to X". A plan that the second line of management has never seen. CVs that gloss over a two-year gap. And, subtle but reliable, management teams that can't disagree with each other in the room. And what looks good? A second line that answers questions without being prompted. A CEO who volunteers what they're bad at. And previous evidence of delivering under PE ownership, which is a different sport from founder ownership.

§9.4.4Legal and tax DD: the red-flag view

Deal teams don't do the legal due diligence themselves, but they do need to know which findings matter. Here are the legal headlines.

  • Change-of-control clauses. These are contracts, with customers, suppliers, landlords, licensors or lenders, that terminate, or can be renegotiated, when the business is sold. A top customer holding a change-of-control right means getting its consent before completion, and that gives the customer a window to negotiate.
  • Litigation and disputes. Quantify the exposure. If it's genuinely a one-off, handle it through an indemnity or an escrow, rather than the price.
  • Ownership of IP. Does the company actually own its core intellectual property? Or does it sit with the founder personally, with a contractor who never assigned it, or with an academic collaboration? Fixing the chain of title to IP before closing is routine; discovering the gap after closing isn't.
  • Employment. Look for contractors who've been misclassified, meaning an "outsourced" workforce that's legally employed; missing restrictive covenants on key staff; and promises of bonuses that were never documented.
  • Arrangements with related parties. For example, property leased from the founder's pension fund at above-market rent, or services bought from family businesses. These aren't necessarily sinister, but every one of them has to be identified, repriced to market in the EBITDA, and then either terminated, or moved onto arm's-length terms at completion.

Tax due diligence hunts for historic exposures, such as aggressive schemes, the treatment of VAT, the employment status of workers, and transfer pricing, and quantifies them. The standard treatment is an indemnity, or increasingly, W&I insurance with a specific tax policy. Remember the rule from Lesson 1: identified risks are excluded from standard W&I cover, so a known hole in the tax position needs its own solution, whether that's a specific indemnity, an escrow, or the price.

§9.4.5Insurance DD and W&I

Insurance due diligence does two jobs. The first is a gap analysis of the target's existing cover. That might reveal underinsured property, missing cyber cover, or limits on professional indemnity that haven't kept pace with the size of contracts. The findings become fixes after closing, and occasionally items in the price, such as premiums stepping up on renewal.

The second job is supporting the placement of W&I insurance. Remember the mechanics. The policy stands behind the seller's warranties, so the buyer claims against an insurer rather than the seller. That's essential when the seller is a fund that wants a clean exit, and won't leave money behind in escrow. Here's the angle for diligence. W&I underwriters read the due diligence reports, and exclude anything that was inadequately diligenced, or specifically flagged. So thin diligence produces a policy full of holes. That creates a virtuous discipline: doing the work properly is what makes the risk transferable.

§9.4.6ESG as a diligence lens

Treat ESG in diligence as a lens for finding real risks and items of value, not as a compliance checkbox.

  • Environmental. Contamination on sites the business owns is a genuinely priceable liability, and estimates of the cost of remediation go straight into the funds flow. Also look at energy intensity, against rising costs of carbon, and at products facing a regulatory phase-out.
  • Social. Labour practices in the supply chain are a reputational bomb, with a fuse of unknown length. Safety records matter too; a rising rate of accidents is also a signal about operational quality. And look at staff turnover compared with the norms for the sector.
  • Governance. This is the quiet workhorse. It covers transactions with related parties, controls that are easily overridden, and an owner-manager who treats the company account as their own. Findings on governance correlate strongly with findings on the quality of earnings, because the same instincts produce both.

There are two practical reasons why ESG earns its place. The first is financing. Margins on sustainability-linked loans, and some lenders' appetite, now move with ESG credentials. The second is the exit. The universe of buyers in five years' time, including trade acquirers with net-zero commitments, and larger funds with exclusions driven by their LPs, may simply not include anyone willing to buy an asset with an unresolved ESG problem. An ESG finding that narrows the pool of future buyers is really a finding about the exit multiple, wearing different clothes.

§9.4.7Pulling the workstreams together

Here's a useful closing exercise. Notice how often the same underlying issue surfaces in several workstreams, wearing different labels. Dependence on the founder shows up in management due diligence, as a missing second line; in legal due diligence, as IP in the founder's name; in operational due diligence, as every pricing decision being routed through one desk; and in financial due diligence, as an add-back for excess pay. Weak systems show up in financial due diligence, as slow reporting that doesn't reconcile; in operational due diligence, as an absence of KPIs; and in technology due diligence, as a sprawl of spreadsheets. When three workstreams independently brush against the same issue, that issue is structural. It belongs at the top of the issues list, priced in or fixed, rather than scattered across three appendices as minor observations. Synthesis, as Lesson 1 said, is the deal team's real job.

Lesson 9.5/Due Diligence

The Red-Flags Catalogue

30 min read
In brief

This lesson is a structured catalogue of twenty classic red flags in diligence, grouped into five areas: the quality of earnings, customers, the market, management, and legal matters. For each one, it shows what it looks like in the data, why it matters, and whether the right response is a price chip, a structural fix, or walking away.

  1. 9.5.1How to use this catalogue
  2. 9.5.2Family 1: Earnings quality
  3. 9.5.3Family 2: Customers and revenue base
  4. 9.5.4Family 3: Market and competitive position
  5. 9.5.5Family 4: Management and governance
  6. 9.5.6Family 5: Legal, tax, and compliance
  7. 9.5.7Reading flags in combination
  8. 9.5.8The discipline of the issues list

§9.5.1How to use this catalogue

This lesson is the reference core of the module. It contains twenty flags that you'll actually meet, grouped into five families. For each one, there's what it looks like in the data, so that you can find it; why it matters, so that you can argue it; and the default treatment, whether a price chip, a structural fix, or walking away, using the framework from Lesson 1.

There are three rules to keep in mind before the tables. First, the treatment column shows a default, not a law. A flag that's certain and can be quantified chips the price; a flag that's a contingent risk gets structured; and a flag that poisons trust, or the thesis itself, means walking away. The same flag can move between categories depending on how severe it is. Customer concentration of 25% is a conversation about price, while 60% is a conversation about walking away. Second, flags compound in a non-linear way. Two medium flags that share a root cause, such as channel stuffing and a founder who blocks customer references, are worse than four unrelated ones. Third, the most dangerous flag is the one you rationalise. If you catch yourself building the seller's defence for them, hand the finding to the most sceptical person on the team.

§9.5.2Family 1: Earnings quality

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
1 Revenue recognised ahead of substance Revenue spikes in Q4/period-end; debtor days climbing (58→74); bill-and-hold or ship-to-distributor terms; deferred income falling while revenue grows Earnings are borrowed from next year — the year you own Price chip on restated EBITDA; walk if deliberate and pervasive
2 Channel stuffing Distributor/wholesale sales outgrowing end-market sell-through; extended payment terms or return rights on late-period orders; distributor inventory building Post-close revenue air-pocket as the channel destocks; often shades into misstatement Price chip on normalised run-rate; walk if concealed
3 Serial "one-offs" The same category of add-back (legal, restructuring, "exceptional" hiring) appears 3+ years running One-offs that recur are opex; adjusted EBITDA is overstated by the recurring level Price chip — add back only the excess over run-rate
4 Provision releases flattering EBITDA Warranty/bad-debt/stock provisions falling while the activity that drives them grows; releases credited to P&L Non-cash, non-recurring profit inside "clean" EBITDA; may signal under-provision building future cost Price chip — strip releases, restate provision to adequate level
5 Rising capitalisation of costs Capitalised development/commissions jump (e.g. £0.4m→£1.6m) with no policy note; amortisation lags Costs moved from P&L to balance sheet inflate EBITDA ~pound-for-pound; conversion to cash worsens Price chip — normalise to historic capitalisation rate; check cash conversion
6 Weak cash conversion EBITDA-to-operating-cash conversion <80% with no growth-capex story; working capital absorbing cash every year EBITDA is an opinion, cash is a fact; leverage is serviced with cash Price chip (value on cash-adjusted earnings); investigate before assuming benign
7 Peg games / window-dressed balance sheet Completion NWC well below 12-month monthly average; creditor stretch and debtor blitz in final quarter Seller extracts value through working capital rather than price Structure fix — set the peg on the monthly average; pound-for-pound true-up

§9.5.3Family 2: Customers and revenue base

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
8 Customer concentration Top customer >20–25% of revenue (or, worse, of gross profit); top 5 >60% One renegotiation resets margins; one loss impairs the thesis; lenders cut leverage for it Price chip via lower multiple; structure (earnout/retention tied to renewal); walk above ~40% with a near-term renewal
9 Hidden churn under headline growth GRR <90% with growth driven by new logos; recent cohorts churning faster than old ones The engine leaks — growth stops the moment acquisition spend does; declining new-cohort quality says the leak is worsening Price chip — underwrite the CDD case, not the plan
10 Contract cliff Large contracts or framework agreements expiring within 12–18 months of close; renewal history thin The revenue you are pricing may not survive year one Structure fix — condition or earnout on renewal; chip if renewal terms already known to be worse
11 Loss-making "strategic" revenue Named contracts at negative or near-zero gross margin, justified as market entry or "land and expand" Revenue quality overstated; exiting the contract shrinks the top line the price was set on Price chip — value the business excluding it; make management's expansion story an earnout
12 Pricing erosion beneath list prices Realised price/mix falling while list prices rise; discount dispersion widening; rebates growing The pricing "lever" in the model runs backwards; competitive position weaker than claimed Price chip on forecast; revisit thesis if pricing is the value-creation plan

§9.5.4Family 3: Market and competitive position

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
13 Share loss dressed as market growth Target CAGR 3% in a market growing 7%; win rates falling; expert calls name a rising competitor You are paying a growth multiple for a share-loser; the gap compounds Price chip at best; walk if the thesis was "market leader"
14 Structural demand risk Core product exposed to regulation, technology substitution, or a single channel shifting (e.g. retail to D2C); customers' own industries declining Terminal value is the majority of any price; a melting terminal value cannot be chipped accurately Walk in most cases — or price as a run-off with structure carrying the tail risk
15 Cyclical peak presented as trend Record year driven by a commodity spike, post-crisis catch-up, or one-off regulation change; "normalised" year never defined Buying peak earnings at a full multiple is double-counting the cycle Price chip — underwrite through-cycle EBITDA; structure with earnout if seller disputes the cycle

§9.5.5Family 4: Management and governance

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
16 Founder dependence All key relationships, pricing decisions, and technical knowledge route through one person; no second line in meetings; IP or customer contracts in the founder's personal orbit The asset walks out of the door at completion — or holds you hostage after it Structure fix — rollover, earnout, retention, pre-close hires; walk if the founder is also exiting fully
17 Inconsistent answers / data access friction The same question gets different answers over time; basic data "not tracked"; management access rationed through advisers Either systems cannot produce truth or someone prefers you not to have it — both are findings, and the second is disqualifying Escalate and test; walk if the pattern persists — trust is not warrantable
18 Related-party transactions Sales to, purchases from, or leases with entities owned by directors/family; terms not benchmarked; e.g. founder's brother as top supplier Margins may be artificial in either direction; post-close continuity at those terms is not assured; governance signal Price chip — restate to arm's-length terms; structure the transition; walk if concealed rather than disclosed

§9.5.6Family 5: Legal, tax, and compliance

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
19 Change-of-control traps CoC clauses in top customer contracts, key licences, or property leases; consents required to complete Key counterparties gain a renegotiation window your completion timetable pays for Structure fix — consents as conditions precedent; chip for known re-pricing
20 Historic tax/compliance exposure Aggressive schemes in the ledger; contractor workforce with employee characteristics; VAT treatment inconsistent with rulings; data-protection posture incompatible with the customer base Crystallisation costs cash and reputation post-close; standard W&I excludes identified issues Structure fix — specific indemnity or escrow, quantified; walk if exposure threatens licence to operate

§9.5.7Reading flags in combination

Single flags have prices, but patterns have verdicts. Here are three patterns to memorise.

The manufactured year. Flags 1, 4, 5 and 7 together, meaning revenue pulled forward, provisions released, costs capitalised and working capital squeezed, describe a business that's been groomed for sale. Each item on its own might be worth £0.3m to £0.8m of EBITDA. Together, they mean that the whole of the current year is unreliable, and your baseline should be built from previous years, plus changes to the run-rate that have been verified. Expect the true EBITDA to be 15 to 25% below the headline, and expect the seller to know it.

The dependent business. Flags 8, 16 and 18 together, meaning concentrated customers, dependence on the founder, and supply from related parties, describe a business that's really a web of personal relationships, dressed up as a company. No price chip fixes this. Only structure, through rollover, earn-outs and long transitions, keeps the relationships attached to the asset, and even then only partly.

The treadmill. Flags 9, 11 and 12 together, meaning leaky retention, bought revenue and eroding prices, describe growth that costs more than it returns. This is the classic value trap covered in the next lesson. It looks cheap, and it's cheap for a reason.

§9.5.8The discipline of the issues list

Every flag you find goes onto the issues list from Lesson 1, with four entries: the evidence, the amount, the proposed treatment, and the owner. There are two closing disciplines. First, quantify even the awkward ones. "Customer concentration: bad" isn't something anyone can act on. But a position like this is: "a 25% chance of losing the top customer at renewal puts £2.1m of gross profit at risk, which at the deal multiple justifies a chip of £6m to £8m, or an earn-out of a similar size." Second, track the total. Deals rarely die of a single flag, but sometimes they should die of twelve. If the combined impact on EBITDA of everything on the issues list exceeds about 20% of the headline number, the question is no longer "what's the right chip?" It's "is this the business we thought we were buying?" And that question belongs in front of the investment committee, not buried in a schedule.

Lesson 9.6/Due Diligence

What Good Looks Like

25 min read
In brief

This lesson sets out the anatomy of a high-quality asset: visibility of revenue, diversified customers, cash conversion, depth of management, and clean data. It explains why quality compounds, through better exits and easier financing, when paying up beats buying a value trap, and how the findings from diligence are assembled into genuine conviction at the investment committee.

  1. 9.6.1Why "good" needs its own lesson
  2. 9.6.2The anatomy of a high-quality asset
  3. 9.6.3Why quality compounds
  4. 9.6.4Paying up versus value traps
  5. 9.6.5How conviction is actually built: the IC memo
  6. 9.6.6The closing test

§9.6.1Why "good" needs its own lesson

Five lessons of scepticism can leave the impression that diligence is an exercise in finding faults. It isn't. It's an exercise in calibration, and it can fail in either direction. Missing a red flag costs money. But failing to recognise quality costs deals, because quality assets go to the bidder who diligences quickly enough to underwrite boldly. The funds that consistently win good auctions aren't the most optimistic ones. They're the ones whose diligence lets them tell the difference between expensive and worth it, and just expensive.

So this lesson turns the catalogue upside down. What does a genuinely high-quality asset look like in the data? Why does quality compound, rather than simply add up? And how does a deal team turn the output of diligence into the thing an investment committee actually buys, which is conviction?

§9.6.2The anatomy of a high-quality asset

Five traits recur in the assets that make funds' track records, and each one can be observed in diligence.

1. Visibility of revenue. At the start of the year, how much of that year's revenue is already secured? Here's the spectrum, from best to worst. Contracted recurring revenue, from multi-year contracts and auto-renewing subscriptions, comes first. Then re-occurring revenue, meaning repeat purchases with no contract, which have high retention in practice, but no legal commitment. Then the backlog, or order book, then the pipeline, and finally walk-in business. Here's a worked test. A business with £50m of revenue, where £38m renews under contract and historic GRR is 96%, starts the year needing to find £12m. A business of the same size, with only £8m contracted, needs to find £42m. It's the same P&L, but an utterly different risk. So what does good look like? Visibility of at least 70% at the start of the year, renewal rates that are stable across cohorts, and, the detail that separates real visibility from decoration, contracts that customers actually honour. So check the history of enforcement, not just the terms.

2. Diversified, sticky customers. The top customer is under 10% of revenue, and the top ten are under 40%. Churn is low, and boring, with the losses concentrated in small accounts, and none of them caused by a reference customer becoming dissatisfied. On top of that, there's stickiness with a mechanism you can name, such as switching costs, integration, accreditation, or lock-in through data, rather than just habit.

3. Cash conversion. The conversion of EBITDA into operating cash stays at 90% or more, year after year. Working capital grows more slowly than revenue. And maintenance capex is modest, and honestly separated from growth capex. Cash conversion is the trait that lenders price most directly, and it's the hardest one to fake for long. Over five years, the cumulative free cash flow either turned up, or it didn't.

4. Depth of management. There's a second line that runs the business day to day, decisions that survive the CEO going on holiday, visible candidates to succeed every key person, and a team that has already operated with proper governance, with board packs and budgets that it holds itself to. Depth turns key-person risk from a structural flaw into a question about personnel.

5. Clean data, and self-knowledge. This is the trait that predicts all the others. Monthly accounts are closed within five days, and reconcile to the audit. The KPIs quoted in the CIM can be reproduced from the raw data. And management know their churn, their price realisation and their margin by customer, including the unflattering numbers. A business that measures itself honestly almost always comes through diligence cleanly, because the habits are the same.

Notice what isn't on the list: the growth rate. Growth is an amplifier, not a quality. Fast growth on a leaky base is the treadmill from Lesson 5, and even fast, profitable growth built on one customer is fragile. Quality is about how durable the economics are, and growth then multiplies whatever durability is there.

§9.6.3Why quality compounds

Quality traits don't just add up; they multiply, through three loops, and all three pay out at exit.

The financing loop. Lenders lend more, more cheaply, and on looser terms, against visible revenue and strong cash conversion. Here's a worked example. Take two businesses, each with £10m of EBITDA. The quality asset supports 5.0× leverage at SONIA plus 375 basis points, while the mixed asset supports 3.5× at SONIA plus 500. At identical entry multiples, the buyer of the quality asset puts in £15m less equity, and over a five-year hold, pays roughly £2m less in cash interest. That gives a higher MOIC, before either business does anything differently. Debt capacity is the market's real-time score for quality.

The exit loop. The next buyer's diligence will find what yours found. A business that comes through diligence cleanly, with its data room ready, its KPIs reproducible, and no skeletons, commands a broader universe of buyers, with trade buyers, larger funds and an IPO all available. It gets a faster process, and a fuller multiple. Multiple expansion is often described as luck. But buying assets whose quality the next diligence process will confirm is the version of it that you can underwrite. The reverse is true too. Every unresolved flag you accept at entry becomes a chip that the next buyer takes at exit. You don't buy red flags once; you rent them.

The optionality loop. Quality assets survive their own bad years. Strong cash conversion and headroom mean that a downturn is a slow year, not a breach of covenant. A crisis becomes a chance to buy a weakened competitor, rather than a forced sale. Over a five-year hold, something always goes wrong, and quality decides whether "wrong" is a chapter, or the ending.

§9.6.4Paying up versus value traps

Here's the perennial argument at investment committee: pay 11× for the clean asset, or 7× for the flawed one? The honest maths is less forgiving of "cheap" than intuition suggests.

Here's a worked example. Asset A has £10m of EBITDA, bought at 11.0×, an EV of £110m, with 5.0× debt, and quality traits throughout. We underwrite EBITDA growth of 6%, and an exit at 10.5×, allowing for some modest compression. Year-5 EBITDA is £13.4m, the exit EV is £140.7m, and the debt has been paid down to, say, £30m. That leaves equity of £110.7m on £60m put in, which is about 1.85× MOIC, with a narrow spread of outcomes. Asset B also has £10m of EBITDA, bought at 7.0×, an EV of £70m, but it has a leaky base. We underwrite no net growth, because churn offsets the wins, with 3.5× debt, and an exit to a buyer who diligences the same flaws you found, at 6.0×. Year-5 EBITDA is £10m, the exit EV is £60m, and the debt is down to £20m. That leaves equity of £40m on £35m put in, which is about 1.14× MOIC, with a wide spread of outcomes, including some zeros. The trap is that Asset B's entry price looks like the bargain. But you exit through the same door you came in by, and the discount travels with the flaws.

This isn't an argument that quality always wins. It's an argument about which question to ask. For the premium asset, ask: "what has to be true for 11× to work, and does diligence support it?" For the cheap asset, ask: "is the flaw something we can fix, that's priced in, and that can be re-rated at exit, or is it the permanent reason for the price?" A flaw that can be fixed, such as weak reporting, no discipline on pricing, or an underinvested sales force, is a value-creation thesis wearing a discount. A permanent flaw, such as structural decline, or customer concentration that can't be shifted, just means a smaller multiple forever. Turnarounds and deep-value deals can make spectacular returns, but only for funds that resource them deliberately, and never by accident, for a buyer who mistook cheap for safe.

§9.6.5How conviction is actually built: the IC memo

Diligence ends in an investment committee memo. And the diligence section of a good memo has a specific architecture. It isn't a summary of the reports; it's a chain of underwriting logic.

  1. The thesis, stated in a way that could be proved wrong. For example: "We're buying the number two player in a consolidating £450m niche, underwriting 4% organic growth and two bolt-ons." A thesis that can't be wrong can't be diligenced.
  2. What we tested, and what we found. Each leg of the thesis is mapped to the workstream that tested it under load, and the evidence that came back, including the tests that failed and changed the plan. For example: "Commercial due diligence supports 4%, not management's 7%, so we underwrite 4%."
  3. The issues list, dealt with. Every material finding, with its treatment. It's either chipped, so the price moved from £108m to £101m because of the quality-of-earnings findings; structured, with an £8m earn-out against the disputed contract; protected, with a specific tax indemnity and a £3m escrow; or accepted with eyes open, such as 25% concentration in the top customer, where the renewal history is strong and the downside case has been run. Nothing is merely "noted".
  4. A downside case that still works. This isn't the base case minus 10%. It's a named scenario, built from the actual flags. For example: "The top customer halves its spending at renewal, and price rises come through at 1%. EBITDA is £8.2m, the covenants hold with £1.4m of headroom, and the equity returns 1.2×." Conviction doesn't mean believing the base case. It means knowing that the specific downside is survivable.
  5. Why we win. In an auction, the honest question is this: what do we see that the underbidder doesn't? Is it a genuine angle, such as synergy with a portfolio company, insight into the sector, or operational capability? Or is it just a higher number? "We're paying more because we know more" is a thesis. "We're paying more" is the winner's curse.

The tell of a weak memo is adjectives where there should be numbers: "strong management", "an attractive market", "robust margins". The tell of a strong one is that a sceptical reader can find the assumptions bearing the weight within five minutes, because they're labelled as such. Done properly, diligence doesn't manufacture certainty. It buys down the cost of being wrong, and tells you precisely what you're still betting on.

§9.6.6The closing test

Before the investment committee votes, the best deal teams can answer five questions, in one sentence each. What exactly are we buying, meaning the diligenced EBITDA, not the CIM's? What are we paying for it, and what did diligence move? What do we believe that the market doesn't, and what evidence supports that belief? What kills this deal, and why does the structure survive it? And who buys this from us in five years, and what will their diligence find? If the answer to the fifth question is "the same flags we're rationalising today", then the deal has failed the whole test of this module. Because in the end, the exit is just somebody else's due diligence.

Lesson 10.1/Value Creation

The Value Creation Plan

24 min read
In brief

This lesson explains what a value creation plan, or VCP, is. It sets out the full taxonomy of levers: revenue, margin, efficiency with cash and capital, the multiple, and leverage. It shows how much each lever typically contributes to returns, why the plan is written before the deal closes, and what actually goes into a 100-day plan, with a worked example of returns attribution.

  1. 10.1.1From deal thesis to value creation plan
  2. 10.1.2The five levers
  3. 10.1.3How much each lever contributes
  4. 10.1.4Why the plan is written pre-close
  5. 10.1.5The 100-day plan
  6. 10.1.6What deal teams actually ask

§10.1.1From deal thesis to value creation plan

Every deal is bought on a thesis. That's a claim, two or three sentences long, about why this business, at this price, will make money. "It's a fragmented market, and we'll consolidate it." "The product is under-priced, and we'll fix the pricing." "It's a great product, with an amateur cost base." The value creation plan, or VCP, is what that thesis turns into when someone forces it to be specific. It's a programme, lever by lever, with named initiatives, owners, timelines, and, critically, numbers that reconcile to the returns model that the investment committee approved.

The distinction matters. A thesis is a belief, but a VCP is a budget. If the model at investment committee assumes EBITDA grows from £10m to £15m over five years, the VCP has to say which £5m. That might be £2m from pricing, £1.5m from procurement, £1m from opening new sites, and £0.5m from mix. Each of those lines then gets an initiative, an owner, a cost to achieve it, and a plan of milestones. When the deal team presents to the investment committee, a good committee asks exactly this question: "Show me the bridge from today's EBITDA to your exit EBITDA, line by line, and tell me who delivers each line." A deal where the answer is "growth" is a deal where nobody has done the work.

For someone in a PE data team, this document is your map of the next five years. Every initiative in the VCP eventually becomes a KPI that someone has to track, a dashboard that someone has to build, and a monthly variance that someone has to explain. Read the VCP on day one, and you'll know what the fund really cares about.

§10.1.2The five levers

All value creation in PE breaks down into five levers. Everything a portfolio company does fits somewhere in this taxonomy, and every returns attribution you'll ever build uses it.

Lever What it means Typical initiatives
Revenue growth Grow EBITDA by growing the top line Pricing, salesforce effectiveness, new products/markets, cross-sell, bolt-on acquisitions
Margin expansion Grow EBITDA at constant revenue Procurement, spans & layers, footprint consolidation, shared services, automation, zero-based budgeting
Cash & capital efficiency Convert more EBITDA into cash; use less capital Working-capital reduction (stock, debtors), capex discipline, sale-and-leaseback
Multiple expansion Sell the same EBITDA for a higher multiple Reposition the business (recurring revenue, sector re-rating), improve growth profile, professionalise reporting, buy-and-build arbitrage
Leverage / deleveraging Debt paydown transfers enterprise value to equity Amortisation from free cash flow — the mechanical partner of the cash lever

Two of these deserve a flag. Multiple expansion is the lever the deal team controls least. Most of it is market exposure, meaning what sector multiples do over the hold, and only some of it is earned, by making the business genuinely higher in quality. Underwriting a deal on an assumption of multiple expansion is how funds overpay at the top of cycles, and most investment committees force the base case to assume that the exit multiple equals the entry multiple. Leverage isn't really a value-creation lever at all; it's an amplifier. Paying down debt moves value from the debt column into the equity column, but the cash that pays the debt down was generated by the operating levers.

§10.1.3How much each lever contributes

The industry's own attribution studies, the kind consultancies publish every year, tell a consistent story about how the mix has shifted. In the 1980s, most buyout returns came from leverage and multiple expansion. You bought cheaply, geared up, and rode the market. Entry multiples were low, and debt was the product. Today, with entry multiples of 9 to 12× for quality assets, and every auction fully competitive, roughly half or more of the value created in a typical modern buyout comes from EBITDA growth. That's split between revenue growth, which is the largest single contributor, often 30 to 50% of the value created, and margin expansion, which is typically 15 to 25%. Multiple expansion and deleveraging share the rest. Treat these figures as framing, not physics. Attribution varies hugely by vintage, sector and strategy, and a buy-and-build deal will show a very different mix from a carve-out of a single asset. But the direction of travel is unambiguous: you can no longer buy your returns; you have to build them.

Here's the standard attribution arithmetic, on a worked example. A fund buys a business at 10.0× EBITDA of £10.0m, which is an EV of £100m, funded with £60m of debt and £40m of equity. Five years later, it exits at 11.0× EBITDA of £15.0m, which is an EV of £165m, with the debt paid down to £30m.

Entry Exit
EBITDA £10.0m £15.0m
Multiple 10.0× 11.0×
Enterprise value £100.0m £165.0m
Net debt £60.0m £30.0m
Equity value £40.0m £135.0m

The gain in equity is £95.0m, which is a gross MOIC of 3.4×. Here's the attribution.

Lever Calculation Value created Share
EBITDA growth £5.0m × 10.0× entry multiple £50.0m 53%
Multiple expansion 1.0× × £15.0m exit EBITDA £15.0m 16%
Deleveraging £60.0m − £30.0m £30.0m 32%
Total £95.0m 100%

A note on convention. Multiple expansion is measured on the exit EBITDA, and EBITDA growth at the entry multiple. The cross term has to sit somewhere, and this is the standard way of allocating it. The shares are rounded. So what looks good in an attribution? EBITDA growth dominating. And what looks bad? A deal where most of the gain is multiple expansion. The deal team will hear "you got lucky" at the next fundraise.

§10.1.4Why the plan is written pre-close

The VCP is drafted before the deal closes, usually alongside confirmatory due diligence, and there are hard commercial reasons for that.

  1. It disciplines the price. The maximum price you can pay depends on the value you can create. If the VCP can only find £3m of improvement in EBITDA, you can't pay a price that needs £5m. Writing the plan before closing forces the deal team to underwrite initiatives, not hopes, and the investment committee will mark the model to the plan.
  2. Due diligence is the evidence base. Commercial and operational due diligence is the one window when consultants are crawling all over the business, at the fund's expense. Their findings, such as the spread of prices, benchmarks for procurement, and data on spans of control, are the raw material of the VCP. If you wait until after closing to plan, you pay twice for the analysis.
  3. The first 100 days are the window. Organisations accept change at the moment ownership changes hands, in a way they never do in a steady state. A new owner asking for a price rise, a new reporting pack, or a redesign of the organisation in month two is just "the new owners' way of doing things". The same request in month eighteen is a fight. You can't make the most of that window if you spend it deciding what to do.
  4. Management's alignment is negotiated at closing. The management incentive plan is agreed at completion, and management need to know what they're signing up to deliver. Agreeing the VCP, or at least its headlines, with the CEO before closing is how you find out whether the incumbent team believes in the plan, and whether you believe in them.

The practical consequence is this. By the time the wire transfer clears, the fund should already know its top five initiatives, who owns each one, and what the first board meeting will demand.

§10.1.5The 100-day plan

The 100-day plan is the front end of the VCP, where execution begins. It isn't a strategy document, but a schedule for mobilising during the first three months of ownership. Its jobs are to take control, build the baseline, bank the quick wins, and launch the big initiatives properly. A real one looks like a grid of workstreams, not an essay.

Workstream Owner By day 30 By day 60 By day 100
Cash & controls CFO Daily cash reporting live; banking mandates changed; capex approvals >£50k to board 13-week cash-flow forecast embedded Working-capital reduction targets set per site
Management reporting CFO + data team Define monthly KPI pack; baseline data pulled First monthly pack delivered ≤10 working days after month end Dashboard automated; budget reforecast complete
Pricing Commercial director Price/discount data extracted; dispersion analysis done Discount authority matrix imposed; list-price rise announced Price increase in market; realisation tracked weekly
Procurement Ops director Spend cube built; top-20 suppliers identified RFQs out on top categories First renegotiated contracts signed; savings run-rate tracked
Organisation CEO Top-team assessment complete Key hires launched (typically CFO/CRO); spans & layers review scoped Any structural changes announced
VCP mobilisation Deal team Initiative owners confirmed; targets cascaded Initiative charters signed off at board Full VCP tracking in monthly board pack

Notice what is, and isn't, in there. What's in it: diagnostics, baselines, control systems, quick wins, which almost always means pricing and procurement, and the launch of work with a long cycle. What isn't in it: completing a warehouse consolidation, an ERP migration, or a change of culture. Those take years. The job of the 100-day plan is to start them from a position of knowledge, not to finish them. A 100-day plan that promises structural transformation by day 100 is a red flag in itself, because it means nobody has scoped the work.

§10.1.6What deal teams actually ask

When you see a VCP, whether it's yours, or one attached to a competitor's asset coming to market, here's the checklist for judgement.

  • Does the bridge tie to the model? Add up the initiatives. If they come to £4m, and the model needs £6m, the gap is being filled with hope. The other way round, a plan showing £8m against a need of £5m has either sandbagging or double counting in it.
  • Are the top three initiatives evidenced by due diligence? A "pricing opportunity of £2m" should trace back to a specific finding, such as data on the spread of prices, or cost inflation that hasn't been passed on, rather than a benchmark percentage applied to revenue.
  • Who delivers it? Every initiative needs a named owner inside the business. A plan whose owners are all "consultants, to be confirmed" will cost twice as much, and deliver half.
  • What does it cost? Every programme to cut costs has one-off costs to achieve it, such as redundancies, exiting sites, and systems. A plan with savings, but no costs, is unfinished.
  • What breaks if it slips? The debt package was sized on the plan. So ask which initiatives the covenant headroom depends on. Those get tracked at board level from the first month.

The rest of this module walks through the levers one at a time. There's revenue in lesson 2, margin and cost in lesson 3, and buy-and-build in lesson 4, which is the lever that spans revenue and the multiple at once. Lesson 5 covers the governance machine that makes any of it actually happen.

Lesson 10.2/Value Creation

Revenue Levers

24 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the revenue side of the value creation plan. It explains why pricing is the most underused lever, with a worked example of a 3% price rise flowing through to EBITDA. It covers the effectiveness of the sales force, new products and markets, cross-selling, and programmes of commercial excellence. And it explains why growth investments that hurt EBITDA in the short term are often exactly the right call.

  1. 10.2.1Why pricing is the most underused lever
  2. 10.2.2Worked example: 3% through to EBITDA
  3. 10.2.3Salesforce effectiveness
  4. 10.2.4New products, new markets, cross-sell
  5. 10.2.5Commercial excellence programmes
  6. 10.2.6When growth investment hurts EBITDA — and why that's fine
  7. 10.2.7What deal teams actually ask

§10.2.1Why pricing is the most underused lever

Ask an operating partner which lever delivers the most EBITDA for each unit of effort, and the answer is almost always pricing. The reason is pure arithmetic: a price increase, after any loss of volume, flows straight through to EBITDA. There's no cost of goods against it, no headcount to hire, and no capex. Compare the three classic 1% moves, on a business with £100m of revenue, £60m of variable costs, £30m of fixed costs, and £10m of EBITDA.

Move EBITDA impact Why
+1% price (volume held) +£1.0m (+10%) 100% flow-through
+1% volume +£0.4m (+4%) Only the 40% contribution margin flows through
−1% variable cost +£0.6m (+6%) 1% × £60m

So price is worth two and a half times as much as volume. And yet mid-market companies systematically under-price, for reasons that are organisational, not economic. Founders price on a cost-plus basis, and never revisit it. Sales reps have unlimited authority to discount, and they're paid on revenue, not margin. List prices haven't moved since the last crisis, because "our customers won't wear it". And nobody owns pricing; it falls between sales, finance and marketing. That's why pricing is nearly always in the 100-day plan. The opportunity is usually large and quick, and the previous owner couldn't see it.

§10.2.2Worked example: 3% through to EBITDA

Let's take a distribution business with revenue of £100.0m, a gross margin of 25%, which is £25.0m, overheads of £17.0m, and EBITDA of £8.0m, an 8.0% margin. The new owner pushes through a price increase of 3% across the whole book.

Case 1 assumes no loss of volume. Revenue becomes £103.0m. The cost of goods sold is unchanged at £75.0m, because the same number of units are shipped, and overheads are unchanged too. So every pound of the increase lands in profit.

£m Before After
Revenue 100.0 103.0
COGS (75.0) (75.0)
Gross profit 25.0 28.0
Overheads (17.0) (17.0)
EBITDA 8.0 11.0

A 3% move in price produces a 37.5% increase in EBITDA. At an 8× multiple, that £3.0m is worth £24m of enterprise value. On a business worth £60m to £80m, that's potentially a third of the equity cheque, from a single initiative. This leverage is why low-margin businesses, such as distributors, logistics and services, are the most sensitive to price in value-creation stories, not the least. The thinner the margin, the more violently it flows through.

Case 2 allows for some churn. Suppose 2% of the volume walks away. The retained volume is 98%, priced 3% higher, so revenue is £100.0m × 0.98 × 1.03, which gives £100.9m. The cost of goods sold falls in line with volume, to £75.0m × 0.98, which is £73.5m. So gross profit is £27.4m, and EBITDA is £10.4m. That's still up 30%. Now run the break-even. With a 25% gross margin, the price rise only destroys value if volume falls by more than roughly 3 divided by 25 plus 3, which is about 11%. In practice, well-executed price increases on B2B business that isn't under contract lose a low single-digit percentage of volume, at worst. That asymmetry is the whole point: even the downside case makes money.

So what evidence on pricing do deal teams look for in due diligence? The spread of prices: the same product sold to similar customers at prices 10 to 20% apart, where the low end is pure leakage. Input inflation that hasn't been passed on: supplier costs up 8%, but prices up only 2%, which shows up as erosion of the gross margin. Discounting without governance: no approval matrix, and discounts clustering just below whatever threshold triggers sign-off. And no price rise for two years or more. Each of these turns into a sized opportunity, which is exactly the exercise in this module's case study.

§10.2.3Salesforce effectiveness

The second commercial lever is getting the existing sales force to sell more. Here are some typical findings in the mid-market, and the fixes.

  • Coverage, and the design of territories. The best rep produces four to five times as much as the worst, and the territories reflect history, rather than opportunity. Rebalancing the accounts, and putting the best people on the biggest untapped opportunities, is free capacity.
  • Discipline on activity and the pipeline. There's no hygiene in the CRM, no definitions of the stages, and the forecasts are guesses. Instrumenting the funnel, which is work for the data team, turns sales management from anecdote into arithmetic. If win rates are 20%, and the plan needs £10m of new revenue at an average deal size of £100k, then the pipeline has to hold £50m. Is it there?
  • Incentives. Reps who are paid on revenue will discount to close a deal. Move their pay towards gross margin and mix, and their behaviour follows within a quarter.
  • Pricing the funnel, not just the book. That means approving discounts at the quoting stage, setting floor prices for each segment, and tracking wins and losses on price.

None of this is glamorous, and that's the point. Sales force effectiveness is an uplift in revenue of 5 to 15%, hiding in process, and it's measurable within two quarters.

§10.2.4New products, new markets, cross-sell

Here are the revenue levers with longer cycles, in rough order of risk.

  1. Cross-selling means selling existing products to existing customers who only buy one line. It's the lowest risk, because both the product and the relationship already exist. The diagnostic is a simple matrix of customers against product lines, filled in with revenue. In most businesses with several lines, the matrix is startlingly empty. If the average customer buys 1.4 of the 5 lines, and the best accounts buy 4, then the gap is the opportunity. But be honest about why it's empty, because sometimes the products genuinely aren't bought together.
  2. New segments and geographies for existing products carry medium risk. The product is proven, but the route to market isn't. Bolt-on acquisitions, covered in lesson 4, are often a faster way into a new region than entering it organically.
  3. New products carry the highest risk, and the slowest payback. Developing a genuinely new product rarely pays back within a hold of four to five years. So PE funds mostly buy new products, through bolt-ons, rather than building them, unless the pipeline was already at a late stage at entry.

So what looks good? A growth plan weighted towards cross-selling and share of wallet, evidenced from the customer matrix. And what looks bad? A hockey stick driven by products that don't exist yet, in markets the company has never sold into.

§10.2.5Commercial excellence programmes

"Commercial excellence" is the umbrella term for doing all of the above as one programme, rather than piecemeal. It brings together governance of pricing, sales force effectiveness, instrumenting the funnel, plans for key accounts, and managing churn, under a single owner, often a newly hired Chief Revenue Officer, with a single dashboard. Structurally, it mirrors a programme to cut costs, with a baseline, charters for each initiative, a weekly rhythm, and tracked benefits. And that structure is what separates it from "we told sales to try harder".

The data team bears a lot of the weight here. Every programme of commercial excellence runs on three datasets that typically don't exist at entry. There's a price file at the level of each transaction, with every invoice line showing the customer, the product, the list price, the price actually achieved, and the cost; this powers the analysis of price spread. There's a clean pipeline, with probabilities for each stage. And there's customer revenue by cohort, showing retention, churn and share of wallet by vintage. Building these is often, quite literally, the first quarter of the programme. That's why providers of commercial due diligence, and operating teams, now bring data engineers along, not just strategists.

Here are some typical economics for a programme, for calibration. Pricing and plugging leakage alone deliver an uplift in revenue of 2 to 5% within 12 to 18 months. Sales force effectiveness and cross-selling add a further 3 to 10% over the hold. The pricing tranche flows through at a margin of close to 100%, while the volume tranche flows through at the contribution margin.

§10.2.6When growth investment hurts EBITDA — and why that's fine

Here's the tension every owner faces. Most of the revenue levers beyond pricing cost money before they pay off. New sales hires take 6 to 12 months to ramp up. A new site loses money for 18 months. Entering a new geography means a year of overheads before the revenue arrives. All of it depresses EBITDA now, in order to build EBITDA later. And since the business is valued as a multiple of EBITDA, undisciplined thinking says, "protect this year's number."

Run the arithmetic instead. EBITDA today is £10.0m, and let's assume an exit at 8× either way. In Option A, you cut £2.0m of growth spending. EBITDA goes up to £12.0m straight away, but growth stalls, so EBITDA at exit is £12.0m, giving an EV of £96m. In Option B, you keep investing. EBITDA stays at £10.0m this year, but compounds to £15.0m by the exit, giving an EV of £120m. Option B is worth £24m more. In reality, the gap is even wider, because a business that exits with visible growth sells at a higher multiple than one that's been harvested. Buyers at exit will run the same quality-of-earnings analysis that your fund ran at entry, and "EBITDA propped up by cutting sales capacity" is one of the first adjustments they'll make.

So here's the rule of judgement that deal teams apply: short-term pain in EBITDA is fine when it's legible. That means three things. First, the investment is ring-fenced and reported separately; boards often track "EBITDA before growth investment" as a memo line, so the underlying engine stays visible. Second, the case for payback is explicit, using cohort economics for sales hires and site-level P&Ls for new locations, and it's tracked against the actual results. And third, the capital structure can afford it. Covenant headroom is measured on actual EBITDA, and a levered balance sheet can turn a sensible investment into a default. What looks bad is the mirror image: EBITDA "investment" that's really just erosion of margin with a story attached, never ring-fenced, never tracked, and never paying back. The difference between the two comes down to a discipline in reporting, which means it's the data team's job to make the difference visible.

§10.2.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show me the price you actually achieved, by customer, for your top products." The chart showing the spread of prices is the single fastest diagnostic of pricing there is.
  • "When did you last raise your list prices, and what happened to volume?" The answer is usually "2022", and "nothing", and that's the opportunity in a single sentence.
  • "What's the trend in gross margin?" Gross margin eroding while volumes are stable means input inflation isn't being passed through. That's a pricing initiative, already sized.
  • "What does a rep cost, what does a fully ramped rep produce, and how long does the ramp take?" These are the unit economics that justify, or kill, an expansion of the sales force.
  • "Which growth spending would you cut if you had to protect EBITDA, and why haven't you?" This is the question that reveals whether management can tell investment apart from waste.
