Lesson 10.3/Value Creation

Margin & Cost Levers

24 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the cost side of the value creation plan: procurement, spans and layers, consolidating the footprint, shared services, automation, and zero-based budgeting. It includes a worked margin bridge from an EBITDA margin of 15% to 19% over three years, and the credibility tests that deal teams apply to plans for cutting costs, especially the scrutiny of the one-off costs of achieving them.

  1. 10.3.1Why margin is the "bankable" lever
  2. 10.3.2Procurement: the reliable first wave
  3. 10.3.3Organisational levers: spans, layers, and shared services
  4. 10.3.4Footprint, automation, and zero-based budgeting
  5. 10.3.5Worked example: the 15% → 19% margin bridge
  6. 10.3.6Costs to achieve: where cost-out plans go to be audited
  7. 10.3.7What deal teams actually ask

§10.3.1Why margin is the "bankable" lever

Revenue levers create the most value over a hold, but margin levers are the ones that lenders and investment committees treat as bankable. You can size them from data the business already has, they don't depend on customers doing anything, and delivering them is largely within management's control. That's why a debt package will often give partial credit for cutting costs, but none for growth. A bank will believe that you can renegotiate your freight contract; it won't believe your hockey stick of cross-selling.

The flip side is that cutting costs is finite, and margin expansion has a floor. You can take a business from an EBITDA margin of 15% to 19% once, but you can't do it on every hold, and a buyer at exit will ask, "what's left?" A VCP that leans entirely on cost, with no growth story, tends to exit at a lower multiple, because buyers pay for engines, not squeezed lemons. The craft is in the sequencing. Bank the cost levers early, because they fund the growth investment and pay down debt, and let the growth levers carry the story at exit.

Here are the standard cost levers, in rough order of how quickly they work.

Lever Typical timing Typical size
Procurement Months 3–18 2–5% of addressable spend
Zero-based budgeting (discretionary) Months 3–12 10–20% of discretionary opex
Spans & layers Months 6–18 5–10% of management cost
Shared services Year 1–2 15–30% of back-office cost
Automation / digital Year 1–3 Varies; longest payback
Footprint consolidation Year 1–3 Site fixed costs, net of transfer costs

§10.3.2Procurement: the reliable first wave

Procurement is nearly always the first big initiative on costs, because the money is real, the method is proven, and nobody gets made redundant. Here's the playbook.

  1. Build the spend cube. That means every supplier invoice line coded by category, supplier, site and unit price. This is work for the data team, it takes four to eight weeks, and it's the one thing everything else depends on. Most mid-market companies can't tell you their top 20 suppliers by addressable spend on day one.
  2. Segment the addressable spend. Not all spending can be negotiated this year. Some of it is under contract, some comes from a monopoly supplier, and some is locked in by the specification. Out of £50m of spending with third parties, perhaps £35m can be addressed in the first wave.
  3. Pull the levers for each category. That means competitive tenders, sending requests for quotes to three to five suppliers; consolidation, such as moving from 8 packaging suppliers to 2 for better volume pricing; changes to the specification, by asking whether you really need this grade; payment terms; and simple renegotiation. A supplier that has held the account unchallenged for six years has some margin to give.
  4. Track the savings at run-rate, and lock them in. A negotiated price reduction of 4%, which purchasing then erodes through maverick buying off contract, is worth nothing. Tracking compliance is, once again, a data problem.

For calibration, 2 to 5% of addressable spend within 18 months is the standard range to underwrite, for a business that has never run professional procurement. Claims above 5% need evidence category by category. On £35m of addressable spend, that's £0.7m to £1.75m of EBITDA, which is often the largest single line in the bridge for the first year.

§10.3.3Organisational levers: spans, layers, and shared services

Spans and layers is the analysis of how many people each manager manages, which is the span, and how many levels of management sit between the CEO and the front line, which are the layers. The benchmarks are spans of 6 to 10 for most functions, and 5 to 6 layers for a mid-market business. What due diligence often finds instead is spans of 2 or 3, "managers managing managers managing one person", and 8 layers, built up by years of promoting without restructuring. Removing one thin layer of, say, 16 roles, at a fully loaded cost of £50k each, saves £0.8m. But the real benefit is speed, because every layer adds delay to approvals, and dilutes accountability.

Shared services consolidates duplicated back-office functions, such as finance, HR, payroll and IT support, into one centre. These are often scattered across sites, or across companies that were acquired and never integrated. The typical saving is 15 to 30% of the cost base affected, from removing the duplication and standardising processes. It's also what makes buy-and-build possible, as lesson 4 explains. A platform with a working shared-service centre can strip the back office out of every bolt-on it buys, and that's where much of the case for synergies lives.

Here's the point of judgement on cutting organisational costs. It's the lever with the highest execution risk for every pound saved. Redundancy programmes cost money up front, which we'll come to below under costs to achieve. They take up management's attention for months. And if they're done badly, they take out the wrong people, so the institutional knowledge walks out of the door, and the politics stays.

§10.3.4Footprint, automation, and zero-based budgeting

Consolidating the footprint, meaning closing a site and serving its demand from the rest of the network, trades savings in fixed costs against the costs of the transfer. The arithmetic has to be done honestly. Closing a warehouse that costs £1.5m a year only saves £0.7m net, if freight to the transferred customers rises by £0.6m and you're left carrying £0.2m of stranded costs. Closing sites also has the longest tail of one-off costs, such as breaking leases, dilapidations, redundancy and running two sites in parallel, and the most operational risk. Service levels dip during the move, and in distribution businesses, customers notice within a week.

Automation and digital covers everything from robotic processing of invoices in finance, to warehouse-management systems, to replacing the manual generation of quotes. Paybacks take longer, from 18 months to 3 years, and the business cases are routinely oversold. So investment committees typically want automation in the plan, but not bearing any weight in the bridge. Here's the honest framing: automation mostly buys capacity and accuracy first, and reduces headcount second.

Zero-based budgeting, or ZBB, rebuilds discretionary budgets from zero every year, so every line has to be justified afresh, rather than being "last year plus 3%". Applied to travel, marketing, professional fees, subscriptions and facilities, it reliably finds 10 to 20% of discretionary spending in the first pass. Most of that is legacy commitments that nobody had looked at. Here's the caution, though. Applying ZBB crudely to spending that matters for growth, such as marketing that drives the funnel, or sales tools, is how you end up harvesting the business by accident. So ring-fence the growth investment, as lesson 2 described, before you zero-base anything.

§10.3.5Worked example: the 15% → 19% margin bridge

A business with revenue of £100.0m and EBITDA of £15.0m, which is a 15.0% margin, is underwritten to reach a margin of 19.0% over three years. We'll hold revenue flat to keep things clear. In reality, revenue grows and the percentages move, but it's the pounds that matter. Here's the bridge that the investment committee signed off.

Bridge item Initiative detail Year landed EBITDA impact
Opening EBITDA £15.0m
Procurement waves 1–2 Tender top categories; £50m spend, 3% on addressable Yr 1–2 +£1.5m
Spans & layers Remove one management layer: 16 roles × £50k Yr 2 +£0.8m
Footprint consolidation Close site 4 of 4; £1.2m fixed cost saved, −£0.5m transfer freight Yr 2–3 +£0.7m
Shared services Consolidate 3 finance/HR teams into one centre Yr 2–3 +£0.4m
Automation Invoice processing + warehouse WMS Yr 3 +£0.6m
Zero-based budgeting Discretionary opex: travel, marketing agencies, professional fees Yr 1 +£0.5m
Inflation & reinvestment Unrecovered wage inflation; new pricing/data roles Yr 1–3 −£0.5m
Exit EBITDA £19.0m

Let's check the arithmetic. The gross initiatives come to 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.7 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.5, which is £4.5m. Net of the £0.5m line for inflation and reinvestment, that's plus £4.0m, landing at £19.0m on £100.0m, which is 19.0%. At an 8× multiple, that £4.0m is worth £32m of enterprise value.

Three features make this bridge credible, rather than decorative. First, every line is an initiative with a mechanism, not a percentage. It says "procurement, 3% on addressable spend of £50m", not "efficiencies, £1.5m". Second, it includes a negative line. Real bridges leak. Wage inflation outruns the recovery in prices, and the VCP itself needs new hires. A bridge with no negative items hasn't been stress-tested. Third, it's phased over time. Nobody delivers spans and layers in month six, or automation in year one, and that phasing drives the covenant headroom in the debt model.

§10.3.6Costs to achieve: where cost-out plans go to be audited

Every one of the savings above comes with a one-off price tag. "Costs to achieve" is where deal teams, lenders, and buyers at exit apply the most scrutiny. Here they are for the bridge above.

One-off cost £m
Redundancy (spans & layers + shared services) 1.0
Site exit: lease break, dilapidations, dual-running 1.1
Systems: WMS, invoice automation, shared-service platform 0.7
Consultant support (procurement wave 1) 0.4
Total costs to achieve 3.2

That's 0.7 times the £4.5m of gross run-rate savings, which is comfortably inside the typical range of 0.5 to 1.5 times. Programmes led by redundancies run at about 0.5 to 1.0 times, while those heavy on sites and systems push towards 1.5 times. A plan claiming big savings at 0.2 times their cost is either genuinely low-hanging fruit, which is possible in a founder-run business that has never been optimised, or it hasn't been priced. And a plan at 2.0 times or more needs a very long hold to pay back.

Here are the credibility tests to run on any plan to cut costs.

  • Run-rate, or in-year? "£4.5m of savings" that lands in December contributes almost nothing to that year's EBITDA. So ask for both numbers, phased by quarter.
  • Where do the one-off costs sit? The classic game is to book the savings in EBITDA, while pushing the costs to achieve them below the line as "exceptional items". That inflates the adjusted EBITDA that a buyer or lender sees. It's fine if it's disclosed, and genuinely one-off. It's a red flag when "exceptionals" recur in every year of the hold.
  • Are they net of inflation and reinvestment? £1.5m of procurement savings, in a year when input costs rose by £1.0m, is only £0.5m of net margin. Bridges that are gross of inflation count things twice.
  • Double counting across initiatives. The same back-office role can't be saved by spans and layers, and by shared services, and by automation. Add up the reductions in headcount by department, and check them against the actual organisation chart.
  • Attrition, or redundancy? Plans that assume half the reduction will come free, through natural attrition, need the attrition rate to support that. And attrition doesn't choose which roles it removes.

§10.3.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show me the bridge with dates, owners and costs to achieve, all on the same page." A savings number without its cost and its calendar is a press release, not a plan.
  • "What's the addressable spend, and who said 3% was achievable?" This is about where the benchmark came from. A consultant's benchmark at the level of each category is evidence; "industry standard" isn't.
  • "Which of these savings will the customer notice?" Consolidating the footprint, and automation that touches service, carry a risk to revenue that has to appear in the bridge, not in the footnotes.
  • "What did last year's exceptional items contain?" This is the quickest test of whether this management team runs one-offs through EBITDA honestly.
  • "If we only did procurement and ZBB, what would we get?" That's the no-regrets floor. Good plans have a bankable core, plus upside. Bad plans need every single initiative to land.

Lesson 10.4/Value Creation

Buy-and-Build

25 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the economics of platforms and bolt-ons. It works through an example of multiple arbitrage, with a platform bought at 9x and bolt-ons at 5 to 6x, and the maths of the blended entry multiple. It explains what makes a good platform, the realities of integration, meaning systems, culture and double counting of synergies, and the classic ways roll-ups fail, which deal teams screen for.

  1. 10.4.1The strategy in one sentence
  2. 10.4.2The multiple arbitrage engine
  3. 10.4.3What makes a good platform
  4. 10.4.4Integration realities
  5. 10.4.5Roll-up failure modes
  6. 10.4.6What deal teams actually ask

§10.4.1The strategy in one sentence

Buy-and-build means acquiring one company as a platform, and then bolting on smaller competitors or adjacent businesses, integrating them into a group that's worth more than the sum of its parts. It's the single most common strategy in mid-market PE. By some counts, most mid-market deals are now either platforms bought with a thesis of building, or bolt-ons to existing platforms. That's because it pulls two levers at once. It drives revenue growth, because you buy revenue that you couldn't grow organically, and it drives multiple expansion, through arbitrage and scale, as we'll see below. Done well, it manufactures a larger, more professional and more diversified business, which a bigger buyer pays a bigger multiple for. Done badly, it manufactures a pile of unintegrated acquisitions sharing a letterhead, and the market has seen enough of those to check.

§10.4.2The multiple arbitrage engine

The core arithmetic rests on a lasting feature of private markets: small companies trade at lower multiples than big ones. A business with £2m of EBITDA sells for 5 to 6×, because of key-person risk, customer concentration, a lack of management depth, and few buyers. A business with £20m of EBITDA in the same sector sells for 9 to 10×, because it has professional management, it's diversified, it can be financed with debt, and both trade buyers and larger funds can bid for it. Buy small, sell as part of something big, and the same pound of EBITDA gets re-rated.

Here's a worked example. A fund buys a platform with £10.0m of EBITDA at 9.0×, which is an EV of £90.0m, and then carries out four bolt-ons over three years.

Acquisition EBITDA Multiple Price
Platform £10.0m 9.0× £90.0m
Bolt-on A (regional competitor) £3.0m 6.0× £18.0m
Bolt-on B (adjacent service line) £2.0m 5.0× £10.0m
Bolt-on C (regional competitor) £2.0m 5.5× £11.0m
Bolt-on D (small tuck-in) £1.0m 5.0× £5.0m
Total £18.0m 7.4× blended £134.0m

The bolt-ons contribute £8.0m of EBITDA for £44.0m, an average of 5.5×. That pulls the blended entry multiple down to £134.0m ÷ £18.0m, which is 7.4×.

Now for the arbitrage. Suppose the group simply exits at the platform's own entry multiple of 9.0×, with no organic growth, and no synergies at all. That gives £18.0m × 9.0×, which is £162.0m, against £134.0m invested. That's £28.0m of value from arbitrage alone, and it's exactly the £8.0m of bolt-on EBITDA re-rated from 5.5× to 9.0×, since £8.0m × 3.5× = £28.0m. Now layer on what a real deal underwrites. Say £1.5m of synergies and organic growth take the group's EBITDA to £21.0m. And add a re-rating for scale, to 9.5×, because a group with £21m of EBITDA clears the size threshold for larger buyers. Then the exit EV is £199.5m. The strategy compounds three levers: EBITDA that's bought, EBITDA that's built, and the re-rating of both.

There are two honesty checks on this maths. First, the costs of transactions and integration are real. Each bolt-on carries fees of 3 to 5% of the deal value, plus the costs of integration, such as migrating systems, rebranding and redundancies. So the true blended cost is higher than the headline. In the example above, it might be £4m to £6m across the whole programme. Second, the arbitrage only turns into money if the integration is real. Buyers at exit run a simple test: is this one company, or five? Five P&Ls consolidated in Excel, five ERP systems, five brands, and five managing directors who never meet, gets valued as five small companies, at small-company multiples. And the arbitrage evaporates at exactly the moment you try to bank it.

§10.4.3What makes a good platform

The choice of platform matters more than any individual bolt-on, because everything bolts onto it. Here's what deal teams screen for.

  • A fragmented market, with willing sellers. You need a pipeline: dozens of targets with £1m to £5m of EBITDA, typically owned by founders with problems over succession. A "roll-up" of a market with three targets is really just three deals.
  • Infrastructure that can scale. The platform's systems, finance function and management have to be able to absorb acquisitions. That's why funds often over-invest in the platform's ERP, shared services and CFO before the first bolt-on. The integration factory is built once, and reused.
  • Management that can integrate, not just operate. Running one company and absorbing four are different jobs. The best platforms have, or hire, a lead for M&A and integration, and treat integration as a repeatable process with a playbook. That means a day-1 checklist, a 100-day integration plan for each target, and a standard migration of systems.
  • A genuine logic for sharing. The group has to be worth more together. That might come from shared purchasing scale, products that can be cross-sold, national coverage that wins contracts no regional player could, or a single brand. If the only logic is "they're in the same sector", you're assembling a conglomerate, not building a company.
  • Headroom in the multiple. The arbitrage needs a real gap between the prices paid for bolt-ons and the platform's exit multiple. In sectors where roll-ups are crowded, such as vets, dentists and managed IT service providers at various points in the cycle, the prices of bolt-ons get bid up from 5× towards 8×, and the engine stalls.

§10.4.4Integration realities

The gap between the model and reality is integration, and three issues dominate.

Systems. Every bolt-on arrives with its own accounting system, customer file, product codes and payroll. Until they've been migrated, "group reporting" means consolidating spreadsheets with mismatched charts of accounts. The month-end close takes longer with every deal, and nobody can answer the question, "what do we sell to customer X across the whole group?" The angle for the data team is blunt: integration is mostly a programme of data migration, with a company attached. The answer in the playbook is a standard target operating model, with one chart of accounts, one instance of the ERP, and one CRM. Every acquisition is migrated onto it within a defined window, usually 6 to 12 months, and there's a layer of group-wide KPIs that works even before the migration is complete.

Culture and people. Bolt-ons are usually founder businesses. The founder often leaves after an earn-out, and the staff's loyalty was to the founder. Heavy-handed integration, such as rebranding on day one, stripping out the local office, or imposing group processes everywhere, can trigger the departure of exactly the client relationships you paid for. The craft lies in deciding what has to be standardised, such as finance, systems, governance of pricing, and safety, and what stays local, such as client relationships and the style of service. And then in saying so explicitly, on day one.

Double counting of synergies. Synergies are underwritten deal by deal, and the same saving gets counted again and again. Bolt-on A's case includes "consolidating purchasing", and so does B's, but there's only one consolidation of purchasing to be had. The same thing happens with back-office headcount, and with cross-selling, where A's case sells to B's customers, and B's case sells to A's. The discipline is to keep a single tracker of synergies at the group level, with each initiative counted once, netted off against the dis-synergies, such as group insurance, the salaries of the integration team, and the costs of systems, and reconciled to the actual P&L, rather than to a stack of deal models.

§10.4.5Roll-up failure modes

The strategy has a well-documented graveyard, and the ways roll-ups fail tend to rhyme.

  1. Choosing speed over quality. The model rewards the number of deals, so the pipeline gets less picky. That means weaker businesses, higher prices and stretched geographies. EBITDA "grows" while quality falls, and the diligence done on each deal shrinks as the team gets saturated.
  2. Integration debt. Each unintegrated deal adds systems, entities and complexity. Like technical debt, it compounds quietly, and then surfaces all at once, usually as chaos at month end, a failed audit, or in the buyer's due diligence at exit.
  3. Leverage on synergies that haven't landed. Debt is raised against pro-forma EBITDA that includes synergies still "to come". If integration slips, the actual EBITDA misses the pro-forma figure, leverage ratios spike, and the acquisition line gets pulled, at exactly the moment when the pipeline was the whole point. Many famous roll-up collapses happened through this mechanism.
  4. The acquisition treadmill hiding organic decline. Group revenue grows every year, because deals close every year, while the like-for-like revenue of the businesses already owned shrinks. Buyers at exit now routinely demand a split between organic and acquired growth, and a platform that can't produce one is assumed to be hiding the answer.
  5. Founder dependence that's been transferred, not solved. Ten founder businesses whose founders have all left means ten sets of orphaned relationships.

So, for calibration, what looks good? A platform doing two to four well-integrated bolt-ons a year, month-end close times that stay flat or fall, a single stack of systems, positive like-for-like growth, and a synergy tracker reconciled to the P&L. And what looks bad? The number of deals used as the KPI, "integration to follow", and pro-forma adjustments making up a growing share of EBITDA.

§10.4.6What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show me organic growth against acquired growth, like for like." That's the first question every buyer at exit asks, so ask it of yourself from year one.
  • "What's the blended multiple, including fees and the costs of integration?" That's the honest denominator, not the headline one.
  • "Walk me through the last integration: the timeline, what slipped, and what it cost." One real post-mortem beats any playbook document.
  • "Which synergies are in the bank, and which are only in the model?" Banked means visible in the P&L, and reconciled. Everything else is a plan.
  • "If you stopped acquiring today, what would next year look like?" That's the treadmill test. A good platform is a good business, even standing still. A bad one is a growth story that dies the moment the music stops.

Lesson 10.5/Value Creation

Governance & the Operating Cadence

24 min read
In brief

This lesson shows how PE actually makes the plan happen. It covers the board after the deal, operating partners, KPI dashboards, and the monthly rhythm of reporting, which is where data teams become critical. It explains when and why funds change management, how to build readiness for exit from year one, and the trade-off between margin and growth that an owner debates every single year.

  1. 10.5.1Governance is the delivery mechanism
  2. 10.5.2The post-deal board
  3. 10.5.3The KPI dashboard and the monthly rhythm
  4. 10.5.4Changing management
  5. 10.5.5Exit readiness from year one
  6. 10.5.6The annual debate: margin now or growth later
  7. 10.5.7What deal teams actually ask

§10.5.1Governance is the delivery mechanism

Everything in lessons 1 to 4 is a plan, and governance is why it actually happens. The uncomfortable truth about value creation is that most initiatives fail, not because they were wrong, but because they were never really run. There was no owner, no baseline, no rhythm, and no consequence for slipping. PE's genuine edge over public-company ownership isn't a cleverer strategy. It's concentrated ownership, combined with a relentless rhythm. A small board owns the company, meets every month, tracks a dozen numbers, and acts within weeks when they move the wrong way. A public company reviews its strategy once a year, for the market. A PE portfolio company reviews delivery every month, for its owner. Over a five-year hold, that difference in clock speed is the value creation.

§10.5.2The post-deal board

At completion, the board is rebuilt around the deal. A typical mid-market configuration has five to seven seats.

Seat Who Role on the board
Chair External, fund-appointed Runs the board; coaches the CEO; often ex-CEO of a larger business in the sector
CEO Management Delivers the plan
CFO Management Owns the numbers and the board pack
Investor directors (1–2) Deal partner + principal The fund's voice; own the returns model
Operating partner / NED Fund operating team or external Functional depth — pricing, ops, digital — matched to the VCP's biggest lever

There are three points of design. First, the chair is usually the single most important hire of the hold. An experienced chair turns the fund's pressure into action by management, without the deal partner having to manage the CEO directly. Second, the board is deliberately small. It's a committee for delivery, not a showpiece of governance. There are no quotas for independence, and everyone in the room is economically aligned, either through the fund or through the management incentive plan. Third, real power also runs through what sits around the board. The rights of shareholder consent in the investment agreement, covering approval of the budget, M&A, senior hires, and capex above a threshold, mean that the fund's control doesn't depend on board votes.

Operating partners deserve a note of their own, because they're the growth industry within PE. The models vary from fund to fund. Some have a generalist bench of "portfolio talent". Some parachute functional specialists, in pricing, procurement, or digital, into particular initiatives. And some second full-time executives as an interim CFO or Chief Revenue Officer. The tension to manage is accountability. An operating partner who quietly becomes a shadow CEO destroys the management team's ownership of the plan. Best practice makes it explicit: operating partners accelerate the initiatives, while management owns the P&L.

§10.5.3The KPI dashboard and the monthly rhythm

The operating rhythm runs on a monthly board pack, and building it is usually the first serious piece of data work in the hold; it appears in every 100-day plan, as lesson 1 showed. Here's the standard shape.

  • A summary of trading. Revenue, gross margin and EBITDA, compared with budget and the previous year, with a bridge explaining the variances. That means not just the numbers, but the why.
  • Cash. The closing cash, a rolling 13-week forecast, and the covenant headroom. In the first year, and always in leveraged deals, cash gets more of the board's time than profit.
  • A KPI dashboard. Ten to fifteen leading indicators, chosen to track the VCP. These might include the price actually achieved compared with list, coverage of the pipeline, order intake, churn, on-time-in-full delivery, procurement savings at run-rate, and headcount compared with plan. The design rule is that every big initiative in the VCP gets a KPI that moves before the P&L does. If pricing is the thesis, then tracking the price actually achieved goes on page one.
  • A tracker of initiatives. Each workstream in the VCP is shown with its owner, the status of its milestones, the benefits banked compared with the plan, and a red, amber or green status. Red items get a page of their own, with a named plan for recovery.

Here's the rhythm around the pack. There's a monthly board meeting, within about 10 working days of the month end. There's a short weekly call on trading, covering sales, cash and operations, during the first year, or whenever performance wobbles. There are quarterly deep dives on a single topic, such as pricing, a bolt-on, or the technology stack. And there's the annual budget, negotiated hard in the fourth quarter.

This is where the data team of a fund, or of a portfolio company, becomes critical infrastructure. At entry, most mid-market companies can't produce this pack. The ERP can't report the price achieved by customer, the "pipeline" lives in a rep's notebook, and the month-end close takes more than 20 working days. So the data agenda for the first year bears the weight of the entire VCP. It means automating the monthly pack; ten working days is a discipline, and it's won by automating the pipeline, not by heroics. It means building the price file at the level of each transaction, instrumenting the sales funnel, and creating a single version of the truth, so that board meetings argue about actions, rather than whose spreadsheet is right. Here's a useful test of any portfolio company's maturity: how many days after the month end can the board see reliable numbers, and how many manual steps does it take?

§10.5.4Changing management

The evidence across the industry is consistent, and blunt: in roughly half or more of buyouts, the CEO is replaced during the hold. The CFO is changed even more often, frequently in the first year, because the disciplines of reporting and cash described above demand a CFO who has done this before. Almost every review after a deal says the same thing: we moved too slowly on people.

Here's the framework of judgement that deal teams use.

  • Upgrade for the next phase, rather than punishing the last one. The founder's CFO who got the business to £8m of EBITDA may simply never have run a leveraged business, governed by a board, on a monthly rhythm. That's a mismatch, not a failing, but it's still a change.
  • Decide on evidence, and quickly. The first two board cycles tell you most of what you need to know. Does the CEO own the plan, or keep reopening the argument about it? Do the numbers arrive on time, and survive scrutiny? Is bad news volunteered early? Six months of doubt is itself a decision.
  • Sequence the changes deliberately. Change the CFO first, because the numbers have to be trustworthy before anything else can be decided. Change the commercial leadership where the thesis is commercial. And change the CEO only when there's a plan for succession, because an empty CEO chair part-way through the hold costs a year of momentum.
  • Cost it honestly. Changing the CEO costs 6 to 12 months of drift, plus the costs of search and severance. Keeping the wrong CEO costs the plan. Both of those numbers belong in the discussion.

The management incentive plan is the other half of this lever. The terms for leavers' equity, good leaver or bad leaver, top-up pools for new hires, and re-vesting all get negotiated at the moment of change. The deal structuring module covers how they're structured.

§10.5.5Exit readiness from year one

Funds increasingly run the hold as a five-year preparation for the sale, because the difference between a prepared exit and an unprepared one is measured in turns of the multiple. Building readiness for exit from year one means four things.

  • Numbers that survive diligence. That means monthly packs reconciled to the audited accounts, a clean policy for recognising revenue, a split between organic and acquired growth maintained continuously, as lesson 4 described, and no items building up in adjusted EBITDA that "we'll explain at exit". The buyer's quality-of-earnings team will find in week two whatever you hoped to explain away in year four.
  • A track record of forecasting. A company that has hit or beaten its budget for three years in a row can sell its forecast. One that misses every year can only sell its history. Boards manage this deliberately, setting budgets to be beaten from about year three.
  • Documented value creation. The margin bridge, the pricing programme and the playbook for integration, written up as evidence of how EBITDA grew. That's what persuades the next buyer that the growth can be repeated, and it supports their own VCP too.
  • A data room that's always warm. Contracts, statutory accounts, board minutes and the history of KPIs are maintained continuously, rather than assembled in a six-week panic that distracts management at exactly the moment when trading mustn't dip.

Routes to exit, and vendor due diligence, get full treatment in the exits module. The point here is that being ready for exit is an operating habit, not a project that starts when the bankers arrive.

§10.5.6The annual debate: margin now or growth later

Every budget season, the board has the same argument. It's worth staging explicitly, because it's the whole problem of ownership in miniature. The company can spend the next £1.0m on growth, such as sales hires, a new site, or a product, or it can let it drop through to EBITDA. Take a business with £10.0m of EBITDA in year 3 of a five-year hold, with an assumed exit at 8×.

  • If it harvests, EBITDA reaches £11.0m by the exit, giving an EV of £88m. The covenants are comfortable. But the buyer sees revenue slowing, and prices in the risk to growth, at perhaps 7×, which gives an EV of £77m.
  • If it invests, EBITDA is £10.0m now, and £12.5m by the exit, as the investment pays back. That gives an EV of £100m at 8×. And a growth engine that has been demonstrated can re-rate the multiple higher still.

The honest answer is that it depends on three things that the board has to weigh every year. The first is the time left until exit. Growth spending in the final year rarely pays back before the sale, although a visible growth story still sells. The second is covenant headroom. A levered balance sheet can make harvesting temporarily rational; leverage both disciplines and distorts. The third is legibility. Growth spending that's ring-fenced, tracked and evidenced by cohorts gets credit from buyers, while vague "investment" reads as erosion of margin, which was lesson 2's rule. What looks bad isn't either answer. It's drift: a board that never decides, under-invests and misses on margin, and arrives at the exit with neither story. The operating rhythm exists precisely so that this trade-off gets made once a year, on evidence, and out loud.

§10.5.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "How many days does it take to close the month, and how many manual steps are there in the pack?" That's the one-question test of the maturity of the finance and data stack.
  • "Which KPI tells us that the pricing programme is working, before the P&L does?" Every initiative needs a leading indicator, or slippage surfaces two quarters too late.
  • "If we could only keep five numbers on page one, which five would they be?" This forces the board pack to mirror the thesis, rather than the ERP's default reports.
  • "Would you hire the CFO again today?" This is asked at every portfolio review, and a hesitant answer is the answer.
  • "What would a buyer's quality-of-earnings team flag if they arrived on Monday?" That's the audit of readiness for exit, run years before the exit itself.

Lesson 11.1/Exits

Exit Routes Compared

24 min read
In brief

This lesson sets out the menu of exit routes: a trade sale, a secondary buyout, an IPO, a continuation vehicle, a dividend recap, and a minority sale. It compares them on process, valuation dynamics, certainty and speed, identifies who the natural buyers are, and explains why strategic buyers can pay more, but often don't.

  1. 11.1.1The exit is the investment case
  2. 11.1.2Trade sale: selling to a strategic
  3. 11.1.3Secondary buyout: selling to another sponsor
  4. 11.1.4IPO: selling to the public markets
  5. 11.1.5Continuation vehicles: selling to yourself, properly
  6. 11.1.6Partial exits: dividend recaps and minority sales
  7. 11.1.7The comparison table
  8. 11.1.8Why strategics can pay more — and often don't

§11.1.1The exit is the investment case

A PE fund doesn't make money when it buys a company; it makes money when it sells one. Every investment committee paper has a slide titled "exit routes", written before the fund has owned the business for a single day. That's because the underwriting question is always the same: who will buy this from us in five years' time, and why will they pay more than we did? If the deal team can't name two or three credible future buyers at entry, the deal usually dies.

The menu is short. The full exits are selling to a strategic acquirer, which is a trade sale; selling to another sponsor, which is a secondary buyout, or "SBO"; or selling to public market investors, through an IPO. A fourth route, the continuation vehicle, or CV, sells the asset to a new fund managed by the same GP, funded largely by secondaries investors. And there are partial exits. A dividend recapitalisation returns cash by putting more debt on the business, and a minority sale brings in a new investor for part of the equity, while the fund stays in control.

Each route trades off four things. There's price. There's certainty, meaning the probability that the deal actually closes at the agreed number. There's speed, meaning the time it takes to get the cash. And there's cleanliness, meaning how much of the position is actually realised, and what liabilities the seller keeps. No route wins on all four, and choosing between them is the judgement this module teaches.

§11.1.2Trade sale: selling to a strategic

A trade sale means selling the whole business to a corporate acquirer. That might be a competitor, a customer, a supplier, or a company entering the market. It's the classic route to "the best price", because a strategic buyer can pay for synergies that no financial buyer has access to, and there's more on that maths below.

The process. It's usually an auction run by a sell-side bank. Module 6 covered the buyer's view, and lesson 3 of this module covers the seller's. Strategic buyers move more slowly than sponsors. They need approval from their board, and sometimes from their shareholders, and their internal M&A teams run diligence alongside their day jobs. Expect six to nine months from launch to completion, and longer if antitrust review bites. A strategic buyer acquiring a direct competitor is exactly the kind of transaction that competition authorities exist to examine. A Phase 1 review by the CMA or the European Commission adds months. A Phase 2 adds six months or more, and carries a real risk of the deal being blocked, or remedies being forced on it.

The dynamics of valuation. This route has the highest potential price, and the widest variance. A motivated strategic buyer with real synergies can pay one to three turns of EBITDA above the price at which financial buyers would clear. An unmotivated one bids below the sponsors, because its board sees no urgency.

Certainty and speed. Certainty is medium, because boards can change their minds, and antitrust can intervene, and speed is medium to slow. But it's a clean, full exit. The whole business is sold, with cash on completion. And strategic buyers often accept a lighter package of warranties than sponsors demand, because they know the industry.

So when is it the right answer? When a strategic buyer genuinely needs the asset, as in plays to consolidate a market, filling a gap in technology or capability, or entering a new geography, and when the antitrust risk can be managed.

§11.1.3Secondary buyout: selling to another sponsor

An SBO sells the company to another PE fund. To outsiders, that looks circular, "PE selling to PE". But it's the single most common route to exit in the European mid-market, routinely making up 40 to 50% of sponsors' exits by number. The logic is straightforward. The buying fund has a different angle, such as a bigger fund, a buy-and-build thesis, or a sector platform. The business has another leg of growth left, which the selling fund can't stay around for. And sponsors are fast, reliable buyers, who do this for a living.

The process. It can be an auction, or a bilateral deal. Sponsors run their diligence in weeks rather than months, use debt markets that they know intimately, and don't need any drama with boards or antitrust. Competition issues are rare, because funds seldom own direct competitors at scale. It takes three to five months from end to end.

The dynamics of valuation. The price is capped by the maths of the LBO. The buyer has to underwrite its own IRR of 20% or more, so it pays what its leverage and its value-creation plan can support. That's typically at, or slightly below, the ceiling a strategic buyer could reach. When debt markets are hot, SBO prices rival trade prices. When credit tightens, the SBO bid is the first to fall.

Certainty and speed. This is the route to a full exit with the highest certainty, and the quickest, especially with committed financing. Sponsors rarely try to renegotiate the price without a reason, because their reputation with advisers is an asset that they protect.

So when is it the right answer? When it's a good business with more growth to come, there's no natural strategic buyer at a full price, and the seller values speed and certainty. That's very common when the selling fund is late in its life, and needs DPI, meaning distributions to paid-in capital.

§11.1.4IPO: selling to the public markets

An IPO lists the company's shares on a public exchange. Two things make it unlike every other route. First, it isn't an exit on day one; it's the start of one. The fund typically sells only 20 to 40% of its stake in the offering. It's then locked up for 180 days, and sells the rest in blocks over 18 to 36 months, at whatever the market price happens to be by then. Second, the price is set by fund managers building a book, rather than by a single buyer in a negotiation. And IPOs are priced at a discount, often 10 to 15% below fair value, to make sure the shares trade upwards.

Here's a worked example. A fund owns all of a company worth £600m of equity. At the IPO, it sells 30% for £180m, priced at a 10% discount. Suppose the shares then drift down by 20% during the lock-up, and the fund sells the remaining 70% at the lower price. It collects another £336m, making £516m in total, compared with £600m from a clean trade sale at £600m. So the IPO route delivered 86p in the pound, and took two extra years. That's why deal teams call an IPO "a route to liquidity, not liquidity itself".

So when is it the right answer? For very large businesses, which are too big for most sponsors, and have few strategic buyers; for strong growth stories that the public market will pay up for; and when the windows for equity are open. IPO markets shut abruptly, and stay shut for quarters at a time, so nobody sensible runs an IPO as their only track.

§11.1.5Continuation vehicles: selling to yourself, properly

A CV moves the asset from the current fund into a new vehicle, managed by the same GP. It's funded by secondaries investors, plus whichever existing LPs choose to roll over. The LPs in the old fund get a genuine choice: cash out at the deal price, or roll into the CV. The GP carries on managing the asset, typically with reset economics, and fresh capital for the next phase.

Here's why it exists. Sometimes the best asset in the fund still has years of compounding left, but the fund has run out of time, and out of capital for follow-on investment. Selling a great business in year 9 of a 10-year fund because the fund has expired, rather than because the asset is finished, destroys value. The CV lets the GP keep the winner, while still handing cash to the LPs who want it.

The obvious problem is that the GP sits on both sides of the price. That problem, and the machinery that manages it, such as approval by the LP advisory committee, fairness opinions, checks against the market, and the mechanics of the LPs' elections, get a full lesson later in this module. For the purposes of comparing routes, here's the summary. The price is usually at, or near, the level a third party would pay, but rarely above it. Certainty is high. Speed is moderate, at four to six months including the LPs' election. And the fund's realisation is partial by construction, typically 30 to 50% in cash, with the rest rolled over.

§11.1.6Partial exits: dividend recaps and minority sales

A dividend recap isn't a sale at all. The company borrows more, and pays the proceeds to its shareholders. Here's a worked example. A portfolio company has £20m of EBITDA, and current net debt of £30m, which is 1.5x. Lenders will support 4.0x, so the company raises new facilities of £80m, repays the £30m, pays £2m of fees, and distributes £48m to the fund. If the fund's equity cost £60m, it has now returned 0.8 times its money, while still owning the whole business. What looks good is taking risk off a winner part-way through the hold, and resetting the IRR clock on capital that was just sitting in the asset. What looks bad is recapping a fragile business. The extra leverage is still there when trading turns, and the lenders, the management and the next buyer will all remember who took the money out.

A minority sale sells, say, 20 to 30% of the equity to a new investor, at a negotiated valuation. That investor might be a minority or growth fund, a sovereign fund, or occasionally a strategic buyer. It delivers some cash, an external valuation mark that validates the carrying value, and sometimes a useful partner. The costs are complexity in governance, through consent rights and exit provisions, and a signal that buyers read carefully: why sell a slice, rather than the whole thing? Partial exits are tools for managing the hold, not substitutes for the real exit.

§11.1.7The comparison table

Route Typical price vs field Certainty Speed to cash % realised Right answer when…
Trade sale Highest potential (synergies) Medium (boards, antitrust) 6–9 months 100% A strategic truly needs it; antitrust manageable
Secondary buyout At/near market, capped by LBO maths High (committed financing) 3–5 months 100% Asset has another PE-shaped leg; seller wants certainty/DPI
IPO Discounted at pricing; market sets the rest Low (windows close) 2–4 years for full exit 20–40% at IPO Very large, strong growth story, open window
Continuation vehicle At/near market, rarely above High once priced 4–6 months 30–50% cash, rest rolled Fund expiring, asset isn't; LPs get real choice
Dividend recap n/a (no sale) High if debt available 2–3 months Partial cash, 0% of equity De-risk a stable winner mid-hold
Minority sale Negotiated, often with structure Medium 3–6 months 20–30% Need validation, partner, or partial liquidity

Deal teams run dual-track, or even triple-track, processes precisely because these profiles differ. They prepare an IPO and an M&A sale in parallel, let each one discipline the other's price, and choose late.

§11.1.8Why strategics can pay more — and often don't

Let's start with the maths of synergies. The target has £15m of EBITDA, and a standalone value of 9.0x, which is £135m. A strategic acquirer expects £4m of annual synergies, from savings in procurement, merging the head offices, and cross-selling products. Capitalise those at the same 9.0x, and the business is worth £135m plus £36m, which is £171m, to that buyer. That's 11.4x the standalone EBITDA. Any price below £171m creates value for the strategic buyer. A sponsor with no synergies, on the other hand, is stuck at around 9.0x, plus whatever its leverage and operating plan can justify.

So why do sponsors win so many auctions? Because the ceiling set by the synergies isn't the same as the bid.

  • Discipline. Corporate boards refuse to "pay away the synergies". A common internal rule is to concede no more than a third to a half of the value of the synergies to the seller. So the bid becomes £147m to £153m, not £171m.
  • The risk of integration. Synergy cases fail often enough that experienced acquirers haircut them before they bid. So £4m on paper becomes £2.5m in the board pack.
  • No clock. A fund in year 8 has to transact. A strategic buyer can wait for the next asset, the next cycle, or the next CEO.
  • Friction in the process. There's slower diligence, board calendars, antitrust conditions, and the negotiation over remedies and break fees that comes with them. Sellers discount uncertain bids. An offer of £300m with a six-month regulatory tail isn't worth £300m.
  • Cycles. The appetite for corporate M&A rises and falls with the cycle, and is driven by confidence, whereas sponsors with committed funds are structurally always in the market.

So what do deal teams actually ask when they compare routes? Who are the three most likely buyers, and what does each one's maths support? And what does each route's price look like once it's adjusted for certainty and time, rather than just the headline? A disciplined seller writes down, for every serious option, the headline EV, the expected proceeds after conditions and retained risks, and the expected number of months until the cash arrives. The best exit is the best number adjusted for risk and time. And as the rest of this module shows, that's frequently not the biggest headline.

Lesson 11.2/Exits

Exit Timing and Preparation

22 min read
In brief

This lesson shows how deal teams decide when to sell, using the framework of incremental IRR, market windows, and pressures at the level of the fund. It covers how they prepare: the checklist for exit readiness, and grooming the equity story. And it explains why selling "too early" is often the right call.

  1. 11.2.1Two clocks, one decision
  2. 11.2.2The incremental-IRR framework
  3. 11.2.3Market windows: the multiple you don't control
  4. 11.2.4The exit readiness checklist
  5. 11.2.5Grooming the equity story
  6. 11.2.6When selling "too early" is right
  7. 11.2.7What the IC actually debates

§11.2.1Two clocks, one decision

Every decision about whether to hold or sell is a fight between two clocks. The IRR clock started ticking on the day the equity was wired. Every extra month of holding divides the same gain by a longer period, so IRR decays, even while value keeps rising. The value clock runs the other way. The plan still has levers that haven't been pulled, EBITDA is compounding, and selling now means handing that growth to the next owner.

The mistake juniors make is arguing about which clock "matters more". Deal teams settle it with a single number: the incremental IRR of the extension. That's the annual return on the money you could take off the table today, but choose to leave in. So frame every debate about holding or selling like this: if we sold today, would we reinvest the proceeds in this same asset, at today's price? Because economically, that's exactly what holding is.

§11.2.2The incremental-IRR framework

Here's a worked example. Three years ago, a fund invested £100m of equity. Today, the position is worth £250m, which is 2.5x, an IRR of 2.51/3−1=35.7%2.5^{1/3}-1 = 35.7\%2.51/3−1=35.7%. The value creation plan says that two more years of trading, and one more bolt-on, will take the exit to £320m, which is 3.2x.

Holding looks obviously right, because 3.2x beats 2.5x. But run the marginal maths.

Incremental IRR=(320250)1/2−1=13.1%\text{Incremental IRR} = \left(\frac{320}{250}\right)^{1/2} - 1 = 13.1\%Incremental IRR=(250320​)1/2−1=13.1%

The last two years of this deal earn 13.1% a year on £250m of LPs' capital. The fund underwrites new deals at 20 to 25%. If the team believes in its own pipeline, then the £250m will work harder in the next deal than in this one. Meanwhile, the blended IRR deteriorates.

Sell now (yr 3) Hold (yr 5)
MOIC 2.5x 3.2x
IRR 35.7% 26.2%
Incremental IRR of the extension — 13.1%

Neither answer is automatically correct. A return of 13.1% from low-risk compounding, in an asset you know intimately, can beat 22% of underwritten hope, in an asset you've never met. But the question has to be asked in this form. What looks bad in an investment committee memo? "We're holding because the business is performing." The performance is already in the price. What looks good? Something like: "the extension earns 13%, against our redeployment rate of 22%, but the risk of executing the rest of the plan is minimal, and the exit multiple is easier to defend once the bolt-on is integrated. So we'll hold for 12 more months, not 24."

Deal teams apply one refinement. The future £320m isn't certain, so haircut it for the risk to the plan. With an 80% weight on £320m, and a 20% weight on a stumble to £260m, the expected exit is £308m, and the incremental IRR drops to (308/250)1/2−1=11.0%\left(308/250\right)^{1/2}-1 = 11.0\%(308/250)1/2−1=11.0%. Adjust both sides for certainty before you compare them.

§11.2.3Market windows: the multiple you don't control

Roughly half of a typical exit outcome comes from the multiple, and the multiple is rented from the market, not earned. Sentiment about the sector, the availability of debt, and public comparables move exit multiples by two to four turns across a cycle. That's far more than a year of good trading is worth.

The treadmill maths makes the point. Enter at 12.0x on £20m of EBITDA, and the EV is £240m. Two years later, EBITDA is £26m, up 30%, but the sector has been de-rated to 9.0x. So the EV is £234m, which is lower than at entry, despite 30% growth in EBITDA. With net debt constant at £90m, the equity has gone from £150m to £144m. You can grow into a falling multiple, and stand still.

Here are the practical implications.

  • Sell into strength, rather than at the top. Nobody rings a bell at the peak. A team that waits for the perfect multiple usually sells a year after it. Here's the discipline: when the market pays a multiple that your underwriting never dared to assume, that's the signal.
  • Windows for debt matter as much as windows for equity. The prices for SBOs and recaps are set by what lenders will fund. When the leveraged loan markets are wide open, financial buyers can pay prices at the level of strategic buyers. When credit tightens, the sponsors' bid drops by a turn within months.
  • IPO windows are either open or shut. M&A markets soften, but IPO markets close. It's normal for a dual-track process to lose its IPO leg part-way through, and that's why the M&A leg is never optional.
  • Windows are specific to sectors. A market that's shut for consumer assets can be wide open for software close to infrastructure, in the same quarter.

So what do deal teams actually ask at every portfolio review? If we launched this asset in four months' time, what would it clear at today? Keeping a live, honest answer to that question, with updated comparables, sounding-out conversations with bankers, and a log of inbound interest, is what separates the funds that catch windows from the funds that read about them.

§11.2.4The exit readiness checklist

Buyers pay for what they can verify, and discount what they can't. Preparing for exit is mostly about turning true things into provable things before the process starts. Here's the core checklist.

Item Why buyers care Typical time to fix
Clean financials — audited accounts, fast monthly close, revenue recognition defensible, data room-ready MI Every unresolved question becomes a price chip or an escrow 6–12 months
Locked-in management — CEO/CFO committed through exit and beyond, MIP rollover agreed in principle, no key-person gaps Buyers underwrite the team; a wobbly CFO in management presentations costs a turn 6–12 months
Resolved legal issues — litigation settled or provisioned, tax structure defensible, change-of-control consents mapped, IP assignments complete Open legal items become indemnities, escrows, or Phase 2 questions 3–18 months
Demonstrated run-rate — pricing and cost initiatives visible in delivered monthly P&L, not in an "adjusted" bridge Buyers pay ~1.0x credit for delivered EBITDA vs heavily-discounted credit for pro-forma claims 6+ months of trading

The last row is the one that data teams touch the most. A £3m pricing initiative that went live in January is worth its full value in a September process, because nine months of actual results prove it. The same initiative launched in July is an "adjustment", which buyers will haircut by half, and which quality-of-earnings advisers will attack. That's why preparing for exit starts 12 to 24 months before the launch. The run-rate needs time to become history.

Here's the overarching rule: fix it, or disclose it, but never just hope. Any issue that the seller finds first can be framed, priced and papered. Any issue that the buyer finds first costs double: the issue itself, plus the credibility of everything else in the data room.

§11.2.5Grooming the equity story

The equity story is the two-line answer to the question, "why will the next owner make money?" And it gets engineered, legitimately, in the final 12 to 24 months.

  • Positioning. Reclassify and report the revenue base in the way the target universe of buyers values it: the split between recurring and non-recurring revenue, net revenue retention, and the behaviour of cohorts. A business that's 70% recurring, but has never reported it that way, is leaving a turn of multiple on the table. This is real work for the data team, because the definitions of the KPIs have to survive diligence, not just decorate the CIM.
  • Pruning. Sell or close the loss-making side business now. A division losing £1m inside a company with £20m of EBITDA doesn't reduce the price by £1m. At 10x, it reduces it by £10m, and it muddies the story. A clean perimeter gives a cleaner multiple.
  • Proving the next leg. Buyers pay for a value-creation plan they can believe in. Sign one bolt-on, or have one credibly in the pipeline, to prove the M&A thesis. Land one flagship customer in the new segment, to prove the thesis for expansion. One proof point that's been delivered beats ten slides about the size of the market.
  • Leaving something in the tank. It's counter-intuitive, but essential: the next owner needs some upside of their own. A business that's been squeezed to perfection, with pricing maxed out, costs cut to the bone and capex deferred, offers the buyer nothing to underwrite. And sophisticated buyers price deferred capex and channel stuffing negatively, once they spot them.

So what looks bad, and gets found? Cost cuts that degrade the product, such as slashing support headcount two quarters before the launch. Pulling revenue forward. Capitalising costs that were always expensed before. And "run-rate" adjustments for initiatives that have no history of running. Every one of these is a standard test in quality-of-earnings work. Window dressing doesn't just fail; it contaminates the genuine adjustments sitting next to it.

§11.2.6When selling "too early" is right

"We left money on the table" is the most survivable mistake in private equity. The opposite mistake, riding a winner into a window that's closed, is the one that ends up in the footnotes of the fund's track record. Selling early is right systematically, and more often than it feels, for reasons that are structural, not psychological.

  • You're paid for certainty, not perfection. A 2.8x banked today beats a 60% chance of 3.5x in two years' time, on almost any weighting of risk. And the incremental IRR of that gamble is usually below the fund's bar anyway.
  • The buyer needs the next leg. The best exits happen while the story still has an obvious chapter left, because that chapter is what the buyer underwrites. Sell the future to the buyer, rather than consuming it yourself.
  • The maths of the fund outranks the maths of the deal. A fund in year 7 or 8 that's raising its successor needs DPI, meaning cash distributed, not paper valuations. LPs re-up on DPI. One realised 2.8x does more for the next fundraise than two unrealised valuations at 3.5x. The deal team's instinct to "hold for more" is routinely, and correctly, overridden by the managing partners, for exactly this reason.
  • Concentration risk compounds. A winner that has grown to 25 to 30% of the fund's remaining NAV is no longer a decision about a deal; it's a decision about the portfolio. Taking risk off the fund can justify accepting an incremental IRR on the asset that's below the bar.

Here's the honest test for "too early". Would you buy this business at this price today, with fresh capital and a fresh five-year clock? If the answer is yes, genuinely yes, at this price, then holding may be right. Or a continuation vehicle may be the honest structure, as lesson 4 covers. If you hesitate, you're holding out of attachment, not analysis.

§11.2.7What the IC actually debates

To pull it all together, the section on exit timing in a portfolio review answers five questions, in order.

  1. What is it worth today? That means live comparables, sounding out the bankers, and inbound interest. It should be a real number, not the valuation it's being held at.
  2. What's the incremental IRR of holding? Compare it against the fund's redeployment rate, with both sides adjusted for certainty.
  3. Is the window open? For this asset, in this sector, in today's debt market. And what's the cost of missing it? That's the treadmill maths from above.
  4. Are we ready? Go through the checklist: the financials, management, legal matters and the run-rate. If we're not ready, what's the quickest credible path to being ready, and will the window still be open by then?
  5. What does the fund need? Think about DPI, concentration, and the timing of the next fundraise. The best answer for the asset and the best answer for the fund differ more often than investment committee memos admit. And when they do, the fund wins.

A team that can answer all five questions with numbers is prepared. A team that answers with adjectives is holding by default. And holding by default is a decision too; it's just one that nobody has examined.

Lesson 11.3/Exits

Running the Sell-Side

24 min read
In brief

This lesson sets out the seller's playbook. It covers hiring and paying the bank, vendor due diligence and how buyers read it, writing the CIM, engineering tension in the auction, handling pre-emptive bids, stapled financing, and managing management's conflicts of interest during a sale.

  1. 11.3.1The seller's job is manufacturing competition
  2. 11.3.2Hiring the bank
  3. 11.3.3Vendor due diligence: paying for the buyer's homework
  4. 11.3.4The CIM, written from this side of the table
  5. 11.3.5Engineering auction tension
  6. 11.3.6Pre-emptive bids
  7. 11.3.7Stapled financing
  8. 11.3.8Managing management's conflicts

§11.3.1The seller's job is manufacturing competition

Module 6 walked through an auction from the buyer's side: the CIM lands, the IOI goes in, and the process grinds on. This lesson turns the table around. From the seller's chair, an exit process has one objective: to make several credible buyers believe, all at the same time, that they might lose. Everything in the sell-side playbook, from the bank and the vendor due diligence to the CIM and the design of the process, exists to create and sustain that fear of losing. That's because it's the fear of losing, rather than the output of any spreadsheet, that moves a bid from 9.5x to 11x.

The seller's second objective is nearly as important: certainty that the deal will close. A process that collapses is expensive. Management are exhausted, competitors have read the CIM, staff have heard the rumours, and the asset has been "shopped". Buyers price a shopped asset lower the second time around. So every choice of design below trades a little price for a lot of certainty, or the other way round, and a good sell-side adviser is explicit about which.

§11.3.2Hiring the bank

The process starts with a beauty parade, or pitch process. Three to five banks present their view of the value, the list of buyers, the positioning, and the design of the process. Reading the pitches is an art.

  • The bank pitching the highest valuation is often buying the mandate, and it will walk the number back down after signing. So ask how it gets to the number: which buyers, at which multiples, and anchored to which precedents. A headline of £450m, supported by two named strategic buyers with a logic that makes sense at board level, beats a headline of £500m supported by "momentum in the sector".
  • The list of buyers is the real product. The right bank knows which head of corporate development answers its calls, which sponsor has just raised a fund and needs to deploy it, and which "obvious" buyer is quietly broken on the inside. Coverage of the sector beats the brand.
  • Conflicts have to be brought out into the open. Is the bank also lending to likely bidders, running a competing sell-side process, or angling to offer staple financing, which we'll come to below?

Fees are almost entirely based on success. In the mid-market, they're typically 0.75 to 1.5% of enterprise value, with higher percentages on smaller deals, plus a modest monthly retainer that's usually credited against the success fee. There's a structural problem here. A flat percentage pays the bank for any deal that closes, not for a good one. On a £400m deal, the difference between a great outcome and a mediocre one might be £40m to the seller, but only £0.4m to the bank, while a collapsed process pays the bank almost nothing. So banks are biased towards getting a deal done. The fix is a ratchet, or incentive fee: say, 1.0% up to £380m, plus 3 to 5% of any proceeds above £380m. Now the bank's marginal economics point the same way as the seller's. So what do deal teams actually ask when they review an engagement letter? Where does the ratchet kick in, and who chose that number? Because a ratchet that starts below the expected clearing price is just a disguised increase in the fee.

§11.3.3Vendor due diligence: paying for the buyer's homework

Vendor due diligence, or VDD, turns the normal arrangement upside down. The seller commissions financial due diligence, of the kind a Big 4 firm would do, and often commercial, tax and legal due diligence too, on its own company, and shares the reports with all the bidders. Sellers willingly pay £300k to £1m or more for this, for the following reasons.

  • It controls the narrative. The first quantified view of the quality of earnings that any bidder sees is the seller's. It's professionally prepared, but it frames every judgement call, such as revenue recognition, add-backs and run-rates, the seller's way. And anchoring works.
  • It keeps the auction wide. Six bidders can all stay in the process, without each of them spending £500k on their own advisers at the stage of indicative offers. That means more bidders, for longer, spending less of their own money, which is precisely the tension the seller wants.
  • It compresses the timetable. The bidders' confirmatory work shrinks from months to weeks, and speed means certainty. Fewer weeks in exclusivity means fewer chances for the markets, trading, or nerves to break the deal.
  • It flushes out issues early, on the seller's terms. A £2m problem with revenue recognition, found by your own VDD in month one, gets framed and priced. The same problem, found by the buyer's quality-of-earnings work during exclusivity, costs a price chip plus your credibility.

The winning bidder usually gets reliance on the VDD report. That means the adviser owes them a duty of care, up to a cap, and that's what makes the report more than just marketing.

Here's how buyers read VDD, and over a career your team will sit on both sides. Start with the scope section, not the numbers. What was excluded, what was sampled rather than tested, and what was "confirmed by management" rather than verified, is where the bodies are buried. Read the databook before the prose, because the prose is negotiated, and the databook less so. Treat every judgement call as an opening position, not a finding. When VDD says adjusted EBITDA is £22m, it means the seller's paid adviser could defend £22m. Buyers' quality-of-earnings teams routinely land £1m to £2m lower, on the same facts. And notice what the VDD is conspicuously quiet about. Silence in a report commissioned by the seller is a hint, never an accident.

§11.3.4The CIM, written from this side of the table

The Confidential Information Memorandum is the seller's brief. It runs to 60 to 100 pages, covering the company, the market, the financials and the projections. Here are the rules for writing it that experienced sellers enforce.

  • Everything in the CIM will be diligenced. The CIM is advocacy, but every number in it becomes an item on the checklist for the buyer's advisers. A claim that dies in diligence costs more than it ever earned, because renegotiations anchor on broken claims. Ambitious framing, yes; numbers that can't be supported, never.
  • The adjusted EBITDA bridge is the most-read page. Each add-back should be defensible on its own, with the evidence sitting ready in the data room. One add-back that can't be defended, such as pro-forma synergies from a bolt-on that hasn't been signed, taints the four legitimate ones next to it.
  • Projections should be ambitious, but anchored. The forecast should extend the momentum that's already been delivered, rather than hockey-sticking away from it. Buyers underwrite their own numbers anyway; the forecast in the CIM mostly signals how credible management are. A plan showing 12% growth, after three years of delivering 11%, is believed. A plan showing 25%, after 11%, is discounted, and remembered.
  • Write for the second reader. The first reader is the deal partner, and the second is their investment committee. Give the deal team the slides they need to sell the asset internally, because that's what the CIM is actually for.

§11.3.5Engineering auction tension

Here's a standard two-round process. A teaser and an NDA go to 30 to 80 parties, and those who sign get the CIM. Indicative offers, or IOIs, come in after about four to six weeks. A shortlist of four to six bidders goes into round two, with management presentations, the data room, and access to the VDD. Binding offers, with a marked-up SPA, come in after about six to eight weeks. Then the seller chooses, negotiates and signs. Here are the seller's levers for creating maximum tension.

  • Keep at least three credible bidders into the final round. Two is a negotiation, and one is a hostage situation. Bidders can smell an empty room. Banks work the phones to keep the third and fourth bidders warm. And sensible sellers give losing bidders honest feedback quickly, because the same funds will bid in the seller's next process.
  • Ration information, and the calendar. Set simultaneous deadlines, control the Q&A, and grant access to management in equal, scheduled doses. Unequal access leaks, and leaks kill tension.
  • Never lie about the competition, but never volunteer clarity either. "The process is competitive" must always be technically true. Banks that invent phantom bidders get caught, and their next ten processes suffer for it.
  • Use the SPA as a dimension of the bid. Final bids are ranked on price, and on the mark-up: conditions, caps on warranties, demands for escrow, and financing outs. A bid of £405m with a clean SPA beats £415m with a financing condition and a six-month regulatory tail. So force the bidders to compete on certainty, by scoring it openly.

Here's a worked example of what tension is worth. A process with only one bidder settles at that bidder's walk-away discipline, say 9.5x on £30m of EBITDA, which is £285m. The same asset, with three bidders in the final round, each afraid of losing, clears at 11.0x, which is £330m. That £45m difference is pure process design, on the same asset. And it's why sellers accept the cost, the risk of leaks, and the distraction to management of a full auction.

§11.3.6Pre-emptive bids

A pre-emptive bid is a buyer's attempt to shoot the auction before it starts. It's a strong price, with heavy conditions attached to speed. For example: "£210m, with proof of funds attached, and four weeks of exclusivity starting on Friday, withdrawn if the process launches." The buyer is explicitly paying a premium to avoid having to compete.

So when should a seller take it? Do the maths on expected value, rather than reacting to the headline. Suppose the bank believes that a full auction would clear at £220m, with a 75% chance of closing there. And a failed process means running a shopped asset again a year later, at about £190m. So the expected headline from the auction is:

0.75×£220m+0.25×£190m=£212.5m0.75 \times £220m + 0.25 \times £190m = £212.5m0.75×£220m+0.25×£190m=£212.5m

And that's before counting five extra months of time, the distraction to management, and the risk of leaks. A credible pre-emptive bid at £210m, with 95% certainty and cash in eight weeks, is better than that, on any view adjusted for risk and time. So what makes a pre-emptive bid credible enough to accept? Diligence that's complete, because they've clearly done the work already; committed financing; a short period of exclusivity that expires automatically; and a reputation for closing at the agreed number. What looks bad is a fat headline from a bidder with a history of renegotiating. That isn't a pre-emptive bid. It's a free option on your asset, paid for with your process's momentum.

§11.3.7Stapled financing

Stapled financing, or a "staple", is a pre-arranged debt package that the sell-side bank's leveraged finance desk offers to any winning bidder. The terms are "stapled" to the back of the CIM. For example, 4.5x total leverage, at agreed pricing, available to whoever wins.

Here's why sellers like it. It sets a floor under every sponsor's bid, so no bidder can plead that "we couldn't raise the debt". It levels the playing field between large sponsors, with their captive relationships with lenders, and smaller ones without them. It speeds up the process, because the diligence on financing has already been done. And it signals the bank's own conviction. A bank that refuses to lend against its own sell-side story is telling you something.

The conflict is obvious. The same bank earns an advisory fee from the seller, and financing fees from the buyer. And a bank that's keen to see any deal close on its staple isn't neutral when it advises on which bid to accept. There are standard ways to mitigate this. Bidders are free to bring their own financing; the staple is a floor, not a requirement, and it's usually beaten. The advisory and financing teams sit behind information barriers. And the seller's board sees a comparison of the bids built by the deal team, not by the financing desk. In practice, staples are used most when debt markets are shaky, which is exactly when the floor is worth the most, and the conflict is worth tolerating.

§11.3.8Managing management's conflicts

The most under-managed risk in any sell-side process is that the people presenting the asset have interests that diverge from the seller's. Management will work for the winner. Sponsors know this, and court them, with a generous management incentive plan in the new company, hints about the terms of rollover, and flattery about the next chapter. A trade buyer, by contrast, may be buying synergies, and management's head office is the synergy. So picture a CEO choosing between Sponsor A, offering sweet equity, a bigger platform, and keeping their job, and Strategic B, offering a higher price for the fund, an integration committee, and a probable exit for the CEO. That CEO has every human reason to shine in one management presentation, and go through the motions in the other. A flat performance from the CEO can move a bid by a turn, which is £30m on an asset with £30m of EBITDA, without anyone doing anything visibly wrong.

Here are the standard guardrails.

  • Pay management for the price, not for the buyer. An exit bonus that scales with the proceeds, and the existing MIP itself, which pays out on the same waterfall, point their economics at the seller's outcome, whoever wins.
  • Sequence the conversation about packages. There should be no discussion between management and the bidders about future packages, rollover, or equity in the new company until the seller permits it. That's typically only with the final one or two bidders, with the seller's adviser in the room. Sponsors will push to start earlier. The process letter says no, and breaches get bidders thrown out. And it has to be enforced at least once to be believed.
  • Control the channel. All contact between buyers and management is scheduled and chaperoned by the bank. There are no private dinners, and no side calls. That isn't paranoia; it's hygiene.
  • Diligence your own management first. The seller should know the CEO's view of each bidder, their plans for retirement, and the maths of their MIP, before the buyers do.

So what do deal teams actually ask when a process wobbles? Have management picked a winner? That's the first hypothesis for any unexplained imbalance, such as one bidder's questions getting answered faster, or one management presentation being mysteriously sharper. The fix is rarely punishment; it's realignment. Because by the final round, a motivated management team, selling hard to every remaining bidder, is the single cheapest source of price tension the seller has.
