Lesson 11.4/Exits

Continuation Vehicles and the Secondaries Market

25 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the mechanics of GP-led secondaries, and the machinery for handling their conflicts of interest, meaning the LP advisory committee, fairness opinions, and checks against the market. It also covers LP-led secondaries and NAV lending, compares continuation vehicles holding a single asset with those holding several, explains how an LP should judge the choice a continuation vehicle offers, and sets out what each exit choice signals about the asset.

  1. 11.4.1The secondaries market in one page
  2. 11.4.2Why GP-leds exist
  3. 11.4.3Mechanics of a GP-led CV
  4. 11.4.4The conflict, and the machinery that manages it
  5. 11.4.5LP-led secondaries and NAV lending
  6. 11.4.6Single-asset vs multi-asset CVs
  7. 11.4.7Judging a CV as an LP: sell or roll?
  8. 11.4.8What the exit choice signals

§11.4.1The secondaries market in one page

Private equity's original design flaw is a mismatch in timing. Funds have ten-year lives, but the LPs' needs for liquidity, and the maturity of the assets, follow their own calendars. The secondaries market exists to trade around that mismatch. It has two halves, which share a name, but little else.

  • LP-led secondaries. Here, an LP sells its interests in funds, meaning its stakes in one fund or many, to a secondaries buyer. The GP's role is limited to consenting to the transfer. This is portfolio trading, and the underlying companies never notice.
  • GP-led secondaries. Here, the GP starts a transaction on an asset, or several, in its own fund, overwhelmingly through a continuation vehicle, or CV. This is a route to exit, which is why it gets most of this lesson.

The market has grown from a distressed backwater into core infrastructure, with well over $150bn of volume a year in recent years, roughly half of it GP-led. The buyers are dedicated secondaries funds, and the secondaries arms of the mega-managers. For a deal team, they're now a standing part of the universe of buyers, alongside strategic buyers and sponsors.

§11.4.2Why GP-leds exist

Lesson 1 gave the short version: sometimes the fund has run out of time, but the asset hasn't. Here's the fuller list of legitimate motives.

  • Keeping the winner. The best business in a fund from the 2016 vintage might have five more years of compounding at 20% or more ahead of it. Selling it in year 9, just because a document signed in 2016 says so, destroys value for everyone. The CV moves it into a vehicle with a fresh clock.
  • Fresh capital. The old fund's reserves for follow-on investment have been spent. The CV raises new money for the next acquisition programme, alongside the stake that's rolled over.
  • DPI without saying goodbye. LPs in years 8 and 9 want distributions, which is lesson 2's maths at the level of the fund, while the GP wants to keep the asset. A CV pays cash to the LPs who choose to leave, while the GP carries on managing what it knows best.
  • Crystallising, and resetting, the economics. The carry on the old fund's gain is realised. The GP typically rolls it over, and earns new carry, often tiered, on future performance.

Notice what isn't on the list: "we couldn't sell it". A CV for an asset that failed in an auction is a warehouse for a problem. Secondaries buyers, who see hundreds of these, price it accordingly, or walk away.

§11.4.3Mechanics of a GP-led CV

Here's the standard sequence, which takes four to six months from end to end.

  1. Selecting the asset, and hiring an adviser. The GP mandates a secondaries adviser to structure the deal and run the discovery of the price.
  2. Discovering the price. The adviser runs a competitive process among secondaries buyers, which is effectively a mini-auction, to find a lead investor who sets the price and anchors the new vehicle. This check against the market is the single most important protection in the whole structure. A price set by competing third parties, writing nine-figure cheques, is evidence. A price set by the GP's own valuation of its holding isn't.
  3. Engaging the LP advisory committee. The fund's LP Advisory Committee, or LPAC, reviews the conflict, the process and the terms, and, as the LPA requires, either waives or approves the conflicted transaction. A fairness opinion from an independent adviser is commonly obtained too.
  4. The LPs' election. Every LP in the old fund chooses. They can sell, taking cash at the deal price, or roll, converting into the CV, often on materially similar economics. That second choice is the option that regulators and ILPA's guidance push for, as a "status quo" choice. The standard is an election window of 20 business days or more, with full packs of disclosure.
  5. Closing. The CV, a new fund with the same GP, buys the asset from the old fund. The LPs who sell get cash, and the LPs who roll get interests in the CV. The lead secondaries investor funds the balance, plus fresh capital for follow-on investment. And the GP typically rolls all of its crystallised carry into the CV, and adds a new GP commitment.

The terms of a CV differ from those of a classic fund. Management fees are closer to 1% on invested capital, and carry is tiered. For example, 10% up to 1.5x, 15% up to 2.0x, and 20% above that. So the GP is paid mostly for future performance, rather than for revaluing the past.

§11.4.4The conflict, and the machinery that manages it

Strip the structure away, and the problem is stark: the GP sets the price at which it sells an asset from investors it owes duties to, to other investors it also owes duties to, and its own economics sit on both sides. A low price cheats the old fund's LPs. A high price cheats the CV's investors, including every LP who rolls over. Nobody involved is neutral, least of all the GP, whose carry crystallises at whatever number comes out.

The market's answer is process, built up in layers.

Safeguard What it actually does
Competitive market check Real third-party capital sets the price; the more genuine bidders for the lead role, the better the evidence
LPAC approval The conflict is disclosed and formally waived by LP representatives before the deal proceeds
Fairness opinion Independent adviser opines the price is within a fair range — a floor of protection, not a substitute for competition
Status quo election LPs who do nothing (or roll) keep economics no worse than they had; nobody is forced to sell
GP rolls its carry The GP's crystallised gain goes back in alongside rolling LPs — it eats the price it set
Adequate time and disclosure 20+ business day elections with full information packs; rushed elections are the classic red flag

So what looks bad? LPs are increasingly saying so. An election window of ten days, over a holiday period. A price supported only by a fairness opinion, with no check against the market. A GP taking part of its carry in cash, rather than rolling it over. And any hint that taking part in the CV is linked to access to the GP's next flagship fund. That's a soft staple, and both buyers and regulators watch out for it.

§11.4.5LP-led secondaries and NAV lending

Two neighbouring tools complete the toolkit for liquidity.

LP-led secondaries. An LP sells its stakes in funds at a negotiated percentage of NAV. Interests in buyout funds commonly trade at 85 to 100%, while venture funds, and funds near the end of their lives, trade lower. The sellers are rarely distressed. They're rebalancing, perhaps because of the "denominator effect" after public markets fall; exiting a strategy; or freeing up capital to re-up. Here's a worked example of why buyers like it. Pay 85% of a NAV of £100m, which is £85m, for a mature fund that then distributes £120m over three years. That's 120/85=1.41x120/85 = 1.41x120/85=1.41x, on a portfolio that's short-dated, already diversified, and already has much of its risk removed. The discount, plus the shorter duration, is the whole trade. For a deal team's purposes, activity in LP-led secondaries matters as a signal. Heavy selling by LPs at deep discounts means LPs need cash, and that feeds straight back into how much pressure your own fund is under to deliver DPI.

NAV lending. A NAV facility is a loan to the fund itself, secured against the NAV of the whole portfolio, typically at a conservative loan-to-value of 5 to 20%. The legitimate uses are funding follow-on investments when the fund is fully drawn, and bridging to an exit that's been signed. The controversial use is borrowing in order to pay the LPs a distribution, which is known as "levered DPI". The cash is real, but the exposure hasn't been reduced. The LPs still own the same assets, now with leverage at the level of the fund on top, and interest running at meaningful spreads. Here's a worked example. A fund with a NAV of £500m borrows £50m, a loan-to-value of 10%, and distributes it. DPI ticks up. But if the portfolio takes three more years to exit, the facility might cost £15m in interest, paid out of the LPs' proceeds, just to move a distribution forward, rather than to create one. ILPA's guidance now pushes for disclosure, and for consultation with the LPAC, precisely because a figure for DPI needs a footnote: was this earned through exits, or borrowed against them?

§11.4.6Single-asset vs multi-asset CVs

  • CVs with a single asset are the trophy format: the fund's best company, moved on its own. Secondaries buyers can diligence it like a direct deal, and price it sharply, and the logic of "keeping the winner" is at its cleanest. The cost is concentration. The CV is a fund with one company in it, and its investors underwrite it on that basis. This is where the machinery for handling conflicts matters most: one asset, one price, and nowhere to hide.
  • CVs with several assets move a number of companies, sometimes the entire tail of a fund, into a single vehicle. Diversification makes them easier for some buyers to hold, and they can be an honest way of giving an old fund's stragglers more time. But blending the assets blends the prices too. Strong assets can subsidise weak ones, inside a single headline number. And historically, the format has been used to sweep problems into a vehicle where the fees keep running. So buyers apply discounts at the level of the portfolio, and LPs should read the pricing asset by asset, not just the total.

Here's a rule of thumb that the market itself uses. CVs with a single asset are done from strength. CVs with several assets need to prove that they aren't being done from weakness.

§11.4.7Judging a CV as an LP: sell or roll?

The election lands on an LP's desk, with a few weeks to answer. Here's a disciplined checklist.

  1. How was the price set? A competitive check against the market, with named lead investors, is credible. A fairness opinion on its own is weak. The price compared with the fund's most recent valuation matters too. A CV at, or above, the carrying value is ordinary. One below recent valuations raises the question of why the valuation was where it was.
  2. Is the GP rolling everything over? If it rolls all of its crystallised carry, plus new money of its own, the GP is eating its own price. If it cashes out part of its carry, the GP is telling you about its own appetite for risk, so listen.
  3. What are the new economics? Tiered carry that only rewards future performance, and fees of about 1% on invested capital, are the market standard. A full 20% carry from the reset base means the GP is being paid twice for the same gain.
  4. Do I have the capacity to underwrite the asset? Rolling over is a new investment decision, in a concentrated position. An LP without the resources to diligence a single company is structurally a seller, and that's fine. It describes most LPs.
  5. What does my portfolio need? The same logic of DPI and redeployment that funds apply, from lesson 2, applies to the LP too. It's cash today, at a price checked against the market, versus a concentrated continuation of a known winner.

In practice, most LPs choose to sell, commonly 70 to 90% of them. That's driven as much by their preference for liquidity, and their bandwidth, as by any view on the asset. It isn't a verdict on CVs. It's what the option exists for.

§11.4.8What the exit choice signals

Let's finish where lesson 1 started. The route chosen is information in itself, and buyers, LPs, and the diligence teams of the next fund all read it.

  • A trade sale is the strongest external validation. An informed player in the industry paid a premium for synergies, which says that the asset matters strategically.
  • A secondary buyout means that a sophisticated financial buyer underwrote the next five years, at a full price. It's healthy and ordinary, and it says that the value-creation story has another chapter, which somebody else believes in.
  • An IPO means the public markets validated the scale and the growth. But the fund still owns most of its position, so its conviction is being expressed with risk that it has kept.
  • A continuation vehicle should be read with the checklist above. Done well, with a competitive price, the GP rolling everything over, and the LPs choosing freely, it signals the GP's highest conviction: it had a market price, and chose to stay invested. Done badly, it signals the opposite: an asset that couldn't clear a real process, warehoused at a negotiated valuation.
  • A dividend recap without a sale, when it's repeated, means cash is being manufactured from leverage, rather than realised from buyers. That's fine once, in a strong business, but it's a pattern worth questioning the second time.

So what do deal teams actually ask when they see any exit announced in their sector? Who bought it, who set the price, and what did the seller keep? Those three answers, more than the headline multiple, tell you what the people with the most information really believed. That habit of reading exits as evidence, rather than just as outcomes, is the skill this module has been building, and it's exactly the judgement that the case study now asks you to exercise.

Lesson 12.1/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

What Deal Teams Watch and Why: The Monthly KPI Stack

25 min read
In brief

This lesson covers the monthly stack of KPIs that deal teams actually track: trading against budget, headroom on liquidity and covenants, and leading indicators. It explains why variance against the thesis matters more than variance against the budget, and sets out the ladder of escalation that kicks in when the numbers slip.

  1. 12.1.1The thesis is a forecast — monitoring is how you test it
  2. 12.1.2The trading block: revenue and EBITDA versus budget
  3. 12.1.3The cash block: liquidity headroom and covenant headroom
  4. 12.1.4Leading indicators: the numbers that move before the P&L
  5. 12.1.5Variance-to-budget versus variance-to-thesis
  6. 12.1.6The escalation ladder: what happens when numbers slip
  7. 12.1.7Why this is your job

§12.1.1The thesis is a forecast — monitoring is how you test it

Every deal in the portfolio was bought on a thesis. That's a specific, numerical story about how X pounds of equity becomes two and a half times X in five years. For example: "grow revenue by 12% a year, expand the EBITDA margin from 18% to 22%, deleverage from 4.5× to 2.0×, and exit at the entry multiple." The investment committee approved that story, and the fund wired the money. From completion day onwards, the thesis stops being a plan, and becomes a hypothesis under continuous test.

Portfolio monitoring is that test. Every month, each portfolio company sends numbers up to the fund, and the deal team's job is to answer one question: is the thesis still on track, and if not, how early can we know, and how quickly can we act? A five-year hold is short. A company that drifts for 18 months before anyone reacts has burned through a third of the holding period. And because IRR is weighted by time, delay is expensive, even when the problem is eventually fixed.

If you work in a PE data team, the monthly cycle of monitoring is probably where you spend most of your time. This lesson is about what the deal teams using your output are actually looking for, so that you can build reports that answer their questions, rather than just displaying data.

§12.1.2The trading block: revenue and EBITDA versus budget

At the top of every monthly pack is the summary of trading. It shows actuals against budget and against the previous year, for the month and for the year to date. Here's a typical extract.

£m, YTD June Actual Budget Var Prior year Var
Revenue 24.0 22.5 +1.5 20.9 +3.1
Gross profit 14.4 14.4 0.0 13.6 +0.8
Gross margin 60.0% 64.0% −4.0pts 65.1% −5.1pts
EBITDA 4.8 4.9 −0.1 4.7 +0.1
EBITDA margin 20.0% 21.8% −1.8pts 22.5% −2.5pts

Read that table the way a deal team would. Revenue is 6.7% ahead of budget, which is a good headline. But gross profit is exactly on budget, despite £1.5m more revenue. That means every extra pound of sales came in at a gross margin of roughly zero, or, more likely, that the whole book is being discounted. And EBITDA is flat, against a budget that assumed growth. The company is running harder just to stand still.

So what looks good? Revenue and EBITDA both ahead, margins stable or expanding, and the beat explained by volume or price in the segments the thesis said would grow. And what looks bad? A beat on revenue with a miss on margin, which means growth is being bought. Or a "beat" on EBITDA driven by deferring costs, such as cutting marketing, freezing hiring, or pushing maintenance back, which is borrowing from next year's P&L. And what do deal teams ask? "What's driving the fading gross margin? Is it mix, price, or cost inflation that we haven't passed on? Show me the split between price, volume and mix."

§12.1.3The cash block: liquidity headroom and covenant headroom

EBITDA is an opinion, but cash is a fact. That's a line you met in quality of earnings, and it runs the whole way through monitoring. Two numbers matter every month.

Liquidity headroom is cash, plus undrawn committed facilities, usually the revolving credit facility, less any minimum operating cash that the business needs. A company with £3.4m of cash and an undrawn RCF of £2.5m has £5.9m of liquidity. Whether that's comfortable depends on the monthly profile of the cash. A business with a £2m swing in working capital within each month, and a quarterly interest payment of £1.2m, has far less real headroom than the headline suggests. Deal teams want a rolling 13-week cash forecast whenever headroom gets thin, because insolvency is an event about cash, not about the P&L.

Covenant headroom measures how far the business is from the tests in the credit agreement. Module 8 covered how covenants are set; here, you live with them. The workhorse is the net leverage covenant, tested every quarter on EBITDA for the last twelve months, or LTM.

Net leverage=Gross debt−CashLTM EBITDA\text{Net leverage} = \frac{\text{Gross debt} - \text{Cash}}{\text{LTM EBITDA}}Net leverage=LTM EBITDAGross debt−Cash​

Here's a worked example. Gross debt is £42.0m, cash is £3.4m, LTM EBITDA is £9.7m, and the covenant says leverage must be no more than 4.25×.

  • The current leverage is (42.0−3.4)/9.7=38.6/9.7=3.98×(42.0 - 3.4) / 9.7 = 38.6 / 9.7 = 3.98×(42.0−3.4)/9.7=38.6/9.7=3.98×
  • The minimum EBITDA before a breach, holding the debt constant, is 38.6/4.25=£9.1m38.6 / 4.25 = £9.1m38.6/4.25=£9.1m
  • So the EBITDA headroom is 9.7−9.1=£0.6m9.7 - 9.1 = £0.6m9.7−9.1=£0.6m, which is about 6%.

Six per cent of EBITDA headroom is thin. Lose one customer, or have one bad quarter rolling into the LTM figure, and the company is negotiating a waiver. Notice the double jeopardy in the formula. If the company burns cash, net debt rises at the same time as weaker EBITDA cuts the denominator, so the ratio deteriorates from both ends. That's why deal teams track covenant headroom as a monthly line, even though the test is only quarterly. They want to see a breach coming two quarters ahead, while there's still time to fix it cheaply.

So what do deal teams ask? "What does the covenant look like at the next two test dates, on the current run-rate, and what would have to go wrong for us to breach it?"

§12.1.4Leading indicators: the numbers that move before the P&L

Revenue and EBITDA are lagging indicators. By the time they slip, the damage was done months ago. The best monthly packs give equal weight to the numbers that predict the P&L.

  • The pipeline, and pipeline coverage. That's the qualified pipeline, divided by the target for new business in the next period. Coverage of three to four times is a common rule of thumb for B2B sales. Coverage falling from 3.5× to 2.1× tells you, in the second quarter, that fourth-quarter revenue is at risk, while you can still do something about it.
  • Order intake, and book-to-bill. For industrials, that's orders divided by the revenue in the period. Below 1.0× for two quarters in a row means the backlog is being eaten up.
  • Churn and retention. For subscription businesses, that means gross revenue churn, churn of customers, and net revenue retention, or NRR. Gross churn moving from 8% to 14% a year is a flashing red light, even while reported revenue is still growing, because new bookings are temporarily masking the leak.
  • Canaries in working capital. Days sales outstanding, or DSO, creeping up from 52 days to 68 can mean that discipline on collections is slipping. Or it can mean that sales are being "bought" with extended payment terms. Or, worse, that disputed invoices are piling up because the quality of delivery has fallen.
  • People. That means regretted attrition, how long roles have been open, and sales headcount compared with plan. A growth thesis with an understaffed sales team is a fantasy with a spreadsheet attached.

The specific set of indicators varies by sector, following the same logic as the lens of unit economics from Module 3. But the design principle doesn't change: every driver of the thesis needs at least one indicator that moves a quarter or more before the P&L does.

§12.1.5Variance-to-budget versus variance-to-thesis

Here's the subtlety that separates good monitoring from box-ticking. Budgets are set every year by management, and management has learned to sandbag. A budget you beat by 5% every year is an artefact of negotiation, not a forecast. The benchmark that really matters is the deal model, the underwriting case the investment committee approved, because the fund's returns are tied to it.

Here's a worked example. The deal model said revenue of £52m in Year 2, and EBITDA of £12.5m, which is a 24% margin. Management's budget for Year 2, set after a soft Year 1, says £46m and £9.7m. The actuals come in at £47.5m of revenue, and £10.0m of EBITDA.

£m Actual vs budget vs deal model
Revenue 47.5 +1.5 (+3.3%) −4.5 (−8.7%)
EBITDA 10.0 +0.3 (+3.1%) −2.5 (−20.0%)

The board pack's narrative writes itself as a success: ahead of budget on both lines. But against the thesis, EBITDA is 20% adrift. If that gap lasts until exit, at the model's multiple of 10×, that's £25m of enterprise value gone, which is probably most of the planned upside in the equity, once leverage magnifies it, following the maths of Module 7. A monitoring system that only shows variance against budget will report green for two years, while the deal quietly dies. Good deal teams, and good data teams, keep the underwriting case in the reporting stack permanently, and show both variances side by side. The budget tells you how management is performing against its own promises. The deal model tells you whether the fund is going to make its returns.

So what do deal teams ask? "Are we behind plan, or behind the plan we paid for?"

§12.1.6The escalation ladder: what happens when numbers slip

Monitoring only matters if it triggers action. Most firms run a ladder of escalation, either explicitly or implicitly. It's worth knowing where a company sits on that ladder, because the demands for information on the portfolio company, and on the data team, escalate along with it.

  1. Green means routine. There's a monthly pack and a quarterly board meeting, and the thesis is on track. The deal team spends a few hours a month on it.
  2. Amber means the watch list. A driver of the thesis has slipped, with two soft quarters, leading indicators deteriorating, or covenant headroom below about 15%. Reporting steps up. There are weekly flash numbers on the KPI that's causing concern, a named plan for remediation with milestones, and the deal partner talking to the CEO between board meetings. The fund's own valuation of the asset may be nudged down.
  3. Red means intervention. The thesis is broken, or cash is at risk. Now the toolkit gets heavy. There's 13-week cash forecasting, and a change of management, statistically starting with the CFO. Operating partners or advisers are deployed, board meetings become monthly, and a dialogue with the lenders is opened before the covenant test is failed. Waivers are cheapest when they're asked for early, and most expensive when the lender finds out from the compliance certificate.
  4. Workout. This is the territory of restructuring: a reset of the covenants, or an equity cure, new money, and possibly handing over the equity in exchange for the debt. The goal shifts from maximising the return to protecting whatever equity value is left.

The whole point of the KPI stack is to catch problems at amber, where the fixes are operational, rather than at red, where they're financial, and dilute the equity. An equity cure, where the sponsor injects cash to cure a covenant breach mathematically, costs the fund real money. Noticing DSO creeping up six months earlier costs a phone call.

§12.1.7Why this is your job

Everything above lands on a data team's desk as a build request, sooner or later: the variance pack, the covenant bridge, the dashboard of leading indicators, and the overlay of the underwriting case. The teams that add the most value don't wait for the request. They know that a beat on revenue with flat gross profit is a story about discounting, that DSO and churn are the canaries, and that covenant headroom needs a view forwards, not a snapshot in the rear-view mirror. And they raise the question before the deal team asks it. The rest of this module builds that capability layer by layer. Lesson 2 covers the infrastructure that gets the data in. Lesson 3 covers the valuation and LP reporting it feeds. Lesson 4 covers the performance analytics on top. And lesson 5 covers where data work genuinely changes the outcomes of deals.

Lesson 12.2/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

Portfolio Monitoring Infrastructure: How the Numbers Actually Flow

25 min read
In brief

This lesson follows the pipeline that moves numbers from the finance teams of portfolio companies to the partners' screens. It covers the data quality problems that are endemic in portfolio companies, and the way the definitions of KPIs drift. And it explains why standardisation is hard, and valuable, and exactly where a data team earns its keep.

  1. 12.2.1The pipeline: five hops from ledger to partner
  2. 12.2.2Why portco data is messy: the endemic problems
  3. 12.2.3KPI definition drift: same word, different formula
  4. 12.2.4Why standardisation is hard — and valuable
  5. 12.2.5Where the data team adds leverage
  6. 12.2.6Worked example: one number, end to end

§12.2.1The pipeline: five hops from ledger to partner

Lesson 1 covered what deal teams want to see. This lesson is about how those numbers reach them. The gap between "the portfolio company knows its revenue" and "the partner can see it" is where most of the effort in monitoring goes, and where most monitoring failures happen.

The standard pipeline has five hops.

  1. First, the portfolio company's finance team closes its books, usually to a timetable measured in working days, such as a "WD5 close", meaning five working days after the month end. It produces management accounts in whatever system it runs.
  2. Second, a reporting template, typically an Excel workbook or a web form that the fund issued at completion, is filled in by the portfolio company's finance team. It covers the P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, KPIs, the calculations for the covenants, and a section of commentary from management.
  3. Third, fund operations, or the data team, receives the templates from every portfolio company. It checks them, chases whatever's late or broken, and loads them into whatever the firm uses as a central store, which might be anything from a consolidation spreadsheet to a proper data warehouse.
  4. Fourth, dashboards and packs are built from the central store. There's a monthly pack for each company for the deal team, a summary across the portfolio for the partnership, flags on covenants and liquidity, and the quarterly inputs to valuation and LP reporting, which Lesson 3 covers.
  5. Fifth, the partners and deal teams use the output, and fire questions back down the pipe. That's how you know it's being read.

A portfolio of ten companies reporting every month means 120 template submissions a year, each with hundreds of line items. At a firm with thirty portfolio companies, the monitoring pipeline is an industrial process, and it's usually run by a team of two to four people. That ratio, thousands of data points per person every month, is why automation and validation aren't luxuries.

The timetable matters too. Here's a typical cycle. Portfolio companies close by working day 5, and the templates are due by working days 8 to 10. The data team validates them and chases by working day 12, and the packs go out by working day 15. The deal team reviews them in week three, and the board meetings happen in week four. Anything that slips at the top slips everything below it. One of the most useful metrics a data team can publish is simply the rate of submissions that are on time, and right first time, for each company. Late reporting that's full of errors is itself a leading indicator of a finance function in trouble.

§12.2.2Why portco data is messy: the endemic problems

Portfolio companies aren't FTSE 100 finance functions. A business with £60m of revenue typically has a finance team of four to eight people, one mid-market ERP system, or three after some acquisitions, and a finance director who inherited the chart of accounts from a predecessor. Problems with data quality aren't occasional; they're structural.

  • Restatements without any flag. March's pack shows revenue for the year to February of £8.4m, but the February pack said £8.6m. Someone reclassified a rebate, and nobody mentioned it. Your stored history is now silently wrong, unless you detect the change.
  • Late and partial submissions. The commentary tab is filled in, but the cash flow isn't. And the KPI tab says "to be confirmed" for churn, for the third month running.
  • Fragile spreadsheets. Templates come back with inserted rows, broken formulas, hard-coded overrides where there used to be links, or last month's file resubmitted with a new filename. If your loader assumes that cell B14 is EBITDA, one inserted row corrupts the whole load.
  • Churn in the chart of accounts. A new CFO re-maps the cost lines. "Distribution costs" moves from cost of sales into overheads, and gross margin jumps 3 points, with no change in trading at all.
  • Changes in the perimeter. A bolt-on acquisition, as in Module 10, joins part-way through the year. Is it in the budget? Is it in the comparative for the previous year? Organic growth and reported growth now differ, and if the pack doesn't split them, every variance is ambiguous.
  • Non-financial KPIs of unknown origin. Finance owns the P&L, but churn comes from the CRM, the pipeline from the sales director's own tracker, and headcount from HR. Each has an owner, a lag in being refreshed, and its own idea of what "as at" dates mean.

None of this is malice, and only occasionally is it manipulation. Mostly, it's small teams doing their best under time pressure. But the consequence is the same: numbers that reach the fund without being validated are numbers the fund will eventually be embarrassed by, whether in an investment committee paper, an LP report, or a covenant certificate.

So what looks good? A portfolio company that submits on time, flags restatements without being asked, and reconciles its KPI tab to its source systems. And what looks bad? Persistent lateness, KPIs marked "to be confirmed", or management accounts that don't tie to the audited statutory accounts at the year end. Deal teams treat the quality of reporting as a proxy for the quality of management, and with good reason.

§12.2.3KPI definition drift: same word, different formula

The deepest problem with data quality isn't errors; it's definitions. Across a portfolio, the same name for a KPI routinely hides different formulas. Here's a concrete example: three portfolio companies all report "gross churn of 2% for the quarter".

Portco A Portco B Portco C
Basis Logo count Revenue (MRR) Revenue (ARR)
Numerator Customers lost Churned MRR only Churned + downgraded ARR
Denominator Opening customers Opening MRR Average ARR in quarter
Timing Cancellation notice date Service end date Renewal date

All three cells say "2%", but they aren't comparable. Portfolio company A lost 4 of its 200 customers. But if those 4 were worth £1.6m out of £16m of ARR, then its churn by revenue is 10%, five times what the pack implies. And because Portfolio company C includes downgrades, it looks worse than B, on identical trading. If you rank these companies on a dashboard, you're ranking their formulas, not their retention.

The same drift infects the financial lines. "EBITDA" is the worst offender. One company reports before IFRS 16, with rent as a cost, and another after IFRS 16, with rent as depreciation and interest, so its EBITDA is higher by the whole rent bill. One includes the management fee paid to the sponsor as a cost, and another adds it back. And exceptional items are self-declared. Two portfolio companies with identical economics can report EBITDA margins 4 points apart. "Net debt" drifts depending on whether lease liabilities, earn-out obligations and shareholder loans count. "Organic growth" drifts depending on how many months an acquisition has to be owned before it counts as organic. Even "revenue" drifts, in businesses with questions about whether they're acting as a principal or an agent, as in Module 1.

So why does drift happen? Because each definition was rational in its local context. It matched the company's old board pack, its credit agreement, or its previous owner's habits. Nobody chose to be inconsistent. It built up, deal by deal, with each template negotiated at closing, under time pressure, by a deal team focused on getting the deal done, rather than on comparability across the portfolio.

§12.2.4Why standardisation is hard — and valuable

Standardisation sounds like a memo: "from next quarter, everyone will report churn on the ARR basis." In practice it's a negotiation, and it's worth understanding the resistance.

  • Genuine differences. A software company and a distribution company shouldn't report identical KPIs. Standardisation means a common core, covering the P&L, cash, net debt, headcount and a defined EBITDA, plus sets of KPIs specific to each sector. It doesn't mean one template to rule them all.
  • Credit agreements pin down definitions. Covenant EBITDA is defined in the loan documents, and it can't be "standardised" away. The fix is to report both the covenant EBITDA and the fund's own basis for EBITDA, with an explicit bridge between them.
  • Management's time is finite. Every extra field in the report competes with running the business, and CFOs push back, often rightly. The template that gets filled in accurately is the one that's no longer than it needs to be.
  • History has to be restated. Changing a definition breaks the trend lines, unless someone rebuilds the historical series on the new basis. That's real work, and it belongs to the data team.

Against that cost, here's the value. There's comparability, meaning you can see which portfolio company's churn problem is real. There's aggregation, meaning revenue, EBITDA, net debt and covenant status across the portfolio that the CFO and the IR team can trust. There's speed, because validated data loads straight through, instead of taking a month of manual tidying. And there's institutional memory, so that when the deal team asks "what did DSO do in the last downturn?", the answer exists. Firms increasingly pitch exactly this to LPs, as evidence of a professionalised platform.

So what do deal teams ask? "Is that churn number on our standard basis, or theirs?" And if the answer is a shrug, the dashboard has already lost the room.

§12.2.5Where the data team adds leverage

Pull the threads together, and the data team's most valuable contributions are concrete.

  1. A dictionary of KPIs. One page per metric, covering its name, formula, source system, owner, basis of reporting, and any known exceptions for each company. It's agreed with each portfolio company when it joins. The first 100 days, from Module 10, are the moment of maximum leverage for setting expectations about reporting, because everything's being renegotiated anyway.
  2. Validation at the point of loading. Automated checks run before any number enters the store. Does the balance sheet balance? Does the movement in cash tie to the cash flow? Does the year to date this month equal the year to date last month, plus the month? Is any figure more than 20% off trend, without any commentary? With those checks in place, a restatement triggers a flag, rather than silently overwriting the history.
  3. A versioned central store. Every submission is kept as it was submitted, and every restatement is tracked. That way, "what did we believe about June, as of July?" can be answered. That matters enormously when a number that went into an LP report later changes.
  4. An overlay of the underwriting case. Load each deal's investment committee model into the same store, so that variance against the thesis, from Lesson 1, becomes a standing column, rather than a one-off analysis.
  5. Outputs that put exceptions first. Partners don't read 30 packs. They read a one-page report of exceptions: covenant headroom below the threshold, EBITDA more than 10% behind the thesis, trends in DSO breaching their limits, and late submissions. The dashboard's job is triage.

Notice what isn't on the list: exotic modelling. The compounding value in monitoring infrastructure comes from boring things, done relentlessly: definitions, validation, lineage and timeliness. Lesson 5 covers where genuine data science lands, and it lands on top of this foundation, or not at all.

§12.2.6Worked example: one number, end to end

Let's trace a single figure, to see the whole system at work. Portfolio company Kestrel's July template arrives on working day 9, showing revenue for the year to date of £14.2m. Validation flags two issues. First, June's stored year-to-date figure was £12.4m, which implies July revenue of £1.8m, against a trend of £2.1m. Second, the KPI tab says "invoiced revenue" is £15.0m. The chasing email goes out on working day 10. Here's the answer. A credit note of £0.3m was issued against a disputed invoice from the second quarter, so June is restated to £12.1m. And the £0.8m gap to invoiced revenue is deferred income on annual licences. That's fine. But the credit note relates to the same customer whose receivable has been outstanding for 95 days.

The data team logs the restatement, updates the store with its lineage, and adds one line to the report of exceptions: "Kestrel: £0.3m credit note against a disputed invoice from Q2; the same customer is 95 days overdue on a further £0.4m, which raises a question about collectability." The deal team walks into the board meeting asking about a specific customer dispute, rather than discovering it in the fourth quarter, when the receivable gets written off. That's the difference between a data team that forwards spreadsheets, and one that produces intelligence. And no part of it needed anything fancier than validation rules and a suspicious mind.

Lesson 12.3/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

Valuation and Fund Reporting: Marks, NAV, and What LPs See

25 min read
In brief

This lesson explains how sponsors value their unrealised holdings every quarter, using valuation based on multiples, with calibration under the IPEV guidelines. It covers what NAV is and who uses it, how reporting to LPs at the level of the fund works, including DPI and TVPI and capital account statements, and why the valuations are smoothed.

  1. 12.3.1From monitoring to marks
  2. 12.3.2The workhorse: a multiples-based mark
  3. 12.3.3NAV: one number, many consumers
  4. 12.3.4What LPs receive each quarter
  5. 12.3.5Why marks are smoothed — and how to read them
  6. 12.3.6Where the data team sits in all this

§12.3.1From monitoring to marks

Everything that the monitoring pipeline collects has a second life. Once a quarter, the same figures for EBITDA and net debt that fed the board pack feed a different machine. That machine produces the valuation of every unrealised holding, the fund's Net Asset Value, and the quarterly report to the LPs. If you work in a PE data team, the end of the quarter is when your numbers stop being internal management information, and become the basis of what investors are told their stake is worth. The tolerance for error drops to zero. That's because these numbers are audited, they appear in the LPs' own accounts, and they underpin the track record that the firm will raise its next fund on.

Public equities are priced by the market every second. But a private company owned by a fund has no price, so the sponsor has to estimate its fair value. That's the price that would be received in an orderly transaction between market participants at the date of measurement. The phrase comes from the accounting standards, IFRS 13 and ASC 820. The practical playbook for applying it to private companies is the IPEV guidelines, which stands for the International Private Equity and Venture Capital Valuation guidelines. They're the industry's shared rulebook. IPEV doesn't prescribe a single method. Instead, it requires the valuer to choose appropriate techniques, use them consistently, and, crucially, calibrate them to the price that was actually paid at entry.

§12.3.2The workhorse: a multiples-based mark

For a cash-generative buyout asset, the standard technique is exactly the method of comparable multiples from Module 4, applied every quarter.

Equity fair value=Maintainable EBITDA×Multiple−Net debt (adjusted)\text{Equity fair value} = \text{Maintainable EBITDA} \times \text{Multiple} - \text{Net debt (adjusted)}Equity fair value=Maintainable EBITDA×Multiple−Net debt (adjusted)

Here's a worked example. Fund III bought Osprey Group in January 2024.

  • At entry, the EV was £90m, on LTM EBITDA of £10.0m, which is an entry multiple of 9.0×. It was funded with £54m of net debt and £36m of equity.
  • At entry, the chosen basket of listed comparables traded at 10.0×. So Osprey was bought at a 10% discount to the comparables, for size, for liquidity, and for the usual arguments about private companies from Module 4.

Now it's the second quarter of 2026. LTM EBITDA is £12.0m, net debt has fallen to £38m, and the basket of comparables trades at 9.5×.

Calibration is the discipline that turns this into a valuation you can defend. At entry, the model, with comparables at 10.0×, and the actual price, at 9.0×, differed by 10%. Unless something has changed about Osprey's relative quality, that 10% discount should persist. So:

  • The calibrated multiple is 9.5××0.90=8.55×9.5\times \times 0.90 = 8.55\times9.5××0.90=8.55×, so say 8.5×.
  • The enterprise value is 12.0×8.5=£102m12.0 \times 8.5 = £102m12.0×8.5=£102m
  • The fair value of the equity is 102−38=£64m102 - 38 = £64m102−38=£64m
  • The valuation compared with cost is 64/36=1.78×64 / 36 = 1.78\times64/36=1.78×. So it's carried at a MOIC of 1.8×, unrealised.

Notice what moved the valuation. Two thirds of the gain came from EBITDA growth and paying down debt, which are facts from the monitoring pipeline, and the multiple actually fell. A valuation that went up purely because the valuer nudged the multiple upwards would attract very different scrutiny from the auditors and the LPs. There are common adjustments layered on top. The valuer uses maintainable EBITDA rather than raw LTM EBITDA, stripping out the one-offs, which is the quality-of-earnings mindset from Module 9 again. They deduct the costs of a transaction or an exit. And they reflect the structure. If the sponsor holds preferred instruments, as in Module 8, the equity value has to be run through the waterfall before it becomes the fund's share.

There are other techniques that IPEV sanctions. There's DCF, usually as a cross-check, and the price of a recent transaction; the entry price itself is the best evidence of fair value for the first few quarters. There are metrics specific to particular industries, and approaches based on NAV for businesses heavy in assets. A recent funding round, or a credible offer, for the asset beats any model. But for mainstream buyouts, calibrated multiples do the work.

§12.3.3NAV: one number, many consumers

Add up the fair values of every holding, add the cash at the level of the fund, and subtract the fund's liabilities, and you have the fund's NAV. It's a number that a surprising range of people rely on.

  • LPs book their share of NAV in their own accounts. A pension fund's asset allocation, and its own funding ratio, move with your valuations.
  • Auditors test the valuations every year. Valuation is almost always the key matter in a fund's audit.
  • The secondaries market prices LPs' stakes as a percentage of NAV, as in "a bid at 92% of NAV". If the valuations are stale, secondary pricing is where the market says so, out loud.
  • The next fundraise. Fund III's interim performance is mostly unrealised valuations, the RVPI component that we'll meet below. LPs diligence the valuations of the current portfolio hard when they're deciding on Fund IV. That includes comparing the uplift from entry to the current valuation of each asset with what those assets eventually exit at, which is called analysis of "valuation accuracy".
  • The GP itself. NAV drives the accruals of carry in the waterfall model, it drives any fund financing facility based on NAV, and, increasingly, it drives conversations about pay. The incentive to value generously is obvious, and that's exactly why process, calibration and audit exist.

§12.3.4What LPs receive each quarter

The quarterly package for LPs is the fund's shop window, and the data team usually builds large parts of it.

  1. The capital account statement is each LP's ledger. It shows the capital committed, the capital called to date, the distributions received, their share of NAV, and the movement in the period. This is the document that an LP's back office actually reconciles.
  2. Metrics at the level of the fund. These are the measures from Module 5, updated. DPI is distributions divided by called capital, which is the cash actually returned. RVPI is the remaining NAV divided by called capital, which is the unrealised valuations. TVPI equals DPI plus RVPI. And there's the net IRR. Here's a worked example. A fund with £400m committed has called £280m, distributed £140m, and holds a NAV of £250m. So DPI is 140 divided by 280, which is 0.50×. RVPI is 250 divided by 280, which is 0.89×. And TVPI is 390 divided by 280, which is 1.39×. An LP reads that as: on paper it's 1.4×, but only half my capital has come back, and the rest is valuations.
  3. Pages for each portfolio company. There's one page for each holding, showing its cost, its valuation, its MOIC, the ownership stake, a summary of trading, meaning revenue and EBITDA, on an LTM basis and against the previous year, its leverage, and a paragraph of commentary. This is monitoring data, redacted and polished.
  4. The quarterly letter. And for larger LPs, there's reporting on fees, expenses and carry using ILPA's template, plus a growing stack of special requests from side letters: ESG data, cuts of exposure by geography and sector, and splits by currency. Every bespoke request lands on the data team. That's why firms increasingly push LP reporting onto the same central store as monitoring: one source, with many views.

So what looks good to an LP? DPI growing steadily in the middle of the fund's life, valuations that exits later confirm, since "exited at or above the last valuation" is a talking point for any track record, and clean, punctual reporting. And what looks bad? TVPI built entirely on RVPI deep into a fund's life, meaning everything's been written up, and nothing's been sold. Valuations that fall precisely when an asset goes to market. And capital accounts that get restated.

§12.3.5Why marks are smoothed — and how to read them

Compare a PE fund's quarterly valuations with an index of listed small caps, and you'll see that the fund's line is far smoother. In 2022, public software comparables fell by 30 to 50%, but typical sponsors' valuations of software assets fell by a fraction of that. Four mechanisms produce this smoothing.

  • Calibration, and discretion. The valuer chooses the basket of comparables, the maintainable EBITDA, and how much of a public de-rating to pass through. They can also argue that the discount at entry has narrowed. Each choice can be defended on its own, but together they damp down the volatility, overwhelmingly in the downward direction.
  • Fundamentals that offset each other. If EBITDA grew by 15%, while the comparables were de-rated by 15%, then the valuation is genuinely flat. Private valuations mix price and performance into a single number.
  • Lag. First-quarter valuations are finalised weeks after the end of the quarter, often anchored on LTM figures that are three months old. So a fall in the market in March may not fully land until the June valuations.
  • Step-ups driven by events. Many sponsors hold assets at close to cost until an event justifies a step-up, such as a strong audited year, a refinancing, or a partial sale. So value arrives in a staircase, rather than a wiggle.

Here's what that means for interpretation, which is the layer of judgement.

  • Don't read quarterly moves in NAV as market prices. A flat valuation, against comparables down 25%, isn't evidence that PE assets are immune. It's a modelling choice, plus a lag. The informative check is on the assumptions. Did EBITDA actually grow? What multiple is implied, and how does it compare with the comparables, and with the entry multiple?
  • Smoothed valuations flatter the metrics of risk. The reported volatility and correlation of PE returns are artificially low, which flatters Sharpe ratios and models of asset allocation. LPs know this; "volatility laundering" is the sceptic's phrase for it. The sophisticated ones remove the smoothing from the series before they use it.
  • The truth arrives at exit. DPI is the audit of RVPI. Over a fund's life, the valuations and reality have to converge. That's why comparing exits against the last valuation is one of the most informative analyses a data team can maintain, as Lesson 4 explains.
  • Losing trust is expensive. A sponsor that values aggressively, and then exits below its valuations, poisons its next fundraise. So most sponsors value conservatively, but smoothly, and the typical pattern is exits that come in modestly above the final valuations.

§12.3.6Where the data team sits in all this

Valuation at the end of the quarter is a process with hard deadlines and audit trails, and it runs on monitoring data. Here are the data team's points of leverage. Make sure the LTM EBITDA and net debt that the valuation team uses reconcile exactly to the monitoring store, because the auditors will trace them. Maintain the sets of comparables, and pull the trading multiples at the end of the quarter in a reproducible way. Keep the history of calibration for each asset, meaning the entry multiple against the comparables at entry, and every quarter since; that's a table both auditors and LPs love. Automate the calculations for the capital accounts and the fund metrics, so that DPI and TVPI are generated, rather than built by hand. And build the backtest of valuation accuracy, comparing, for every exit, the final valuation with the proceeds actually realised. None of it's glamorous, but all of it compounds. In fund reporting, the firm's product is credibility, and credibility is a property of data quality.

Lesson 12.4/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

The Value Bridge and Performance Analytics

25 min read
In brief

This lesson shows how to build a value bridge for a portfolio company, with a worked example, and how to attribute returns across the deals in a fund. It covers loss ratios and analysis of concentration, what tracking the underwriting against actual results teaches a firm, and the benchmarking datasets that a data team can build.

  1. 12.4.1Why attribution is the firm's mirror
  2. 12.4.2The portfolio-company value bridge: worked example
  3. 12.4.3Fund-level attribution: which deals made the fund
  4. 12.4.4Loss ratios and concentration
  5. 12.4.5Underwriting versus actual: the institutional learning loop
  6. 12.4.6Benchmarking: the portfolio as its own dataset

§12.4.1Why attribution is the firm's mirror

Monitoring, from Lesson 1, asks: "is this deal on track?" Attribution asks a harder question: where did the money actually come from? A fund can make 2.5× without knowing whether it came from skill in operations, courage with leverage, or luck with multiples. And a firm that can't answer that question can't honestly tell its LPs what it's good at. It can't underwrite the next deal any better, and it can't see its own bad habits. The tools in this lesson, meaning value bridges, attribution across the fund, loss ratios, analysis of concentration, and comparing underwriting with actual results, are how a firm holds up a mirror to itself. They're also, not by coincidence, almost entirely things that the data team delivers. They need clean data from entry, consistent valuations, and the underwriting cases kept in a form that can be queried.

§12.4.2The portfolio-company value bridge: worked example

You met the idea in Module 7, as returns attribution. Here, it becomes a standing report. The bridge breaks the change in the equity value down into three drivers: EBITDA growth, the change in the multiple, and deleveraging.

Here's an example in the style of Osprey, with a five-year hold.

Entry Exit
Revenue £50.0m £65.0m
EBITDA £10.0m £15.0m
EV multiple 10.0× 10.4×
Enterprise value £100.0m £156.0m
Net debt £60.0m £24.0m
Equity value £40.0m £132.0m

The gain in equity is £92m, which is a MOIC of 3.3×. Here's the standard breakdown.

  • EBITDA growth, valued at the entry multiple, is (15.0−10.0)×10.0=£50m(15.0 - 10.0) \times 10.0 = £50m(15.0−10.0)×10.0=£50m
  • Multiple expansion, on the exit EBITDA, is (10.4−10.0)×15.0=£6m(10.4 - 10.0) \times 15.0 = £6m(10.4−10.0)×15.0=£6m
  • Deleveraging, meaning the net debt paid down, is 60.0−24.0=£36m60.0 - 24.0 = £36m60.0−24.0=£36m
  • As a check: 50+6+36=£92m50 + 6 + 36 = £92m50+6+36=£92m ✓

Here's a note on honesty. How the cross term, growth multiplied by the change in the multiple, is split is a convention. Here, multiple expansion is measured on the exit EBITDA. Some houses measure it on the entry EBITDA instead, and price growth at the exit multiple. That gives (10.4−10.0)×10=£4m(10.4-10.0)\times 10 = £4m(10.4−10.0)×10=£4m and (15−10)×10.4=£52m(15-10)\times 10.4 = £52m(15−10)×10.4=£52m, the same £56m gain in EV, with different labels. It rarely changes the story. But a data team has to pick one convention and apply it identically to every deal, or comparisons across deals get quietly corrupted. It's the problem of drifting definitions from Lesson 2, in miniature.

The bridge gets more useful the further you push it.

  • Split EBITDA growth into revenue and margin. Revenue growing from £50m to £65m, at a constant margin of 20%, contributes 15×0.20×10=£30m15 \times 0.20 \times 10 = £30m15×0.20×10=£30m. And margin expanding from 20.0% to 23.1%, on the exit revenue, contributes (0.231−0.200)×65×10=£20m(0.231-0.200)\times 65 \times 10 = £20m(0.231−0.200)×65×10=£20m. Now ask: did the thesis say margin, or growth? A deal underwritten as a growth story that delivered through cutting costs didn't prove its thesis. It just got lucky in a different way.
  • Split organic growth from M&A. If two bolt-ons added £2.5m of the £5m growth in EBITDA, then organic growth was half the headline. And the bolt-ons used up capital that belongs in the denominator.
  • Question the deleveraging line. Paying down £36m of debt means cash that the business threw off. If it came from genuine cash conversion, that's excellent. But if £10m of it came from squeezing working capital, or starving capex, then some of that value was borrowed from the buyer. Those are exactly the adjustments that a vendor due diligence process, from Module 11, will probe.

So what looks good? Value built mainly on EBITDA growth, ideally the kind that the thesis predicted. And what looks bad? A bridge dominated by multiple expansion. That's market exposure, which the firm can't repeat, and LPs discount it accordingly. And what do deal teams ask? "Run the bridge at the entry multiple. Would we still have carry if the market hadn't been re-rated?"

§12.4.3Fund-level attribution: which deals made the fund

Add everything up across the portfolio, and patterns appear. Here's a stylised Fund II, with all the figures showing total value, both realised and valued, against the cost invested.

Deal Invested Value MOIC Gain/(loss)
Alpha £50m £150m 3.0× +£100m
Beta £60m £120m 2.0× +£60m
Gamma £40m £100m 2.5× +£60m
Delta £45m £45m 1.0× £0m
Epsilon £35m £15m 0.4× −£20m
Fund £230m £430m 1.87× +£200m

Read it the way a partner would. Alpha alone accounts for half of the fund's gains, and Alpha, Beta and Gamma together account for all of them, because the other two net out to minus £20m. That's typical. Buyout returns are less skewed than venture returns, but they're still concentrated. And it drives real decisions. Which partners' deals actually made the money? That's where the politics of carry live. Do the fund's winners share a sector, or a playbook? That's strategy. And what should the pacing and sizing of the next fund look like? Cut the same table by sector, by deal size, by year of entry, by sourcing channel, auction versus proprietary, and by the entry multiple paid. Every cut is a question about what the firm is good at, and the data team is the only place where the cuts can be produced consistently.

§12.4.4Loss ratios and concentration

There are two lenses on risk that LPs apply to every track record.

The loss ratio is the share of invested capital in deals returning less than their cost. In Fund II above, Delta returned exactly 1.0×, so it isn't a loss, while Epsilon's £35m returned 0.4×. So the loss ratio is 35 divided by 230, which is about 15% of the capital in losing deals. The harsher variant, capital impairment, is the capital actually destroyed: 35 minus 15, divided by 230, which is about 9%. Buyout LPs typically expect loss ratios of 10 to 20%. A loss ratio of 5%, in a fund returning 1.6×, suggests either admirable discipline, or too little appetite for risk. A loss ratio of 35% needs a very good story. The two variants get mixed up constantly, so a data team should publish both, with definitions, for each fund vintage.

Concentration is how much of the fund rides on a few names. In Fund II, Alpha is 150 out of 430, which is 35% of the total value. So the timing of a single asset's exit now dominates the fund's DPI. Funds manage this in advance, with limits on positions, commonly no deal above 10 to 15% of commitments at cost. And they manage it afterwards, by watching how concentrated the value is. The fund's CFO watches it too, for the covenants on any NAV facility. There are related cuts, too: the top three assets as a percentage of NAV, concentration by sector, and, more subtly, concentration in shared factors. Five deals that are all "US consumer discretionary with floating-rate debt" are really one bet, wearing five names.

§12.4.5Underwriting versus actual: the institutional learning loop

The single most valuable dataset that a PE data team can build is also the simplest to describe: for every deal, the underwriting case approved by the investment committee, frozen at closing, and joined to the actual results forever. Most firms have this in principle, but few can query it. Here's what it teaches.

Question Typical finding
Do we hit Year-1 EBITDA? Underwriting misses Y1 by 5–10% at many firms — the "J-curve of optimism". If your firm's Y1 miss averages 8%, ICs can haircut systematically.
Which assumptions miss most? Revenue growth is usually the optimistic line; cost synergies in buy-and-build second. Exit multiples underwritten flat-to-entry are usually the conservative line in rising markets.
Where do we win? If actual outperformance clusters in one sector or one operating lever (pricing, say), that is the firm's genuine edge — bid harder there, staff it better.
Are our marks honest? Join to Lesson 3: final mark versus exit proceeds, per deal. A firm that exits 10% above final marks can prove conservatism to LPs with a table, not an adjective.

The cultural obstacle is obvious: this dataset grades the past promises of named partners. Building it anyway, neutrally and systematically, without editorialising, is one of the clearest ways a data function can show that it works for the firm, rather than for any single deal team. The output shows up directly in investment committee memos, along the lines of "our last four industrial deals underwrote 12% growth and delivered 7%, so why is this one different?" That's precisely the currency for earning a seat at the table, which Lesson 5 is about.

§12.4.6Benchmarking: the portfolio as its own dataset

A firm with 25 portfolio companies is sitting on a private benchmarking asset that no consultant can sell it, as long as the data is standardised, as Lesson 2 described. Here are some useful things to build, in rough order of effort.

  1. Benchmarks of KPIs across the portfolio. These might cover DSO, DPO, inventory turns, EBITDA margin by sector, revenue per head, and IT spending as a percentage of revenue. A portfolio company's CFO who's told "your DSO is 68, against a portfolio median of 49 for similar businesses" has been handed a target, with the evidence attached.
  2. Benchmarks of functional costs. That means the cost of the finance function as a percentage of revenue across the portfolio, and the rates paid for the same categories of procurement, such as insurance, freight and software licences. These feed procurement programmes across the whole portfolio, which is a classic value-creation lever from Module 10.
  3. Benchmarks of pricing and retention. That means the price increases actually achieved against list, churn by cohort and by tier, and the depth of discounts by sales rep. These can be compared across software companies in the portfolio on a standard basis, and acted on immediately inside each one.
  4. Joining external data. That means the multiples of public comparables, which feed the calibration in Lesson 3, conditions in the credit markets, and datasets for each sector. The problems with joining are real, such as company identifiers, financial years that don't line up, and currency. Solving them robustly is unglamorous work, but it compounds.

So what looks good in a firm's stack of analytics? A single store, standard definitions, the overlay of the underwriting case live, reporting driven by exceptions, and every number in an investment committee paper or LP report traceable back to its source. And what looks bad? Five spreadsheets that disagree about last quarter's EBITDA, attribution rebuilt by hand for each fundraise, and a "data team" that spends the end of every quarter retyping numbers. The difference between the two is rarely about tools. It's about whether the firm decided that the history of its portfolio is an asset worth engineering. The final lesson turns to where that asset, and the person who builds it, change the actual outcomes of deals.

Lesson 12.5/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

The Data-Driven PE Firm: Where Data Work Changes Deal Outcomes

25 min read
In brief

This lesson looks at where data science genuinely lands in PE: signals for sourcing, analytics in diligence, work on pricing and churn in the portfolio, and preparing for exit. It covers the realistic limits, how a data professional earns a seat at the deal table by speaking the language of returns, and finishes with a closing synthesis: how to read any company through the eyes of a deal team.

  1. 12.5.1Separating the real from the deck-ware
  2. 12.5.2Sourcing: signals before the banker calls
  3. 12.5.3Diligence: the data room as a dataset
  4. 12.5.4Portfolio: pricing, churn, and the operating levers
  5. 12.5.5Realistic limits: where data science doesn't land
  6. 12.5.6Earning the seat: speak returns, translate to thesis
  7. 12.5.7Closing synthesis: reading any company through the deal lens

§12.5.1Separating the real from the deck-ware

"Data-driven private equity" appears in every fundraising deck. Inside firms, though, the reality ranges from a genuinely industrialised capability, to one analyst with a Bloomberg login. This lesson maps out where data work has actually changed the outcomes of deals, where it reliably disappoints, and, since you're the person doing it, how to turn analytical work into standing in an organisation led by deals. Here's the honest headline. The wins are concentrated in four places, and none of them looks like a Kaggle competition. They look like the deal lifecycle from Module 6, with better inputs at each stage.

§12.5.2Sourcing: signals before the banker calls

The economics of sourcing reward being early. A proprietary conversation started a year before a process means a relationship, an advantage in information, and sometimes a pre-emptive bid, as in Module 6. Data work is one of the few scalable ways of getting there.

Here's what works in practice: an engine of universes and signals. Build the universe of companies in the firm's target sectors and range of sizes, from filings, registries and commercial databases. In the UK, filings at Companies House give you revenue, margins and debt for private companies, with a lag. Then layer on signals that suggest change, or quality. These include the speed of hiring by function, where a spike in sales hiring implies ambitions for growth; the trajectory of web traffic and reviews; scores from customer reviews compared with competitors; changes to the technology stack; the age and tenure of the founder; lease events; grant awards; and records of imports and exports. Score and rank the companies, feed the top of the list to the sector teams as call sheets, and track the conversion from signals, to meetings, to deals.

There are two truths about the design. First, the model's job is triage, not prediction. It reduces 40,000 companies down to the 200 that a human should ring this quarter. What matters is precision at the top of the list. A plausible-looking company that agrees to a meeting is a success, even if it never transacts. Second, most of the moat lies in the plumbing. That means resolving entities, such as matching "Hartwell Systems Ltd" across five databases, removing duplicates against the CRM, and keeping the signals fresh. Firms that treat data science for sourcing as an engineering problem of matching and freshness get compounding value. Firms that treat it as a modelling problem build an impressive notebook, and quietly stop using it.

§12.5.3Diligence: the data room as a dataset

Module 9 covered what diligence asks; data teams change what it can answer. Modern processes drop data at the level of each transaction into the data room, such as invoice lines, subscription logs, and sales by product. A team that can process a few million rows in a week can test the claims that the CIM makes in prose.

  • Analysis of cohorts and retention, from raw data on subscriptions or repeat purchases. Calculate NRR and churn yourself, rather than accepting management's definition. It's the problem of drifting definitions from Lesson 2, in its adversarial edition. A classic finding is a headline of "95% retention" that's really 84%, once downgrades and a quirk in the definition have been unwound.
  • Pricing forensics, from the invoice lines. Look at the price actually achieved against list, the depth of discounts by rep and segment, and how well price changes stick. A classic finding is that list prices rose by 5%, but the prices actually achieved rose by only 1.4%. In other words, the pricing lever that the thesis relies on has never actually been pulled successfully.
  • Customer concentration, and cross-selling, calculated from the transactions, rather than from the table of the top 10 customers that the vendor curated. That includes the revenue at risk from customers who are already shrinking year on year.
  • Speed as an advantage. In a compressed auction, as in Module 6, producing the cohort analysis in three days, rather than outsourcing it for three weeks, changes what the deal team can know before the bid deadline. Sometimes, that's the difference between having the conviction to stretch, and passing.

The same skill set points the other way at exit, in Module 11, as sell-side analytics. Preparing for exit increasingly means building the clean dataset of KPIs eighteen months early. That way, vendor due diligence tells a verified growth story, and the buyers' data teams find order, rather than excuses to chip the price. A data team that knows its portfolio company's numbers will be recalculated by someone exactly like them prepares accordingly.

§12.5.4Portfolio: pricing, churn, and the operating levers

Inside the portfolio, data work is value creation, as in Module 10, but with a keyboard. There are two recurring wins.

Pricing. Most mid-market companies under-price through inertia. They don't take their annual increases, they don't manage their discounts, and they don't segment. The analytical work is often mundane: analysing the spread of prices, meaning who pays what for the same thing, and why. But the value isn't mundane. Here's a worked example. Take a portfolio company with £40m of revenue, where analysis shows that the customers paying the lowest quartile of prices are no more sensitive to price than the median. A targeted increase of 3% in the price actually achieved, on half of the book, adds 40×0.5×0.03=£0.6m40 \times 0.5 \times 0.03 = £0.6m40×0.5×0.03=£0.6m of revenue, at a flow-through of about 90%. That's £0.54m of EBITDA, worth about £5m of EV at an exit multiple of 9×. That's a result the partners can see, from six weeks of SQL.

Churn and retention. The value of a churn model isn't its accuracy score; it's the economics of intervening. Here's an example. A portfolio company with £30m of ARR is losing 12% gross. Scoring the accounts for risk, and triggering plays to save them, cuts gross churn by 2 points. That retains £0.6m of revenue a year. At an incremental margin of 70%, that's £0.42m of EBITDA. And at an exit multiple of 10×, that's about £4.2m of enterprise value, before any compounding, as the retained customers renew again. Presenting it that way, from points of churn, to EBITDA, to value at exit, rather than as model metrics, is the difference between analytics and value creation.

Beyond these, there's forecasting demand for portfolio companies that carry heavy inventory, analytics on procurement across the portfolio, the productivity of sales forces, and the benchmarks across the portfolio from Lesson 4. The pattern holds. The technique is rarely new; the leverage comes from linking it to a lever in the thesis, and quantifying it in the currency of deals.

§12.5.5Realistic limits: where data science doesn't land

Being clear-eyed about the limits is an asset for your credibility in itself.

  • A small number of cases, with huge stakes. A firm does four to eight deals a year, and a fund's outcome hinges on two or three of them. You can't train a model on "will this deal work?" using 25 observations from a regime of interest rates that has vanished. Choosing deals remains a matter of judgement. Data narrows the funnel, and arms the judgement.
  • The decisive variables often aren't quantified. The quality of management, a founder's real reason for selling, or a competitor's next move: the diligence findings that kill deals are frequently qualitative, and the model sees none of them.
  • Relationships still win deals. Proprietary deal flow is mostly about trust, and years of coffee. A signals engine gets you the meeting sooner, but it doesn't get you the deal.
  • Analytics can't fix a bad thesis. No dashboard rescues an asset in structural decline that was bought at 11×. The lens from Module 3 comes first.
  • The cost of integration is chronically underestimated. Every model needs the foundation from Lesson 2: definitions, pipelines and validation. Firms that hire data scientists before they build the data plumbing produce demos, and then disillusionment.

So what looks bad, from the deal team's chair? Black-box scores with no explanation, analysis that arrives after the decision has been made, theatrical precision, such as four significant figures on rubbish inputs, and any answer that can't survive the question, "so what should we do?"

§12.5.6Earning the seat: speak returns, translate to thesis

Here's the recurring career question for data professionals in PE: how do you stop being a service desk, and start being in the room? Across firms, the pattern is consistent.

  1. Express everything in terms of returns. The firm's native units are EBITDA, the multiple, IRR, MOIC and covenant headroom. "Churn is down 2 points" is a KPI. "That's about £4m of equity value at exit, or roughly 0.1× on this deal's MOIC" is a contribution. You now have the whole course's vocabulary, so use it in every piece of work you deliver.
  2. Anchor yourself on the thesis. Before you analyse anything, read the investment committee paper. Every piece of analysis should locate itself on a driver of the thesis. Does it support, threaten, or quantify the case we underwrote? Analysis that has no position on the thesis is trivia.
  3. Volunteer the question, not just the answer. This is Lesson 1's discipline. A data team that asks, before the board meeting, "revenue beat the budget, but the incremental gross margin was 30%, so are we buying growth?", becomes part of the deal conversation for good.
  4. Be flawless on the boring cycle. The monitoring pack, the data for the quarter-end valuations, and the LP reporting, delivered on time and reconciled, twelve times a year. Trust in PE is built on operational reliability first, and the interesting work is given to the people who have it.
  5. Pick one deal, and go deep. Knowing one portfolio company down to the depth of its board pack, meaning its position on covenants, its story on DSO, and its pricing cohorts, teaches you more about what deal teams need than broad work on tools. And it makes you the person the deal partner actually rings.

§12.5.7Closing synthesis: reading any company through the deal lens

This module brings the course to a close, so let's zoom out. Twelve modules ago, a set of accounts was a compliance document. Now, handed any company, you can run the full read that a deal team would.

  • What does it sell, and why do customers stay? That's Module 3: the moat and the unit economics, before any multiple.
  • Are the earnings real? That's Modules 1, 2 and 9: cash conversion, working capital, one-offs, and the instincts of quality-of-earnings work.
  • What is it worth, and to whom? That's Module 4: multiples, with scepticism about calibration, and always distinguishing EV from equity.
  • How would a deal be built? That's Modules 5 to 8: who funds it, how much leverage it can carry, the structure and covenants, and what the maths of returns requires of the exit.
  • What would you do with it, and how would you leave? That's Modules 10 and 11: the levers, the 100-day plan, the route to exit, and its timing.
  • And how would you know that it's working? That's this module: the KPI stack, variance against the thesis, the valuations, and the bridge.

That last question is yours, professionally. Every lesson in this course ultimately described a forecast that someone made with other people's money. Portfolio monitoring is where the forecast meets the actual results, and the data team is where that meeting is engineered honestly. Do it well, and you're not just sitting next to the investing; you're the part of the machine that tells the firm the truth. There's no more valuable seat to earn.
