Case C1/Case studies

Hilton: The Best Buyout That Nearly Wasn't

GoodReal deal15 min read

USD 26bn take-private at the peak, rescued by a debt restructuring, roughly USD 14bn of profit

Sponsor
Blackstone
Sector
Hotels & hospitality
Period
2007–2018
In brief

Blackstone bought Hilton at the top of the market in 2007, and watched the value of its equity get marked down heavily in the financial crisis. It restructured the debt, pivoted the business towards fees, and ended up with what's widely cited as the most profitable buyout ever.

  1. C1.1Snapshot
  2. C1.2The business and the thesis
  3. C1.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C1.4What went wrong
  5. C1.5What went well
  6. C1.6Outcome
  7. C1.7Lessons for deal teams

§C1.1Snapshot

This is a real deal. The figures are rounded from public reporting, and they're approximate, so check the primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsor Blackstone (real estate and private equity funds)
Announced / closed July 2007 / October 2007
Enterprise value About USD 26bn
Funding About USD 20.5bn debt, about USD 5.6bn equity
Implied equity cushion Roughly 21% of the price
Exit route IPO December 2013, then staged sell-downs to 2018
Outcome Widely reported profit of about USD 14bn
Verdict Good, but only after surviving a near-miss

§C1.2The business and the thesis

Hilton Hotels owned, managed and franchised hotels, under brands including Hilton, Hampton, Embassy Suites, DoubleTree and Conrad. It had three quite different economic engines inside one company.

  • Owned real estate. This was capital-heavy and cyclical, but it meant valuable land and buildings.
  • Management contracts. These earned fees for running hotels that other people own.
  • Franchising. This earned royalties on revenue, for letting owners use the brand and the booking system.

Blackstone's thesis had three parts. First, the fee businesses were undervalued inside a listed company that was heavy in real estate. Second, the pipeline of brands could grow globally with little capital. And third, a large portfolio of owned hotels gave the support of hard assets for a lot of debt. Blackstone also owned other hotel businesses, and knew the sector well.

§C1.3Entry and deal structure

The deal was priced at the peak of the credit boom before the crisis, and it shows in the structure.

Sources USD bn Uses USD bn
Debt (mortgage, mezzanine, corporate loans) 20.5 Purchase of equity and refinancing 26.1
Blackstone equity 5.6
Total 26.1 Total 26.1

Around four fifths of the price was borrowed. A large share of the debt was secured on the owned hotels, with layers of mezzanine debt above it. That's a structure that works well while hotel revenue is growing, and becomes dangerous very quickly when it falls.

§C1.4What went wrong

The timing could hardly have been worse. The deal closed months before the financial crisis. In 2009, US hotel revenue per available room fell sharply, as business travel and conferences were cut. And because hotel operating costs are highly fixed, profits fell much faster than revenue.

Blackstone marked down its equity in Hilton steeply, by around 70% at the low point, according to press coverage at the time. With roughly USD 20bn of debt against collapsing earnings, the equity was close to worthless on a mark-to-market basis, and several maturities were approaching.

§C1.5What went well

Three things turned it around.

  1. Restructuring the debt from a position of relative strength. In 2010, Blackstone negotiated with lenders who didn't want to own a hotel company in the middle of a recession. It bought back about USD 2bn of debt for about USD 800m, which was a large discount. And lenders converted a further USD 2bn or so into preferred equity. Debt fell to around USD 16bn, and the maturities were pushed out.
  2. New management, and a leaner centre. Chris Nassetta became CEO in late 2007. He cut corporate overheads, moved the headquarters from Beverly Hills to Virginia, and pushed a consistent culture of performance across the brands.
  3. An asset-light engine for growth. Growth came mainly from new franchised and managed hotels, built with other people's capital, especially internationally. Every new room added fee income, without adding any debt. The development pipeline grew to become one of the largest in the industry.

The cycle also recovered, and that matters. Operational work gets you the rebound, but it doesn't guarantee one.

§C1.6Outcome

Hilton relisted on the New York Stock Exchange in December 2013, in one of the largest hotel IPOs on record. Blackstone then sold down its stake in stages. In 2017, Hilton spun off its owned real estate into a separate listed REIT, and its timeshare business into another company. That left a hotel manager and franchisor driven by fees, which was valued at a much higher multiple. Blackstone sold its final shares in 2018.

Measure Approximate figure
Equity invested (original plus 2010 injection) USD 6.4bn
Reported total profit USD 14bn
Implied multiple of money About 3x
Hold period About 10.5 years

A crude calculation on those figures, treating it as a single exit, gives an IRR in the low teens. The true figure was higher, because a large share of the proceeds came from 2013 onwards, rather than at the very end. Here's the lesson in the numbers: an enormous absolute gain can come with a return that's only solid on an annual basis, when the hold is long.

§C1.7Lessons for deal teams

  • The capital structure decides whether you survive long enough to be proved right. Covenant-light terms, and maturities a long way off, gave Blackstone time. A tighter structure would probably have handed Hilton to its lenders.
  • Negotiate restructurings early. Lenders facing losses will often accept a discount to avoid having to own the asset.
  • Separate the things that the market values differently. Splitting the owned real estate away from the fee business re-rated the company.
  • Absolute profit and IRR tell different stories. So quote both when you describe a deal.

Case C2/Case studies

Harbourline Testing: A Textbook Buy-and-Build

GoodFictional12 min read

14 bolt-ons bought at 6x, platform sold at 12x, 4.7x money in five years

Sponsor
Aldermoor Capital (fictional)
Sector
Testing, inspection & certification
Period
2016–2021
In brief

This is a fictional deal in the UK mid-market. It involves a fragmented services market driven by regulation, a platform bought at 9x, fourteen small bolt-ons bought at 6x, real work on integration, and an exit at 12x. The value bridge shows exactly where the return of 4.7x came from.

  1. C2.1Snapshot
  2. C2.2The business and the thesis
  3. C2.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C2.4What went well
  5. C2.5What went wrong
  6. C2.6Outcome
  7. C2.7Lessons for deal teams

§C2.1Snapshot

This is a fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All of the figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Aldermoor Capital, UK mid-market buyout fund
Business Electrical, fire-safety and lift inspection for commercial buildings
Entry 2016 at 9.0x EBITDA of £10.0m, EV £90.0m
Exit 2021 to a large sponsor at 12.0x EBITDA of £25.0m, EV £300.0m
Equity in / out £49.0m / £230.0m
Returns 4.7x MOIC, about 36% IRR
Verdict Good

§C2.2The business and the thesis

Harbourline carried out statutory inspections that building owners are legally required to commission: checks on electrical installations, servicing of fire alarms, and examinations of lifts. Demand is driven by regulation, rather than by the economy, and about 80% of revenue repeated every year.

The market was highly fragmented. Hundreds of small regional firms, each with £0.5m to £1.5m of EBITDA, served local customers. Meanwhile, national facilities managers wanted a single provider covering the whole country. That gap was the thesis, and it had four steps.

  1. Buy a well-run regional leader as the platform.
  2. Acquire small operators at low multiples, because small businesses sell cheaply.
  3. Integrate them onto one scheduling system, one brand, and one sales team.
  4. Then sell a national business, which is larger and lower in risk, at a platform multiple.

§C2.3Entry and deal structure

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (9.0x £10.0m) 90.0 Unitranche loan (4.5x) 45.0
Transaction fees 4.0 Aldermoor equity 44.0
Management rollover 5.0
Total 94.0 Total 94.0

The unitranche came with an uncommitted accordion. That's extra debt for acquisitions, subject to a test of leverage on a pro-forma basis. Management rolled over £5.0m, and received a management incentive plan on top. The returns below are shown on total equity, before any dilution from the incentive plan.

§C2.4What went well

  • Disciplined pricing of the bolt-ons. Fourteen acquisitions added £9.0m of EBITDA, for £54.0m in total, which is an average of 6.0x. £34.0m of that came from the accordion, and £20.0m from the company's own cash.
  • Integration before the next deal. In 2018, the team paused acquisitions for six months, to move every business onto a single system for scheduling jobs. The utilisation of engineers rose, and overlapping depots were closed. That delivered £2.0m of cost synergies.
  • Organic growth. The platform's EBITDA grew by 7% a year, from £10.0m to £14.0m, helped by cross-selling fire and lift work to electrical customers.
  • A better business to own. At exit, no customer made up more than 3% of revenue, and national contracts made up a growing share. A buyer could underwrite it with confidence.

§C2.5What went wrong

  • Two of the early bolt-ons lost their founders within a year, and with them, some key customer relationships. So Aldermoor moved to longer earn-outs, and retention packages, for the later deals.
  • One acquisition in 2019 had weak record-keeping on safety. Putting it right cost £0.6m, and a warning from the regulator was a reputational scare. After that, diligence on compliance became a standard workstream.
  • Leverage only fell from 4.5x to 2.8x because EBITDA grew so fast. Net debt itself actually increased.

§C2.6Outcome

Exit EBITDA build £m
Platform EBITDA at entry 10.0
Organic growth 4.0
Acquired EBITDA 9.0
Integration synergies 2.0
Exit EBITDA 25.0

The exit EV is 12.0x × £25.0m, which is £300.0m. Net debt at exit was £70.0m, leaving £230.0m of equity. So the MOIC is 230 ÷ 49, which is 4.7x. Over five years, that's 4.691/5−1≈36%4.69^{1/5} - 1 \approx 36\%4.691/5−1≈36%.

The value bridge explains the £181.0m gain in equity.

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (25.0 − 10.0) × 9.0x entry multiple 135.0
Multiple expansion (12.0 − 9.0) × £25.0m exit EBITDA 75.0
Change in net debt £45.0m at entry to £70.0m at exit (25.0)
Entry fees (4.0)
Total equity gain 181.0

The £9.0m of acquired EBITDA was bought at 6.0x and sold at 12.0x. That arbitrage alone was worth £54.0m.

§C2.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Buy-and-build works in fragmented markets that aren't cyclical, where small firms trade at a genuine discount to scaled platforms.
  • The arbitrage is only real if the integration earns the higher multiple. A buyer paying 12x wants one business, not fourteen.
  • Watch the net debt line. Growing EBITDA can hide debt that's rising in absolute terms.
  • Earn-outs and retention packages protect people businesses. In services, the customers often follow the founder.

Case C3/Case studies

Alliance Boots: A FTSE 100 Take-Private and a Strategic Exit

GoodReal deal13 min read

£11.1bn take-private funded with about £9bn of debt, exited to Walgreens in two steps

Sponsor
KKR with Stefano Pessina
Sector
Pharmacy retail & pharmaceutical wholesale
Period
2007–2015
In brief

KKR, together with Alliance Boots' largest shareholder, took a FTSE 100 company private just weeks before the credit crunch. Defensive earnings carried the debt through the crisis, and a sale to Walgreens in two stages produced a strong return.

  1. C3.1Snapshot
  2. C3.2The business and the thesis
  3. C3.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C3.4What went well
  5. C3.5What went wrong
  6. C3.6Outcome
  7. C3.7Lessons for deal teams

§C3.1Snapshot

This is a real deal. The figures are rounded from public reporting, and they're approximate, so check the primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsor KKR, alongside executive deputy chairman Stefano Pessina
Closed June 2007
Price About £11.1bn, the first FTSE 100 company taken private by a PE firm
Funding About £9bn of debt
KKR's own equity About £1.22bn
Exit Walgreens bought 45% in 2012 and the rest by the end of 2014
Outcome KKR and partners were reported to be on course to almost triple their money
Verdict Good

§C3.2The business and the thesis

Alliance Boots was formed in 2006, by merging Boots, the UK high-street health and beauty retailer, with Alliance UniChem, a pan-European pharmaceutical wholesaler led by Stefano Pessina.

The thesis rested on three points.

  • Defensive cash flows. Prescriptions and everyday health products hold up in downturns, and that supports heavy borrowing better than most of retail.
  • A partner who was both owner and operator. Pessina already owned a large stake, and ran the combined group. Rolling his stake into the deal aligned the main manager with the sponsor.
  • Room to improve. Boots had underperformed as a listed company. The integration of the merger, savings in procurement, and international expansion were all already under way.

§C3.3Entry and deal structure

The consortium won after a competitive bidding process. About £9bn of the funding was debt, arranged by a large syndicate of banks at the peak of the market. The equity came from KKR's funds and balance sheet, Pessina's rolled-over shares, and co-investors.

The debt was large, even for a defensive business. The banks were left holding much of it when the credit markets froze, just weeks after closing, and they had to sell it later at a loss.

§C3.4What went well

  • Earnings held up. Trading proved resilient through the recession of 2008 and 2009, just as the thesis had predicted. That kept the company comfortably able to pay its interest.
  • Operational delivery. Integrating the merged group, savings from buying on a much larger scale, and the growth of Boots' own brands, including No7, all improved profits.
  • International expansion. The wholesale arm grew in new markets, which made the group more attractive to a global buyer.
  • An elegant exit. In 2012, Walgreens paid about USD 6.7bn, in cash and shares, for 45% of the business, with an option to buy the rest. It exercised that option in 2014, and the combined group became Walgreens Boots Alliance. Selling in stages let the sponsors realise part of the value early, while keeping some upside through Walgreens shares.

§C3.5What went wrong

  • Timing, and syndication. Closing just before the credit crunch left the lending banks with losses. That didn't hurt the equity directly, but it did damage relationships.
  • Tax, and public scrutiny. The group moved its headquarters to Switzerland, and benefited from interest deductions on its debt. In the UK, it faced criticism over how little tax it paid.
  • The legacy after the exit. Boots in the UK later struggled under Walgreens' ownership, with cuts to pharmacy funding and store closures. That came after the sponsor had exited. But it's a reminder that a good return for the sponsor doesn't settle the question of whether the business was strengthened.

§C3.6Outcome

KKR invested about £1.22bn of equity in 2007. At the time of the Walgreens deal in 2012, KKR and its partners were widely reported to be on course to almost triple their money. Much of the consideration came in the form of Walgreens shares, so the final result also depended on the Walgreens share price after 2014.

§C3.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Defensive earnings are the best protection against bad timing. Alliance Boots and Energy Future Holdings closed in the same year. One business held on to its earnings, and the other didn't.
  • A strategic buyer can pay for things that a financial buyer can't. Walgreens valued the scale of global purchasing, and international expansion.
  • Staged exits can bridge gaps in valuation. An option structure let both sides agree a deal, when a full sale might have stalled on price.
  • Reputation is part of the return. Questions about tax and jobs can follow a deal long after the exit.

Case C4/Case studies

Northgate Packaging: Carve-Out Done Properly

GoodFictional12 min read

Neglected division bought cheaply, stood up alone, restructured, sold to a trade buyer at 3.0x

Sponsor
Calderstone Partners (fictional)
Sector
Industrial packaging
Period
2014–2018
In brief

This is a fictional corporate carve-out. The parent's EBITDA overstated the profits of the business as a standalone company, the TSA ran late, and the switchover of IT went badly. And yet work on procurement, consolidating plants and pricing still delivered 3.0x in four years.

  1. C4.1Snapshot
  2. C4.2The business and the thesis
  3. C4.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C4.4What went well
  5. C4.5What went wrong
  6. C4.6Outcome
  7. C4.7Lessons for deal teams

§C4.1Snapshot

This is a fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All of the figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Calderstone Partners, European mid-market fund
Business Rigid plastic containers for food and chemicals, seven UK plants
Seller A listed industrial group exiting non-core businesses
Entry 2014, EV £120.0m: 6.0x reported EBITDA, 7.5x standalone EBITDA
Exit 2018 trade sale at 9.0x EBITDA of £28.0m, EV £252.0m
Equity in / out £70.0m / £212.0m
Returns 3.0x MOIC, about 32% IRR
Verdict Good

§C4.2The business and the thesis

Northgate was a steady, but neglected, division. The parent had starved it of capital and management attention for a decade. The plants were under-used, raw materials were bought separately at each site, and price increases lagged behind the cost of resin.

Carve-outs often sell cheaply, because the seller wants a clean, quick exit, and few buyers can handle the complexity. Calderstone's thesis was that the discount it was paid for taking on the complexity was larger than the cost of solving it.

§C4.3Entry and deal structure

The first job was to work out the true earnings. Inside the parent, Northgate received shared services, such as IT, finance, HR and insurance, for less than their real cost.

EBITDA bridge £m
EBITDA as reported within the parent 20.0
Standalone costs to replace group services (4.0)
Standalone EBITDA 16.0

The headline price of 6.0x looked cheap. But on standalone EBITDA, it was 7.5x, which is a fair price. The sponsor underwrote the deal on the lower number.

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value 120.0 Term loan B (4.0x standalone) 64.0
Transaction fees 6.0 Calderstone equity 70.0
One-off separation costs 8.0
Total 134.0 Total 134.0

A transitional services agreement, or TSA, let Northgate keep using the parent's IT and payroll for 18 months, while it built its own.

§C4.4What went well

  • Procurement. Buying resin centrally across all the plants, with indexed contracts, saved £3.0m a year.
  • The footprint. Closing two of the seven plants, and moving their volume to the others, saved £4.0m a year, after £10.0m of one-off restructuring costs.
  • Pricing. New contracts included clauses to pass through the cost of resin, which added £2.0m. Margins stopped swinging with the price of oil.
  • Growth in volume. With capital finally available, new lines for chemical customers added £3.0m.
  • Management. A new CFO and a new operations director joined within the first 100 days. The division's managing director stayed on, and was given real authority for the first time.

§C4.5What went wrong

  • The TSA overran by nine months, which cost £2.0m more than planned.
  • The switchover of IT disrupted invoicing. For two months, many invoices went out late, debtor days rose sharply, and the company drew £5.0m on its revolving credit facility to cover the gap in cash.
  • A plant closure cost a customer. One food customer disliked being moved to a more distant plant, and left, taking £1.0m of EBITDA with it.

None of these problems was fatal, because the plan had buffers of cash, and the core levers were within management's control.

§C4.6Outcome

EBITDA at exit was £28.0m. That's the £16.0m standalone figure, plus £3.0m from procurement, £4.0m from the footprint, £2.0m from pricing and £3.0m from volume, with the lost customer already reflected in the volume figure. A European packaging group paid 9.0x, valuing Northgate at £252.0m. Net debt was £40.0m, so the equity was worth £212.0m.

So the MOIC is 212 ÷ 70, which is 3.0x. Over four years, that's 3.031/4−1≈32%3.03^{1/4} - 1 \approx 32\%3.031/4−1≈32%.

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (28.0 − 16.0) × 7.5x standalone entry multiple 90.0
Multiple expansion (9.0 − 7.5) × £28.0m 42.0
Debt paydown £64.0m at entry to £40.0m at exit 24.0
Entry fees and separation costs (14.0)
Total equity gain 142.0

§C4.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Price carve-outs on standalone EBITDA. The seller's reported figure hides real costs.
  • Budget more time and cash for the separation than the plan says. TSAs and IT migrations almost always run late.
  • Operational levers within management's control are the safest way to create value. None of the upside in this deal needed the market to recover.
  • Strategic buyers pay for businesses that have been fixed. A cleaned-up, focused asset fitted a trade buyer's network, and earned a higher multiple.

Case C5/Case studies

Kestrel Software: Great Operations, Average Return

AverageFictional11 min read

EBITDA more than doubled, but paying 20x and selling at 14x left 1.8x

Sponsor
Wrenfield Equity (fictional)
Sector
Vertical software (SaaS)
Period
2017–2022
In brief

This is a fictional software buyout. Management more than doubled EBITDA, and yet the entry multiple, paid in a hot auction, and the reset in valuations in 2022 absorbed most of the gain. The value bridge shows how compression of the multiple cancels out operational success.

  1. C5.1Snapshot
  2. C5.2The business and the thesis
  3. C5.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C5.4What went well
  5. C5.5What went wrong
  6. C5.6Outcome
  7. C5.7Lessons for deal teams

§C5.1Snapshot

This is a fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All of the figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Wrenfield Equity, technology-focused buyout fund
Business Software for residential property managers: rent collection, maintenance, compliance
Entry 2017 at 20.0x EBITDA of £10.0m, EV £200.0m, about 5.0x ARR of £40.0m
Exit Late 2022 to another sponsor at 14.0x EBITDA of £22.0m, EV £308.0m
Equity in / out £146.0m / £260.0m
Returns 1.8x MOIC, about 12% IRR
Verdict Average: above the hurdle, well below the fund's target

§C5.2The business and the thesis

Kestrel sold subscription software to letting agents and property managers. Customers rarely left, because switching meant migrating tenants' records and retraining staff. Here's how it looked at entry.

Metric Value
Annual recurring revenue (ARR) £40.0m
ARR growth 20%
Gross revenue retention 93%
Net revenue retention 108%
EBITDA margin 26%

The thesis was to keep growth at 15 to 20%, raise prices, add modules for payments and insurance to lift the revenue from each customer, and expand margins as the business grew in scale.

§C5.3Entry and deal structure

The sale was run as a competitive auction, with six bidders. Wrenfield won by paying 20.0x EBITDA.

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (20.0x £10.0m) 200.0 Recurring-revenue loan (1.5x ARR) 60.0
Transaction fees 6.0 Wrenfield equity 146.0
Total 206.0 Total 206.0

The recurring-revenue loan was sized on ARR rather than on EBITDA, which is a common structure for software. At 6.0x EBITDA, it looked high, but lenders were comfortable with how sticky the customers were. The equity cheque was large: 71% of the total.

§C5.4What went well

  • Operational delivery. ARR reached £75.0m, and EBITDA more than doubled, to £22.0m.
  • The payments module. Collecting rent through Kestrel created a new stream of revenue, worth £6.0m of ARR by the exit.
  • Pricing. Annual price rises of 5 to 7% stuck, with little extra churn.
  • Resilience. Covid barely touched the business, because rent still had to be collected.

§C5.5What went wrong

  • Growth slowed. ARR growth fell from 20% to 11%, because the easy customers had already been won. Net revenue retention slipped to 104%.
  • A costly rebuild of the platform. The old code base couldn't scale. Rebuilding it took two years and cost £15.0m of R&D, which held back margins and delayed the new modules.
  • The market was re-rated. In 2022, rising interest rates cut software valuations sharply. Buyers who would have paid 20x in 2021 offered 14x a year later.
  • Holding on didn't help. Waiting for multiples to recover would have lengthened the hold, and cut the IRR further, while the fund needed to show realisations in order to raise its next fund.

§C5.6Outcome

The exit EV is 14.0x × £22.0m, which is £308.0m. Net debt at exit was £48.0m, so the equity was worth £260.0m.

So the MOIC is 260 ÷ 146, which is 1.8x. Over five years, that's 1.781/5−1≈12%1.78^{1/5} - 1 \approx 12\%1.781/5−1≈12%.

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (22.0 − 10.0) × 20.0x entry multiple 240.0
Multiple compression (14.0 − 20.0) × £22.0m (132.0)
Debt paydown £60.0m at entry to £48.0m at exit 12.0
Entry fees (6.0)
Total equity gain 114.0

Management created £240.0m of value by growing the earnings. The compression of the multiple took back more than half of it.

§C5.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Your entry multiple is a bet on the exit multiple. Paying 20x assumes that someone else will pay something similar later.
  • Model a case where the multiple compresses. An exit at 14x should have been a standard downside test, not a surprise.
  • Low leverage limits the downside, but it also limits the upside. An equity cheque of 71% protected the deal, but it diluted the returns.
  • Check the technology during diligence. A proper review of the code and the architecture would have found the need to rebuild the platform, and priced it in.

Case C6/Case studies

Ashworth Foods: When a Dividend Recap Flatters the IRR

AverageFictional11 min read

Flat EBITDA and a supermarket price war; a recap lifted IRR but cut MOIC

Sponsor
Belvoir Capital (fictional)
Sector
Food manufacturing
Period
2012–2019
In brief

This is a fictional supplier of chilled ready meals, squeezed by its supermarket customers. Nearly all of the return came from paying down debt. And a dividend recap in year three raised the IRR, while lowering the multiple of money.

  1. C6.1Snapshot
  2. C6.2The business and the thesis
  3. C6.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C6.4What went well
  5. C6.5What went wrong
  6. C6.6Outcome
  7. C6.7Lessons for deal teams

§C6.1Snapshot

This is a fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All of the figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Belvoir Capital, UK mid-market fund
Business Chilled ready meals, mostly supermarket own-label
Entry 2012 at 7.0x EBITDA of £18.0m, EV £126.0m
Dividend recap Year 3: £40.0m of new debt paid out to shareholders
Exit 2019 to a food group at 7.0x EBITDA of £19.0m, EV £133.0m
Equity in / total returned £58.0m / £107.0m
Returns 1.8x MOIC, about 12% IRR
Verdict Average

§C6.2The business and the thesis

Ashworth made ready meals for two of the big four UK supermarkets. It was efficient, with modern factories and a strong record on food safety. Belvoir's thesis was to win a third supermarket as a customer, launch a premium branded range, and use its scale to cut costs.

The obvious risk sat in the list of customers: the top two customers made up 70% of revenue. The investment committee accepted it, because the relationships went back a long way, and switching suppliers of chilled food is hard.

§C6.3Entry and deal structure

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (7.0x £18.0m) 126.0 Senior debt (4.0x) 72.0
Transaction fees 4.0 Belvoir equity 58.0
Total 130.0 Total 130.0

§C6.4What went well

  • Cash generation. Strong control of costs, and tight working capital, meant the business paid down debt steadily every year.
  • An early dividend. By year three, EBITDA had reached £21.0m, and leverage had fallen. Belvoir borrowed another £40.0m, and paid it out as a dividend. The fund had got 69% of its money back within three years.
  • The record on food safety. Seven years without a single product recall kept both key customers loyal.

§C6.5What went wrong

  • A price war among the supermarkets. From 2014, the discounters Aldi and Lidl grew fast. The big supermarkets pushed price cuts down onto their suppliers. And with 70% of its revenue coming from two customers, Ashworth had no negotiating power.
  • The third customer never came. A long tender was lost on price.
  • Inflation in input costs. After sterling fell in 2016, imported ingredients and packaging became more expensive. And the contracts didn't allow price increases to be passed on quickly.
  • The branded range failed. £5.0m of marketing spend produced little lasting revenue.

EBITDA went from £18.0m at entry to £21.0m in year three, then down to £17.0m in year five, and only recovered to £19.0m by the exit. After seven years, the business was earning barely more than when it was bought.

§C6.6Outcome

The exit EV is 7.0x × £19.0m, which is £133.0m. Net debt at exit was £66.0m, leaving £67.0m of equity. Adding the £40.0m dividend, Belvoir received £107.0m for its £58.0m.

So the MOIC is 107 ÷ 58, which is 1.84x. The IRR on cash flows of minus 58 in year 0, plus 40 in year 3, and plus 67 in year 7, is about 12%.

What if there had been no recap?#

Let's assume that the £40.0m had stayed in the company, saving interest at 6% for four years, which is about £10.0m. Net debt at exit would then have been about £16.0m, and the equity about £117.0m.

With recap Without recap
Total proceeds £107.0m £117.0m
MOIC 1.84x 2.02x
IRR 12.3% 10.6%

The recap raised the IRR, by returning cash early, but it lowered the multiple, because the extra debt cost interest. Which of those matters more depends on the fund. IRR drives carry and the league tables, while the multiple is the money that LPs actually receive.

Where the return came from#

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (19.0 − 18.0) × 7.0x 7.0
Multiple change 7.0x to 7.0x 0.0
Cash generation used to repay debt and fund the dividend (72.0 + 40.0) − 66.0 46.0
Entry fees (4.0)
Total gain including the dividend 49.0

Almost the whole return came from generating cash, not from building a better business.

§C6.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Customer concentration is a risk to margins, not just to revenue. Large customers may stay, but they'll take your profit.
  • Check whether the contracts let you pass on increases in costs. Ask how quickly, and how fully.
  • Always show IRR and MOIC together. Recaps and early distributions can move them in opposite directions.
  • Deleveraging on its own gives average returns. Top-quartile deals need growth in earnings, or a better multiple.

Case C7/Case studies

Debenhams: A Great Sponsor Return, a Weakened Business

MixedReal deal12 min read

Over 3x in under three years for the sponsors; the company later failed under its debts and leases

Sponsor
CVC, TPG and Merrill Lynch Private Equity
Sector
Department store retail
Period
2003–2006 (company collapsed 2019–2021)
In brief

A take-private worth £1.7bn returned more than three times the sponsors' equity within three years, helped by selling property and cutting costs. The business went back to the stock market carrying more debt and more rent, and eventually closed. It's a case study in who a return is actually good for.

  1. C7.1Snapshot
  2. C7.2The business and the thesis
  3. C7.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C7.4What went well, for the sponsors
  5. C7.5What went wrong, for the business
  6. C7.6Outcome
  7. C7.7Lessons for deal teams

§C7.1Snapshot

This is a real deal. The figures are rounded from public reporting, and they're approximate, so check the primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsors CVC Capital Partners, TPG and Merrill Lynch Private Equity
Closed Late 2003
Price About £1.7bn
Sponsor equity About £600m
Exit Stock market relisting in May 2006
Sponsor outcome Reported at more than three times their equity in under three years
Company outcome Administration in 2019, all stores closed by 2021
Verdict Mixed: excellent for the sponsors, poor for the business long term

§C7.2The business and the thesis

Debenhams was one of the UK's largest chains of department stores, with prime sites in town centres and shopping centres, and it owned many of them. The sponsors saw three sources of value.

  • Property. The owned stores could be sold to property investors, and rented back, releasing cash that was tied up in buildings.
  • Cost and working capital. Stock levels, terms with suppliers, and central costs all had room to be tightened.
  • A quick relisting. A leaner business, with higher margins, could be sold back to public investors at a good price.

§C7.3Entry and deal structure

The consortium won a contested bid, paying about £1.7bn, with about £600m of equity. The rest was debt. The plan was for a short hold, so taking cash out and making a quick exit were central from the very start.

§C7.4What went well, for the sponsors

  • Sale and leaseback. Stores were sold to property companies, and leased back on long leases. The cash raised helped to fund large returns to the owners.
  • Tighter operations. Stock was cut, suppliers were paid more slowly, and costs were reduced. The reported margins improved.
  • A quick, successful exit. Debenhams was floated again in 2006, at a value similar to what the sponsors had paid. But they had already taken out large sums. The three firms were reported to have made more than three times their £600m, in under three years.

§C7.5What went wrong, for the business

  • Rent replaced ownership. After the leaseback, the company paid rent on buildings it used to own, often on long leases with rent reviews that could only go up. Those costs were fixed, whatever happened to sales.
  • More debt at the relisting. The company went back to the stock market with far more debt than it had before the buyout.
  • Under-investment. Cutting capital spending improved cash flow in the short term, but it left the stores looking tired as online shopping grew.
  • A weak start on the public market. Within about two years, after a series of profit warnings, the share price fell well below the price at the IPO. Investors who bought at the IPO lost money.

Debenhams struggled for years afterwards. Its leases and its debt left little room to invest as shoppers moved online. It went into administration in 2019, with the lenders taking control, and the Covid closures finished it off. All of the stores had closed by 2021, and the online retailer Boohoo bought the brand name.

§C7.6Outcome

Perspective Result
Sponsors Reported more than 3x their equity in under three years
IPO investors Large losses as the share price fell
Company Weaker balance sheet, higher fixed costs, eventual failure
Employees Many thousands of jobs lost when the business closed

It's too simple to blame the 2003 buyout alone for a collapse that came sixteen years later. Online shopping, the decisions of many other owners, and Covid all played a part. But the deal did leave the company less able to adapt, with less property to borrow against, higher fixed rents, and more debt.

§C7.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Sale and leasebacks create costs that behave like debt. Rent is a fixed claim on cash flow. So count leases when you judge leverage, as the IFRS 16 accounting rules now require.
  • A quick flip moves the risk onto the next owner. If you're buying into an IPO backed by a sponsor, ask what was taken out, and what was cut.
  • Returns, and the health of the business, can diverge. Judge a deal by what it did to the company, as well as by its multiple of money.
  • Reputation matters for fundraising. Deals like this one shaped public and political views of private equity for years.

Case C8/Case studies

Corrigan Leisure Clubs: Add-Backs, Leases and a Lost Company

BadFictional12 min read

Paid on adjusted EBITDA that never arrived; hidden lease leverage and Covid handed it to the lenders

Sponsor
Hartwell Capital (fictional)
Sector
Gyms & leisure
Period
2018–2023
In brief

This is a fictional chain of gyms, bought on generously adjusted EBITDA, with obligations for rent that made its real leverage far higher than it looked. A plan for expansion, closures, and a shock in energy prices forced an equity cure, and then a swap of debt for equity that wiped out the sponsor.

  1. C8.1Snapshot
  2. C8.2The business and the thesis
  3. C8.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C8.4What went wrong
  5. C8.5Outcome
  6. C8.6Lessons for deal teams

§C8.1Snapshot

This is a fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All of the figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Hartwell Capital, mid-market buyout fund
Business 60 mid-price gyms in UK towns and cities
Entry 2018 at 9.0x "adjusted" EBITDA of £25.0m, EV £225.0m
Additional equity £20.0m equity cure in 2020
Outcome 2023 debt-for-equity swap; lenders take 90% of the company
Sponsor returns 0.0x: £114.0m lost
Verdict Bad

§C8.2The business and the thesis

Corrigan ran mid-price gyms, with pools and classes, and its membership had grown steadily. The plan was to open 20 new clubs in five years, raise prices, and cut costs through central buying and digital sign-up.

§C8.3Entry and deal structure

The sale process marketed adjusted EBITDA of £25.0m. But the sponsor's own review of the quality of earnings told a different story.

EBITDA bridge £m QoE view
Reported EBITDA (before IFRS 16) 21.0 Supported
Run-rate profit from 8 recently opened clubs 2.5 Optimistic: assumes mature membership levels immediately
"One-off" pre-opening and launch marketing 1.5 Recurring while the company keeps opening clubs
Adjusted EBITDA 25.0 Supportable figure closer to 21.0–22.0

In a competitive auction, Hartwell paid 9.0x the adjusted number. On reported EBITDA, that was 10.7x.

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (9.0x £25.0m) 225.0 Unitranche (5.5x adjusted EBITDA) 138.0
Transaction fees 7.0 Hartwell equity 94.0
Total 232.0 Total 232.0

A further capex facility of £40.0m funded the new clubs. The covenant allowed net leverage of up to 7.0x, measured on adjusted EBITDA, before rent was treated as a financing cost.

The leverage nobody headlined#

Corrigan paid about £28.0m a year in rent, on long leases. Under IFRS 16, those leases were worth about £250m as liabilities. Counting them, the true leverage at entry, adjusted for leases, was well above 15x. A business with high fixed rent, high staff costs, and high energy costs has very little room when revenue falls.

§C8.4What went wrong

  • The add-backs didn't materialise. EBITDA in 2019 was £22.0m, against a plan of £28.0m. The new clubs matured slowly, and some took members from nearby Corrigan clubs.
  • Budget competitors. Low-cost gyms open 24 hours a day opened near a third of the estate, pulling away members who were sensitive to price.
  • Covid closures. The clubs were shut for much of 2020 and 2021. EBITDA was negative, at minus £6.0m, in 2020. And the rent still had to be paid, or negotiated.
  • An equity cure. To avoid defaulting on a covenant in 2020, Hartwell put in £20.0m of new equity. The lenders agreed to a holiday from the covenants, and let the interest roll up, rather than being paid in cash.
  • A shock in energy prices. In 2022, heating pools and running air conditioning became far more expensive. EBITDA only recovered to £14.0m.

By the end of 2022, net debt had grown to £190.0m, from drawing on the capex facility and from the rolled-up interest. Leverage was 13.6x, before counting the leases.

§C8.5Outcome

In 2023, the lenders and the sponsor agreed a restructuring.

Item Result
Debt Cut from £190.0m to £100.0m
Lenders Took 90% of the equity in exchange for the debt written off
Management 10% through a new incentive plan
Hartwell Nothing. Its £94.0m plus the £20.0m cure were lost

Some of the weaker clubs were closed, and several landlords agreed to cut the rent as part of the process.

§C8.6Lessons for deal teams

  • Price on the EBITDA that the quality-of-earnings work supports. An auction doesn't make weak add-backs real.
  • "One-off" costs that come round every year aren't one-offs. Pre-opening costs are normal for a business that keeps opening new sites.
  • Count leases as leverage. Businesses that are heavy on rent carry far more fixed obligations than their debt alone suggests.
  • An equity cure should be a decision, not a reflex. Before putting in more money, ask whether it saves the investment, or only delays losing it.
  • Stress-test against a real shock. A collapse in revenue lasting three months is a useful test for any business with high fixed costs.

Case C9/Case studies

Toys "R" Us: Debt That Left No Room to Adapt

BadReal deal12 min read

USD 6.6bn buyout with more than USD 5bn of debt; about USD 400m a year in interest; liquidated in 2018

Sponsor
KKR, Bain Capital and Vornado Realty Trust
Sector
Specialty retail
Period
2005–2018
In brief

Three sponsors bought the toy retailer with heavy debt. Interest costs of around USD 400m a year absorbed cash that could have modernised its stores and its online sales, while Amazon, Walmart and Target took market share. A failed IPO, bankruptcy and liquidation followed.

  2. C9.2The business and the thesis
  3. C9.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C9.4What went wrong
  5. C9.5Outcome
  6. C9.6Lessons for deal teams

§C9.1Snapshot

This is a real deal. The figures are rounded from public reporting, and they're approximate, so check the primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsors KKR, Bain Capital and Vornado Realty Trust
Closed July 2005
Price About USD 6.6bn
Funding More than USD 5bn of debt, about USD 1.6bn of sponsor equity
Interest burden About USD 400m a year by 2017
Exit attempt IPO filed in 2010, withdrawn in 2013
Outcome Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2017; US stores liquidated in 2018
Verdict Bad

§C9.2The business and the thesis

Toys "R" Us was the leading specialist toy retailer in the US, with a large international business, and the Babies "R" Us chain. Its market share had been falling for years, as discount retailers used toys to bring shoppers into their stores.

The sponsors' thesis combined three things.

  • The value of the real estate. The company owned many of its stores, and Vornado, a property investor, brought expertise in extracting value from that estate.
  • Babies "R" Us. This was a growing, profitable format, with loyal customers.
  • Operational improvement. That meant better control of stock, better store formats, and better pricing, to fight back against the discounters.

§C9.3Entry and deal structure

Most of the price was borrowed, and the debt was placed on the company's balance sheet. The store property was held in separate property companies, with the operating business paying rent to them.

Item Approximate figure
Purchase price USD 6.6bn
Debt More than USD 5bn
Sponsor equity USD 1.6bn

Toy retail is highly seasonal. A large share of the year's profit comes in the weeks before Christmas, while the debt and the rent have to be paid all year round. That makes high leverage riskier than the headline annual EBITDA suggests.

§C9.4What went wrong

  • Interest crowded out investment. Paying around USD 400m a year in interest left little for upgrading stores, technology or e-commerce, while rivals were investing heavily in all three.
  • The market moved online. Amazon grew quickly in toys, and Walmart and Target used toys as loss-leaders. Toys "R" Us couldn't compete on either price or convenience.
  • A failed exit. An IPO was filed in 2010, but weak results and market conditions meant it was withdrawn in 2013. Without an exit, the sponsors couldn't reduce the debt through a sale.
  • Refinancing got harder. Every year, the company needed to refinance large maturities of debt. And suppliers, worried about whether they'd be paid, started demanding cash up front before the holiday season in 2017.

§C9.5Outcome

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2017, with around USD 5bn of debt. A weak holiday season followed. In 2018, the US business was liquidated, rather than restructured, and more than 30,000 jobs were lost. The UK business collapsed in the same year.

Party Result
Sponsor equity USD 1.6bn effectively lost
Sponsors' fees and interest received Reported at about USD 464m over the hold, according to an advocacy group's analysis
Employees More than 30,000 jobs lost; severance became a public controversy
Creditors Large losses

The fees partly offset the sponsors' losses, and that became a central part of the public debate about the deal.

§C9.6Lessons for deal teams

  • Leverage and disruption don't mix. A business that's losing share to structural change needs cash to adapt, and heavy debt takes that option away.
  • Seasonality multiplies the risk of leverage. Judge the debt against the weakest part of the year, not just against the annual EBITDA.
  • The value of property isn't the same as operating strength. Owning the stores gave the lenders security, but it didn't make the retail business competitive.
  • Always have a second route to exit. When the window for the IPO closed, there was no clear plan B.

Case C10/Case studies

TXU / Energy Future Holdings: The Biggest LBO and a One-Way Bet

BadReal deal13 min read

USD 45bn buyout betting on high gas prices; shale gas collapsed them and about USD 8bn of equity was wiped out

Sponsor
KKR, TPG and Goldman Sachs Capital Partners
Sector
Power generation & utilities
Period
2007–2014
In brief

The largest leveraged buyout ever was, underneath it all, a bet that natural gas prices would stay high. The US shale boom pushed them sharply down, cut power prices in Texas, and left a business with around USD 42bn of debt in bankruptcy.

  1. C10.1Snapshot
  2. C10.2The business and the thesis
  3. C10.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C10.4What went wrong
  5. C10.5Outcome
  6. C10.6Lessons for deal teams

§C10.1Snapshot

This is a real deal. The figures are rounded from public reporting, and they're approximate, so check the primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsors KKR, TPG and Goldman Sachs Capital Partners, with co-investors
Closed October 2007
Enterprise value About USD 45bn including debt, the largest LBO in history
Sponsor equity About USD 8bn
Outcome Chapter 11 in April 2014 with roughly USD 42bn of debt
Sponsor returns Equity wiped out
Verdict Bad

§C10.2The business and the thesis

TXU was the largest power company in Texas. After the buyout, it was renamed Energy Future Holdings, and it had three parts.

Business What it did Economic profile
Luminant Coal, lignite and nuclear power stations Profits depend on wholesale power prices
TXU Energy Selling electricity to homes and businesses Competitive retail
Oncor Regulated transmission and distribution network Stable, regulated returns

The core of the thesis was simple. In the Texas power market, the wholesale price of electricity is usually set by gas-fired plants. TXU's coal and nuclear plants cost much less to run. So when gas was expensive, power prices were high, and TXU earned wide margins. In 2007, gas prices were high, and had been rising, and the sponsors bet that they would stay that way.

§C10.3Entry and deal structure

The buyout was financed mostly with debt, placed on the businesses that generated and retailed the power. Oncor was ring-fenced. The regulators required it to be kept legally separate, so that its customers would be protected if the rest of the group failed.

To win public support, the sponsors also agreed to cancel most of TXU's plans to build new coal plants.

§C10.4What went wrong

  • The shale gas revolution. New drilling techniques unlocked huge supplies of gas in the US. The benchmark US gas price fell from above USD 13 per million British thermal units in mid-2008, to below USD 2 in 2012.
  • Power prices followed. Cheap gas pushed down wholesale electricity prices in Texas. Luminant's margins collapsed, and much of the company's debt depended on those margins.
  • The hedges ran out. Hedges on gas prices protected earnings for the first few years. But they were set to expire, and they couldn't be renewed at the old prices.
  • The recession cut demand. Lower use of power by industry added to the pressure.
  • Buying time made the hole deeper. Swaps of debt, and extensions of maturities, from 2009 to 2013 delayed the default, but the interest kept building up.

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway bought about USD 2bn of the company's bonds early on. Buffett later called the purchase a major mistake.

§C10.5Outcome

Energy Future Holdings filed for Chapter 11 in April 2014, with roughly USD 42bn of debt. It was one of the largest non-financial bankruptcies in US history.

Party Result
Sponsors and co-investors About USD 8bn of equity lost
Generation and retail creditors Took ownership; the business became Vistra Energy in 2016
Oncor Protected by the ring-fence; later sold to Sempra Energy in 2018

§C10.6Lessons for deal teams

  • Know what you're really betting on. Strip away the complexity, and this was a leveraged bet on the price of natural gas.
  • Never put high leverage on a single variable that you can't control. No amount of operational improvement could offset a structural fall in the price of the commodity.
  • Stress-test the thesis itself, not just the plan. The key question was: what if gas prices halve, and stay low? And the answer was bankruptcy.
  • Hedges buy time, not safety. They protect cash flow in the near term, but they expire.
  • Size and prestige don't reduce risk. The biggest deal, backed by the most experienced sponsors, still failed on its central assumption.
